00 Index

Market, Competitor and Ecosystem Intelligence V1 — index

The first live execution of L-04. The competitor and ecosystem model was schema-only with an explicit note: "No competitor research was conducted." This objective conducts it.

Scope: 30+ organisations across Australia and internationally, plus five adjacent fields and the market-access environment. Public sources only. Every substantive claim labelled verified fact · public organisational claim · inference · strategic hypothesis · unknown.

Authority: advisory. A-17 characterises; it does not decide MFC's response. Everything implying a positioning change is escalated to Hunter.

The four findings that matter

1. "Mental fitness" is not an unclaimed category. Eleven-plus claimants. Gotcha4Life (definitional since ~2017) and Smiling Mind (definitional since a Sept 2024 repositioning to "Lifelong Mental Fitness") both use it as their organising frame. The AIS Mental Fitness Program (Australian Institute of Sport + Black Dog Institute) is a free, national, government-backed schools program using the literal name. BetterUp published MFC's exact distinction in March 2021. → [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/01-category-language-and-positioning-risk|01]]

2. But nobody has built what the word promises. Gotcha4Life's "Mental Fitness Gym" converts 8% of workshop participants. Smiling Mind publishes 9.8M downloads and no retention data. R U OK? measures intentions. The Resilience Project has the field's best evidence — and it shows nothing measurable before year 6. → The gap is not the word. It is the practice.

3. MFC's biggest asset is that it hasn't started yet — and the measurement gap is the way to use it. Every strong evidence base in this field is developer-conducted; the one program with independent multi-country replication (KiVa) is the one that scaled internationally. More importantly: nobody can measure the construct. The standard battery — WHO-5, K10, SWEMWBS, PERMA — all measures state, i.e. the mental health side of K-05. Nobody measures how often, in real life, a person actually deployed a capability when an opportunity arose. The instruments to do it are free and two are Australian. → [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/10-measurement-white-space|10]]

4. The schools market is the wrong first target; the adult market MFC already serves is the least contested. Three independent lines of evidence converge here: category-language crowding, evidence-gated procurement, and a free government-backed incumbent using MFC's own term. → [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/07-market-access-and-procurement|07]]

Two corrections to Hunter's framing

  1. healthymindsprogram.com is Healthy Minds Australia (Dr Tom Nehmy, Adelaide, for-profit, ex-Flinders PhD) — not Richard Davidson's Healthy Minds Innovations. It is the closest structural match to MFC found anywhere in this research: non-clinical, skills-not-therapy, practice-and-consistency, "lifelong tools", preventive, workshop-delivered, schools + workplaces, Australian. It uses "psychological skills", not "mental fitness" — so the category term survives against this competitor. Its evidence is unpublished and unciteable. It is listed on the NSW catalogue. MFC is not.

  2. The NSW link is a market-access gate, not a competitor directory. ~60 quality-assured programs; criteria informed by a Murdoch Children's Research Institute literature review; entry by periodic tender (none open as at 1 Aug 2026). Smiling Mind, The Resilience Project, batyr and Healthy Minds Enterprises are all listed.

Highest-value follow-up actions

Ranked. All are strategic hypothesis — recommendations to Hunter, not decisions.

  1. Obtain the MCRI literature review behind the NSW catalogue criteria. It encodes the evidence bar for Australia's largest school system and tells MFC exactly what its pilot must meet. Cheapest high-value artefact identified.
  2. Design the first pilot for evidence credibility, not just outcomes — pre-register, pre-specify primary outcomes, publish a COI statement, use at least one non-self-report measure, retain an arm's-length evaluator with the contractual right to publish nulls. Near-zero cost now; unpurchasable retrospectively.
  3. Commission the public comprehension study (SWM-13, SWM-22) — does the Australian public distinguish "how we are doing" from "what we are able to do"? Smiling Mind ran the adjacent study, published it, and turned it into $3.3M in federal funding.
  4. Run an IP Australia register search and take qualified trade mark advice before naming any certification-shaped product.
  5. Open an Indigenous-led process on MFC's relationship to SEWB. Recorded as an unowned risk; route to A-12.
  6. Add implementation intentions to every workshop — Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006), 94 tests, d = .65. Free, immediate, evidence-backed.
  7. Explore Black Dog Institute as a partner, not only a competitor.
  8. Commission a dedicated teardown of Healthy Minds Australia.

Honest status and limits

  • Public sources only. No competitor's internal strategy, finances or effectiveness is inferred from marketing material.
  • Two research streams failed (API error and a stall). Their scope was recovered by direct research, but coverage of six adjacent fields is thinner than intended — health insurer prevention programs, TGA regulation of wellbeing apps, Men's Sheds/community models, ADF and emergency-services programs, peer-support and lived-experience workforce models, and the VIA character-strengths instrument are recorded as known gaps, not as low priority.
  • Several claims could not be verified and are marked unknown rather than estimated: TRP revenue (no public obligation), Gotcha4Life workshop dosage (unpublished), R U OK? current reach (published as images), the MCRI review, Triple P training prices, WHS enforcement volume.
  • Entries older than 180 days must be flagged stale per A-17's method. stale_after: 2027-01-28.
  • No specialist evaluation has been run against this output. A-17's role card records last_evaluation: NOT_RUN and live-use count: 0. This objective is that first live use — the live-proof requirement was "one live L-04 competitor scan."

01 Category Language And Positioning Risk

Category language and positioning risk — the headline finding

A-17 characterises; it does not decide MFC's response. Everything below is evidence and analysis. The positioning decision is Hunter's, per the role card's human gate: any conclusion implying a change to MFC positioning.

The finding, stated plainly

"Mental fitness" is not an unclaimed category. It is an actively contested term with at least eleven identified claimants, two of which are major Australian charities that use it definitionally, and one of which is a government-backed national schools program that uses it as a literal program name.

This directly contradicts two entries in the Strategic World Model. See [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/08-strategic-world-model-contradictions|08 — Strategic World Model contradictions]].

strategic hypothesis It is also the clearest proof that the metaphor has enormous latent public appetite in Australia — and that in this category, distribution and ritual beat evidence for reach, but produce a fundraising vehicle rather than a capability-building institution. MFC's differentiator against it is precisely the lifelong-practice claim: the Push-Up Challenge runs 24 days a year and routes money to crisis services. It is a fundraiser wearing the fitness metaphor, not a fitness program.

How close are their definitions to MFC's?

Uncomfortably close.

Gotcha4Life: "the everyday skills, habits and connections that help us navigate life's ups and downs... like physical fitness, mental fitness can be strengthened through regular practice and healthy habits"

Smiling Mind: "the skills and habits needed to feel calm and confident, cope with life's ups and downs, and build healthy relationships, much like physical fitness grows through regular movement"

Danny Frawley Centre: "a lifelong investment in our mental resources, so we can perform at our best and respond effectively to life's ups & downs"

BetterUp: "a proactive practice that ignites well-being, performance, and growth"

MFC (K-04): "how well we navigate life's everyday moments" MFC (K-05): "Mental health is how we are doing. Mental fitness is what we are able to do."

Assessment inference, high confidence: MFC's K-05 is the sharpest and most quotable articulation any of these organisations has produced. No competitor has an equivalent one-liner. But a better sentence about an occupied word is not category ownership.

Note especially: Smiling Mind reached the anti-stigma argument independently, researched it (900 Australians, nearly half aged 5–18, finding people conflate "mental health" with "mental illness"), published it, repositioned the whole organisation on it, and attracted $3.3M in federal funding. That is the same founding insight as MFC's, executed with evidence attached.

The trademark position — precise, not alarmist

verified fact Mental Fitness Australia holds ACCC-assessed Certification Trade Marks. The ACCC has assessed the rules governing "Certified Mental Fitness Star" and "Certified Mental Fitness First Responder" under the Trade Marks Act 1995. Certifications priced at $150 and $250 AUD respectively. They state: "WE ARE THE ONLY GOVERNMENT APPROVED CERTIFICATION PROGRAM."

The important nuance, and it cuts in MFC's favour:

  • These are composite marks — the full phrases including "Certified" and the role noun. They are not a registration of the bare term "mental fitness."
  • "Mental fitness" used descriptively — as MFC uses it — is very unlikely to be blocked by a certification mark over a longer specific phrase. Descriptive terms are weak marks generally.
  • Where a genuine collision would arise: if MFC ever launched a certification or accreditation product using "Mental Fitness" in its name. Given the vault already discusses facilitator models, this is a live and foreseeable path.

verified fact A US registration for "MENTAL FITNESS" exists (Reg. 5193223, filed 2016, registered 2017); owner and goods/services could not be retrieved.

This is not legal advice and A-17 has no authority to give it. The recommended action is a direct IP Australia register search and qualified trade mark advice before any certification-shaped offer is named. Recorded as a gap, not a conclusion.

The strategic reframe

MFC's framing assumes the question is "is 'mental fitness' available?" It is not. Three better questions:

1. Is anyone actually delivering what the word promises?

No. This is the real finding. Every "fitness"-adjacent player promises training and delivers exposure:

Organisation Promise What the numbers show
Gotcha4Life A "Mental Fitness Gym" 114,177 face-to-face participants → 9,566 gym members (~8%)
Smiling Mind "Lifelong Mental Fitness" 9.8M downloads; no published retention or practice-frequency data
R U OK? A conversation skill Peak-day awareness; no skill measurement at all
The Resilience Project Whole-school wellbeing Real evidence — showing nothing measurable before year 6
AIS Mental Fitness "strategies to stay mentally fit" 85% said they were likely to implement — an intention measure

The gap is not the word. The gap is the practice. Everyone in Australia has claimed the gym metaphor. Nobody has built the gym.

2. Who owns the adult, non-school, non-crisis segment?

  • Smiling Mind → children 4–12 and their parents
  • The Resilience Project → schools primarily
  • Gotcha4Life → began with men; ~80% of 2025 participants were young people in schools
  • AIS Mental Fitness → secondary students
  • R U OK? → workplaces, but annually, as a campaign

The general adult population, seeking sustained non-clinical skill development outside a school or an annual campaign, is the least contested segment. MFC currently delivers workshops to adults. strategic hypothesis: that is the right beachhead, and should be treated as the position — not as a stepping stone to schools.

Corollary risk. MFC is "working toward school/organisational programs." The school market is the most crowded, most evidence-demanding, most price-compressed and lowest-margin segment in this landscape — contested by a Be You 4/4-rated for-profit with 1,000+ schools and published pricing, a government-funded charity with 1,792 schools, a free government/AIS program, and a third charity with a university research partnership. Entering it early with no evidence would be MFC's most expensive available mistake. strategic hypothesis, strongly supported.

3. Where is the defensible evidence position?

The most important number in this research is TRP's: no significant effect at 2–3 years; effects at 6+ years.

Every organisation in this landscape sells short-dose interventions while the best available Australian evidence says effects require years. Nobody has published a dose-response curve for adult non-clinical mental fitness training.

MFC has no evidence and no pilot. That is normally a weakness. Here it is the one genuine opportunity: MFC is the only player free to design its first study around the question the whole sector is avoiding.

The critique MFC must be able to answer

verified fact The University of Auckland published a critique titled "Apps won't save us from mental health crisis", aimed directly at this framing:

"Many apps... present mental health as something that should be 'worked on' every day, by everyone. Just as people are advised to exercise and eat a balanced diet to maintain physical health, these apps suggest we should also take time out for our mental health…"

The charge is that the everyday-practice/fitness analogy individualises responsibility for what are structural and social determinants of distress. No organisation in this field has published a good answer.

Related, and more serious: the US Army's Comprehensive Soldier Fitness — which used exactly this metaphor at $125m scale — drew sustained academic attack (Eidelson & Soldz; Eidelson, Pilisuk & Soldz in American Psychologist, 2011) for scaling without a pilot, mandatory participation without informed consent, failing to measure the outcomes that mattered, and minimal effect sizes.

strategic hypothesis Because MFC is claiming the same metaphor CSF used, MFC will inherit CSF's critics by association. MFC's strongest available answer is that K-04's stated boundary already is the disclaimer — "not a way to blame people for distress, trauma, disability, unsafe environments, or lack of support." MFC should lead with that boundary rather than defend it, and should pre-empt the CSF pattern by piloting before scaling, publishing effect sizes rather than p-values, and commissioning independent evaluation.

Where the genuine gap is — precise statement

Taken: the term "mental fitness" · the physical-fitness analogy · the prevention framing · the anti-stigma argument · the school market · the annual-campaign format · free-app-at-scale · the certification-body position.

Genuinely open:

  1. Depth over reach as an explicit position. Every competitor optimises for reach and reports exposure metrics. None optimises for demonstrated capability. "We serve fewer people, more deeply, and we can prove it" is unoccupied and directly consistent with K-00.
  2. Sustained adult practice architecture — the gym Gotcha4Life named but did not build (8% conversion), and Smiling Mind implies but does not evidence.
  3. Published dosage. Nobody in this set publishes session length, count and frequency clearly. Radical dosage transparency is free, immediate differentiation.
  4. Measurement of capability, not sentiment. Competitors publish satisfaction percentages. Measuring what people can do is unclaimed territory that MFC's own definition (K-05) uniquely obliges it to occupy. RULER's own authors concede the field lacks "performance-based assessments... sensitive to change."
  5. A named behavioural protocol for adults. R U OK? proved a four-letter mnemonic can reach a nation. Gotcha4Life has three nouns; Smiling Mind has five abstract pillars. Neither has a verb sequence. MFC has a definition built on capability and no protocol yet — the most valuable unbuilt asset in the space.
  6. Charity-grade transparency as a competitive weapon. TRP is a for-profit publishing no financials; Smiling Mind is independently flagged for publishing no annual report, no privacy policy and no outcome measures; Gotcha4Life publishes no dosage. Full transparency — pricing, dosage, financials, and null results — is cheap for MFC and expensive for all three to match.

The candidate reframe of the category claim

strategic hypothesis — for Hunter's decision, not A-17's.

MFC's current position (SWM-02) is that MFC is defining mental fitness as a category. The evidence does not support that as stated. A claim that does survive contact with the evidence:

Australia has been told what mental fitness is. Nobody has yet shown what training it actually takes.

This claim: survives contact with Gotcha4Life and Smiling Mind; is consistent with the published evidence including TRP's six-year finding; does not require MFC to assert it invented a term two established charities already own; and — critically — is a claim MFC's first pilot can actually go and substantiate.

02 Profiles Australia Direct

Australian direct competitors — full profiles

Four organisations. These are the closest competitors MFC has. Two of them already use "mental fitness" as a definitional term.

Every claim below is labelled: verified fact · public organisational claim · inference · strategic hypothesis · unknown. Marketing copy is never recorded as verified fact. No internal finances, strategy or effectiveness are inferred from marketing material.

ORG-01 — Gotcha4Life

Field Value
Legal structure Gotcha 4 Life Foundation Ltd. Registered charity, Health Promotion Charity, DGR. ABN 82 618 093 762 verified fact
Founded 2017, by Gus Worland public organisational claim
Relationship to MFC direct — category-language competitor

What they do

Face-to-face presentations and interactive workshops to schools, sporting clubs, workplaces, community groups and regional/remote communities, built on a proprietary three-term language set: Mental Fitness, Emotional Muscle, Meaningful Mateship. Also runs a whole-of-school program (Mentally Fit Schools), teacher professional development, a free digital platform (Mental Fitness Gym), and mass-participation fundraising (24 Hour Row). verified fact

Notably, much workshop delivery is executed through third-party delivery partners — Tomorrow Man, Tomorrow Woman and Man Anchor — rather than solely in-house facilitators. verified fact

Theory of change public organisational claim

  • Vision: "A suicide-free world, where no one worries alone."
  • Mission: "Inspire and enable people to take action to build their mental fitness."
  • The reframe: shifting from "What's wrong?" to "What makes us strong?"
  • Mentally Fit Schools draws on CASEL's social-emotional learning framework. verified fact — Western Sydney University, 11 Mar 2025

Delivery and pedagogy

Predominantly in-person, facilitator-led, with lived-experience storytelling and disclosure modelling as the core pedagogical device (inherited from the Tomorrow Man methodology inference).

Dosage is not published anywhere on the public site — no session length, session count, or frequency. unknown — this is a genuine transparency gap and a competitive opening for MFC.

Evidence base — forensic

  • No peer-reviewed outcome evaluation of Gotcha4Life programs was found. verified absence (public search, Aug 2026)
  • Published claims are post-only self-report: "83% reported positive life impact", "93% provided support to someone in need" — no control group, no validated instrument disclosed, no sample size published. This is claimed effective, not evaluated. verified fact re the claim; inference re the assessment
  • MoU signed 11 Mar 2025 with Western Sydney University (School of Health Sciences) to measure outcomes and scalability. verified fact Results not yet public.
  • Mentally Fit Schools first year: 1,991 students, educators and caregivers across NSW. verified fact

After ~8 years and ~$5.2M/yr, Gotcha4Life has no published outcome evidence of its own. Its evidence programme began in 2025. inference — strongly supported by public record

Reach (2025 calendar year) public organisational claim

The single most important number in this profile: 114,177 face-to-face participants → 9,566 gym members. The sustaining practice layer — the thing that makes the fitness metaphor true — reaches roughly 8% of participants. verified (computed from their own published figures)

Despite the male-suicide-prevention origin, ~80% of 2025 participants were young people in schools. inference from their own figures

Funding

$5,184,339 in FY2023-24 verified fact (corrected 2026-08-06 from "~$2.5M annually"; see file 23). Mix of DGR donations, government grants, fee-for-service delivery verified fact. ChangePath: more assets than liabilities, asset coverage ~6 months of expenses, one loss in last five years verified fact. Six months of reserves for a charity this size is thin inference.

Use of "mental fitness" — exact quotes verified fact

"Building a mentally fit future" — primary tagline

Mental fitness is "the everyday skills, habits and connections that help us navigate life's ups and downs."

"like physical fitness, mental fitness can be strengthened through regular practice and healthy habits"

Centrality: total. It is in the mission statement, the tagline, the flagship school program name (Mentally Fit Schools), the digital product name (Mental Fitness Gym), and the third-party sector descriptor. Gus Worland's title on the About page is literally "Mental Fitness Advocate."

What they do really well

  1. Language architecture — three interlocking terms that are memorable, non-clinical, positive-framed, and self-explaining. Travels without a facilitator present.
  2. Reframe discipline — "What's wrong?" → "What makes us strong?" does the entire category-positioning job in one sentence.
  3. Reaching hard-to-reach men in non-clinical settings — 26,607 regional/remote participants in one year is genuinely difficult delivery.
  4. Partner-led scaling — contracted proven delivery specialists rather than building a facilitator bench from zero.
  5. Founder as distribution — Worland's media career gives free national reach.
  6. They named their own weakness and moved on it — the WSU MoU.

Where they lack or struggle

  • No outcome evidence after 8 years verified absence
  • No published dosage — fidelity and depth are unassessable verified absence
  • Digital layer is failing — ~8% conversion from workshop to gym. The "gym" metaphor promises ongoing training; the numbers indicate one-off exposure. inference from their own figures — their sharpest strategic vulnerability
  • High founder dependency verified fact re roles; inference re risk
  • Reserve thinness (~6 months) plus event-dependent fundraising verified fact
  • Mission scope drift: a suicide-prevention charity now ~80% school students inference

MFC can learn

  • Build the language system before the program. Three interlocking terms beat one.
  • Use a provocation sentence as the front door.
  • Partner for delivery capacity early.
  • Sign a university evaluation partnership before scaling, not eight years in. MFC can front-load as a founding design decision what Gotcha4Life is retrofitting.

MFC should NOT imitate

  • Publishing post-only self-report percentages as "impact" — that is a credibility ceiling MFC would inherit.
  • Leaving dosage unpublished. MFC's differentiator is lifelong practice; opacity about session structure destroys the claim.
  • Building the brand on a single founder's media profile — MFC has no Worland.
  • Shipping a "gym" app as an afterthought.

Sources: gotcha4life.org · our-vision · programs · ACNC · ChangePath · WSU partnership — all accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-02 — Smiling Mind

Field Value
Legal structure Registered Australian charity, not-for-profit. ACNC-classified "Large" verified fact
Relationship to MFC direct — category-language competitor

What they do

Three things: (1) a free consumer meditation/mental-wellbeing app; (2) the Primary School Program — curriculum-aligned, teacher-delivered lessons, plus secondary and early-years (Early Minds); (3) research and public-agenda work (State of Mind report with KPMG, Mental Wellbeing Index).

In September 2024 they executed a strategic repositioning from a mindfulness organisation to a "Lifelong Mental Fitness" organisation. verified fact

Theory of change public organisational claim

  • Purpose: "empowering generational change in mental health"
  • Prevention logic: develop wellbeing skills proactively, before mental illness emerges; "shifting from crisis response to early proactive support"
  • Stigma logic — the reason for the rebrand: their own research of 900 Australians (nearly half aged 5–18) found people conflate "mental health" with "mental illness", which suppresses conversation. verified fact
  • Skills logic: these skills are "grounded in science, can be learned and developed, and importantly, remain relevant to improving mental wellbeing over the lifespan."

Delivery and pedagogy

Named framework — the Smiling Mind Mental Fitness Framework, five skill sets: Live Mindfully · Embrace Flexible Thinking · Grow Connections · Act Purposefully · Recharge Your Body. Mindfulness now overlays each pillar as a cross-cutting method rather than being the whole product. verified fact

Who delivers: teachers, not facilitators. Smiling Mind supplies "curriculum-aligned, teacher-ready lessons" plus teacher capability-building. This is the fundamental architectural difference from Gotcha4Life, TRP and MFC. verified fact

Early Minds is specified as 8 weeks, app-based, educator-delivered verified fact. Primary School Program session count not published unknown.

Evidence base — forensic

Strongest research infrastructure of the four. Worth studying closely, including its disappointments.

  • Early Minds pilot cluster RCT — Mindfulness (2021), "Feasibility of the Early Minds Program by Smiling Mind: a Pilot Cluster-Randomized-Controlled Trial". Sample: 25 educators and 188 preschoolers across six Melbourne centres. verified fact

    Read carefully: this is a feasibility/pilot trial with "limited efficacy testing", not an efficacy trial. Smiling Mind's own flagship RCT is explicitly framed as feasibility.

  • 17+ peer-reviewed studies have used the Smiling Mind app across university students, athletes, clinical paediatric populations, adolescents; JMIR mHealth, Mindfulness, Journal of Sports Sciences, ~2015–2020. verified fact

    Crucial distinction: these are independent researchers using the app as a tool, not evaluations of Smiling Mind's programs. MFC should not confuse the two, and should not let Smiling Mind's framing do so either.

  • School program outcomes (2025): 75% of students said the program benefited their wellbeing; 94% of educators observed benefits. Post-only self-report. public organisational claim
  • Research partnerships are currently closed — not accepting new collaboration requests. verified fact

Verdict: genuinely evidence-engaged, with real RCT experience — but direct causal evidence for their own school program at scale remains pre/post and self-report, and their randomised work is pilot/feasibility grade. "Evaluated" ≠ "proven efficacious."

Reach (2025 Annual Impact Report) public organisational claim

Metric Global Australia
App downloads 9.8M 5.4M
Children/young people supported 14.7M 9.45M
Schools in Primary School Program — 1,792

Caution inference: "14.7M children supported" is a downloads-derived reach metric, not engagement or outcome. Treat as exposure, not dosage.

Funding and financial health

  • Federal government funding is material — announced $3.3M to roll the Schools Program out to a further 300 primary schools plus support 800 existing. verified fact
  • Mixed: government grants, philanthropy, corporate partnerships, educator shop / paid school offerings. App is free.
  • ChangePath: Financial Health Score 5/10; asset coverage ~9 months; 2 losses in last five years. Also flags no annual reports on their own website, no privacy policy, no team page, and no outcome measures reported. For a Large charity this is notable. verified fact
  • Revenue figures on commercial aggregators (e.g. $22.9M) are unverified scrapes — do not use.
  • Leadership transition: Dr Addie Wootten (clinical psychologist, long-time CEO) → Director of Strategic Engagement; Sarah La Roche (commercial background) is CEO. verified fact A clinical-founder-led org handing to a commercial CEO simultaneously with a category rebrand signals a push toward revenue diversification and consumer-brand scale inference.

Use of "mental fitness" — exact quotes verified fact

"Mental fitness reflects our ability to be at our best each day, navigate challenges, and support a state of positive mental wellbeing."

Developing "the skills and habits needed to feel calm and confident, cope with life's ups and downs, and build healthy relationships, much like physical fitness grows through regular movement."

Blog titles include "Moving from mental health to mental fitness, smashing the stigma"

September 2024: Smiling Mind "launches Lifelong Mental Fitness platform."

Centrality: since Sept 2024, "mental fitness" is Smiling Mind's organising framework, with a dedicated /mental-fitness page, a named five-pillar model, and "Lifelong" attached.

Direct implication for MFC: Smiling Mind has publicly claimed "lifelong mental fitness" and the mental-health-is-stigmatised → mental-fitness-is-proactive argument. MFC's distinction is a sharper sentence, but it argues a case Smiling Mind has already publicly won for itself — and funded with government money.

What they do really well

  1. Research culture — an actual cluster-RCT, a research page, an annual impact report, a KPMG State of Mind report, a Mental Wellbeing Index. No other org here matches this.
  2. They rebranded onto evidence about language. The 900-person survey finding that "mental health" reads as "mental illness" is exactly the insight MFC is founded on — and Smiling Mind researched it, published it, and repositioned on it.
  3. Teacher-delivered architecture — fidelity at cost, and the program persists after the provider leaves. Most scalable model of the four.
  4. Government relationship — $3.3M federal funding is a validated public-funding pathway.
  5. Free consumer app as top-of-funnel feeding a paid institutional product.

Where they lack or struggle

  • The scale/depth tension is their defining problem. 9.8M downloads vs no published retention or behaviour-change data. Downloads are not practice; practice is not outcome. They publish the first and not the others. inference — well-supported by what is and isn't published
  • Their own randomised evidence is pilot/feasibility grade at n=188 preschoolers
  • Transparency deficits independently flagged — no annual report on own site, no privacy policy, no team page, no outcome measures reported verified fact (ChangePath)
  • Financial volatility: 5/10 health score, 2 losses in 5 years, ~9 months cover
  • Government-funding concentration risk inference
  • Leadership churn at the top during a category pivot
  • Mindfulness legacy drag — a decade as "the meditation app" is a heavy lift to reposition against inference

MFC can learn

  • Research your own category claim and publish it. Smiling Mind's 900-person stigma study is the single most transferable move in this entire report. MFC could run an equivalent study establishing that Australians distinguish "how we are doing" from "what we are able to do." That becomes owned intellectual territory rather than a slogan.
  • Design for the deliverer, not the participant. Teacher- / manager- / coach-delivered content survives the provider's departure.
  • Publish an annual impact report with a consistent metric set from year one.

MFC should NOT imitate

  • Headlining reach metrics that are really download counts. MFC's differentiator is depth of practice; exposure metrics forfeit it.
  • Letting the framework balloon to five broad pillars covering everything from sleep to purpose — that breadth is what makes Smiling Mind hard to distinguish from generic wellbeing.
  • The transparency gaps. Publishing annual reports, privacy policy, team and outcome measures is free credibility.
  • Assuming "we have an app" solves sustained practice. Both Smiling Mind and Gotcha4Life demonstrate the opposite.

Sources: smilingmind.com.au · /mental-fitness · /research · annual impact report · ChangePath · Lifelong Mental Fitness launch, The Sector, 24 Sep 2024 · Early Minds pilot RCT — all accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-03 — The Resilience Project (TRP)

Field Value
Legal structure For-profit commercial business (Pty Ltd), NOT a charity verified fact
Founder Hugh van Cuylenburg
Relationship to MFC direct — competes for the same school/workplace budget line, but NOT for the category word

No ACNC charity registration found. Operates a retail shop, bulk orders, paid online platform and published per-school pricing. This matters: TRP competes on the same school shelf as charities but is under no charity governance, DGR, or ACNC reporting obligation, and publishes no audited financials.

What they do

Sells wellbeing programs into early years services, primary/secondary schools, workplaces, and direct-to-consumer. Core school product is the School Partnership Program: emotionally engaging live or digital presentations, plus a teacher-delivered curriculum, physical resources (journals, emotion cards, books), teacher seminars, parent components, and a login-gated Teacher Resource Hub. Adjacent brand assets: van Cuylenburg's bestselling books and The Imperfects podcast. Sports partnerships: AFL, NRL, Cricket Australia, Netball Australia. Retail partner: Coles. verified fact

Theory of change public organisational claim

GEM — Gratitude, Empathy, Mindfulness — with Emotional Literacy as a fourth element (the research literature calls it GEEM). Explicitly a whole-school approach with three components: curriculum, school environment, and parent engagement. verified fact

Delivery and pedagogy

  • TRP presenters deliver set-piece presentations; teachers deliver the ongoing curriculum. Hybrid model.
  • Face-to-face presentations are available in Victoria only. Everywhere else gets digital presentations. verified fact — a significant and under-discussed fidelity issue: most of Australia buys the recorded version.

Published pricing verified fact:

Product Price
School Partnership — digital $3,900 + $20/student (ex GST)
School Partnership — face-to-face (VIC only) $6,500–$7,900 + $20/student (ex GST)
Early Years $1,250 + $19/child
VIC "Inspire" Program $4,290 incl GST per school
VIC "Engage" Program $23.10 incl GST per student

A 600-student secondary school on the digital partnership pays roughly $15,900 ex GST per year inference.

Evidence base — forensic

TRP has the strongest published outcome evidence of the four. MFC must understand it precisely — including what it does NOT show.

Balasooriya Lekamge, R., Karim, M.N., Chen, L., & Ilic, D. (2025). "Evaluation of a nationwide whole-school approach to mental health and well-being in 40,149 Australian secondary school students: cluster quasi-experimental study." BJPsych Open. Design: cluster quasi-experimental, post-test only, intervention vs control. Sample: 40,149 students across 102 schools (55 intervention, 47 control). COI declared: "None."

Findings are entirely dose-dependent:

Implementation duration Result
2–3 years No significant differences vs control
4–5 years Depression reduction only
6+ years Life satisfaction B=0.627 · Hope B=2.135 · Coping B=0.438 · Anxiety OR=0.658 · Depression OR=0.534

Stated limitations (from the paper): no randomisation; no pre-test data; potential selection bias; low Cronbach's alpha on the coping subscale (0.523); anonymous cross-sectional design limiting causal inference; no data on individual students' actual exposure duration.

  • Be You programs directory rates the School Partnership Program 4/4 for evidence and 4/4 for implementation. verified fact
  • University of Adelaide (~160,000 students, 2019–2021) and University of Melbourne evaluations are referenced by TRP but the underlying publications could not be located — treat as public organisational claim, not verified studies.
  • TRP's own /evidence page is notably weak: it cites general literature on gratitude, empathy, mindfulness (Harvard Medical School, Greater Good Science Center, Psychology Today, a blog called "Happier Human") — i.e. evidence for the ingredients, not for the program. No sample sizes, findings or dates given. verified fact

Verdict: TRP is the only one of the four with a large-n, controlled, independently-authored, peer-reviewed outcome study. It is also the only one whose evidence explicitly shows their program does nothing measurable for the first three years.

Reach public organisational claim

1,900+ organisations · 1,000+ schools · 5,000+ workplaces · 1M+ Australians reached. (The "5,000+ workplaces" vs "1,900+ organisations" figures are internally inconsistent on their own homepage — flagged.)

Funding

Fee-for-service commercial revenue, book sales, podcast, live events, merchandise, corporate/sports partnerships. No audited financials published; no ACNC obligations; revenue unknown. unknown — and this opacity is itself a competitive fact. No revenue figure is estimated here, because none is published.

Use of "mental fitness"

They do not use it. TRP's vocabulary is resilience, happiness, gratitude, empathy, mindfulness, emotional literacy, wellbeing. verified — as far as public pages reach

Strategic note: TRP is MFC's most direct competitor for the school budget line but not a competitor for the category word. Keep these separate in all positioning work.

What they do really well

  1. They enabled real research and published inconvenient results. The 6-year threshold finding is bad for a sales cycle and good for credibility. That is rare, and it is why they own the shelf.
  2. Commercial model discipline — published, transparent per-school and per-student pricing. Schools can budget it. Charities routinely fail at this.
  3. Whole-school architecture — curriculum + environment + parents. They pre-empted the "one-off talk" critique structurally.
  4. Brand ecosystem — books → podcast → live events → school contracts → workplace contracts. Each channel lowers customer acquisition cost for the others.
  5. Sports codes as credibility infrastructure — reaches audiences that don't respond to clinical framing.
  6. Be You 4/4 listing — third-party government-adjacent endorsement that shortens every school's procurement decision.

Where they lack or struggle

  • The dose-response finding is a double-edged sword. Their own best evidence shows no significant effect at 2–3 years. Most schools do not stay 6+ years. verified fact — the most important publicly-evidenced weakness of any organisation in this report
  • Study design limits: post-test only, no randomisation, no pre-test, no individual exposure data. Schools that stay 6+ years are self-selecting and likely differ systematically (well-resourced, stable leadership). Causality is not established.
  • Their evidence page conflates ingredient evidence with program evidence — the weak flank an informed buyer can attack.
  • Face-to-face in Victoria only; the rest of the country buys the recorded version.
  • Founder charisma dependency.
  • Documented critique of the founding narrative — published reviews describe the book as "one big humble-brag" and criticise using a poor Indian village and a named disadvantaged student as a vehicle for Western gratitude (a "poverty as inspiration" objection). verified fact that this criticism exists
  • Conceptual critique: three positive-psychology constructs is thin theory for a whole-school mental health intervention; critical-education literature argues resilience programs individualise structural causes of distress. partially verified
  • No financial transparency while occupying a "social good" market position.

MFC can learn

  • Publish your dosage curve, including where it's flat. TRP's willingness to publish "nothing at 2–3 years" bought more credibility than a 90%-satisfaction stat ever could. MFC has no evidence yet — which means MFC can design its first pilot to answer the dosage question honestly from day one. That is a genuine differentiator.
  • Publish pricing. It converts, builds trust, and lets institutions budget.
  • Build the whole-system product (participant + environment + significant others), not a workshop.
  • Own a distribution channel you control (podcast/book/newsletter).
  • Get listed in Be You and equivalent directories early.
  • Multi-year contracting, not per-event bookings.

MFC should NOT imitate

  • Building an evidence page out of general literature about your ingredients. MFC will be asked "where's your evidence" and pointing at Harvard's gratitude research will not survive a serious funder.
  • Resting the emotional core on a founder's personal story — especially not one using other people's poverty as the gratitude device. That critique is on the public record; MFC should not walk into it.
  • Selling face-to-face in one state and recorded video everywhere else while calling it the same program.
  • Promising outcomes on a 12-month cycle that the best evidence in the sector says take six years.
  • A for-profit-in-charity-clothing posture — MFC is a charity and should make its accountability a visible advantage.

Sources: theresilienceproject.com.au · /evidence · Be You directory · VIC schools pricing · Balasooriya Lekamge et al. 2025, BJPsych Open — all accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-04 — R U OK?

Field Value
Legal structure R U OK? Limited. Registered charity and registered public health promotion charity verified fact
Relationship to MFC category-adjacent — campaign model, not a program

What they do

A national behaviour-change and awareness campaign, not a curriculum. Core assets: R U OK?Day (second Thursday of September), the ALEC conversation model, and free downloadable resource suites segmented by setting (workplaces, schools, community), plus event kits, an Ambassador program, and story-based content. Revenue and reach are heavily partnership-driven. verified fact

Theory of change public organisational claim

"A conversation can change a life." "You don't need to be an expert to reach out — just a good friend and a great listener."

Mechanism: the barrier to helping is not services — it is confidence and permission. So the intervention de-professionalises the helping conversation, gives it a four-step scaffold, and gives it a socially-sanctioned annual moment.

ALEC: Ask → Listen → Encourage action → Check in. verified fact

Delivery and pedagogy

Mass media campaign + free downloadable resources + partner-hosted events. There is essentially no facilitator-delivered curriculum. The public delivers it to itself; employers and schools act as hosts, not trained facilitators.

Dosage is structurally minimal and self-administered — the model's defining characteristic and its defining limitation. ALEC is a four-step mnemonic, not a curriculum: extremely low cognitive load, extremely high memorability, almost no practice architecture.

Evidence base — forensic

Has peer-reviewed evaluation of campaign effect — more than Gotcha4Life — but measures beliefs, intentions and self-reported helping behaviours, not suicide rates and not skill acquisition.

Ross, A.M. & Bassilios, B. (2019). "Australian R U OK?Day campaign: improving helping beliefs, intentions and behaviours." International Journal of Mental Health Systems, 13(1). University of Melbourne. n = 2,013. Awareness 66% (2014) → 78% (2017); participation 19% → 32%; exposure associated with being 2–3× more likely to intend recommended helping actions and "up to six times more likely to reach out." verified fact

  • Ongoing evaluation partnership with Melbourne School of Population and Global Health verified fact
  • Critical read inference, well-grounded in the design: the flagship finding is cross-sectional association between campaign exposure and self-reported helping, not a randomised or longitudinal causal test. People already pro-social and mental-health-engaged are more likely both to notice the campaign and to reach out. The paper itself notes prior service-users showed higher campaign awareness — consistent with a receptivity confound. The "6 times more likely" figure should be read as association, not established causal effect.
  • No published evidence that the campaign changes suicide rates. verified absence
  • No published evidence of ALEC skill acquisition or retention verified absence — this is the awareness-vs-skill gap, and it is real.

Reach

Campaign awareness 78%, participation 32% — but these are 2017 figures, now ~9 years old. Current figures are published as images on their impact page and were not machine-extractable. unknown

Funding

Structured corporate partnership tiers, government funding, donations, fundraising verified fact. Annual report PDF is image-heavy and did not yield text — revenue, expenses and government-grant proportions unknown, not estimated here. A campaign charity with a single-day annual peak has a structurally seasonal revenue profile inference.

Use of "mental fitness"

They do not use it. Vocabulary is conversation, connection, checking in, suicide prevention. verified

What they do really well

  1. The single greatest act of category branding in Australian mental health. "R U OK?" is a sentence, a brand, a date and an instruction simultaneously. MFC will not beat this; it should study it.
  2. Radical simplification. ALEC has four steps and a name you can say aloud.
  3. They gave permission. "You don't need to be an expert" removed the biggest barrier — fear of doing it wrong. That is a psychological design decision, not a marketing one.
  4. The annual date as infrastructure — a recurring calendar anchor creates free annual media, predictable sponsorship, and a socially-sanctioned excuse to act.
  5. Zero-marginal-cost distribution — free resources activated by employers means reach without a delivery workforce.
  6. A decade of sustained independent university evaluation.

Where they lack or struggle

  • The "one day a year" problem is structural, not incidental. Year-round resource use is not published — a conspicuous omission inference
  • Awareness ≠ skill. No published test of whether anyone can competently conduct a supportive conversation or handle a difficult answer. Asking "are you OK?" is the easy step; ALEC's "Listen" and "Encourage action" are where actual skill lives, and no training is provided.
  • The headline "6 times more likely" is associational, presented in marketing without that qualification
  • Key public figures are dated (2017 data still circulating in 2026)
  • No suicide-rate outcome evidence — inherent, arguably unfair, but real for a suicide prevention charity
  • Risk of "checkbox" adoption — employers can discharge perceived duty-of-care with a morning tea and a poster. The campaign's greatest strength (low barrier) is what makes tokenism easy. inference

MFC can learn

  • Name the behaviour, not the concept. "R U OK?" names an action. "Mental fitness" names a state. Consider whether MFC needs an ALEC-equivalent: a four-step, sayable, teachable protocol that is the thing people actually do.
  • Give permission explicitly. "You don't need to be an expert" does enormous work. MFC's non-clinical positioning needs its own version of this sentence.
  • Create a calendar anchor — a recurring date is free annual distribution forever.
  • Partner with a university on a multi-year repeated national survey.
  • Make employer adoption trivially easy with free self-serve resources; monetise the depth tier behind it.

MFC should NOT imitate

  • Building the organisation around a single annual moment. MFC's north star is lifelong practice — an annual campaign is the direct antithesis, and MFC's honest differentiation is precisely here.
  • Reporting intentions and beliefs as if they were behaviour or skill. If MFC's first pilot measures only "participants intend to practise," MFC will have reproduced the exact gap it exists to close.
  • Headlining an associational multiplier without the design caveat.
  • Competing on awareness. That war is over and R U OK? won it.

Sources: ruok.org.au · /our-impact · Ross & Bassilios 2019 · UniMelb evaluation — all accessed 2026-08-01

03 Profiles Australia Adjacent

Australian adjacent organisations

Not direct competitors for MFC's category claim, but they occupy the ecosystem MFC operates in, compete for the same budgets and attention, or hold the boundary MFC's definition depends on.

Labels: verified fact · public organisational claim · inference · strategic hypothesis · unknown.

ORG-05 — AIS Mental Fitness Program (Australian Institute of Sport + Black Dog Institute)

The most consequential domestic finding after Gotcha4Life and Smiling Mind. A government-backed program using MFC's exact category term as its literal name.

Field Value
Structure Partnership: Australian Sports Commission / AIS + Black Dog Institute verified fact
Launched ~2020 verified fact
Relationship direct — category-name collision, government-backed

What they do verified fact: connects current and former high-performance athletes with secondary school students to build resilience and strengthen mental wellbeing. Delivers up to six sessions across terms two and three with "practical, evidence-based strategies to stay mentally fit." Interactive presentations, in person and online. 2026 cohort: 24 athlete ambassadors across Olympic, Paralympic and Commonwealth Games sports. Expanding to sporting clubs, and to Tasmania in 2026.

Cost: Free. Schools book through the AIS website. verified fact

Reach verified fact: Historical cumulative — over 90,000 students across 458 schools and sporting organisations, 800+ presentations. Participation increased ~200% over six years, with 20,000+ students in one recent year. 2026 target: 75 schools, 150 presentations, 7,000+ students.

inference The 2026 target (7,000 students) is markedly lower than the reported 20,000 in a prior year. Either a deliberate narrowing, a reporting-basis change, or a scale-back. Unresolved — worth monitoring.

Evidence public organisational claim: "85 per cent of students indicating they are likely to implement strategies learned during the sessions." inference This is an intention measure, not a behaviour or capability measure — the same limitation as R U OK?. No peer-reviewed outcome evaluation of this program was located unknown.

Definition of "mental fitness": verified as absence — the term is used throughout their materials but never explicitly defined. inference This is a meaningful competitive detail: they own the name at national scale but have not defended the concept. That is precisely the space K-04 and K-05 occupy.

Strategic implications for MFC

  • Free, national, government-backed, clinically-endorsed (Black Dog), and named exactly "Mental Fitness Program." For any Australian secondary school, this is the default zero-cost option. strategic hypothesis This alone should give MFC serious pause about the schools market as an early target.
  • But: it is a presentation-based awareness program measured on intentions, using athlete storytelling. It is not a practice architecture. The gap identified in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/01-category-language-and-positioning-risk|01]] holds here too.
  • strategic hypothesis Black Dog Institute is a potential partner, not only a competitor. They supply clinical credibility to a program that lacks a defined concept and a practice layer — the two things MFC has. A partnership conversation is worth more than a competitive posture.

Sources: ausport.gov.au 2026 launch · Black Dog Institute program page — accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-06 — Mental Fitness Australia

Field Value
Structure unknown — not stated on their site
Relationship direct — category term + IP dimension

What they do verified fact: a certification body. Three offers:

Product Structure Price
Always Mental Fitness Self-paced online, 1–3 hours Free
Certified Mental Fitness Star Online assessment, 20 questions, 100% pass required $150 AUD
Certified Mental Fitness First Responder (MFFR) Training + 100% pass + 1-hour facilitated workshop $250 AUD
Employee Support Program (ESP) Workplace system unknown

Their definition verified fact:

"Mental fitness is the ability to maintain positive wellbeing, even when life becomes challenging. It involves having practical tools, self-awareness and resilience to manage stress, adapt to change and recover from setbacks."

Their claims verified fact:

"WE ARE THE ONLY GOVERNMENT APPROVED CERTIFICATION PROGRAM" "All Mental Fitness Australia certifications are governed by approved Certification Trade Mark (CTM) rules. The ACCC has assessed the Certified Mental Fitness Star and Certified Mental Fitness First Responder trade marks in accordance with the Trade Marks Act 1995." "All Mental Fitness Australia certifications are non-clinical. They do not qualify individuals to diagnose, treat, or provide therapy."

Assessment

  • The trademark position is narrower than it first appears — composite marks on the certification phrases, not the bare term. See [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/01-category-language-and-positioning-risk|01]] for the full analysis.
  • inference "Government approved" is doing heavy lifting. ACCC assessment of certification-mark rules is a competition-law procedural step, not a government endorsement of the program's content or efficacy. A reader would likely misread this. MFC should not adopt similar framing — it sits close to K-08 territory.
  • Where a genuine collision arises for MFC: any future MFC certification or accreditation product using "Mental Fitness" in its name. Get IP advice before naming such a product.
  • Evidence base: none published unknown.
  • Note the structural similarity to Mental Health First Aid's model — a low-cost certification with a licensing tail. Also note MFFR's "recognise early signs of psychological distress" scope is responder training, not capability building — a different product to MFC's despite the shared word.

Sources: mentalfitnessaustralia.au · /certification — accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-07 — Healthy Minds Australia (Dr Tom Nehmy)

The closest structural match to MFC found anywhere in this research — and the organisation behind the URL Hunter supplied. See [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/04-international-and-ruler|04]] for the full profile and the correction distinguishing it from Richard Davidson's Healthy Minds.

Summary: Australian, for-profit (Healthy Minds Enterprises, ABN 20 616 567 465), founded by clinical psychologist Dr Tom Nehmy from Flinders University PhD research. Non-clinical, skills-not-therapy, practice-and-consistency, "lifelong tools", preventive, workshop-delivered, schools + workplaces. Four skill domains: Helpful Thinking · Stress Management · Emotional Regulation · Attention and Focus Control.

They use "psychological skills," NOT "mental fitness." verified The category term remains available against this competitor specifically.

Evidence: references "our controlled evaluation trial" but publishes no citations, studies, effect sizes or outcomes verified as absence.

Listed on the NSW Student Wellbeing external programs catalogue as "Healthy Minds Enterprises." MFC is not. verified fact

ORG-08 — Mental Health First Aid Australia

Field Value
Relationship delivery-adjacent — the model MFC should study for scaling and funding

What they do verified fact: develops and licenses a standardised accredited course (the ALGEE action plan) teaching lay people to recognise and respond to a mental health crisis in someone else. Youth MHFA is a variant.

Delivery model verified fact: independently licensed instructors — MHFA Australia does not employ them. Instructors set their own fees ($220–$450 per person). A decentralised train-the-trainer/franchise network.

Evidence verified fact: the strongest independently peer-reviewed evidence base of any organisation in this research. Multiple PubMed-indexed RCTs and evaluations including a 3-year follow-up RCT on Youth MHFA, and studies across culturally specific cohorts. Consistently shows improved knowledge, confidence and reduced stigmatising attitudes, sustained over time.

Reach public organisational claim: 1.3M+ Australians trained cumulatively; 141,000 in 2025 alone (record year); 9M+ globally across 50+ countries.

Funding verified fact: fee-for-service since July 2002 — moved off government funding. Instructors and licensees pay to be certified; participants pay instructors. Genuinely self-sustaining, non-philanthropy-dependent. Unusual in this sector.

MFC can learn: - The licensed-facilitator fee-for-service model is a proven way to scale nationally without philanthropy dependence — directly relevant to a workshop-based organisation. - Their university research partnership structure is the credibility bar for "evidence-informed."

MFC should NOT imitate: - The "first aid" crisis-response frame — responding to others' crises, not building one's own practice. - One-off certification with no follow-up. A badge with no ongoing engagement won't build "what we are able to do." - inference Quality-consistency risk from a decentralised network of self-employed instructors setting their own fees.

Sources: mhfa.com.au · /mhfa-research · 25th year milestone · Youth MHFA 3-year RCT follow-up — accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-09 — batyr

What they do verified fact: youth-led charity delivering peer-led mental health education workshops in secondary schools (batyr@school) and universities (batyr@uni), plus "Being Herd" workshops training young people with lived experience to structure their story into a public talk. Core mechanic: lived-experience storytelling by trained young speakers to peer audiences, followed by facilitated small-group discussion.

Evidence public organisational claim: cites an unpublished RCT finding reduced stigma and increased help-seeking, maintained at 3-month follow-up. Self-reported surveys: 82–85% rate the program "highly engaging"; 70–78% report increased likelihood of seeking support.

verified fact A 5-year longitudinal evaluation began in 2024, funded by a $1.6m Balnaves Foundation grant. This is a genuine independent research commitment; results not yet published.

Reach public organisational claim: 400,000+ young people cumulatively; batyr@school 200,000+ students across 352 secondary schools.

Uses "mental fitness"? No unknown/absent.

MFC can learn: the near-peer lived-experience storytelling mechanic; and investing early in a rigorous funded longitudinal evaluation partnership — the Balnaves model is exactly the move Gotcha4Life is retrofitting eight years late.

MFC should NOT imitate: treating a single workshop as sufficient dose. batyr's model is fundamentally awareness/destigmatisation, not skills-practice inference.

Sources: batyr.com.au · Balnaves $1.6m grant — accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-10 — Life Ed Australia

What they do verified fact: curriculum-aligned in-person preventive health education to ages 3–13 via 120+ employed trained education specialists, using Mobile Learning Centres that visit schools, with the Healthy Harold mascot. 12 curriculum-aligned modules make up the Primary Program. Underpinned by the WHO Health Promoting Schools Framework public organisational claim.

Reach public organisational claim: ~700,000 children annually, 5,000+ schools/year. The largest sheer reach of any organisation in this research.

MFC can learn: inference The sequenced, multi-year, curriculum-integrated repeat-exposure model is the closest published example of "practice over time" delivered at national scale. Their 12-module structure and educator-training pipeline are worth studying as a structural analogue. Note also that they employ and train their own specialist workforce rather than relying on volunteers — more scalable and quality-controllable.

MFC should NOT imitate: the mascot/juvenile branding (wrong audience for MFC); and the capital-heavy Mobile Learning Centre infrastructure inference.

Sources: lifeed.org.au · evidence-based reports — accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-11 — Geelong Grammar Institute of Positive Education

Why it matters: philosophically the closest Australian organisation to MFC's practice-based ethos.

Theory of change public organisational claim: "Learn it, live it, teach it, embed it" — staff must first personally learn and apply positive psychology to their own lives before teaching students, then embed it in everyday practice.

inference This is the same adults-first sequencing principle as RULER and the same "live it before you teach it" logic as the US Army's Master Resilience Training. Three independent traditions converged on it. See [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/04-international-and-ruler|04]]. This is as close to a settled design principle as this field has.

Delivery: training courses (flagship $880 AUD/person online), whole-school consulting, licensable curriculum. Train-the-trainer. Built on PERMA/PERMAH.

Evidence inference: cites a systematic review of school-based positive-psychology interventions — i.e. references the general literature rather than GGS-specific outcomes. A "28% more engaged" claim has no clearly identified original citation unknown.

MFC can learn: the PERMAH base and the "practitioners must live it before teaching it" principle; a self-sustaining training-revenue business model.

MFC should NOT imitate: the elite-private-school brand association and premium per-person pricing — inconsistent with K-00's universal ambition; and conflating general positive-psychology evidence with program-specific evidence.

Sources: instituteofpositiveeducation.com · Learn it, Live it, Teach it, Embed it — International Journal of Wellbeing — accessed 2026-08-01

ORG-12 — Berry Street Education Model

What they do verified fact: a trauma-informed teaching framework and professional-development product; trains teachers and school leaders. B2B, not direct-to-student. Five domains including Body (regulating the physiological stress response) and Relationship. Active in 400+ Australian schools public organisational claim. Independent University of Melbourne evaluation (2016) verified fact that such an evaluation exists; findings not directly read unknown.

MFC can learn: the five-domain, teacher-actionable framework structure — a template for making an abstract model usable rather than theoretical.

MFC should NOT imitate: inference BSEM is calibrated for trauma/adversity populations. Importing its clinical/stress-response framing wholesale into a universal non-clinical product risks over-medicalising content — a direct K-08 risk.

ORG-13–16 — The boundary organisations

These matter because K-04's category definition depends on the boundary they hold.

Org What they are Why it matters to MFC
Beyond Blue National mental health charity; helpline, Be You (with headspace), NewAccess (structured low-intensity CBT delivered by trained coaches, not clinicians) inference NewAccess's trained-coach model is structurally close to what MFC needs for facilitators. But Beyond Blue's positioning — "reduce impact of illness / support recovery" — is the deficit frame K-05 exists to distinguish from
headspace 154–169 youth mental health centres, 12–25, government-funded. Formally published 10+6 component service model in Early Intervention in Psychiatry inference Publishing a formal peer-reviewed service model is the credibility move MFC should copy. But headspace is early-intervention/treatment-adjacent — a different category, and a crowded government-owned one
Black Dog Institute UNSW-affiliated research institute; research + clinical + prevention + digital tools (e.g. Sleep Ninja, six structured sessions, effectiveness-tested) Also the AIS Mental Fitness clinical partner (ORG-05). strategic hypothesis Potential partner. Sleep Ninja is a good template: a self-contained dosed digital intervention with actual effectiveness testing
ReachOut Digital-first, anonymous, free; PeerChat verified fact Peer-reviewed prospective cohort study, ~2,000 users 16–25 over 3 months: significant reductions in depression/anxiety/stress and high-suicide-risk prevalence falling 12.3% → 8.6%. Rare genuine outcome evidence in this sector — a credibility bar to match

Common lesson inference: none of these four use "mental fitness." They occupy the mental health side of K-05 cleanly. MFC's distinction is doing real work here — the boundary is clear and defensible against these organisations. The competitive pressure comes from the fitness side, not this side.
