04 International And Ruler

International field — RULER and global analogues

The most learnable material in this entire research. RULER in particular is the closest thing to a proven version of what MFC says it wants to do.

Labels: verified = stated in a peer-reviewed paper or primary document read directly · claim = organisation's own unverified assertion · inference · hypothesis · unknown.

Part 1 — RULER (Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence)

What it is

verified A whole-school approach developed at the Yale Center for Emotional Intelligence, a self-supporting unit of the Yale School of Medicine's Child Study Center. Architects: Marc Brackett, Susan Rivers, Peter Salovey, David Caruso, Robin Stern.

Five emotion skills (Nathanson, Rivers, Flynn & Brackett, Emotion Review 8(4), 2016):

Skill
Recognizing emotion in self and others (facial, vocal, bodily, contextual cues)
Understanding causes and consequences of emotions
Labeling emotions with a diverse and accurate vocabulary
Expressing emotions constructively across contexts and cultural norms
Regulating emotions effectively with strategies

verified Theoretical parentage is unusually disciplined: Mayer & Salovey's (1997) four-branch ability model supplies the taxonomy; Bronfenbrenner's (1979) ecological systems theory supplies the implementation logic (change the environment, not just the individual).

The single most MFC-relevant sentence in the RULER literature — Hagelskamp et al. (2013) describe an "achievement model of emotional intelligence": emotional literacy "is acquired through experience and the acquisition of emotion-related knowledge and skills," ideally where "consistent practice using the RULER skills is encouraged; and where feedback is provided by adults who also model the RULER skills."

That is a practice-and-modelling theory of capability, not an information-transfer theory. It is SWM-03 with twenty years of evidence attached.

The four anchor tools — concretely

verified all from Nathanson et al. 2016.

1. The Charter

A collaborative written agreement created by a classroom, staff team, or family. Three questions: (a) How do we want to feel here? (b) What behaviours will produce those feelings? (c) What will we do when someone isn't living up to it? Signed by all members, periodically amended. Staff charters are made as well as student charters.

Design insight: converts an abstract value ("respect") into a named target feeling + a named behaviour + a named repair protocol. It is a standing artefact in the room, not an event.

2. The Mood Meter

The signature tool. Four-quadrant grid: x-axis valence (unpleasant → pleasant), y-axis arousal (low → high energy), from Russell & Barrett's (1999) core affect model. Colour-coded red / yellow / blue / green. Younger children plot with colour + one feeling word; older students and adults plot coordinates + a granular word ("I feel +2, −2; peaceful").

Daily uses: greeting check-ins; building vocabulary until each quadrant holds dozens of words; asking whether the current feeling is ideal for the task about to be done, and if not applying a regulation strategy; plotting a literary character's emotional trajectory.

Design insight: two axes only. Learnable in 60 seconds, usable for a lifetime, scales in granularity with the user. It is a coordinate system, not a curriculum.

3. The Meta-Moment

A process for "extending the time between an emotional trigger and one's response to it." Sequence: sense the trigger → pause/deep breath → envision your "best self" → choose a response consistent with that best self. Worked example: a hurtful comment from a friend — recognise feeling hurt, breathe, ask what the best self would do, then request a conversation instead of posting mean comments online.

Design insight: the "best self" is a pre-loaded identity anchor rehearsed in calm conditions so it is retrievable in hot conditions. This is an explicit mental-rep design — the rep is the pause, and the pause is trainable. Structure: pre-load in calm → retrieve in heat.

4. The Blueprint

A conflict-repair and perspective-taking protocol: "How did I feel, and how did the other person feel?" · "What caused me to feel this way, and what caused them?" · "How did I/they react?" · "What could I/they have done differently?" · "What can I do now?"

Design insight: symmetry. Every question is asked twice — once of self, once of other. Empathy is engineered structurally rather than exhorted.

Beyond the tools

verified The Feeling Words Curriculum (K–8) is introduced only after the anchor tools are embedded with fidelity, "typically in Year 2." It infuses one feeling word (e.g. alienated) into existing academic content — students find causes and consequences in a text, then discuss their own experiences, then learn regulation strategies. High school adds ~20 lessons/year of 45–60 minutes.

The implementation model — the pedagogically distinctive part

a) A team, not a teacher. verified Schools cannot enrol individuals. A RULER Implementation Team is mandatory: minimum 3 people, including at least one school administrator plus at least two teachers or mental-health professionals. Individual educators, consultants, parents and non-K-12 organisations are explicitly ineligible.

inference The administrator requirement is a structural guarantee of leadership buy-in. RULER has hard-coded into its enrolment rules the variable that most commonly kills school programs.

b) Adults first — the defining choice. verified Phase 1 takes one to two years, during which the adults become comfortable with the skills and tools before introducing them to students. Staff create their own Charter, plot themselves on their own Mood Meter, take their own Meta-Moments. Only then does Phase 2 reach classrooms.

Public sequence: staff learning → classroom instruction → family engagement → out-of-school time.

inference This is not politeness. It follows from the theory: children acquire emotion skills where adults also model them. An unregulated adult cannot teach regulation, so adult capability is the rate-limiting input, not a nice-to-have.

c) Cascading. verified Yale trains the team → the team trains the whole staff in-building → staff embed tools in routines → staff introduce tools to students → students take them home. Yale never touches most eventual users. Platform access is granted to trained staff only, not students or parents.

d) Dosage and cost verified:

Format Structure
RULER Institute Online 6 weeks, 2–2.5 hrs/week (≈12–15 hrs team total)
RULER Institute at Yale 2 days in person
On-Site in person at the school

All include 2 years of implementation support: virtual group coaching, webinars, platform access, and an annual assessment of implementation progress.

Cost: Online 2-year package US$6,000 for 3 participants, up to $13,000 for 10; at Yale $7,500–$10,500; then US$1,000 per school per year subscription. inference ≈$6/student in years 1–2 in a 500-student school — cheap per capita, but a real cash line and a substantial time cost, which is the binding constraint.

Theory of change

verified (Hagelskamp et al. 2013, Fig. 1)

INPUTS                    PROXIMAL (classroom-level)        DISTAL
Teacher/leader training  → quality of social-emotional   → classroom organisation
+ anchor tools &            interactions                    + instructional support
  Feeling Words          ↕ (mutually reinforcing)        → academic performance
  Curriculum             → emotional literacy of          → health & wellbeing
                           students AND teachers          → responsible decision-making

The central testable claim: RULER changes the emotional climate first (Year 1); improvements in classroom organisation and instructional quality follow as a consequence (Year 2). Change is setting-level and sustained by daily routine embedding, not lesson delivery.

Evidence — by design tier

Tier 1 — Cluster-randomised controlled trials

Rivers, Brackett, Reyes, Elbertson & Salovey (2013), Prevention Science 14(1). verified 2-year cluster-RCT randomised at school level. 62 urban schools, 155 classrooms, 3,824 students, grades 5–6. Blinded observational coding using CLASS. Year-1 (Hedges' g): warmth/connectedness g=.50 · positive climate g=.55 · regard for student perspectives g=.60 · emotion-focused interactions g=.52.

Hagelskamp, Brackett, Rivers & Salovey (2013), American Journal of Community Psychology 51. verified Same trial, Year-2 plus a mediation test of the theory of change. End of Year 2: emotional support g=.48 · classroom organisation g=.56 · instructional support g=.71. Critical result: the Year-2 gains were partially mediated by RULER's Year-1 impact on emotional climate. The sequencing claim survived an empirical test — rare in this field.

Effect sizes of g ≈ .48–.71 on blind-observer-rated classroom quality are substantial. But note these are classroom-level environmental outcomes, not individual child mental-health outcomes.

Tier 2 — Quasi-experimental

  • Brackett et al. (2012), 273 students: higher year-end grades (partial η²=0.07), work habits, adaptability. Effects small in variance terms (3–7%).
  • Castillo, Fernández-Berrocal & Brackett (2013), Spain, 47 teachers: higher work engagement (η²=.35), better interactions (η²=.37). Adult-outcome evidence — directly relevant to MFC, but small N and self-report.
  • Preschool RULER, n=156: emotion recognition Δ=0.52, labelling Δ=1.39.
  • Reyes et al. (2012), School Psychology Review — the fidelity study. Students had higher EI and better social problem-solving when their teachers attended more trainings, taught more lessons, and were rated by impartial observers as high-quality implementers. Dosage and implementation quality moderate outcomes.

The independence caveat

verified The 2016 author note discloses: "Authors Rivers and Brackett have a conflict of interest management plan in place with Yale University..." The Mood Meter is copyrighted to Emotionally Intelligent Schools, LLC.

inference Essentially all strong RULER evidence is developer-conducted. A specific search for independent or critical evaluations found none of substance. That is not evidence of a problem — but MFC must not describe RULER's evidence as independently replicated.

Reach

claim "Over five thousand schools worldwide" (publisher framing) vs a separately repeated "more than 2,000 schools... over 1 million students." These are inconsistent; treat both as marketing-grade.

verified Nathanson et al. (2016) themselves said only "hundreds of public, charter, and independent schools throughout the US," with implementation evaluated "in dozens of schools."

inference The gap between adoption counts and evaluated implementation counts is roughly two orders of magnitude. This is the single most important number in this report for MFC.

Business model

verified YCEI is self-supporting, funded by foundation and federal grants, corporate support, training revenue and philanthropy. RULER is not free — fee-for-service, institution-only, two-year package plus annual subscription, IP held partly in a private LLC. Brackett's Permission to Feel (2019) is the public-facing category-building asset.

inference The architecture is: university research credibility → third-party accreditation (CASEL SELect) → institutional licence sales → recurring subscription → mass-market book for category legitimacy. Four parts, each reinforcing the others.

Where RULER struggles

  • Effects are conditional on fidelity, and fidelity varies wildly. verified Reyes et al. is RULER's own admission. inference A program whose effects depend on dosage underperforms at scale, because dosage decays fastest in the schools that need it most.
  • Adoption ≫ evaluated implementation. Purchase of a package is not implementation.
  • Enormous time burden on adults — 1–2 years before students see anything, plus institute time, in-building cascade, daily embedding, annual assessment. inference No visible student-facing win for up to two years, which is politically fragile for a principal on a 3-year tenure.
  • Structural dependence on leadership — an administrator is mandatory, so principal turnover is an existential risk with no published mitigation.
  • Schools cannot sustain it independently. verified Ongoing platform access and Yale coaching are structured in; schools renew or lose the platform. inference Good for revenue, bad for the claim that RULER builds durable capability — a genuine tension with MFC's "lifelong practice" positioning.
  • No published evidence that effects sustain after support ends. verified as absence Longest follow-up is 2 years during supported implementation.
  • They cannot yet measure the capability they claim to build. verified The 2016 review names "the lack of developmentally sequenced, performance-based assessments of the full range of EI skills" as a limitation and says future research "needs to coincide with the development of high-quality EI assessments that are sensitive to change." Much of the strong evidence is on classroom climate — an environmental proxy.
  • Adult/workplace applicability largely unevidenced — strongest adult finding is n=47.
  • Institutional gatekeeping excludes the general public. verified Individuals, parents and non-K-12 organisations cannot access training. inference RULER is a school-systems product, not a public capability product. This is the largest strategic opening MFC has relative to RULER.

What MFC can learn from RULER — specifics

  1. Adults first, and say why. The most transferable idea is not a tool, it's a sequence, justified by theory. hypothesis MFC should adopt an explicit, publicly stated sequencing rule (facilitators → parents/leaders → participants) and defend it as a design principle, not an operational convenience.
  2. Tools, not curriculum. The anchor tools are portable, reusable, context-free artefacts that live in the environment. The curriculum is the optional Year-2 layer. hypothesis MFC's workshops should aim to leave behind 3–5 reusable objects, not 3–5 remembered ideas. The unit of retention should be a tool, not a lesson.
  3. Two-axis simplicity that scales in granularity. The Mood Meter is learnable by a five-year-old and still useful to a 45-year-old. One artefact, lifelong ceiling — that is the design bar.
  4. Emotion-labelling granularity as a countable rep. Filling each quadrant with dozens of words over time is rep-based skill accrual with a visible progress surface. hypothesis One of very few SEL constructs that is countable — a candidate MFC metric.
  5. Design the pause explicitly. The Meta-Moment names the target as "extending the time between trigger and response" and gives a rehearsable sequence with a pre-loaded identity anchor. This is SWM-03's "mental reps in real-life moments," already engineered.
  6. Symmetric protocols manufacture empathy — cheap, structural, culturally portable.
  7. Embed in routines, not events. hypothesis MFC's workshops should be judged on what routine they install, not what content they delivered. Define a "routine installed" success metric.
  8. Gate access to force the conditions for success. RULER refuses individuals and requires an administrator. hypothesis MFC should consider a minimum-viable-unit rule for organisational clients (a named internal owner, a second session) — and be willing to lose sales over it.
  9. Publish the theory of change as a testable causal sequence, then test the sequence. Hagelskamp et al. tested whether the order of change matched the model. hypothesis This is the highest-credibility research move available to a small organisation, and far cheaper than a full RCT.
  10. Measure implementation annually as a contracted deliverable — it converts fidelity from a hope into a service.

What MFC should NOT imitate

  • A 1–2 year adult phase before anyone downstream sees value — RULER's biggest adoption tax. Sequence adults-first but compress it, and engineer an early visible win in the first 8–12 weeks.
  • Dependence on the provider as the sustainability mechanism. Build for graduation, not renewal — and find a business model that survives graduation (facilitator certification, tool licensing, alumni practice infrastructure).
  • Gatekeeping out individuals and the public. RULER's institution-only rule is exactly the constraint that leaves "mental fitness as a public category" unclaimed.
  • Letting all your evidence be self-generated. Commission independent evaluation early, while a null result is survivable.
  • Over-claiming reach. Publish evaluated implementation counts alongside adoption counts, and say which is which.
  • Launching a category claim without a measurement instrument. inference If MFC claims mental fitness is a distinct buildable capability, the measure is the load-bearing asset and should be commissioned before scale.
  • Adopting "emotional intelligence" as the frame — a crowded, contested construct with an ability-vs-trait measurement war attached. "What we are able to do" is cleaner precisely because it is behavioural.

Part 2 — International analogues

⚠ Correction — two different "Healthy Minds"

The page Hunter flagged (healthymindsprogram.com/psychological-skills-training) does NOT belong to Richard Davidson's organisation.

Humin (formerly Healthy Minds Innovations) Healthy Minds Australia
URL humin.org (was hminnovations.org) healthymindsprogram.com
Home UW–Madison Center for Healthy Minds, USA Adelaide, Australia
Founder Richard J. Davidson Dr Tom Nehmy (+ director Nick Lee)
Structure Non-profit For-profit — Healthy Minds Enterprises, ABN 20 616 567 465
Model Free consumer app + org services Commercial workshops/webinars for schools & workplaces

Healthy Minds Australia — closest structural competitor to MFC

verified Founded by Dr Tom Nehmy, clinical psychologist, Adelaide. Developed over four years from PhD research at Flinders University under Prof. Tracey Wade. His systematic review found most existing prevention programs were ineffective, "with some actually harmful." Core concept: "psychological immunization." Draws on "cognitive-behavioural theory, positive psychology, therapeutic writing, ACT, and more." Originally an 8-lesson classroom series, later adapted for corporate.

Named skill domains: Helpful Thinking · Stress Management · Emotional Regulation · Attention and Focus Control.

Their language — direct quotes verified:

"Everyone can learn the psychological skills that enhance mental health and wellbeing" teaches "lifelong tools" rather than therapy "mental well-being is a constant process, where individuals need to practice healthy mechanisms" "consistency is key"; "at the cutting edge of preventive psychology" "we aren't offering you therapy"

Evidence verified as absence: the site references "our controlled evaluation trial" and "world-leading research" but provides no citations, published studies, effect sizes or quantitative outcomes. No peer-reviewed publications are linked. I could not locate the underlying trial.

inference This is MFC's positioning almost verbatim: non-clinical, skills-not-therapy, practice-and-consistency, lifelong tools, preventive, workshop-delivered, Australian, schools + workplaces.

The distinguishing gaps MFC can exploit: (a) they are for-profit, MFC is a charity; (b) they use "psychological skills," NOT "mental fitness" — so this particular competitor has not taken the category term; (c) their evidence is unpublished and unciteable; (d) pricing not disclosed.

verified They are listed on the NSW Student Wellbeing external programs catalogue as "Healthy Minds Enterprises." MFC is not.

hypothesis This organisation warrants a full dedicated teardown as a priority — it is the closest structural match found anywhere in this research.

Humin / Healthy Minds Program (USA)

verified Global non-profit from Richard Davidson's Center for Healthy Minds, UW–Madison. Framework: ACIP — Awareness, Connection, Insight, Purpose. Free app with 100+ guided practices.

Language verified: "qualities of mind can be taught" · "wellbeing can be trained through ACIP" · "trainable skills."

inference They deliberately use "trainable"/"training" rather than "fitness." The metaphor is skill acquisition, not gym. MFC's "mental fitness" is a stronger, riskier claim — stronger because it implies capacity and performance, riskier because it invites the "is this measurable like a bench press?" challenge.

Evidence verified: three-arm fully remote RCT (JMIR Mental Health, 2020), N=343, 8 weeks. HMP conditions showed larger improvements in psychological distress, social connectedness and mindfulness vs waitlist.

Critical limitation stated in the paper: only 186/343 (54.2%) completed at least one post-test, and only 166/228 (72.8%) of those assigned even downloaded the app.

inference This is the digital-delivery attrition problem in its purest form, and it is the single strongest evidence-based argument for MFC's workshop-based, in-person model. A free app has near-zero marginal cost and near-zero adherence guarantee.

verified Funders include DARPA and the Templeton World Charity Foundation.

MFC can learn: the free-core/paid-organisational split; ACIP as proof a four-word framework can carry both a research program and a consumer product; the discipline of "trainable" language. Should NOT imitate: app-first delivery; and the mid-flight rebrand (hminnovations.org → tryhealthyminds.org → humin.org). inference For a category-creating org, name stability is the category claim.

Penn Resilience Program / Comprehensive Soldier Fitness — the fitness-metaphor precedent

The most directly relevant precedent for MFC's category claim — and a cautionary tale as much as a model.

Penn Resilience Program (PRP)

verified Positive Psychology Center, UPenn (Seligman). Teaches "science-based tools to build resilience and wellbeing," from "cognitive-behavioral science and Positive Psychology." Delivered in person or virtually using a train-the-trainer model built for scale. claim "Over one million people have attended."

Evidence verified — Reivich, Seligman & McBride, American Psychologist 66(1), 2011: PRP is "one of the most widely researched depression prevention programs," with 19 controlled studies. Meta-analysis (Brunwasser, Gillham & Kim, 2009) found fewer depressive symptoms than controls for as long as 24 months post-training.

Crucially: when Penn curriculum developers trained educators to deliver PRP, students still showed fewer depression symptoms and behaviour problems. inference This is the strongest published evidence anywhere that a cascade delivery model preserves effect — the empirical warrant for MFC's facilitator model.

Comprehensive Soldier Fitness — the language, quoted

verified Launched 2009, ~US$125m. The Army's own headline: "Comprehensive Soldier Fitness addresses mental fitness, resilience." Built on "five dimensions of strength: emotional, social, spiritual, family and physical", framed analogically: "As people develop their holistic fitness strength, they develop psychological resilience..."

For MFC's category claim, this is the key finding: a US$125m US Government program explicitly named psychological capability as "fitness," placed it alongside physical fitness, and used the words "mental fitness" officially. inference The fitness metaphor is already institutionally precedented at national scale. This de-risks the category claim (it is legible to policymakers) and raises the bar (someone big already used it — and got criticised).

Master Resilience Training — the cascade design

verified 10-day course for noncommissioned officers who then teach their soldiers.

Structure: 5 days "learn it and live it" + 3 days "deepen understanding and teach it." PRP had used this split for years and "found that this approach provides a better understanding of course content and instructional training."

Modules: resilience fundamentals + six competencies [2.5 days] · Building Mental Toughness [2.5 days] — ABC (adversity–belief–consequence), Thinking Traps, Icebergs, Energy Management, Minimizing Catastrophic Thinking, Real-time Resilience, "Hunt the Good Stuff" (daily gratitude journalling, shared aloud each morning) · Character Strengths [1 day] · Strengthening Relationships [1 day] — Active Constructive Responding, effective praise, assertive communication.

Pedagogy: "a brief didactic presentation followed by a series of experiential activities such as group discussions, role plays, and application exercises." Breakouts led by one trainer plus four facilitators, with a deliberate civilian + military mixed facilitator team.

inference MFC should study this course design more closely than almost anything else in this research. Four transferable features: (a) the explicit "live it before you teach it" 5:3 ratio; (b) skills named as verbs and moves ("Hunt the Good Stuff", "Real-time Resilience") rather than constructs; (c) a daily shared ritual that makes reps social and public; (d) mixed insider/outsider facilitator pairs to establish credibility with a sceptical population.

The documented criticism — MFC will inherit this

verified - Eidelson & Soldz, "Does Comprehensive Soldier Fitness Work? CSF Research Fails the Test." Failure to measure PTSD, depression or other disorders despite validated measures being available; design failing to control confounds; "minimal associated effect sizes" and multiple significance tests without adjustment. They called for retraction. - Eidelson, Pilisuk & Soldz, "The Dark Side of Comprehensive Soldier Fitness," American Psychologist (Oct 2011). Soldiers were required to participate, with no informed-consent protections. - CSF was rolled out force-wide without pilot testing. - George Bonanno (Columbia): "there's no evidence that any program makes Soldiers more resilient." - Disclosure in Reivich et al.: "Karen J. Reivich earns a salary for providing training services to the Army." Same developer-evaluator entanglement as RULER.

MFC should NOT imitate: inference (a) scaling before piloting — CSF's fatal error and the source of every subsequent attack; (b) mandatory participation; (c) measuring soft proxies while conspicuously not measuring what people care about; (d) developer-as-sole-evaluator; (e) over-claiming from significance without effect sizes.

KiVa (University of Turku, Finland) — the scaling lesson

verified Anti-bullying program, funded by the Finnish Ministry of Education and Culture. Provides lesson plans, presentation graphics, online surveys, computer games, high-visibility vests for recess supervisors, teacher manuals, parent guides.

Distinctive pedagogy inference: KiVa targets bystanders, not bullies — it changes the audience's response, removing the social reward for bullying.

Evidence — genuinely strong and, crucially, independently replicated verified: - Kärnä et al. (2011), Finland RCT: 78 schools, >8,000 children aged 9–12. Victimisation OR=0.68; perpetration OR=0.82. Peer-reported measures stronger (0.55, 0.78). - Nationwide non-randomised rollout, grades 1–9 - Wales, UK: pragmatic cluster RCT — independent team, different country - Netherlands: large-scale replication RCT (Prevention Science, 2020) - UK primary schools: multicentre cluster RCT with cost data - Cost-effectiveness modelling (Prevention Science, 2018) and Netherlands cost-benefit analysis

inference KiVa is the only program in this scan with multi-country independent replication plus published economic evaluation. That combination — not the Finnish origin — is why it scaled.

The licensing model — the actual lesson verified: KiVa licenses to national/regional partners, not schools. "Options for either a single payment covering all costs, or a yearly basic fee and royalties, with contracts signed for 3–5 years." The licence conveys the trademark, a defined region, training for the trainers, all materials, and setup of the implementation infrastructure. Present in 17+ countries.

hypothesis If MFC ever goes beyond Australia, this is the proven template for a research-born non-profit program. Note the sequencing: prove it at home → let others replicate it independently → license. Independent replication is the asset that makes licensing possible.

MindUP — and the most important null result in the field

verified Mindfulness-based, brain-science-framed school program since 2003 (Goldie Hawn Foundation). Mandatory 1-day on-site training, then online support plus a mentor visit. Listed in the CASEL Program Guide. Individual plans US$120/year. Per 990 filings: 73 schools, 48 countries, ~4,000 teachers, 106,000+ students.

verified Uses "mental fitness" in its own homepage copy — equipped people with "mental fitness tools for over 20 years."

Evidence verified: an RCT run in 2007–08 and published in 2015 (a 7-year lag), grade 4–5 Canadian students: better stress regulation, more optimistic and helpful.

⚠ The MYRIAD trial (PMC9340028) — a large, independent, well-powered, cost-effectiveness-inclusive cluster RCT of universal school-based mindfulness training in the UK — found it did not outperform normal school provision for reducing mental-health risk or promoting wellbeing in adolescents.

inference This is the most important null result in this entire field and MFC must know it. A well-funded independent trial of the universal-mindfulness-in-schools category found no benefit over business-as-usual. It is why "we teach everyone a practice at school" is now a contested rather than assumed proposition.

MFC's model differs from MYRIAD's target (workshop-based, capability-framed, adults included, repetition in real-life moments rather than in-class meditation) — but MFC should be able to articulate precisely why it expects a different result, in advance, in writing.

Mentemia (NZ) — and the critique MFC must answer

verified Founded 2019 by Sir John Kirwan (All Black, depression advocate) with Adam Clark. B2B2C, "set up to help employers embed a wellbeing-first culture." Made free to all New Zealanders with Ministry of Health, Kiwibank and Westpac support (2020). Investors include ACC.

verified University of Auckland: "Apps won't save us from mental health crisis." — "Many apps, like Mentemia, present mental health as something that should be 'worked on' every day, by everyone. Just as people are advised to exercise and eat a balanced diet to maintain physical health, these apps suggest we should also take time out for our mental health…"

inference This is the sharpest published academic critique of exactly MFC's framing. The charge: the everyday-practice/fitness analogy individualises responsibility for structural and social determinants of distress. MFC must have a prepared, honest answer. See [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/01-category-language-and-positioning-risk|01]].

Others — briefly

  • Greater Good in Action (UC Berkeley) — practice-library model, 16 "Keys to Well-Being", 600,000+ registered users on the Science of Happiness course, funded by Einhorn Family Charitable Trust and John Templeton Foundation. inference The atomic unit is a single practice with a stated evidence claim, a time cost and a benefit — the most elegantly scalable content architecture in the field. But it solves discovery of practices, not adherence — precisely the problem MFC claims to solve.
  • Anna Freud — Mentally Healthy Schools (UK) — free, "quality-assured" resources. Built by Anna Freud, YoungMinds, Place2Be and The Royal Foundation as a Heads Together legacy; Anna Freud took full ownership 1 April 2020. inference Quality assurance as the product — a trusted curatorial filter over a chaotic field is a defensible charity function. But it's a library, not a program, and it publishes no evidence labelling.
  • Sparklers (NZ) — 50+ free wellbeing activities, Years 1–8, born from post-earthquake Christchurch recovery. Ministries of Health and Education commissioned an external evaluation. inference Get a government ministry to commission your external evaluation — the cheapest credibility available, and it produces curriculum-alignment mapping, which is what actually unlocks school adoption. But they stopped at acceptability evidence ("teachers like it" ≠ "children can do more").
  • Finland — wellbeing as system architecture. verified Embedded in legislation (Basic Education Act; Pupil and Student Welfare Act) and the National Core Curriculum. "Promoting wellbeing is the shared responsibility of all adults in the school community." hypothesis When wellbeing is statutory and curricular, you don't need a program, a licence or a fidelity monitor — the distribution problem dissolves. For MFC, the highest-leverage long game is not selling more workshops but getting "mental fitness" named in curriculum or policy language. A 10-year play — and what makes the category claim strategically serious rather than a marketing frame.
  • Iceland — Planet Youth / Icelandic Prevention Model. verified Iceland moved from among the highest adolescent substance use in Europe (1998) to among the lowest (2013). inference The most under-appreciated model here. It is not a curriculum and not a skills program — it is a data-and-community-mobilisation loop: survey the local population annually → feed results back → the community itself chooses the protective changes → re-survey. Population change came from changing what young people did with their time and with whom, not from what they were taught. hypothesis If MFC's real claim is "capability is built through reps in real-life moments," MFC's most credible scaling mechanism may be closer to Planet Youth than to RULER. Caveat verified: this is a population time-series, not a controlled trial; causal attribution is contested.

What the international field has already solved

Do not reinvent these.

  1. The skills taxonomy. RULER's five, ACIP's four, PRP's six, CASEL's five — the field has converged; residual differences are branding. inference Adopt or adapt an existing taxonomy and spend scarce originality on delivery and measurement, not on inventing a sixth list.
  2. The core toolset. Mood Meter (valence × arousal), trigger-pause-best-self, ABC/thinking traps, gratitude noticing, active constructive responding, a written group agreement, a symmetric conflict protocol. All published and validated. (The Mood Meter is copyrighted to Emotionally Intelligent Schools LLC — but the underlying Russell & Barrett circumplex is not.)
  3. That adults must be trained first. RULER's architecture, Finland's legislation, PRP's validated educator delivery. Settled. Adopt it; don't re-argue it.
  4. That cascade / train-the-trainer preserves effect. The strongest empirical permission slip for a small organisation to scale.
  5. The dosage architecture that works — multi-year, team-based, leadership-anchored, tools embedded in routines, annual implementation assessment.
  6. That fidelity, not content, determines outcomes. Stop optimising content; optimise implementation.
  7. The fitness metaphor's legitimacy — precedented and policy-legible at $125m national scale.
  8. The non-profit revenue architecture — three working templates (free core + paid org services; trademark licensing on 3–5 year fee-plus-royalty; institutional package plus annual subscription).
  9. Content architecture for a practice library — GGIA's atomic format (name / benefit / time / evidence link / rating).
  10. The credibility ladder — university or ministry evaluation → third-party accreditation → institutional adoption → popular book. Four organisations here climbed it in the same order.

What remains genuinely unsolved

This is where MFC can contribute — or fail.

  1. Nobody can measure the capability directly. RULER's own authors state the field lacks performance-based assessments "sensitive to change." Everyone measures proxies. Nobody has an instrument for "what you are able to do." hypothesis MFC's single largest opportunity. A behavioural, performance-based, repeatable mental fitness measure would be a category-defining asset — the thing that makes "fitness" more than a metaphor, because fitness is definitionally measurable. It is also what K-05 logically obligates MFC to build.
  2. Nobody has demonstrated effects sustain after support ends. Longest follow-ups are within supported implementation windows. There is no published evidence anywhere that any of these programs builds a durable lifelong practice. inference MFC's entire "lifelong practice" premise is currently unevidenced by anyone, including its predecessors.
  3. Adherence/repetition in real life. GGIA doesn't track it. Healthy Minds lost 27% before download and 46% before post-test. NHS trials of Headspace and Foundations show the same. How you get a person to do a mental rep, unsupervised, in the moment, repeatedly, over years — is unsolved. hypothesis If MFC's differentiator is real, this is the exact problem it claims to solve, and it should design its evaluation around repetition frequency as a primary outcome — not satisfaction, not knowledge, not wellbeing scores.
  4. Whether universal preventive practice works at all. MYRIAD returned a well-powered independent null. Bonanno's verdict stands unrefuted for the military context. The thesis is live and contested, not established. MFC should state in advance what result would falsify its own model.
  5. The individualisation critique has no good published answer from anyone.
  6. Adult and workplace evidence is thin everywhere. RULER's strongest adult finding is n=47. PRP's million attendees have no published effect sizes at that scale. The adult/workplace segment is evidentially wide open — and it is where MFC already operates.
  7. Transfer across culture and country. KiVa's replications outside Finland consistently attenuate. RULER's non-US evidence is one 47-teacher Spanish study. inference Nobody has shown any of this transports to Australia. Australian-context evidence is not a nice-to-have for MFC — it is the missing evidence for the whole field in this jurisdiction, and generating it is both a contribution and a moat.
  8. Independence. Every strong evidence base here is developer-conducted with a disclosed COI plan or a commercial IP interest. The one program with genuine independent multi-country replication — KiVa — is the one that scaled internationally. inference That is not a coincidence, and it is the clearest strategic instruction in this research: commission independent evaluation early, while a null result is still survivable, because independent replication is what converts a program into a category.

05 Commercial Platforms

Commercial platforms using "mental fitness"

Why this file exists: MFC's category claim depends on whether the term is commercially occupied. It is. These organisations are not competitors for MFC's audience — most are enterprise B2B — but they shape what "mental fitness" means to the public and to funders, and MFC will be compared to them.

BetterUp — the most significant collision

Field Value
Country USA, VC-backed
Valuation ~$4.7–5B public organisational claim via press
Model AI + human 1:1 coaching, enterprise B2B

verified fact Dedicated page at betterup.com/mental-fitness, headline "Transform with Mental Fitness". Their definition:

"Mental Fitness is a proactive practice that ignites well-being, performance, and growth to become more resilient, realize your potential, and thrive."

verified fact Blog post "From Mental Health to Mental Fitness: Raise the Bar on Employee Well-Being", published 19 March 2021, explicitly frames mental fitness as proactive skill-building versus mental health as crisis/clinical care.

This is MFC's K-05 distinction, published five years earlier, by a company press outlets describe as "the largest mental fitness coaching business in the world."

Theory of change public organisational claim: targets the "massive middle" — the ~90% of employees neither clinically ill nor thriving.

Evidence public organisational claim: self-published claim of 77% wellbeing improvement in 3–4 months for low-wellbeing members. Not independently verified.

MFC can learn: their framing is near-identical to MFC's own and is prior art in messaging — worth reading closely, because MFC will be compared to it. MFC should NOT imitate: for-profit, VC-backed, individual-coaching-for-the-few, enterprise-gated — the structural opposite of a public-education charity mission.

Positive Intelligence (Shirzad Chamine)

verified fact Tagline: "Building mental fitness for all." App-guided PQ (Positive Intelligence Quotient) program, NYT bestseller basis, Stanford-affiliated. Framing: "we do physical fitness for our bodies, so why don't we learn mental fitness for our minds?"

verified fact Action for Happiness hosts a page titled "Mental Fitness" built entirely around Chamine's framework — describing "practical methods for how to grow our mental muscles and overcome our inner saboteurs."

inference This is a validation signal (the metaphor resonates publicly) and a differentiation risk (MFC is not the first mover). strategic hypothesis MFC should differentiate from the individual-guru/self-help register, which its charity status and evidence posture make easy.

MFC should NOT imitate: the "inner saboteurs" framing risks reading as pop-psychology rather than evidence-institutional.

The rest of the register

Organisation Usage of "mental fitness" Collision risk
MindUP (Goldie Hawn Foundation) verified fact Homepage copy: equipped people with "mental fitness tools for over 20 years" — but under a "preventative mental health" banner High conceptually. They conflate the two categories K-05 separates. A cautionary example of message dilution, and a named prior claimant
Uprise Health (Australian-founded) verified fact Markets its content library as "mental fitness courses" Medium. Australian origin makes it locally relevant; B2B EAP context differs
Calm / Calm Business verified fact Blog series "Mental Fitness as Part of a Healthy Workplace Strategy"; event "Mental Fitness for the Workplace" Low — descriptive/thematic, not branded
Headspace Health verified fact EAP copy: "brings together mental fitness, coaching, therapy and psychiatry... in one connected model" Low — one service line among several
Total Brain verified fact Term appears (e.g. "custom mental fitness program") but primary branding is "brain optimization" Low
Headversity (Canada) verified fact Mission: "to make practicing mental health skills as routine as developing physical fitness" — conceptually identical, but branded "resilience" Low on term, high on concept
Modern Health · Unmind · Whil · Wysa · Sonder No prominent "mental fitness" branding found Low

verified fact A US trademark registration for "MENTAL FITNESS" exists (Reg. 5193223, filed 2016, registered 2017); owner and goods/services could not be retrieved unknown.

The finding

"Mental fitness" is a moderately crowded, semi-generic term used across at least a dozen organisations globally. No single player dominates it — but no one has to dominate a term for it to stop being available as a category claim.

Two specific consequences for MFC:

  1. strategic hypothesis MFC cannot claim to have created or to be creating the category. BetterUp published the mental-health-vs-mental-fitness distinction in 2021; the US Army used "mental fitness" officially in 2009; MindUP has used it for twenty years.
  2. strategic hypothesis MFC can still own the positioning — non-clinical, non-commercial, population-wide, evidence-generating, and actually delivering the practice the word promises. That is distinct from BetterUp's premium enterprise coaching, Total Brain's clinical-adjacent assessment, Mental Fitness Australia's certification-body model, and Positive Intelligence's individual-guru model.

The commercial register also carries a warning: the term's dominant global association is now enterprise employee performance. inference If MFC does not actively define the term publicly, the default public meaning of "mental fitness" in five years will be a thing your employer buys to make you more productive — which is the opposite of K-00.

06 Adjacent Fields And Structural Forces

Adjacent fields and structural forces

This file covers what was not on the candidate list — the fields, regulations and bodies of evidence that shape MFC's market without appearing as competitors. Several of these matter more than any individual competitor.

A. The behaviour-change evidence — a check on MFC's core assumption

SWM-03 states: capability is built through practice and repetition, not information alone. This is MFC's load-bearing claim. What does the evidence actually say?

The good news — the mechanism is real and well-evidenced

Implementation intentions — Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006) meta-analysis, 94 independent tests, 8,000+ participants: forming an "if situation Y, then I will do X" plan had a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment, d = .65 verified fact. Effective at initiating goal striving, shielding pursuit from unwanted influences, and disengaging from failing courses of action.

inference This is the single most transferable, cheapest, best-evidenced design feature available to MFC. It is a one-sentence structure that can be built into the end of any workshop. If MFC's workshops do not currently end with participants writing specific if-then plans, that is a free improvement with a d=.65 evidence base behind it.

COM-B / Behaviour Change Wheel — Michie, van Stralen & West (2011) verified fact. Behaviour requires Capability (psychological and physical), Opportunity (external factors that make the behaviour possible or prompt it), and Motivation. Nine intervention functions and seven policy categories sit around it.

inference The strategically uncomfortable part for MFC: COM-B says Capability alone is insufficient. MFC's name, definition (K-04) and theory of change are all capability-focused. COM-B holds that capability without opportunity (environmental cues, permission, time, social context) and motivation produces no behaviour. K-04's own boundary statement already concedes this — "what a person can access changes with health, state, previous learning, habits, relationships, support, environment, power, safety." MFC's framework is more sophisticated than its name. That is a communications problem worth naming.

Habit formation — Lally et al. (2010), European Journal of Social Psychology, 96 participants over 12 weeks verified fact. Median time to 95% of asymptotic automaticity: 66 days. But the range was 18 to 254 days — enormous individual variation. Usefully: missing one opportunity did not materially affect habit formation.

inference Two implications. First, any MFC dosage claim shorter than ~9 weeks of daily practice is not supported by habit-formation evidence. Second, the "missing one day doesn't matter" finding is a genuinely useful, evidence-backed, permission-giving message for participants — and it is not what most wellbeing programs tell people.

The bad news — and MFC must sit with this

The training-transfer problem. Blume, Ford, Baldwin & Huang (2010), Journal of Management, meta-analytic review verified fact: while participants often acquire knowledge during training, only a modest portion of that learning transfers into sustained behaviour change. Broad & Newstrom (1992): without ongoing support, newly learned skills decay rapidly, with most people back to old ways of working within six months verified fact.

This is the central risk to MFC's entire model. A workshop is a training event. The training-transfer literature is fifty years of evidence that training events do not, by themselves, change behaviour. MFC's differentiator — practice, not information — is the correct diagnosis of the problem. But the workshop format is the very format the literature says fails, unless specific supports are built in.

What the literature says mitigates it verified fact: motivation and a supportive work/home environment; relapse-prevention components built into the training; scenarios developed by the participants themselves; specific learning goals formulated by participants; participation by superiors/leaders; and rewards or reinforcement in the environment.

strategic hypothesis Every one of those mitigations is a design decision MFC can make now, before its first pilot. Notably, "participation by superiors" and "supportive environment" both point the same way as RULER's adults-first rule and Planet Youth's community-mobilisation model. Three independent literatures converge: the environment around the person matters at least as much as the training given to the person.

The honest summary

Claim Evidence status
Skills can be trained through practice Well supported (PST, implementation intentions, RULER)
Repetition builds automaticity Supported, with large individual variance (Lally)
A brief workshop produces sustained practice NOT supported — contradicted by transfer literature
Workshop + implementation intentions + environmental support + boosters produces sustained practice Plausible and partly supported — but this is a different product than a workshop

strategic hypothesis MFC's theory of change is defensible. MFC's delivery format, on its own, is not. The gap between them is the actual design problem, and naming it honestly is a stronger position than asserting the model works.

B. Workplace psychosocial regulation — the biggest structural force nobody put on the list

What changed

verified fact SafeWork Australia's Model Code of Practice: Managing Psychosocial Hazards at Work (July 2022), following amendments to the Model WHS Regulations, imposes a positive obligation on PCBUs (employers) to manage and guard against psychosocial hazards. Adopted into state law including SafeWork NSW's Code of Practice.

This created a compliance-driven market for workplace mental health services — a large, growing, budget-backed demand signal.

The problem — and it is serious for MFC

verified fact The Code requires employers to first eliminate psychosocial risks where reasonably practicable, then minimise them by applying the hierarchy of controls — "starting with higher-order controls (such as implementing flexible working or redesigning the way work is completed) before relying on lower-order controls (such as training or coping strategies)."

Training sits at the BOTTOM of the hierarchy of controls.

verified fact Named psychosocial hazards include: role overload and underload · role conflict or lack of role clarity · low job control · poor support from supervisors and co-workers · poor workplace relationships and conflict · inadequate reward and recognition · poor procedural justice · poor organisational-change consultation · exposure to traumatic events · remote or isolated work · violence and aggression · bullying · sexual harassment.

verified fact The accompanying critique in the professional literature is explicit: "Offering resilience training is not enough." · "EAPs and resilience training sit at the bottom; they must not replace job redesign, workload restructuring, or scheduling changes." · "Job design is the biggest driver — workload, pace, autonomy, and role clarity cause more harm than interpersonal conflict."

⚠ The study that will be quoted at MFC

Fleming, W.J. (2024), Industrial Relations Journal 55:162–182 — "Employee well-being outcomes from individual-level mental health interventions: cross-sectional evidence from the United Kingdom." verified fact

46,336 workers across 233 organisations. Found no significant wellbeing differences between participants and non-participants in mindfulness, resilience/stress management, relaxation classes or wellbeing apps. For resilience training specifically, participants reported worse mental health than non-participants.

Fleming's stated implication: organisational interventions — scheduling, management practice, staffing, performance review, job design — are the more promising lever.

The honest reading inference: this is cross-sectional, so the resilience-training finding is very plausibly selection (people who are struggling opt into resilience training), not harm. But the headline travelled widely (Forbes, AJMC, UPI, Jan 2024) and is now part of buyers' mental furniture.

strategic hypothesis MFC will meet procurement officers who have absorbed "wellbeing training doesn't work" as settled fact. MFC needs a prepared, non-defensive answer that (a) concedes the point about individual-level interventions substituting for work redesign, (b) names the selection-effect limitation accurately without hiding behind it, and (c) explains what MFC does differently. Pretending this study doesn't exist is not viable.

ISO 45003 note verified fact: ISO 45003:2021 is a guidance standard containing no requirements — you cannot be certified to it. Providers routinely blur this. MFC should not.

What this means for MFC

  1. verified fact A "mental fitness" skills program cannot satisfy an employer's psychosocial-hazard duty. It is a lower-order control. An employer who buys MFC workshops instead of fixing work design is not compliant, and a regulator would say so.
  2. strategic hypothesis This is simultaneously a threat and MFC's cleanest differentiator. The threat: MFC will be sold into a compliance market where it cannot deliver compliance, and will be blamed when it doesn't. The opportunity: MFC can be the organisation that says this out loud — "we do not fix your work design, and nothing we sell you will discharge your WHS duty" — which is both true and a trust-building differentiator against every vendor implying otherwise.
  3. inference This connects directly to the individualisation critique in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/01-category-language-and-positioning-risk|01]]. The regulator has effectively codified the academic critique: don't put the burden on the individual when the hazard is structural. MFC's answer to the University of Auckland critique and its answer to the WHS hierarchy are the same answer, and K-04's boundary statement already contains it.
  4. strategic hypothesis MFC should consider stating a red line in K-08 terms: MFC does not claim its programs discharge, satisfy or substitute for any WHS psychosocial duty. This is a claims-boundary question and belongs to the committee.

The three defensible workplace positions strategic hypothesis

  1. Sell to managers and leaders, not workers. Manager behaviour — support, procedural justice, change consultation, role clarity — is itself a named hazard domain. A mental fitness program aimed at leaders sits inside the hazard rather than beside it. This is the strongest available position, and it is not the one most vendors take.
  2. Position explicitly as a complement, in writing. "This does not discharge your psychosocial duty; it is a lower-order control that assumes you have done the higher-order work." Saying this out loud is a differentiator in a market full of providers implying otherwise.
  3. Avoid "resilience" as the lead frame. It is now the specifically contested term — and the one Fleming's finding attaches to. K-05's "what we are able to do" is orthogonal to resilience-as-endurance, but only if MFC actively distinguishes them rather than letting buyers collapse the two.

unknown — worth commissioning: enforcement volume under the Australian psychosocial provisions. Prosecutions and improvement notices are the true demand signal, and nobody in this research has that number.

C. Triple P — the most instructive Australian precedent

verified fact University of Queensland origin, now the most widely disseminated parenting intervention in the world.

The tiered model — five levels of increasing intensity: Level 1 universal media/communication strategy · Level 2 brief primary-care developmental guidance · Level 3 four-session active skills training for mild-moderate problems · Level 4 intensive 8–10 session group or individual training · Level 5 enhanced/intensive for complex cases.

inference Why tiering matters, and why MFC should care: it lets one organisation serve an entire population at proportionate cost — cheap universal reach at the top, expensive intensive support only where needed — while using a single coherent framework and a single practitioner-accreditation pipeline across all levels. It solves the reach-versus-depth tension that [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/01-category-language-and-positioning-risk|01]] identifies as the unclaimed space. Nobody in the Australian mental fitness landscape has a tiered model. This is a genuinely available structural design.

The evidence verified fact: Sanders et al. (2014) systematic review and meta-analysis — 116 eligible studies over 33 years, 101 studies comprising 16,099 families analysed quantitatively. Significant positive effects across child, parent and family outcomes.

The criticism — and this is the part MFC must internalise verified fact:

Wilson et al. (2012), BMC Medicine, "How evidence-based is an 'evidence-based parenting program'?" Found significant positive effects on maternal reports of child behaviour (ES = .61) — but raised serious concerns about investigator bias, inadequate reporting, and conflicts of interest. Specifically: many studies were authored by Triple P-affiliated personnel; no trials were registered; only two papers contained conflict-of-interest statements.

verified fact A subsequent finding: Dutch research performed independently of the Triple P developers found Triple P was not more effective than care-as-usual.

verified fact The Wilson review documented pervasive conflicts of interest, with authors of the bulk of articles receiving royalties and other financial rewards from the promotion of Triple P.

What MFC learns

  1. Tiered universal-to-targeted design is a proven, available, and unclaimed structure in this market.
  2. Practitioner accreditation is simultaneously a scaling mechanism and a revenue model — same lesson as MHFA and KiVa.
  3. An evidence base is a strategic asset — Triple P's 116 studies are why governments fund it.
  4. But developer-conducted evidence is a reputational time bomb. Triple P, RULER and the US Army's MRT all have the same disclosed entanglement. Triple P's is the one that produced a published attack in a major journal and an independent replication failure.

strategic hypothesis This is the fourth independent line of evidence in this research pointing at the same conclusion: commission independent evaluation early, register trials in advance, publish conflict-of-interest statements, and publish null results. For MFC — which has no evidence yet — doing this from the first pilot costs almost nothing and buys a defensible position that Gotcha4Life, Smiling Mind, Triple P and RULER all now have to retrofit.

D. Sport and performance psychology — a prior claimant MFC should know about

verified fact Psychological Skills Training (PST) is a decades-old established field: "the systematic and consistent practice of mental skills for the purpose of enhancing performance." Core techniques: imagery/mental rehearsal, self-talk, goal setting, arousal regulation, cognitive restructuring, pre-performance routines.

Evidence verified fact: a Web of Science bibliometric analysis covering 405 articles and reviews, 1992–2021. A review of reviews (2023, International Journal of Sport and Exercise Psychology) found 90% of reviews concluded PST interventions can enhance performance. Also a meta-regression of single-case designs, and RCTs comparing PST against mindfulness training.

Why this matters to MFC

  • inference This field has been "training the mind" with measurable outcomes for forty years. It is the one domain that has genuinely operationalised the fitness metaphor — because sport supplies an unambiguous outcome measure (performance) that wellbeing does not.
  • It is a prior claimant to MFC's framing — "psychological skills training" is exactly the term Healthy Minds Australia uses, and it comes from here.
  • verified fact The AIS — which runs the AIS Mental Fitness Program (ORG-05) — sits in this tradition, as do the College of Sport and Exercise Psychologists. This is why an Australian sports institute was the body that put "mental fitness" into schools.
  • strategic hypothesis The transferable lesson is the outcome-measurement discipline, not the techniques. Sport psychology could evidence itself because it had a scoreboard. MFC's equivalent challenge — building a performance-anchored measure of "what we are able to do" — is identified in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/04-international-and-ruler|04]] as the largest unsolved problem in the field. Sport psychology is the field that has come closest to solving it, and MFC should look there before looking at SEL.

E. Indigenous Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEWB) — a serious risk, not a checkbox

verified fact SEWB is the established, culturally-grounded Australian framework for holistic wellbeing. It comprises seven interconnected domains: connection to body · mind and emotions · family and kinship · community · culture · Country · spirituality and ancestors. It represents "a cultural understanding of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander relationality, identity, and holistic individual, family, and community health," and explicitly foregrounds historical and social determinants.

verified fact The Gayaa Dhuwi (Proud Spirit) Declaration states that all parts of the Australian mental health system should be guided by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander concepts of social and emotional wellbeing, mental health and healing, in combination with clinical approaches. A formal SEWB Policy Partnership exists as a shared decision-making structure between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander leaders and governments.

Why this is a genuine strategic and ethical risk for MFC

MFC is a non-Indigenous organisation proposing to define a wellbeing category for Australia. SEWB is an existing, Indigenous-led, government-recognised framework that already does holistic wellbeing in this country — and does it with a relational, collective, Country-connected model that is philosophically different from an individual-capability model.

inference Three specific risks:

  1. Talking over. A claim to be "defining the category of mental fitness in Australia" (SWM-02) is, read from a SEWB standpoint, a claim to define wellbeing — which is already defined, differently, by the people whose framework has policy standing.
  2. Philosophical collision. SEWB locates wellbeing in connection to family, community, culture and Country. MFC's K-04 locates it in individually-accessible skills. These are not incompatible — K-04's boundary statement explicitly names relationships, environment, power and safety — but MFC has not stated the relationship between its model and SEWB anywhere in the vault. That is a gap.
  3. The individualisation critique lands harder here. The critique in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/01-category-language-and-positioning-risk|01]] — that everyday-practice framing individualises structural problems — is sharpest in relation to populations whose distress is most clearly structural and historical.

strategic hypothesis This warrants a dedicated piece of work, led by Indigenous advisors, not a paragraph written by AI. A-17 has no standing to determine MFC's position here, and this file records it as an unowned risk requiring human and Indigenous-led resolution. Recommend routing to A-12 (exclusion/safeguarding) and escalating to Hunter as a category-claim constraint.

F. Other fields worth noting

Field Relevance Status
Character education — Jubilee Centre for Character and Virtues (Birmingham); VIA Institute on Character and the VIA Survey of character strengths The VIA survey is already used inside the US Army's MRT (Character Strengths module, 1 full day). A validated, free, widely-used instrument for making abstract qualities concrete and measurable Worth direct investigation — closest available off-the-shelf measurement instrument
Health insurer prevention — Medibank, Bupa, HCF wellbeing programs Large, funded, and competing for the same "prevention" narrative; a potential funding/partnership channel unknown — not researched
Digital therapeutics and TGA regulation of wellbeing apps in Australia Determines what MFC could and could not claim if it ever ships a digital product; relevant to K-08 unknown — not researched
Men's Sheds / community connection models The non-clinical, non-program, environment-based route to the same outcome — closer to Planet Youth than to a curriculum unknown — not researched
ADF and emergency-services resilience programs (Australia) Domestic instances of the CSF tradition; likely already use fitness language unknown — not researched
Peer-support and lived-experience workforce models An established, funded workforce category MFC's facilitator model will be compared against unknown — not researched

These six are recorded as known gaps in this research pass, not as low-priority. Three of them (TGA regulation, insurer channel, lived-experience workforce) could each materially change MFC's options.

Structural forces — the eight findings that matter most

  1. Training sits at the bottom of the WHS hierarchy of controls. A mental fitness program cannot discharge an employer's psychosocial duty. → MFC should say so explicitly and make honesty the differentiator.
  2. The training-transfer literature says workshops don't produce sustained behaviour change without specific supports. → MFC's format is the risk; its theory is sound. Build in implementation intentions, boosters, environmental support and leader participation before the first pilot.
  3. Implementation intentions have a d = .65 meta-analytic effect and cost nothing to add. → Free, immediate, evidence-backed improvement to every workshop.
  4. Habit automaticity takes a median 66 days with an 18–254 day range. → Any dosage claim under ~9 weeks is unsupported. Also: "missing one day doesn't matter" is a true, evidence-backed, permission-giving message nobody else is using.
  5. COM-B says capability alone is insufficient. → MFC's name emphasises exactly the one-third of the model that doesn't work alone. K-04's boundary already concedes this — the framework is ahead of the branding.
  6. Tiered universal-to-targeted design (Triple P) is proven, available, and unclaimed in this market. → The structural answer to the reach-versus-depth tension.
  7. Developer-conducted evidence is a reputational time bomb — demonstrated at Triple P, RULER and CSF. → Register trials, publish COI statements, commission independent evaluation, publish nulls. Costs almost nothing now; impossible to retrofit.
  8. SEWB is an existing Indigenous-led Australian wellbeing framework with policy standing, and MFC has no stated position on it. → Unowned risk. Requires Indigenous-led resolution, not an AI-drafted paragraph.
