NewAccess / Before Blue — the honest adjacency assessment

This is the section the brief asked for, and the answer is more uncomfortable than "structurally adjacent."

What NewAccess actually is verified fact: an Australian adaptation of the UK's Improving Access to Psychological Therapies (IAPT) programme. Structured, manualised, low-intensity CBT, delivered in six sessions by trained coaches who are not clinicians, under clinical supervision, free at point of use, no referral or diagnosis required.

Where it genuinely resembles MFC's position: - Non-clinical deliverers. The workforce is coaches, not psychologists. verified fact - Explicitly not therapy in its consumer framing — "mental health coaching," accessed without a GP referral or treatment plan. verified fact - Skills and tools framing: participants "develop and work through your own tailored plan"; Before Blue is described as equipping people with "long-term skills, continuity of care, and a focus on wellbeing before issues escalate," explicitly contrasted with EAPs that "often focus on short-term crisis support." verified fact - Prevention/early-intervention positioning under Strategy 2023+ — "Earlier. Easier. Together." verified fact

Where the resemblance breaks, and it breaks hard: - NewAccess measures clinical symptom reduction on clinical instruments. NASBO's headline outcome is "clinically significant improvement … on the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ9) and/or the Generalized Anxiety Disorder Questionnaire (GAD7)" — 76% of participants verified fact. This is a treatment model with a non-clinical workforce, not a capability-building model. The construct it moves is symptom severity, which is precisely the construct K-05 distinguishes MFC from. - Entry is by distress. You come to NewAccess because you are stressed or overwhelmed. You do not come because you want to get better at something. inference, strongly supported by all public framing. - Dose is bounded and terminal. Six sessions (or eight), then you exit. There is no sustaining practice layer, no lifelong architecture. verified fact re the session cap; inference re the implication.

Published evidence base verified fact: - Multi-site cohort study, 2013–2016, published in Journal of Mental Health (2023, vol 32 no 1) as "The Australian version of IAPT: clinical outcomes of the multi-site cohort study of NewAccess" — reliable recovery ~68% at post-treatment. Cohort, not randomised; no control group. - A PricewaterhouseCoopers evaluation reported a 72% recovery rate public organisational claim — PwC was engaged by Beyond Blue; this is not independent academic evaluation. - inference Recovery rates of 68–72% without a control arm cannot be attributed to the intervention. Natural remission of mild-to-moderate anxiety and depression over six to twelve weeks is substantial. The UK's own IAPT-equivalent benchmark is ~42% recovery / ~60% improvement, and an independent 2026 review notes 30–40% of low-intensity CBT users do not improve meaningfully. NewAccess's higher headline number is a reason for scepticism about comparability, not a reason for confidence.

The finding that changes MFC's picture: the Commonwealth has nationalised this model

On 1 January 2026 the Commonwealth launched the National Early Intervention Service, branded "Medicare Mental Health Check In," delivered by St Vincent's Health Australia. Free, no referral, no diagnosis, aged 16+, low-intensity CBT delivered by trained practitioners (not necessarily psychologists) by phone or video, six-week tailored plan, self-guided versions from May 2026. Funding: $588.5 million over eight years from 2024-25, then $113.4 million per year ongoing. Expected to reach over 150,000 people per year by 2029. verified fact — Department of Health, Disability and Ageing; The Conversation, 9 April 2026

Beyond Blue's own 2024-25 report claims paternity: "Beyond Blue has advocated for a national approach to Low-intensity Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (Li-CBT) for over 10 years and has been encouraged by the Commonwealth's investment in a new National Early Intervention Service." verified fact

strategic hypothesis, high confidence: Beyond Blue spent a decade proving the coach-delivered low-intensity model, then watched the Commonwealth build it at national scale and award it to someone else. The "coaching, not therapy, free, no referral" space is now occupied by a $588.5M government service with a Medicare-adjacent brand.

What this means for MFC, stated plainly: any MFC positioning that leans on "non-clinical, no referral needed, skills-based, accessible" as its differentiator is now competing against a free national government service on those exact attributes. MFC's differentiation cannot be access, cost or non-clinicality — those are commoditised as of January 2026. It has to be the thing NEIS structurally cannot do: entry without distress, and practice without an endpoint. This sharpens K-05 rather than threatening it — but only if MFC states it that way.

What Beyond Blue actually measures

Almost everything published is satisfaction, self-reported knowledge, self-reported feeling, or intention verified fact, with two exceptions: - NASBO's PHQ-9/GAD-7 clinically significant improvement (76%) — a real instrument, but pre/post with no control. - The K10 completed 446,000+ times on the website — a screening tool, not an outcome measure.

Representative claims, all post-only self-report from opt-in surveys (Beyond Blue discloses this: "Some surveys are opt-in and not compulsory… statistics represent findings from the sample of those individuals who completed the survey" verified fact): 86% received the information they sought · 75% felt less distressed · 82% felt heard · 77% intended to act · 97% of Before Blue participants learned skills · 90% of Speaker Program audiences had greater awareness.

inference Beyond Blue — the best-resourced mental health charity in the country, with $52.6M of public money and a Deloitte audit — publishes an impact report in which the strongest outcome evidence is an uncontrolled pre/post on 7,900 coaching sessions, and everything else is an opt-in satisfaction survey. This is not a criticism unique to Beyond Blue; it is the sector's ceiling. It is also MFC's single clearest opening: the bar for "credible evidence" in Australian mental health promotion is far lower than the bar in the learning-science literature MFC is actually built on.

Strategic read for MFC

Referral pathway — yes, and only that. The Support Service (303,000+ contacts) is the correct escalation destination for any MFC participant who discloses distress, and naming it is a safeguarding asset, not a competitive concession. strategic hypothesis

Partner — unlikely and not worth pursuing now. Beyond Blue's board is its funders; partnership decisions are effectively government decisions. MFC has no track record to bring. inference

Competitor — for philanthropic dollars, yes. Beyond Blue is raising $17.9M/year in a market it describes as challenging, while running deficits. verified fact

Evidence-generation model — and the null result MFC must read

Black Dog is the only organisation in this entire market-intelligence objective that runs adequately-powered randomised trials of its own programmes and publishes them when they fail.

Werner-Seidler A, Mackinnon A, Batterham PJ, et al. (2025). "Future Proofing Study: a cluster randomised controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of a universal school-based cognitive–behavioural programme for adolescent depression." BMJ Mental Health, 28(1):e301426. Design: cluster RCT, 1:1 allocation, Australian secondary schools, Aug 2019 – Dec 2022. Sample: 134 schools (71 intervention, 63 control); 6,388 students at baseline; 4,841 at primary endpoint (75.8% retention). Intervention: SPARX — gamified self-directed digital CBT, seven 20-minute modules, delivered by smartphone app with schools instructed to provide in-class time. Primary outcome: change in PHQ-A depressive symptoms, baseline to 12 months. Result: "Intent-to-treat analyses showed no difference in depression change between groups from baseline to 12 months" (p = 0.75). Engagement: only 22% of intervention participants completed ≥4 of 7 modules; 43% did not engage at all. Authors' stated limitations: low engagement, schools' failure to provide scheduled class time, COVID-19 timing, 31% consent rate.

This is the most important single study in MFC's entire competitive research corpus, and it is not about a competitor's brand — it is about MFC's delivery assumption.

  1. The largest, best-designed Australian trial of a universal school-based digital skills programme found nothing at 12 months. verified fact
  2. The stated mechanism of failure was not that the content was wrong — it was that nobody did the practice. 43% zero engagement, 22% reaching four modules. verified fact
  3. inference This is the same failure mode already documented for Gotcha4Life (114,177 participants → 9,566 gym members, ~8%) and suspected for Smiling Mind (9.8M downloads, no retention data published). Three independent organisations, three different models, one identical result: the sustaining-practice layer does not sustain.
  4. strategic hypothesis MFC's entire thesis rests on practice over time. The best evidence in this market says practice over time is exactly what does not happen when you ship it as content and hope. MFC's design problem is therefore not "what should the skills be" — that is well covered — it is "what makes an adult actually do the rep next week." If MFC's first pilot does not answer that question with behavioural data, MFC will have reproduced a 6,388-student null result at smaller scale.

Other Black Dog evidence assets verified fact: ClearlyMe® (CBT app for 12–17s) supported by an RCT of 569 young people with depressive symptoms showing lower depressive symptoms and improved quality of life; Sleep Ninja (six structured sessions, effectiveness-tested, already noted in file 03).

inference Note the contrast within Black Dog's own portfolio: a targeted, symptomatic digital CBT tool (ClearlyMe, n=569) produced a positive result; a universal, whole-population digital CBT programme (SPARX, n=6,388) produced a null. That contrast is a design lesson, not a coincidence — universal programmes have to solve motivation before they can deliver content.

AIS Mental Fitness Program — extension of ORG-05

Black Dog's own page for the programme returned only a title on fetch (2026-08-06) and could not be read; the programme detail in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/03-profiles-australia-adjacent|ORG-05]] stands unamended. What this profile adds:

  • inference Given Black Dog explicitly does not receive ongoing government funding, the AIS partnership is most likely grant- or fee-for-service-funded delivery, sitting inside the $11.4M "clinical services, online treatments and education programs" expense line or the $6.0M fee-for-service revenue line. Not verified — the annual report does not disaggregate by programme. unknown
  • strategic hypothesis A research institute that competitively bids for delivery work, has 132 research staff, has just published its own null result, and lends its name to a programme called "Mental Fitness Program" that never defines mental fitness, is the most partner-shaped organisation in this entire market. MFC brings a defended definition (K-04, K-05) and a practice architecture; Black Dog brings trial capability and the credibility MFC cannot buy. This is the highest-value relationship identified anywhere in this objective.

Strategic read for MFC

Partner — first priority. strategic hypothesis Competitor — only via the AIS programme's use of the category name. verified fact Evidence benchmark — the standard MFC will be measured against. A cluster RCT with published nulls is what "evidence-based" means when a serious funder asks. inference

Three findings that reframe R U OK? completely:

  1. Government funding is 9.3% of revenue — around $800,000, essentially flat for three years. verified fact The most recognised mental health brand in Australia is almost entirely privately funded. Every assumption that R U OK? is a government-backed institution is wrong.
  2. Merchandise is 36.1% of revenue — $3.1M, more than donations. verified fact inference R U OK? is, financially, a branded-goods business attached to a suicide prevention message. Inventory on the balance sheet is $1.04M. This is a genuinely unusual and, on the evidence, effective funding model — and it depends entirely on the brand remaining desirable to wear and display.
  3. FY2025 is a deficit year (−$503,306) with revenue down 2.4%, following a 2.4% fall the year before. Cash at bank fell from $2.41M to $0.46M (offset by term deposits rising $6M → $7M). verified fact inference The revenue line has been flat-to-declining for three consecutive years while employee costs rose 43% from FY23 to FY25. That is a compression, not a crisis — total assets are $9.39M against $1.07M current liabilities — but the trend is one direction.

The measurement problem — now precisely characterisable

What R U OK? measures, verbatim, FY2024-25 verified fact (all sourced to Verian (June, 2025) R U OK? Impact Tracker, a commissioned market-research tracker):

  • 87% of Australians are aware of R U OK?
  • ~3 in 5 associate R U OK? with encouraging people to talk
  • Of those engaged: 56% called and 52% messaged someone about a troubling issue
  • 77% agree it's important to check in regularly any day of the year
  • 90% of people say being asked "are you OK?" made them feel grateful, supported and cared for
  • Those engaged are "20% more confident they can recognise the signs"

inference, well-grounded: every one of these is awareness, association, attitude, self-reported feeling, or self-reported behaviour collected by a brand tracker. Not one is an observed behaviour, a validated instrument, a skill demonstration, or a health outcome. The construct genuinely moved is campaign salience. The construct claimed is suicide prevention capability. That gap has not narrowed since the 2019 Ross & Bassilios paper; it has been re-instrumented.

The comparison problem — what happened to the reach data verified fact: - 2017 (Ross & Bassilios, peer-reviewed, n=2,013): awareness 78%, participation 32%. - 2023 (KANTAR Public tracker): figures published as images on the impact page, machine-unreadable. - 2025 (Verian tracker): awareness 87%. Participation is no longer published.

inference The tracker provider changed (KANTAR Public → Verian), and the participation metric — the one that measures whether people actually did anything — stopped appearing while the awareness metric, which only goes up, remained the headline. This may be entirely innocent (Verian is KANTAR Public rebranded). But the effect is that the only R U OK? number that could show stagnation is no longer in the public record. MFC should treat any R U OK? "impact" figure as brand-tracking data unless the underlying question wording is published. Neither the Verian tracker instrument nor its methodology is public — unknown; publication of the tracker questionnaire and sampling frame would verify.

Campaign vs capability — the model stated honestly

R U OK? says it itself: "We're not a service provider or a registered training organisation." verified fact Its theory of change is Joiner's Interpersonal Psychological Theory of Suicidal Behaviour — increase belonging and social connection verified fact. Its intervention is free resources plus an annual date plus permission ("Ask R U OK? — No qualifications needed").

Delivery footprint FY2024-25 verified fact: Rail R U OK? reached 120,000+ employees across 183 organisations with 314 Rail Champions; Healthy Heads in Trucks & Sheds engaged 136 organisations and 224 champions with 93% of participants reporting greater confidence; ~3,000 participants at the Australasian Police & Emergency Services Games; Conversation Convoy workshops ("Locals Know Best") building ALEC self-efficacy; Stronger Together in its sixth year with resources translated into Arrernte, Luritja, Pitjantjatjara and Walpiri.

inference Note what the Convoy workshops are: R U OK? has quietly built a facilitator-delivered skills layer under the campaign — small, regional, and unmeasured in outcome terms, but real. The campaign/capability boundary is less absolute than the 2026-08-01 profile implied. It remains true that no published evidence tests whether anyone can competently conduct the conversation. verified absence

Strategic read for MFC

Not a competitor — a proof and a warning. strategic hypothesis The proof: a $8.7M organisation with 9% government funding built the most recognised mental health brand in Australia on merchandise and sponsorship. That funding model is available to MFC and nobody in the "mental fitness" category is using it. The warning: fourteen years in, with 87% awareness, the organisation still cannot say whether anyone acquired a skill — and its revenue is now declining. Awareness compounds; capability does not follow it automatically.

The crisis ← → prevention spectrum

Placement is inference from each organisation's own published description of what it does and who it is for.

Position Organisation Entry condition Construct actually moved
Acute crisis Lifeline (13 11 14), Kids Helpline, 13YARN "I am in crisis now" Immediate distress, safety
Crisis-adjacent support Beyond Blue Support Service "I am distressed" Distress, information, referral
Complex / enduring SANE Australia "I live with a complex condition" Coordination, connection, coping
Treatment (youth) headspace, Orygen clinics "Something is wrong and I want help" Clinical symptoms
Condition-specific treatment + prevention Butterfly Foundation Both — helpline and BodyKind Symptoms; body-image attitudes
Low-intensity intervention NewAccess / Before Blue / NEIS "Check In" "I am stressed or overwhelmed" PHQ-9 / GAD-7 symptom scores
Early intervention, digital ReachOut, Black Dog digital tools "Something is off and I'll look online" Literacy, symptoms, self-efficacy
Universal prevention, institutional Be You, AIS Mental Fitness Program, BodyKind Schools "My school/club booked it" Educator confidence; student awareness
Awareness / social norm R U OK? "It's September" / "there's a poster" Campaign salience; helping intentions
Research and system Black Dog, Orygen, Mental Health Australia n/a Evidence; policy
Non-clinical capability building, entered by choice, practised indefinitely — nobody — "I want to get better at this" What we are able to do

Does any of them occupy MFC's position?

No — and the gap is now sharper than it was in the 2026-08-01 analysis, not vaguer. inference

Every organisation in this tier is entered through a problem. Distress, symptoms, a condition, a crisis, a booked assembly, a calendar date. Not one is entered because a person decided they wanted to become more capable. The closest structural approach — NewAccess/Before Blue — reaches the non-clinical workforce and the skills language, and then measures itself on a depression scale.

The two organisations that come nearest on any single dimension: - NewAccess / Before Blue / NEIS own non-clinical delivery of structured skills, free, without referral. As of 1 January 2026 the Commonwealth owns this at $588.5M scale. MFC cannot differentiate on access, cost or non-clinicality. - Be You and the AIS Mental Fitness Program own free universal institutional delivery. Between them they are in >70% of Australian schools and 458+ schools and sporting organisations. MFC should not enter schools as an early market. This is now the third independent line of evidence pointing the same way.

What remains unoccupied, precisely: 1. Entry without a problem. No large institution can market to people who are fine, because their funding is justified by need. 2. Practice without an endpoint. Every model here has a session cap, a call length, a campaign day or a module count. verified fact across all of them. 3. Measurement of capability rather than symptoms or satisfaction. ReachOut has publicly conceded this is not attempted; Beyond Blue uses clinical scales; R U OK? uses a brand tracker.

strategic hypothesis These three are one position, not three, and it is the position K-04 and K-05 already describe. The institutional tier does not threaten it. What the institutional tier proves is that the position is empty because it is hard to fund, not because it is unwanted — funders buy need, and MFC's proposition is definitionally not about need. That is the real strategic problem this research surfaces, and it is a funding-model problem, not a positioning problem.

Three Australian organisations have already solved the funding-model problem without government: R U OK? (36% merchandise, 9% government), yourtown/Kids Helpline (a lottery business), and Mental Health First Aid Australia (fee-for-service since 2002, per [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/03-profiles-australia-adjacent|ORG-08]]). None of the three depends on demonstrating deficit to get paid.

16 Kindness And Connection Cluster

Kindness and social-connection cluster (Australia)

Commissioned to profile ALLKND and the surrounding Australian kindness / social-connection / loneliness cluster.

Labels used on every substantive claim: verified fact (URL given) · public organisational claim (they say it, nobody independent checked it) · inference · strategic hypothesis · unknown.

Method constraint on this pass: ACNC charity-register pages are JavaScript-rendered and could not be retrieved (confirmed by direct attempt — the register page returns a shell with no financial content). Every charity revenue figure in this document is therefore unknown, with the verification route named. ABN/legal-entity data was verified directly against ABN Lookup, which is server-rendered.

Year discipline: every figure below carries the year it refers to. Today is 2026-08-06.

Headline judgements (read this first)

  1. ALLKND is a startup-scale charity, not a competitor tier. 3,081 people trained in its flagship programme, lifetime, as displayed on its own homepage 2026 public organisational claim. It is a real registered Health Promotion Charity with DGR status verified fact, run by a strong personal-brand founder, with disproportionate social-media reach relative to its programme throughput. It is a positioning and attention competitor for the Gen Z audience, not a delivery competitor.
  2. The only organisation in this cluster using MFC's category term is The Push-Up Challenge — it describes itself using "mental fitness" language public organisational claim. It reaches 234,000 Australians a year and 785 schools (2025) public organisational claim. This is materially more consequential to MFC's category position than anything ALLKND does. It belongs with the AIS Mental Fitness Program (file 03) on the category-collision watchlist.
  3. The cluster's evidence base is thin, and one name collision is actively dangerous. "Kindness Curriculum" is two different things: the Australian Kindness Factory product (no published independent evaluation found) and the UW-Madison Center for Healthy Minds Mindfulness-Based Kindness Curriculum (two RCTs). They are not the same programme and their evidence does not transfer. Anyone citing "the Kindness Curriculum is RCT-backed" in an Australian schools context is very likely conflating them. MFC must never repeat that conflation, and can gain credibility by being the organisation that names it.
  4. The strongest evaluation practice in this cluster is Live4Life and Raise, not the kindness brands. If MFC wants a model for how an Australian charity builds a defensible evidence position, those two are the templates.

1. ALLKND — primary target

Scale verdict, stated plainly: startup-scale. A five-year-old charity whose flagship programme has trained ~3,000 people in total. Its social-media reach is roughly 1,600× its cumulative programme throughput. That is a media brand with a programme attached, not a delivery organisation at competitive scale. Treating it as a competitor tier would be an error.

inference The QLD 4165 registered location sits oddly against ALLKND's public presentation as a Surry Hills / Sydney organisation (its Facebook page lists Surry Hills NSW). Most likely explanation is a registered-office or director's address in Queensland with operations in Sydney. Not material, but do not describe ALLKND as "a Sydney charity" as though that were verified.

It was the sole file contradicting the register position and was cited in 42-committee-approval-pathway.md as proof the vault could not settle the matter. The vault could; this line was simply stale.

Founder and origin story

Founder: Milly Rose Bannister verified fact — allknd.org/about. Origin story as told publicly public organisational claim: she founded ALLKND a decade after supporting her best friend through a mental-health crisis when she was 15, an experience that showed her how unprepared young people are to support each other. She is described on the site as an award-winning speaker and social-impact strategist working on prevention, belonging and youth wellbeing.

inference This is a classic single-founder personal-brand charity — the founder's speaking profile and the charity's reach are hard to separate. That is a strength for attention and a structural risk for institutional durability (key-person dependency). The same risk pattern applies to Kindness Factory and OneWave.

What it actually does

Two programmes verified fact (both listed on allknd.org):

  1. Good Mate Training — a free, online, ~60-minute course teaching young people how to support a friend through a tough time. Presented as "Australia's first digital peer-to-peer mental health first aid training certificate," designed by mental health professionals to land with a younger audience public organisational claim.
  2. Cause Club — a national community that gathers young people for local social-volunteering events; explicitly framed as making friends while doing good public organisational claim.

Delivery format: digital self-paced course + in-person community volunteering events. Dosage: Good Mate Training is a single ~60-minute session, one-off public organisational claim. Cause Club dosage is unknown (event frequency per member not published).

Reach — all public organisational claim, homepage counters, retrieved 2026-08-06

Metric Figure
Young people trained in peer mental health first aid 3,081
Cause Club members 4,362
Australian cities with Cause Club members 73
Monthly social-media content views 5,128,447

Source: allknd.org. These are undated lifetime counters — no year is stated on the page, so treat them as "as at 2026-08-06, cumulative since some unstated start." A separate search snippet showed 3,079 trained, i.e. the counter is live and moving slowly — roughly two additions between two retrievals days apart inference.

The ratio matters more than the absolute numbers. 5.1 million monthly social views against 3,081 lifetime trainees inference means the conversion from attention to programme completion is very low, or that the social reach is a separate product (awareness/stigma) that is not being measured against training at all. Either reading is instructive for MFC.

Schools presence

unknown, and probably minimal. No schools programme, school count, curriculum, or education-sector offer appeared anywhere on ALLKND's own about page or homepage. Its volunteer listings describe it as a youth mental-health charity, not a schools provider. What would verify: an ALLKND impact or annual report, or an education-sector listing (e.g. a state education department approved-provider register). None found this pass.

Funding and revenue

Revenue: unknown. ACNC register page not retrievable (JS-rendered). What would verify: ALLKND Limited's ACNC Annual Information Statement (an AIS for FY2022 is known to exist on the register), or an annual/impact report PDF on allknd.org — no such PDF was found this pass.

Named supporters public organisational claim — listed on allknd.org/about: lululemon, Siganto Foundation, Perpetual Foundation, Pinterest, Instagram, The Inspired Unemployed, Frank Body, Boring Without You, Four Pillars of the Community, Brightbox Consulting, plus individual donors.

inference That donor mix — two social platforms, several youth-culture consumer brands, two established foundations — is a brand-partnership funding model, not a government-contract or fee-for-service model. It fits the media-reach profile. It is also the most volatile funding base in this cluster: consumer-brand partnerships turn over fast.

Evidence base

Weak / unknown. No evaluation, trial, pre-post data, published paper, or independent review was found for Good Mate Training or Cause Club. The site says the course was "designed by mental health professionals" public organisational claim — that is a design-input claim, not an outcome claim. Testimonials are the only impact evidence displayed.

Relationship to the kindness evidence base: effectively none, in the technical sense. Despite the brand name, ALLKND is not running a kindness intervention (prosocial-acts-of-kindness research à la Curry et al., Nelson-Coffey et al.). It is running peer mental-health-literacy / gatekeeper training — a different literature entirely, closest to Mental Health First Aid. "Kindness" here is brand language, not a construct. inference, and a firm one.

Claims risk to note: "Australia's first digital peer-to-peer mental health first aid training certificate" is a first-mover claim, not an efficacy claim, and it sits close to the accredited Mental Health First Aid Australia trademark space. strategic hypothesis — a 60-minute unaccredited digital course carrying "mental health first aid certificate" language is a positioning MFC should study for what not to imitate: it borrows credibility from an accredited regime it is not part of. K-08 red-line thinking applies.

Construct claimed

"Being a better mate" / peer support capability / belonging / stigma reduction public organisational claim. No use of "mental fitness" language found. verified fact (absence across homepage and about page).

MFC overlap · difference · learning

WHERE MFC OVERLAPS inference - Both are Australian preventive (not clinical) mental-health charities working upstream of services. - Both teach a capability to people who are well, rather than treating people who are unwell. - Both use short, structured, non-clinical training as the delivery unit. - Both compete for the same brand-partnership and foundation philanthropy pool. - Both are founder-led with the founder as the primary public voice.

WHERE MFC DIFFERS inference - Direction of the skill. ALLKND teaches you to support someone else. MFC teaches you to train your own mental fitness. Other-directed vs self-directed — this is the cleanest differentiation in the whole cluster and MFC should use it. - Dosage architecture. ALLKND is one 60-minute one-off. MFC's model is repeated deliberate practice (Mental Reps) over time. MFC's entire theory of change is dosage; ALLKND's has no dosage. - Evidence discipline. MFC has a controlled evidence library, K-08 claim red lines, and a source register. ALLKND publishes testimonials. - Audience. ALLKND is explicitly Gen Z. MFC's current demand work is adult-facing. - Category. ALLKND is in mental-health-literacy. MFC is asserting mental fitness as a trainable-skill category.

WHAT MFC COULD LEARN strategic hypothesis - The free-front-door funnel is real and cheap. A free, 60-minute, certificate-issuing digital asset is a legitimate top-of-funnel for a charity with no budget. MFC has no equivalent free digital entry product; it has workshops. - Distribution before product. ALLKND built audience first and programme second. Whether or not that is the right order, it demonstrates that in this cluster attention is winnable by a tiny organisation with no evidence base. MFC's constraint is not credibility, it is reach. - The named-supporter wall is a credibility device, and it works on funders even though it proves nothing about outcomes. - The cautionary lesson is the more valuable one: ALLKND shows what MFC would look like if it optimised reach ahead of evidence. MFC's claims discipline is currently a competitive disadvantage on speed and a competitive advantage on durability. Naming that trade-off explicitly, rather than pretending it doesn't exist, is the honest position.

2. Kindness Factory (and The Kindness Curriculum)

Field Value
Founder Kath Koschel verified fact — kindnessfactory.com/about
Structure Not-for-profit, based in Australia and the USA public organisational claim
Commercial arm Kind Group — "The Culture Intelligence Company"; Koschel is Managing Director; profits stated to go to Kindness Factory public organisational claim (kindgroup.co)
Legal entity / ABN unknown — not verified this pass
Revenue unknown — verification route: ACNC AIS, or a Kindness Factory annual report PDF

What they do public organisational claim: run a global "acts of kindness" movement with a logging platform, and publish The Kindness Curriculum — a free downloadable SEL programme for schools, launched 2020, designed in partnership with Kaplan to cover early learning through Year 12. Three school offerings: Kindness Curriculum Activities (free download), a Kindness Curriculum SEL Program, and Kindness Keynotes (thekindnesscurriculum.com/education-offerings).

Reach public organisational claim, figures as reported in 2024–2025 coverage and on their own sites: - 3,500+ Australian schools have downloaded the free activities; 3,500+ schools across Australia, the USA and the UK in the wider claim. Note the ambiguity — the same 3,500 number is used both for Australia alone and for AU+US+UK combined across different pages. inference At least one of those statements is imprecise; do not cite either as settled. - 50,000+ total downloads. - 7 million+ acts of kindness recorded on the platform.

Download ≠ delivery. A downloaded free activity pack is the weakest possible reach metric — it counts intent, not dosage, not completion, not exposure. inference MFC should treat "3,500 schools" as 3,500 download events, and should never adopt a comparable metric itself.

Dosage: unknown. The free activities are self-selected by teachers; no prescribed session count, duration or sequence was found.

Evidence base — weak, plus a serious name-collision risk. - Kindness Factory describes its content as "evidence-based" and "research-informed," created by "academics and behavioural scientists," and says it funds research into kindness public organisational claim. No published, independent evaluation of the Kindness Factory Kindness Curriculum was found this pass. verified fact (absence, after targeted search). Reported outcomes are school feedback about "positive changes in behaviour" — uncontrolled, self-reported. - The collision: the other "Kindness Curriculum" is the Mindfulness-Based Kindness Curriculum (MBKC) from the UW-Madison Center for Healthy Minds. It is a different programme and it does have trials: - Flook et al., 2015 — RCT, n=68 preschoolers, 24 lessons over 12 weeks (~10 hours), delivered by mindfulness experts. Intervention group showed greater social competence, better sharing, higher report-card ratings; control group showed more selfish behaviour over time. Authors explicitly cautioned that larger studies were needed. PubMed 25383689 - Applied Multi-Site RCT, 2023, Mindfulness — 16 preschool/4K classrooms, 245 children (57.6% ethnically diverse, 69.8% low SES), teacher-delivered rather than expert-delivered. Teacher ratings favoured MBKC on social-emotional skills, executive function and academic skills. doi 10.1007/s12671-023-02210-8 - Caveat MFC must carry if it ever cites this: the 2023 results retrieved are teacher-rated outcomes in a study where teachers delivered the intervention and were not blind. That is a known inflation risk. Whether child- or parent-reported measures showed the same pattern, and what the effect sizes were, is unknown — the full text was paywalled at fetch time. Do not cite effect sizes for this study without reading it. - Wider field: a 2026 scoping review of interventions promoting kindness in primary schools exists (doi 10.1080/00221325.2026.2677924) — not read this pass, flagged as the highest-value single read for anyone building MFC's kindness evidence position. Earlier field commentary notes that beyond the MBKC work, school-based kindness programmes have largely not been systematically evaluated verified fact (as characterised in the literature surfaced).

Construct claimed: kindness as a teachable disposition, plus school culture and belonging public organisational claim. "Mental fitness" language: not found.

MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: same funder pool; same "teachable skill, not treatment" premise; both produce structured curriculum-style content for a non-clinical audience; both rely on a founder's story. DIFFERS inference: Kindness Factory's unit is a free downloadable resource with no dosage and no completion tracking; MFC's unit is a delivered workshop with defined practice. Kindness Factory targets K-12 school culture; MFC's current demand work is adult. Kindness Factory says "evidence-based" without a published evaluation; MFC's K-08 red lines would prohibit that exact sentence about its own material. LEARN strategic hypothesis: (a) free-to-download destroys distribution friction — 50,000 downloads with no sales team is a distribution result MFC cannot match through workshops alone; (b) the commercial-arm-funds-the-charity structure (Kind Group → Kindness Factory) is a funding model MFC should actively evaluate — a paid corporate/culture offer subsidising free community delivery is the most replicable thing in this file; (c) the warning: an unevaluated free resource at 3,500 schools has already occupied the schools-kindness shelf space. If MFC ever enters schools, the incumbent is not better evidenced — it is better distributed. Beat it on distribution, not on argument.

Exact 2025 duration and daily target: unknown — not captured this pass; verification route is the challenge's own rules page.

What they measure: participation, teams, communities, schools, push-ups, dollars raised. They do not publish outcome measurement. MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: the category term itself — this is a direct language collision, alongside the AIS Mental Fitness Program (file 03). Both MFC and Push-Up use the physical-training analogy as the core communication device. Both are non-clinical, both go into schools, both target the general well population. DIFFERS inference: Push-Up is an annual campaign with an awareness-and-fundraising theory of change; MFC is a capability-building programme with a practice theory of change. Push-Up delivers facts daily; MFC delivers reps. Push-Up measures participation; MFC intends to measure outcome. Push-Up's "fitness" is literal physical exercise used as a hook; MFC's "mental fitness" is a claim about trainability of a mental skill — and Push-Up's usage actively muddies MFC's, because it teaches 234,000 Australians a year that "mental fitness" means "doing push-ups for mental health." LEARN strategic hypothesis: (a) the countable daily unit (push-ups) is why this scales — a Mental Rep is MFC's equivalent and is currently far less countable; making reps countable is the single highest-leverage design borrow available; (b) team/community structure drives participation — 30,000 teams is a social-obligation engine, not a motivation engine; (c) schools came to them, via student ambassadors, not via a sales process; (d) the risk lesson: Push-Up proves you can reach a quarter of a million Australians annually while publishing zero outcome evidence. MFC's answer cannot be to match them on scale — it has to be to own the measurement ground they have vacated (see file 10, measurement white space).

4. Ending Loneliness Together

Field Value
What it is Australia's peak body on loneliness and social isolation; a national network of universities and industry partners public organisational claim (endingloneliness.com.au/about-us)
Started 2016 public organisational claim
Leadership Associate Professor Michelle Lim, CEO and Scientific Chair verified fact
Network size ~65 organisations public organisational claim
Revenue unknown — verification route: ACNC AIS / annual report. Publicly describes partner resource and in-kind support without figures

What they do and specialise in: research synthesis, national measurement, public campaigns and policy advocacy for a National Strategy to Address Loneliness. Assisting the Victorian, Queensland and South Australian governments on loneliness activity public organisational claim. Convenes Loneliness Awareness Week — first held August 2023; 2026 dates 3–9 August verified fact (lonelinessawarenessweek.com.au).

Their key data — this is the source MFC would cite: - State of the Nation Report on Social Connection, 2023 — survey of 4,000+ Australian adults. 32% (nearly 1 in 3) report being lonely; 17% (1 in 6) severely lonely. Loneliest age bands: 18–24 and 45–54. Rural 35% vs metro 30%. By jurisdiction: ACT 40%, Tas 37%, Qld 35%. public organisational claim (their own survey, self-published; report PDF) - Youth loneliness report, 2025 — "A call for connection: understanding and addressing youth loneliness in Australia." Over 2 in 5 young Australians experience loneliness; persistent loneliness linked to poorer mental and physical health, financial stress and social disconnection public organisational claim (PDF). - Moments Matter youth public-health campaign, launched August 2025 public organisational claim. - Qualitative research partner: Wallis public organisational claim.

Evidence quality: the strongest research capability in this cluster — university-embedded, methodologically literate, uses validated loneliness measures. But note: these are self-published organisational reports, not peer-reviewed papers. They are advocacy-adjacent. inference Cite them as "Ending Loneliness Together's 2023 national survey found…", never as "research shows…". Effect sizes are not applicable — these are prevalence estimates, not intervention trials.

Construct claimed: loneliness and social connection public organisational claim. "Mental fitness" language: not found.

MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: shared upstream-prevention worldview; loneliness is a plausible mediator of several outcomes MFC cares about; both need the same policy audience to accept that non-clinical intervention is worth funding. DIFFERS inference: ELT is a peak body and evidence broker — it does not deliver programmes; MFC delivers. ELT owns a problem definition; MFC owns a solution method. That makes ELT not a competitor but the single most useful potential ally in this file. LEARN strategic hypothesis: (a) owning the national number is enormous positional power — ELT is quoted every time an Australian journalist writes about loneliness, because it publishes the prevalence figure. MFC has no equivalent owned number for mental fitness. Creating a credible, repeatable national measure of mental-fitness practice would be worth more than any campaign; (b) the network-of-65 model buys legitimacy cheaply; (c) ELT's annual awareness week gives it a guaranteed yearly media moment — a structural asset MFC lacks; (d) practically: MFC should be in ELT's network and should cite its data properly rather than generating its own prevalence claims.

5. OneWave

Founded 2013, Bondi public organisational claim (onewaveisallittakes.com/about)
Model Non-profit surf community — "saltwater therapy," Fluro Friday beach gatherings with an "anti-bad-vibes circle" for sharing public organisational claim
Reach Fluro Friday at 200+ beaches in 50+ countries; Free the Funk school and workplace programmes have "impacted" 65,000+ people; the school programme specifically 45,000 young people across Australia and New Zealand public organisational claim
Revenue unknown. Donations are tax-deductible via the Australian Sports Foundation public organisational claim — i.e. it appears to rely on an auspicing arrangement rather than holding its own DGR. Verification route: Australian Sports Foundation reporting, or OneWave's own annual report
Dosage Fluro Friday is weekly, drop-in, unbounded. School programme dosage unknown
Evidence None found. No evaluation, published study or outcome measurement located verified fact (absence). "Impacted" is undefined
Construct Peer support, openness, stigma reduction, connection public organisational claim. "Mental fitness" language: not found

MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: both non-clinical, both build a repeatable ritual rather than a one-off, both go into schools and workplaces. DIFFERS inference: OneWave's mechanism is environment plus ritual plus disclosure; MFC's is taught skill plus deliberate practice. OneWave has no content to transfer; MFC's content is the product. OneWave's model is inherently place-bound (a beach); MFC's is portable. LEARN strategic hypothesis: weekly, same time, same place, free, no sign-up is the most durable engagement structure in this entire cluster — 13 years and 200 beaches on essentially no content. The lesson for MFC is that a recurring ritual out-survives a programme. MFC's workshop is an event; it has no weekly ritual. Designing one — even a low-content one — is a genuine strategic option. Second lesson: fluro clothing is a visual identity that makes the ritual visible and recruits by sight. MFC has no equivalent visible signal.

6. Live4Life (Youth Live4Life Inc.) — the evaluation benchmark

Field Value
Focus Rural and regional Victoria; youth mental health and suicide prevention; health promotion charity public organisational claim (live4life.org.au)
Model Community-led partnership between schools, councils, local services and community organisations, delivering accredited Mental Health First Aid training to students and community members public organisational claim
Footprint 13 rural Victorian communities public organisational claim
Cost to schools $5,250–$15,750 per year ex GST per school's contribution to full implementation cost public organisational claim
Revenue unknown — verification route: ACNC AIS / annual report
Evidence — the strongest in this file 12-month evaluation by Orygen; a two-year Victorian-Government-funded evaluation covering proof of concept, impact, transferability and SROI; an NHMRC-funded multi-community, multi-year external evaluation led by Prof. Nicola Reavley (University of Melbourne); and a peer-reviewed paper in Australian Psychologist, 2022 — doi 10.1080/00050067.2022.2158063 verified fact (existence of these; effect sizes and any null results unknown — full texts not read this pass)
Construct Mental health literacy, help-seeking, community capacity public organisational claim. "Mental fitness" language: not found

MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: both deliver structured training into schools and communities; both are non-clinical and preventive; both charge for delivery. DIFFERS inference: Live4Life is place-based and partnership-brokered — its product is arguably the local coalition, not the curriculum (the curriculum is licensed accredited MHFA). MFC's product is its own framework. Live4Life is suicide-prevention-framed; MFC is capability-framed. LEARN strategic hypothesis: this is the model for how a small Australian charity builds an unarguable evidence position — stack an academic partner (Orygen/Melbourne), a government-funded evaluation, an SROI, and a peer-reviewed publication, and you become procurement-eligible. That path is open to MFC and is more valuable than reach. Second: publishing the per-school price openly ($5,250–$15,750) is a procurement-maturity signal — it says "we are a purchasable service," which most charities in this cluster cannot say. MFC's school/organisation pricing posture should be deliberate, not absent.

7. zero2hero (WA)

Field Value
Focus Perth-based; empowering young people to manage their own mental health and wellbeing public organisational claim (zero2hero.com.au)
Programmes Camp Hero — a five-day camp covering resilience, compassion, leadership, self-worth, anxiety; Hero High — 45–60 minute presentations, standalone or as a series; suicide-prevention training public organisational claim
Reach, 2024 255 WA high schools; 23,666 students educated on mental health; 768 people trained in suicide prevention; 51,994 people impacted in 2024; 220,000+ over the last decade public organisational claim
Fundraising cape2cape trek — 200+ trekkers, $800,000+ raised (cumulative, year unknown) public organisational claim
Revenue unknown — verification route: ACNC AIS / annual report
Evidence None found this pass. No published evaluation located verified fact (absence)
Construct Self-management of mental health, resilience, leadership public organisational claim. "Mental fitness" language: not found

inference Note the internal gap in their own numbers: 23,666 students educated vs 51,994 impacted in the same year. "Impacted" is doing a lot of work — likely including event attendance and reach. Treat 23,666 as the defensible figure.

MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: the closest construct match in this file — zero2hero's stated aim, young people managing their own mental health, is self-directed capability, which is MFC's territory. Both use a tiered offer (short session → intensive). DIFFERS inference: zero2hero is single-state (WA) and youth-only; its intensive is a residential camp, which is a delivery form MFC does not have. MFC has an explicit framework and claims discipline; zero2hero's content model is unknown. LEARN strategic hypothesis: (a) the tiered ladder — 45-minute presentation as the entry, five-day camp as the deep product — is a clean architecture MFC could mirror (taster workshop → intensive); (b) regional dominance beats national thinness: 255 of WA's high schools is near-saturation of a single state, which is a far stronger procurement story than a scattered national footprint. MFC should consider winning one jurisdiction properly before spreading; (c) a signature fundraising expedition (cape2cape) creates an annual revenue ritual independent of programme income.

8. Raise Foundation

Field Value
Focus In-school youth mentoring for young people at risk of disengagement public organisational claim (raise.org.au)
Reach, 2025 2,753 young people across 189 school programs; plus 117 via Raise Digital public organisational claim
Outcomes targeted Resilience, school belonging, hope for the future, help-seeking public organisational claim
Revenue unknown — their 2025 impact report states audited financials to follow. Verification route: Raise's own annual report PDF (they publish one) or ACNC AIS
Evidence Annual internal evaluation, plus an independent evaluation commissioned by Raise using Federal Department of Health funding (outcome evaluation PDF); SROI of $4.37 returned per $1 invested public organisational claim. Listed in the Be You programs directory verified fact. Effect sizes and nulls unknown — reports not read this pass
Construct Belonging, resilience, help-seeking public organisational claim. "Mental fitness" language: not found

inference "Independent evaluation commissioned and funded by the organisation being evaluated" is standard sector practice but is not independence in the research sense. Be precise if citing. The Be You directory listing is the more useful credential — it is an external gatekeeper's judgement.

MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: schools channel; belonging and help-seeking as outcomes; annual published evaluation as a credibility engine. DIFFERS inference: Raise's mechanism is a trained volunteer mentor relationship over a school year — high-dosage, high-cost, relational. MFC's is taught skill plus self-practice — lower cost per head, scalable. Raise targets at-risk young people; MFC targets the general population. LEARN strategic hypothesis: (a) publish an evaluation report every single year, without exception — Raise's compounding credibility comes from the series, not any one report; (b) get listed in the external directories that gatekeepers actually check (Be You is the Australian one for schools) — this is cheap, and MFC is unknown on whether it is listed; (c) an SROI figure is the language funders and government buy in — MFC has no SROI. Commissioning one is a discrete, fundable piece of work.

9. Big Blue Table (Beyond Blue)

Field Value
What A fundraising and stigma campaign, not a programme: host a meal, have a conversation, raise funds. Run during Mental Health Month (October) public organisational claim (beyondblue.org.au)
Since 2019 public organisational claim
Reach 5,000+ participants since inception; nearly $1 million raised cumulatively public organisational claim
Owner Beyond Blue — a large national mental-health organisation. The campaign's own revenue is a Beyond Blue line item; unknown separately
Evidence None — it is a fundraising mechanic. No outcome claim to evaluate
Construct Stigma reduction through shared meals and conversation public organisational claim. "Mental fitness" language: not found

MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: minimal — shared-meal connection touches MFC's connection territory, but the theory of change is fundraising. DIFFERS inference: MFC teaches a skill; Big Blue Table creates an occasion. No delivery, no dosage, no content. LEARN strategic hypothesis: the host-your-own format costs the charity almost nothing per participant — supporters do the work and supply the venue, the food and the invitation list. Note the scale honestly though: 5,000 participants and ~$1M over 7 years is modest even with Beyond Blue's brand behind it. The lesson is that participant-hosted formats are cheap but not automatically large — MFC should not assume a host-your-own model would scale simply because it is low-cost.

10. Neighbours Every Day / Neighbour Day (Relationships Australia)

Field Value
What Relationships Australia's national social-connection campaign. Neighbour Day is the day of action, last Sunday of March; Neighbours Every Day is the year-round campaign it became public organisational claim (neighbourseveryday.org)
2025 framing Belonging for better mental health; cites nearly 1 in 3 Australians lonely and over 15% often or always lonely public organisational claim
Reach unknown — no participant count found. Verification route: Relationships Australia annual report
Revenue unknown — campaign is a Relationships Australia programme line
Evidence unknown / none found for the campaign's own effect. The loneliness statistics cited are drawn from the broader evidence base, not from campaign evaluation
Construct Belonging, neighbourhood connection public organisational claim. "Mental fitness" language: not found

MFC overlap · difference · learning

OVERLAP inference: both position connection as protective and both address a general, non-clinical population. DIFFERS inference: this is awareness-day infrastructure, run by a large established service provider as an adjunct to counselling services. MFC is a capability programme. LEARN strategic hypothesis: the day-to-campaign evolution is the notable move — Relationships Australia recognised that a single day produces a spike and nothing else, and rebuilt it as "every day." That is precisely MFC's own problem in miniature: a workshop is a Neighbour Day. The question MFC should take from this is "what is our every day?" — and the answer needs to be a designed artefact, not an aspiration.

11–12. Brief profiles

Friends For Good (Vic) — founded 2016, describes itself as Australia's first not-for-profit focused specifically on loneliness and social isolation public organisational claim (friendsforgood.org.au). Runs FriendLine, ArabicLine and MateLine — anonymous friendly-conversation phone lines — plus Walk for Good, a national local-walks programme. Associated with the Australian Loneliness Research Foundation public organisational claim. Revenue unknown; evidence unknown. Construct: loneliness. "Mental fitness": not found. Overlap inference: non-clinical, prevention, connection. Differs: befriending/service model, not skill-building; MFC teaches, Friends For Good listens. Learn strategic hypothesis: the anonymous, no-commitment, no-diagnosis entry point removes the identity cost of asking for help — MFC's offers all require someone to identify as wanting to improve, which is a higher barrier than it looks.

Groundswell Foundation — a foundation convening influential Australians personally affected by mental health and loneliness, to fund and drive better outcomes public organisational claim (groundswellfoundation.com.au). Revenue and grant programme unknown. Not a delivery competitor — a potential funder. inference Action: route to the funder-research workflow rather than treating as a competitor. Learn: its existence confirms loneliness now has a dedicated philanthropic vehicle in Australia — MFC framing that touches connection has a funding pathway it may not have mapped.

What I could not verify

  • Every charity revenue figure in this document. ACNC register pages are JS-rendered and returned no financial content. Routes: each charity's Annual Information Statement on the ACNC register (browser required), or an annual-report PDF on the organisation's own site. Priority order for a follow-up pass: Kindness Factory, The Push for Better Foundation, ALLKND, zero2hero, Raise.
  • ALLKND's revenue, staff count, schools presence, and any evaluation. No impact report or annual report PDF found on allknd.org.
  • ALLKND's homepage counters have no stated date range. They are live counters of unstated vintage.
  • Kindness Factory's legal entity, ABN and the true Australian-vs-global school count. The "3,500 schools" figure is used inconsistently for Australia alone and for AU+US+UK.
  • Effect sizes and null results for the MBKC 2023 multi-site RCT (paywalled), the Live4Life evaluations, and the Raise outcome evaluation. Existence verified; findings not read.
  • The 2026 scoping review of primary-school kindness interventions — identified, not read. Highest-value single follow-up read in this file.
  • The Push-Up Challenge's 2025 duration and daily push-up target, and The Push for Better Foundation's own revenue as distinct from funds raised for partners.
  • Neighbours Every Day participation numbers.
  • Whether MFC is listed in the Be You programs directory — not checked, and it is checkable.
  • The Man Walk, Good Karma Networks, Neighbourhood Connect, Two Good Co, Men's Sheds, parkrun Australia — surfaced or considered, not researched. Declared rather than implied.
