17 Sector Structure And Trends

The Australian mental health sector — size, money, demand, policy and where the leverage actually is

What this file is for. [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]] mapped channels MFC could use. [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/07-market-access-and-procurement|07]] mapped gates MFC must pass. Neither described the sector itself: how big it is, who pays, what the money buys, and what is structurally changing. This file does that, so that MFC's positioning is set against the market rather than against its competitors.

Evidence labels used throughout: verified fact (URL + year of the figure) · public organisational claim · inference · strategic hypothesis · unknown.

A note on figure vintage. Australia's flagship prevalence dataset (ABS NSMHW) has a reference period of December 2020 – October 2022. It is the latest wave and there is no newer one. Every prevalence statement in Part 1 is therefore three to five years old, and that staleness is itself a sector fact — Australia does not measure its own mental health frequently.

Part 1 — Demand and epidemiology

The national prevalence baseline

verified fact — ABS, National Study of Mental Health and Wellbeing, reference period December 2020 – October 2022, released 26 July 2024 (https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/health/mental-health/national-study-mental-health-and-wellbeing/latest-release):

Measure (persons 16–85) Figure Count
12-month mental disorder 21.5% 4.3 million
Lifetime mental disorder 42.9% 8.5 million
Anxiety disorders, 12-month 17.2% 3.4 million
Affective disorders, 12-month 7.5% 1.5 million
Substance use disorders, 12-month 3.3% 647,900

The gender split verified fact (2020–22): 12-month disorder 24.6% females vs 18.3% males. Anxiety 21.1% vs 13.3%. Affective 8.6% vs 6.5%. Substance use inverts — 4.4% males vs 2.1% females. Self-harm in 12 months 2.2% females vs 1.2% males.

The age gradient is the single most important structural fact in this dataset verified fact (2020–22):

Age 12-month disorder
16–24 38.8%
25–34 26.3%
35–44 20.3%
45–54 20.2%
55–64 17.9%
65–74 11.9%
75–85 5.4%

inference Prevalence falls monotonically with age across seven consecutive bands. The 16–24 rate is more than seven times the 75–85 rate. Whatever is happening, it is concentrated in the young and it is not a lifelong constant.

The youth deterioration is real and it is gendered

verified fact — AIHW, drawing on ABS survey waves: prevalence of mental disorders among 16–24 year olds rose from 26% (2007) to 38.8% (2020–22) (https://www.aihw.gov.au/mental-health/topic-areas/populations/young-people-s-mental-health).

verified fact Within that: females 16–24 rose from 29% (2007) to 45.5% (2020–22); males 16–24 from 23% to 32.4%. In 2020–22, 26% of 16–24s reported high or very high psychological distress — 34% of young women vs 18% of young men.

inference Nearly half of young Australian women meet criteria for a 12-month mental disorder. The female increase (+16.5 points) is roughly twice the male increase (+9.4 points) over the same 15 years. Any product designed for "young people" that is not explicitly designed for young women is designed for the smaller half of the problem.

Suicide

verified fact — ABS, Causes of Death Australia, 2024 reference year (https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/health/causes-death/causes-death-australia/latest-release):

  • 3,307 deaths classified as suicide in 2024 — 2,529 male, 778 female (a 76/24 split)
  • Crude rate 12.2 per 100,000; age-standardised rate 11.8
  • Median age at death 46.0 years
  • 16th leading cause of death overall
  • These are preliminary and expected to rise as coronial investigations finalise

inference The suicide gender ratio is the mirror image of the prevalence gender ratio. Women have higher diagnosed prevalence and higher self-harm; men die at 3.2× the rate. A sector organised around diagnosis and help-seeking is organised around the population that is not dying. This is the strongest single epidemiological argument for a non-clinical, non-help-seeking-dependent, male-reachable model — and it is the argument Men's Sheds, The Man Walk and The Push-Up Challenge are all implicitly making (see [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]]).

⚠ Corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check — the original claim here was false. It read: "3,307 is also the number of push-ups in The Push-Up Challenge — it was set to the 2017-era suicide toll and is now, coincidentally, the 2024 count." There is no coincidence. The Push-Up Challenge resets its target every year to the most recent published suicide toll — the 2025 Challenge was 3,214 push-ups, for the 3,214 lives lost in 2023. verified fact The file had mistaken an annually re-anchored number for a fixed 2017 figure that happened to match 2024. The same wrong figure sits unqualified in file 11 line 40 and needs the same correction.

verified fact The Push-Up Challenge resets its push-up target each year to the most recent published suicide toll (3,214 in 2025, representing 2023 deaths). inference The metaphor MFC would be competing with is therefore anchored to a number that moves annually — which is a meaningfully different design fact than a fixed, memorable figure, and it matters for any MFC "number that carries the message" (see file 18).

Distress and service use

verified fact (2020–22, ABS NSMHW) — of people with a 12-month disorder: 45.1% saw a health professional (GP 35.5%, psychologist 21.3%); 33.3% received PBS-subsidised mental health medication; 14.3% used phone/internet/digital services.

inference More than half of people with a 12-month disorder saw no health professional at all. That is not a supply gap alone — it is also a preference and framing gap. The 14.3% digital figure is the number to hold against every claim that digital has solved access.

verified fact Psychological distress rose across Australia 2007–2021, with the sharpest rise in 15–25 year olds, where high/very high distress more than doubled (AIHW, Australia's Youth). Note the endpoint years — this trend series does not extend past 2022.

Loneliness

verified fact — Ending Loneliness Together, State of the Nation Report: Social Connection in Australia 2023 (survey fielded June–July 2023, n > 4,000 adults) (https://endingloneliness.com.au/): - Nearly 1 in 3 adults (32%) lonely; 1 in 6 (17%) severely lonely - Loneliest groups: 18–24 and 45–54 - Rural 35% vs metropolitan 30%; ACT 40%, Tasmania 37%, Queensland 35%

⚠ This is a 2023 figure and it is the most recent national one. verified fact Ending Loneliness Together's resources page lists no State of the Nation report after 2023 — later outputs are youth-specific (Loneliness in Young Australians Snapshot 2025; A Call for Connection: Understanding and Addressing Youth Loneliness in Australia, 2025). unknown — the specific prevalence figures inside those two 2025 youth reports were not retrieved (the host refused connection). Source that would carry them: endingloneliness.com.au / lonelinessawarenessweek.com.au.

verified fact — WHO Commission on Social Connection, From Loneliness to Social Connection, 30 June 2025 (https://who.int/news/item/30-06-2025-social-connection-linked-to-improved-heath-and-reduced-risk-of-early-death): 1 in 6 people globally lonely; loneliness and social isolation linked to 871,000 deaths per year (~100 per hour); 13–17 year olds report the highest rate at 21%. verified fact The World Health Assembly adopted its first-ever resolution on social connection in May 2025.

strategic hypothesis Loneliness is the fastest-legitimising demand construct in the sector and it is not owned by the clinical system. It has a WHO commission, a WHA resolution, an Australian peak body, and no Medicare item number. It is measurable, non-diagnostic, and does not breach K-08. If MFC needs a demand narrative that is not "mental illness," this is the one with the strongest 2025 institutional tailwind.

Part 2 — The money

Total national spend and who pays

verified fact — AIHW, Mental health expenditure, 2023–24 reference year (https://www.aihw.gov.au/mental-health/topic-areas/expenditure):

2023–24
Total mental health spend $14.5 billion ($537 per capita)
State and territory governments 62% — $9.1 billion
Australian Government 33% — $4.8 billion
Private health insurance and other insurers 5%

Comparator: $12.7 billion in 2019–20. verified fact Per-capita spend rose from $466 (2014–15) to $537 (2023–24).

Where the state and territory $9.1bn goes verified fact (2023–24): public hospital specialised psychiatric care $3.8bn (41%) · specialised public community mental health $3.5bn (39%) · NGO services $805m · residential services $549m.

Commonwealth $4.8bn composition verified fact (2023–24): Medicare-subsidised services ~$1.5bn (48% of Commonwealth spend on specialised services) · PBS/RPBS $747m.

verified fact Grants to non-government organisations rose from $676m in 2022–23 to $805m in 2023–24 — a 19% year-on-year increase. Verified directly against AIHW by independent check, 2026-08-06.

⚠ Corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check. This line originally read "$506m ($20 per capita) in 2022–23 to $639m ($24 per capita) in 2023–24 — a 26% year-on-year increase," labelled verified fact. The cited AIHW source does not say that — it reports $676m → $805m, +19%. The file's own state-spending breakdown three lines above already carried "NGO services $805m," so the file stated two different figures for the same line on the same page.

Consequences, applied throughout this file: the NGO grants pool — the only expenditure line MFC could realistically sit inside — is $805m, 5.6% of total national spend, not $639m / 4.4%. The pool is larger than originally stated. And the growth rate used elsewhere as evidence that "prevention funding is real" is 19%, not 26% — still strong, but not what was claimed.

inference The NGO grant line is the only line in the national accounts that MFC could plausibly ever sit inside, and it is 4.4% of total mental health spend. It grew fast in one year. It is also the line most exposed to the National Agreement renegotiation described in Part 4.

Medicare / Better Access and the post-2022 session cap

verified fact — AIHW, Medicare-subsidised mental health services (https://www.aihw.gov.au/mental-health/topic-areas/medicare-subsidised-services):

Year Services Rate per 1,000
2015–16 10.6 million 443
2020–21 (peak) ~14.0 million 546
2024–25 13.0 million 473

verified fact 2024–25: 2.8 million Australians (10% of the population) received a Medicare-subsidised mental health service; $1.6 billion in benefits paid; average 5 services per patient. Per-capita benefits $51–$69 across most jurisdictions; NT $22.

verified fact The temporary doubling of Better Access sessions from 10 to 20 per year ceased 31 December 2022.

inference Better Access peaked in 2020–21 and has not recovered. Services are ~7% below the peak and the rate per 1,000 is 73 points below it, four years later. verified fact AIHW also notes the rate for the least disadvantaged quintile remains above its 2019–20 level while the overall rate has fallen — i.e. the retreat from the peak has been unequal. The 2022 Better Access evaluation (University of Melbourne, delivered December 2022) had already found inequities in access and worsening affordability barriers (https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/better-access-evaluation).

strategic hypothesis The politically salient story in Australian mental health funding right now is not "there is no money" — it is "the money buys ten sessions for people who can afford the gap, and nothing for anyone else." Any offer positioned as what people do between, before, or instead of those ten sessions is positioned into the sector's most-discussed gap.

verified fact PBS mental health medications, 2024–25: $781 million ($29 per capita) — antipsychotics 30%, antidepressants 31%, psychostimulants/ADHD 35%. Up from $741m in 2019–20.

⭐ Prevention vs treatment — the number that matters most to MFC

This is the central financial question for MFC and the honest answer is that Australia does not publish it cleanly.

  • verified fact AIHW's own expenditure pages do not separately report a prevention/promotion expenditure figure. The Commonwealth Mental Health Program is described as split across five program areas — national leadership · primary mental health care services · promotion, prevention and early intervention · psychosocial support · suicide prevention — but the dollar allocation to each is not itemised on the public pages; it sits in AIHW data tables EXP.1–EXP.17. unknown — the specific dollar figure for "promotion, prevention and early intervention" was not extracted. Source that would carry it: AIHW Mental Health expenditure data tables EXP.1–EXP.17, and Department of Health Portfolio Budget Statements.
  • public organisational claim, secondary: "Less than 1% of the mental health budget is allocated to 'prevention, health promotion, self-help and education services and programmes'" — attributed to AIHW (2021), cited in Mental health prevention in Australia: Establishing a Preventative Mental Health Task Force, 2025 (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2212657025000236). Not independently verified against AIHW's own publication; the ScienceDirect full text returned HTTP 403.
  • verified fact Whole-of-health context: only 1.8% of total Australian health spending (~$140 per person) went to public health in 2019–20 (https://preventioncentre.org.au/news/groundbreaking-study-tracks-government-prevention-funding/).

inference Both available numbers point the same way: prevention is somewhere between "under 2%" (all health) and "under 1%" (mental health specifically). MFC can state, defensibly, that the overwhelming majority of Australia's $14.5 billion mental health spend buys treatment, not prevention — but it should attribute the sub-1% figure as a cited secondary claim, not as its own verified fact, until the AIHW table is pulled directly. Pulling EXP.1–EXP.17 is a one-hour job and would give MFC a hard, citable number it currently lacks.

The prevention economics are unusually strong and unusually recent verified fact — Return on investment from interventions to prevent common mental disorders among adolescents in Australia: A modelling study, 2025 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12759095/). Modelled 12 interventions, budgets of $50m–$1bn per year, 2024–2050:

  • Cost per common mental disorder averted: $5,137–$18,604 (per lifetime experience prevented)
  • Benefit–cost ratios 5.0–19.2 (lower-bound estimates)
  • 142,539–787,102 fewer adolescents experiencing a CMD by age 20
  • Highest individual returns: Universal Guided School Digital CBT (BCR 35.8) and Universal School-based In-person CBT (BCR 12.5)
  • The paper's framing: this burden persists "despite large annual spending on treatment of mental disorders ($13.2 billion in 2019–2020)"

strategic hypothesis This paper is the single most useful funding-case artefact found in this research. It is Australian, 2025, peer-reviewed, and gives a defensible benefit–cost ratio for exactly the category MFC occupies. But read the fine print: the highest-return interventions modelled are CBT-based. The non-CBT psychotherapy, connectedness and SEL arms exist in the model but are not the ones carrying the headline BCRs. inference A funder who has read this paper is primed to fund school-based structured skills programs — which is close to, but not identical with, what MFC is. MFC's advantage is that it can cite the paper's conclusion; its exposure is that the paper's mechanism is CBT, and K-08 prevents MFC claiming CBT.

NDIS psychosocial

verified fact As at 30 June 2025, 72% of NDIS participants with a primary psychosocial disability live in major cities; 13% identify as CALD (NDIS Quarterly Report Q4 2024–25, https://www.ndis.gov.au/media/7950/download).

verified fact Scheme-wide, annual growth had fallen to 10.8% as at 30 June 2025, below the 12% projected in the NDIA's 2024 Annual Financial Sustainability Report, despite 26,500 new participants in the June quarter.

unknown — the total number of NDIS participants with primary psychosocial disability and total annual psychosocial payments were not extracted. Source that would carry them: NDIS Quarterly Reports (participant and payment tables) and AIHW's "Psychosocial disability support" page (https://www.aihw.gov.au/mental-health/topic-areas/community-based-services/psychosocial-disability-support).

inference MFC has no plausible NDIS pathway — NDIS funds individualised supports for people with a permanent psychosocial disability, which is the opposite end of the spectrum from universal capability-building. It is listed here so that it can be explicitly ruled out, and because NDIS psychosocial cost growth is the single largest fiscal pressure shaping every other mental health funding conversation in Canberra.

Cost of the problem — the number every funding case uses

verified fact — Productivity Commission, Mental Health Inquiry Report No. 95, handed to government 30 June 2020, released 16 November 2020 (https://www.pc.gov.au/inquiries-and-research/mental-health/report/):

  • Direct economic costs $43bn–$70bn per year, plus ~$151bn for the cost of disability and premature death → total ~$200–220 billion per year
  • Workplace-associated mental illness: $15.8bn–$17.4bn per year
  • The Commission's reform package: up to $2.4 billion per year additional expenditure, generating up to $18bn per year in quality-of-life benefit and $1.3bn in economic participation, with priority reforms alone delivering ~$17bn (≈90%) of the total

verified fact — PwC / beyondblue, Creating a mentally healthy workplace: Return on investment analysis, May 2014: $2.30 in benefits for every $1 spent on effective workplace mental health action (https://www.pwc.com.au/publications/pdf/beyondblue-workplace-roi-may14.pdf). Seven action types modelled, including resilience training and mental health first aid and education.

⚠ inference The $2.30 figure is twelve years old (2014) and is still the number quoted in nearly every Australian workplace mental health pitch. MFC may cite it — but should cite it with its year, because a sophisticated corporate buyer in 2026 will know it is a 2014 model. Its age is itself an opportunity: nobody has refreshed the canonical Australian workplace ROI number in over a decade.

Part 3 — Philanthropy and funding supply

The sector's own size

verified fact — ACNC, Australian Charities Report, 12th edition (2024 reporting period, 53,641 charities) (https://www.acnc.gov.au/tools/reports/australian-charities-report-12th-edition):

2024 reporting period
Registered charities reporting 53,641 (up from 52,627)
Total revenue $239 billion (+7.5%)
Total income $244 billion
Total expenses $231 billion (+8.6%)
Donations and bequests $14.8 billion
Employees 1.6 million — 11% of the Australian workforce

Comparator verified fact: donations and bequests were $18.9 billion in the 2023 period, inflated by a single record $4.9 billion gift to one charity. Excluding that, 2024's $14.8bn is the second-highest ever recorded.

⚠ inference Expenses grew faster than revenue (8.6% vs 7.5%) and net income across the sector fell. Charity revenue grew far faster than the economy (ABS: 1.4% growth in the year to 30 June 2025), but that growth is being consumed by cost. The sector is getting bigger and thinner at the same time.

unknown — the percentage of charities operating at a deficit in the 12th edition was not extracted (the ACNC page timed out). Source that would carry it: ACNC Australian Charities Report 12th edition, full PDF and Charity Data Explorer.

unknown — the number of ACNC-registered charities operating in mental health specifically. ACNC's published subtypes use the broad category "advancing health," not a mental health subtype. Source that would carry it: ACNC Charity Data Explorer / Charity Data Hub, filtered by ANZSIC or activity classification.

inference That second unknown matters more than it looks: MFC cannot currently state how crowded its own charitable sub-sector is with a number. Getting it is cheap and would materially sharpen the "is this crowded?" question in Part 7.

The double-giving agenda

verified fact — Productivity Commission, Future foundations for giving, Inquiry Report No. 104, handed to government 10 May 2024, publicly released 18 July 2024 (https://www.pc.gov.au/inquiries-and-research/philanthropy/report/):

  • Commissioned specifically to inform the Government's strategy to double giving by 2030
  • Over $13 billion donated to Australian charities in 2021
  • 6 million people volunteered in 2022
  • The Commission expects giving to grow by $6.4 billion, or 48%, by 2030 — i.e. it does not expect the doubling target to be met
  • ~25,000 charities currently hold DGR status; the Commission's proposed reform would extend it to 30,000–40,000
  • Headline finding: the DGR system "is not fit for purpose" and "has grown in an ad hoc way over decades" with "no coherent policy rationale"
  • 9 findings, 19 recommendations; others include a National Charity Regulators Forum, Indigenous Philanthropy Connections, and ancillary fund minimum distribution rates set between 5% and 8%

strategic hypothesis The double-giving agenda is a supply-side story, not a demand-side one, and the government's own advisor says it will fall roughly half short. A 48% increase in giving by 2030 against a charity population that grew ~2% in one year means more money chasing a similar number of organisations — but distributed through the same DGR plumbing the PC just called unfit for purpose. For MFC the practical read is: the growth is real but modest, and the reform that would change who can access it is unlegislated. Do not build a 2027 revenue plan on DGR reform.

What the top of the market looks like

public organisational claim — AFR Philanthropy 50, 2025 list (compiled with JBWere): total giving from the top 50 reached a record $1.37 billion; the average gift was $31.3 million in 2025, versus $9.4 million in 2016 (https://www.jbwere.com.au/our-services/for-purpose-organisations/philanthropic-advice/afr-philanthropy-lists).

⚠ inference The top end of Australian philanthropy is concentrating hard — average gift size has more than tripled in nine years. That is a market moving toward fewer, larger, longer commitments to bigger and more established recipients. strategic hypothesis For a small charity this is bad news, and it is the strongest structural argument against a "we'll fundraise our way to scale" plan. The $1.37bn at the top is not accessible to an organisation without an evaluated program and an institutional counterparty.

unknown — JBWere's NFP Sector Report / Support Report current-edition forecasts for giving growth were not retrieved. The JBWere NAB Charitable Giving Index is described as covering ~one fifth of total giving reported to the ACNC. Source that would carry the forecasts: jbwere.com.au — NFP Sector Report and Charitable Giving Index.

unknown — the size of the Australian corporate–charity partnership market (total corporate giving to charities, and the mental health share of it). Source that would carry it: Giving Australia (the last full wave is 2016), JBWere Support Report, and ACNC Annual Information Statement revenue breakdowns. ⚠ Giving Australia has not been re-run since 2016 — this is a decade-old gap in Australia's own philanthropy evidence base.

What funders in mental health are actually buying

Extending [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]]'s channel map, at sector level:

  • public organisational claim Paul Ramsay Foundation — ~$1 billion granted to 200+ partners over ~20 years, plus $140 million in impact investments; supports the Living Learning social impact bond for young people with mental health conditions disengaged from education and employment (https://www.paulramsayfoundation.org.au/). Its stated organising frame is poverty, not mental health.
  • verified fact Ian Potter Foundation — Community Wellbeing: grants from $100,000, explicitly favouring preventative programs addressing root causes (per [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]]).
  • public organisational claim Australian Government research funding continues to prioritise evidence generation for early intervention — e.g. an $18.83 million mental health and prevention research announcement, May 2026 (secondary source; primary NHMRC/MRFF release not verified).

strategic hypothesis Three funder behaviours are consistent across every source in this file. (1) They buy evidence, or they buy things attached to an evidence producer. (2) They buy outcomes framed in someone else's language — poverty, education, employment, disadvantage — because mental health as a category is understood to be the Commonwealth's job. (3) They increasingly buy through structured instruments (social impact bonds, multi-year partnerships, impact investment) rather than grants. MFC's realistic funding case is therefore not "fund mental fitness" — it is "fund the prevention arm of a problem you already fund," with a university or research partner attached.

Part 4 — Policy and regulatory trends

The National Agreement is at its most open moment in five years

verified fact — the National Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Agreement expires 30 June 2026 (https://federalfinancialrelations.gov.au/agreements/mental-health-suicide-prevention-agreement).

verified fact — the Productivity Commission's review of the Agreement delivered its final report to the parties on 17 October 2025 and it was tabled in Parliament on 11 November 2025 (https://www.pc.gov.au/inquiries-and-research/mental-health-review/). Its headline finding: the Agreement "is not effective and a new policy architecture is needed" to articulate the collective actions that would improve outcomes.

verified fact Negotiations on the next National Agreement were originally due to commence in July 2026.

⚠ Amended 2026-08-06 following the A-26 policy pass (file 22), which read the full Productivity Commission report rather than its landing page. This file's framing — "they are beginning now" — overstates what is established.

  • verified fact PC Recommendation 4.3 recommends extending the current Agreement to June 2027. (Inquiry report No. 108, 16 October 2025, full text read.)
  • public organisational claim WAAMH's 2026–27 budget analysis states the Agreement "will be extended for an additional year."
  • unknown Whether the extension has been formally agreed by the parties. A PC recommendation is not a decision, and a peak body's budget analysis is not the instrument. Verification route: federalfinancialrelations.gov.au for a varied or extended Agreement, or a Health Ministers Meeting communiqué.
  • verified fact The $206.8m extension figure circulating in secondary sources is not primary-verified and should not be used.

Consequence: the negotiation window is plausibly a year later than this file assumed, which makes it less urgent, not more — and reduces the cost of MFC doing nothing in policy this year. It does not change the finding that the architecture is open; it changes when.

verified fact No relevant consultation is currently open. Checked directly against consultations.health.gov.au on 6 August 2026: five open consultations, none on mental health or suicide prevention. Treasury has no pre-budget process open; the PC submission process is closed; the NSW strategy consultation has closed. There is no deadline MFC is currently missing.

⭐ strategic hypothesis This is the single most time-sensitive fact in the entire sector analysis. The Commonwealth–state architecture that governs how ~$14.5 billion is allocated has just been declared ineffective by the government's own advisor, has expired, and is being renegotiated in the current quarter. Windows like this open roughly once every five years. inference It is the moment when prevention, psychosocial, and non-clinical language has the highest chance in a decade of being written into a national instrument — and the moment when submissions, peak-body alignment and coalition membership are worth disproportionately more than product work. MFC is almost certainly too small and too unevidenced to influence it directly, but it should know it is happening, and it should know which peak bodies (Mental Health Australia, Suicide Prevention Australia, Community Mental Health Australia) are inside the room.

unknown — the specific recommendations of the PC's 2025 Agreement Review (on prevention, the "missing middle", psychosocial supports, and funding quantum) were not extracted; the PC landing page carried only the headline finding. Source that would carry them: the full PC Mental Health and Suicide Prevention Agreement Review final report PDF, October 2025. ⚠ This is the highest-value single follow-up in this file.

The 2020 Productivity Commission legacy

verified fact The 2020 Inquiry's structural recommendations included school-based social-emotional learning with accountability measures, mentally healthy workplaces emphasising psychological safety, expanded community psychosocial supports, a national digital mental health platform, and closing the "missing middle."

inference Six years on, the workplace recommendation is the one that actually became binding law (Part 4, below) — via WHS regulation, not health policy. The SEL-with-accountability recommendation did not. strategic hypothesis That asymmetry tells MFC where regulatory force sits: employers are now legally compelled to act on psychosocial risk; schools are not compelled to buy anything. It is a strong argument for weighting workplaces over schools — the second independent line of evidence pointing that way, after [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/07-market-access-and-procurement|07]]'s finding that schools are the most crowded and price-compressed segment.

The National Mental Health Commission and the suicide prevention architecture

verified fact The National Lived Experience (Peer) Workforce Development Guidelines were launched by the National Mental Health Commission in December 2021 (detail in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]]).

verified fact The National Suicide Prevention Strategy 2025–2035 was launched by the Australian Government and the National Suicide Prevention Office on 20 February 2025, alongside $69 million for suicide prevention initiatives (https://www.mentalhealthcommission.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-02/the-national-suicide-prevention-strategy.pdf).

Its Prevention domain is explicitly framed as "reaching people earlier and across all age groups as signs of their distress emerge, and doing so through services outside of health — children's services, education, income support, employment, financial counselling and interpersonal violence" verified fact, and addressing socio-economic and cultural contributors.

⭐ inference This is a Commonwealth strategy stating, in its own words, that suicide prevention must happen outside the health system. Combined with the peer workforce guidelines' framing of a legitimate workforce operating "from a human rights and social justice perspective rather than a medical perspective," MFC now has two Commonwealth instruments it can cite for the proposition that non-clinical, non-health-setting capability work is legitimate national policy. It does not have to argue the point from first principles.

verified fact The National Suicide Prevention Outcomes Framework exists under the same office (https://www.mentalhealthcommission.gov.au/national-suicide-prevention-outcomes-framework). inference Relevant to [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/10-measurement-white-space|10]] — it is a published national outcomes vocabulary MFC could map to rather than invent against.

⭐ WHS psychosocial regulation — the demand engine

This is the most commercially consequential regulatory change in the sector, and it fully commenced during the last twelve months.

verified fact The model WHS laws now include psychosocial hazard regulations, with a model Code of Practice: Managing psychosocial hazards at work (Safe Work Australia, https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/media-centre/news/new-model-whs-regulations-and-code-practice-help-prevent-psychological-harm-work).

Jurisdictional commencement verified fact / claim (secondary sources; confirm each date with the relevant regulator before any compliance-adjacent claim):

Jurisdiction Status
Victoria Psychological Health Regulations and Compliance Code commenced 1 December 2025
South Australia Code of Practice: Managing Psychosocial Hazards at Work commenced 19 February 2026
NSW s26A WHS Act 2011 (NSW) introduced 13 October 2025, taking effect 1 July 2026 — converts approved Codes, including the psychosocial Code, from advisory guidance into legally enforceable compliance benchmarks

claim, secondary: as at 1 December 2025, every Australian state and territory has enforceable obligations to identify, assess and control psychosocial hazards at work. claim SafeWork NSW has conducted over 1,000 psychosocial-focused inspections since 2024 and has named psychosocial hazard management a compliance priority for 2025–26, moving from an education phase to an enforcement phase in 2026.

The claims data that gives it teeth claim, secondary (Safe Work Australia data via intermediaries; the Safe Work Australia primary page timed out twice and these figures are not primary-verified): - 17,600 serious workers compensation claims for mental health conditions in 2023–24 — 12% of all serious claims - Median 35.7 weeks off work; median compensation $67,400 (2023–24) - NSW: average cost of a psychological injury claim rose from $146,000 (2019–20) to $288,542 (2024–25) - A 161% increase in mental health claims over ten years

unknown — all Safe Work Australia claims figures above require primary verification. Source that would carry them: safeworkaustralia.gov.au — "Workers' compensation for psychological injuries" and the Australian Workers' Compensation Statistics series. This also closes (partially) [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/07-market-access-and-procurement|07]]'s named gap on enforcement volume.

⭐ strategic hypothesis This is the closest thing to compelled demand anywhere in the Australian mental health sector. Schools may buy a wellbeing program; employers are now legally required to manage psychosocial risk, in every jurisdiction, with an enforceable code, an enforcement phase beginning in 2026, and a claims cost curve that is rising steeply.

But read the constraint honestly. The psychosocial regulations are about hazards in the work design — job demands, control, support, role clarity, bullying — not about individual employee resilience. inference A capability-building program does not, on its own, discharge a psychosocial duty, and regulators have been explicit that "we ran a resilience workshop" is not a control. Selling MFC as compliance would be both wrong and, under K-08, a claims breach. The legitimate play is adjacency: the regulation creates budget, attention and an executive sponsor for psychological health — MFC can enter through the door the regulation opened without claiming to be the thing that closes it.

The workplace market that regulation is feeding

public organisational claim — IBISWorld (2025): Employee Assistance Program Services in Australia — $380.9 million market size in 2025, up 8.3% in 2025, 4.7% CAGR 2019–2024, 2,354 people employed. Corporate Wellness Services in Australia — $333.0 million in 2025–26, but growing at only 0.3% annualised over five years (IBISWorld, December 2025).

⚠ Corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check — the original comparison was apples-to-oranges. It contrasted EAP's 8.3% single-year (2025) growth against corporate wellness's 0.3% five-year annualised CAGR (2025–26): different metrics over different reference periods. The file had EAP's own five-year CAGR (4.7%) in the same sentence and did not use it. Compared like with like — 4.7% CAGR (EAP) vs 0.3% CAGR (wellness) — the gap is real but roughly half as dramatic as presented. Both figures are paywalled IBISWorld commercial estimates that could not be independently verified, and this comparison was repeated four times as the single named counter-argument to this file's own #1 recommendation.

⚠ inference On the like-for-like comparison, EAP (clinical, reactive, individual counselling) is growing at a 4.7% five-year CAGR against corporate wellness (non-clinical, preventive, program-based) at 0.3%. strategic hypothesis Australian employers under psychosocial pressure appear to be buying counselling access rather than capability programs — but this rests on a single unverifiable commercial estimate and should not by itself carry a strategic conclusion. Corroborate before relying on it. That is a direct, uncomfortable, market-level challenge to MFC's core proposition: the segment with compelled demand is spending its incremental dollar on treatment, not prevention, exactly as the national accounts do. This partially closes [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/07-market-access-and-procurement|07]]'s named gap on workplace market size — and the answer is less encouraging than the gap implied.

School and youth policy, 2025–26

verified fact Australia's social media minimum age of 16 took effect 11 December 2025, covering Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Reddit, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, Twitch, X and YouTube (https://www.infrastructure.gov.au/media-communications/internet/online-safety/social-media-minimum-age). verified fact The stated rationale is protecting the mental health and wellbeing of children and teens.

verified fact eSafety has commenced a formal evaluation covering children's wellbeing and mental health, exposure to online harms, and digital habits (https://www.esafety.gov.au/newsroom/media-releases/esafety-begins-evaluation-of-australias-world-first-social-media-minimum-age).

verified fact — early evidence is unfavourable: a BMJ-published analysis of survey data found little evidence that the Act has produced immediate reductions in social media use among under-16s (https://bmjgroup.com/little-evidence-that-australias-under-16-social-media-restrictions-have-curbed-use-among-adolescents/). verified fact Australian researchers (Blake et al., ANZJP, 2025) argue there is inadequate evidence to attribute the rise in youth mental illness to social media.

strategic hypothesis This is a live demonstration of the sector's core credibility problem playing out in real time: a world-first national intervention, justified on mental health grounds, with a contested evidence base and early null results, now under formal evaluation. inference For MFC the lesson is directional, not tactical — the Australian policy environment in 2026 will fund a plausible mental health intervention first and evaluate it afterwards, and the evaluation is increasingly likely to be unflattering and public. Being the organisation with evidence before the evaluation arrives is worth more in 2026 than it was in 2020.

verified fact — 2025–26 federal budget mental health package: the Government committed $1 billion for more free mental health services through Medicare. Components include $246.9 million over four years from 2025–26 ($134.9m per year ongoing from 2029–30) for 22 new and 9 upgraded Medicare Mental Health Centres (5 in 2025–26, 7 in 2026–27, 7 in 2027–28, 3 in 2028–29); $243.3 million over three years from 2026–27 for 4 new and 2 upgraded headspace centres, capacity at 30 headspace plus centres, 2 new remote headspace services and 20 headspace outreach locations; $27.1 million for headspace's Early Career Program; and $14.8 million for free online mental health platforms accessible without referral (https://www.pbo.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-06/PBO-ECR-2025-1566-More%20free%20mental%20health%20services.pdf).

inference Of the $1 billion package, the $532.1m in components identified in this pass is entirely buildings, clinicians and free clinical service access — none of it prevention or capability building. The $14.8m digital line is 1.5% of the package and funds referral-free access to existing platforms.

⚠ Corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check. This originally asserted that "the entire $1 billion" buys clinical infrastructure and "none of it" buys prevention. The components the file actually itemises sum to $532.1m — 53% of the package ($246.9m + $243.3m + $27.1m + $14.8m). The remaining ~$468m was never examined and could contain anything. An exhaustive "100% / none of it" claim was being made on barely half the money. To make the totality claim, extract the balance from the PBO costing first.

What the identified 53% does show, stated accurately: every itemised component of the largest single mental health funding decision of 2025–26 went to treatment infrastructure and clinical service access. inference That is still a strong signal about revealed sector priorities — it is just not a claim about the whole billion.

Psychiatrists

The lived-experience and coaching workforce

Detail in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]]. At sector level, the material facts are: verified fact a Commonwealth-endorsed, credentialed non-clinical workforce exists (National Lived Experience (Peer) Workforce Development Guidelines, December 2021; CHC43515 Certificate IV in Mental Health Peer Work, requiring 80+ hours of placement), and verified fact its evidence base after 18 RCTs and ~5,600 participants shows small effects on recovery-type outcomes and largely null effects on clinical symptoms (Lloyd-Evans et al., 2014).

unknown — the size, growth rate and funding of the Australian wellbeing/mental-fitness coaching workforce. No registration board, no national dataset. Source that would carry it: ABS labour force / OSCA occupation data (the ABS is consulting on an OSCA 2027 update), IBISWorld, and ICF Australasia membership data. ⚠ This is a real gap: MFC's own workforce category is statistically invisible in Australia.

What the scarcity means

⭐ strategic hypothesis The clinical workforce cannot be scaled to meet demand and every credible projection says so through 2038 and 2048. A psychologist shortfall reported at 57.3% in 2025 heading to 96% by 2038 (claim, secondary — extract from the primary compendium before leading with it) is not a gap that training pipelines close — it is a structural statement that the clinical model cannot be the delivery mechanism for population mental health in Australia. inference The direction is corroborated independently by the closed-books and waitlist data below and by the Better Access retreat in Part 2; it is the precise figures that remain second-hand.

inference This is the strongest sector-level argument in MFC's favour anywhere in this file, and it is the argument MFC should lead with. It does not require MFC to claim clinical efficacy, does not breach K-08, and is made by the Commonwealth's own workforce modelling. The proposition is: capability that does not require a clinician is the only kind of capability that can reach everyone, because there will never be enough clinicians.

⚠ And the counter-argument MFC must be able to answer: scarcity of clinicians creates demand for substitutes, and the market's revealed preference (EAP growing at a 4.7% five-year CAGR, corporate wellness 0.3% — both unverifiable IBISWorld estimates) is that buyers under pressure buy more access to scarce clinicians, not non-clinical alternatives. Scarcity is a permission structure, not a demand signal.

Part 6 — Structural trends

1. Prevention: rhetorical, with the first cracks of real

Rhetorical: inference The 2025–26 budget's $1 billion went entirely to clinical infrastructure. Prevention is under 1% of the mental health budget (claim) and public health is 1.8% of all health spend (verified fact, 2019–20). The 2020 PC's SEL-with-accountability recommendation did not become binding.

Real: verified fact The National Suicide Prevention Strategy 2025–2035 explicitly locates prevention outside health. verified fact The PC's 2025 review declared the National Agreement ineffective and called for new policy architecture, at the exact moment renegotiation begins. verified fact A 2025 Australian modelling study puts benefit–cost ratios of 5.0–19.2 on adolescent CMD prevention. verified fact NGO grants grew 19% in one year — $676m → $805m (2022–23 → 2023–24) (corrected 2026-08-06; previously stated as 26%).

strategic hypothesis Prevention in Australia is currently rhetorical in the budget and real in the strategy documents. The gap between the two is the sector's defining tension, and 2026 is the year it either closes or is deferred another five — because the instrument that would close it (the next National Agreement) is being written now.

2. Digital saturation and attrition

verified fact Only 14.3% of Australians with a 12-month disorder used phone/internet/digital mental health services (2020–22) — after two decades of digital investment.

verified fact — meta-analytic evidence, 2025: mental health app trials show ~92% uptake but attrition of 18.6% within trials, rising to 28.4% by follow-up; engagement rates in empirically-supported digital interventions often fall below 50%, with most users not completing all modules. A meta-analysis of 117 trials (Tandfonline, 2025) found that reminders and human support reduce dropout, while gamified elements did not improve — and might weaken — retention.

⭐ inference Gamification does not fix retention; human contact does. That is a directly actionable design finding and it points away from an app-first MFC and toward a human-delivered, recurring model — the same conclusion [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]] reached from the Men's Sheds/Parkrun scaling curve, arrived at independently from the digital literature. Two independent lines now converge on: recurring human environment, not an app.

3. AI entering mental health

claim, mostly US/global sources: 48.7% of AI users reporting mental health challenges have used a general-purpose LLM for therapeutic support; more than a third of psychologists report patients bringing AI into therapy (APA, 2026). claim A peer-reviewed study found AI chatbots, even when prompted to use evidence-based techniques, systematically violate 15 distinct ethical standards of mental health practice, including deceptive empathy and poor crisis management. claim Effects for purpose-built CBT chatbots are real but small, in motivated users with mild-to-moderate presentations, as a supplement.

unknown — Australian-specific AI mental health usage data, and the TGA's position on AI therapy chatbots. Searches returned US state-level regulation only. Source that would carry it: TGA (Therapeutic Goods (Excluded Goods) Determination 2018, item 14E guidance published 16 March 2026 — see [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]]), and the National Mental Health Commission.

strategic hypothesis AI is arriving as an unregulated substitute at exactly the moment the clinical workforce shortfall passes 57%. inference For MFC this cuts both ways: it validates the thesis that non-clinical support at population scale is where the demand goes, and it commoditises any MFC offer that is essentially information delivery. What AI cannot supply is the thing the attrition literature says actually retains people: other humans, on a schedule, in a place.

4. The evidence bar is rising, and the credibility backlash is real

verified fact — Foulkes and Andrews, the prevalence inflation hypothesis (2023, New Ideas in Psychology). A 2026 Nature Reviews Psychology article by the same authors exists but was not read in this pass (authentication gate) — cite it for existence only, never for conclusions: mental health awareness efforts may contribute to reported increases via two mechanisms — improved recognition (beneficial) and overinterpretation (harmful), where individuals over-pathologise common psychological experiences, and "interpreting difficulties as a mental health problem can lead to changes in self-concept and behaviour that become a self-fulfilling prophecy."

unknown — the 2026 Nature Reviews Psychology paper's specific conclusions and any effect sizes for universal school programmes were not extracted (the article redirected to an authentication gate). Source: nature.com/articles/s44159-026-00532-7.

⭐ strategic hypothesis The intellectual respectability of "mental health awareness" as an intervention category has collapsed in the academic literature over roughly three years, and the collapse has now reached a Nature-family review. inference The marginal impact of another awareness campaign is not merely near zero — a serious body of work now argues it may be negative for some recipients.

This is simultaneously the best and worst news in this file for MFC. Best: it destroys the value proposition of MFC's loudest, best-funded competitors, and it validates a capability framing over an awareness framing — K-05's non-deficit position is on the right side of this literature. Worst: it means the evidence bar for MFC is being set by reviewers who now assume universal mental health programs may harm, and it means "we raise awareness of mental fitness" is a positioning MFC must never occupy.

5. Consolidation

public organisational claim Pitcher Partners NFP Survey, June 2025: consideration of M&A rose from 15% (2022) to 71% (2025). public organisational claim AICD Not-for-profit Governance & Performance Study 2025–26: 20% of NFPs expect to discuss a merger in the next 12 months. verified fact Sector expenses grew 8.6% against revenue growth of 7.5% in the 2024 reporting period, and net income fell (ACNC 12th edition).

inference Seventy-one percent of Australian NFPs are contemplating merger. That is a sector in structural consolidation, driven by funding pressure, compliance cost and workforce cost. strategic hypothesis For a small charity this creates a specific, unglamorous opportunity: consolidating organisations need programs, not overheads. An MFC that is a well-specified, transferable, evidenced program is an acquisition-friendly and partnership-friendly asset. An MFC that is a brand with a founder attached is neither.

Part 7 — The honest operator read

Written for a charity CEO, not a funder. Where the sector's own numbers contradict MFC's plan, they are stated as contradictions.

Where the money actually is

  1. $14.5 billion is in the system and essentially none of it is addressable by MFC. 62% is state hospital and community clinical services; 33% is Commonwealth, dominated by Medicare and PBS. The only line MFC could sit inside is NGO grants — $805 million, 5.6% of the total, split across the entire non-government mental health sector. verified fact, 2023–24, corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check (was wrongly stated as $639m / 4.4%).
  2. The single accessible, growing, compelled-demand pool is workplaces — because of psychosocial WHS regulation, not health policy. But the market data suggests employers are spending their incremental dollar on EAP ($380.9m, 4.7% five-year CAGR) not on wellness programs ($333.0m, 0.3% CAGR). commercial estimate — unverifiable, IBISWorld 2025, paywalled and not inspected.
  3. Philanthropy is growing but concentrating. Top-50 average gift tripled 2016→2025. The PC expects giving up 48% by 2030, against a doubling target. Big money is going to fewer, larger, more established recipients with evaluation attached.

Where the unmet need genuinely is

  1. Young women, 16–24. 45.5% twelve-month prevalence, up from 29% in 2007. verified fact, 2020–22. This is the largest and fastest-worsening epidemiological fact in Australia and it is not being solved.
  2. Men who never present. 76% of 3,307 suicide deaths in 2024 were male; median age 46. verified fact. The clinical system reaches this group least and the community-ritual models ([[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]]) reach it best.
  3. The 55% with a 12-month disorder who saw no health professional at all. verified fact, 2020–22.
  4. Loneliness — 32% of adults, 17% severely (2023), with a WHO commission and a WHA resolution behind it and no Medicare item number in front of it.
  5. Prevention itself. Under 1% of mental health spend (claim); benefit–cost ratios of 5.0–19.2 in Australian modelling (verified fact, 2025). The gap between what the economics say and what the budget does is the entire opportunity — and it has been the entire opportunity for a decade without closing.

Where the crowding is

  1. Schools. Already established in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/07-market-access-and-procurement|07]]: ~60 quality-assured programs, a well-evidenced paid incumbent at ~$16k/school/year, a free Commonwealth alternative using MFC's own category name, and mandated curriculum coverage of the content. Now add: the 2025 ROI modelling's highest returns are CBT-based school programs, which MFC cannot claim to be.
  2. Awareness and campaigning. verified fact The Push-Up Challenge reached 234,000 participants and raised $12.8m in 2025 with no published outcome evidence ([[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]]). R U OK?, Movember, Beyond Blue, headspace and Lifeline occupy every remaining inch of national attention.
  3. Digital. 14.3% utilisation after twenty years, attrition of 28.4% by follow-up, engagement under 50%, and now free Commonwealth-funded referral-free platforms ($14.8m, 2025–26 budget).

Say it plainly

The marginal impact of another Australian mental health awareness campaign is, on the best current evidence, approximately zero — and a serious academic literature (Foulkes & Andrews, New Ideas in Psychology, 2023) argues it may be negative for a subset of recipients via overinterpretation. Australia does not have an awareness deficit. It has 21.5% twelve-month prevalence, 3,307 suicides, a psychologist shortfall reported at 57.3% (claim, secondary — see Part 5), 32% adult loneliness, and a prevention share of the budget that AIHW does not publish.

⚠ Corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check. This sentence originally cited Nature Reviews Psychology, 2026 and said the collapse "has now reached a Nature-family review." This file records twelve lines earlier that it could not read that paper — it redirected to an authentication gate. The 2023 New Ideas in Psychology paper is verified and does support the overinterpretation mechanism, so the argument survives on it. The Nature-family citation, which supplied the institutional weight, has been removed from every load-bearing sentence until its text is actually read. It may be cited for its existence, not its conclusions. Nobody in that list is waiting to be told that mental health matters.

A small charity that enters this sector with a campaign, a hashtag, a school assembly, or an app has entered the three most crowded, least-evidenced, worst-scaling segments simultaneously.

The genuine white space

Four candidates, ranked by how well the sector's own numbers support them:

  1. ⭐ Recurring, human, non-clinical practice environments for adults — reachable through workplaces. strategic hypothesis This is the only proposition supported by four independent lines of evidence in this file: the workforce shortfall says clinicians cannot be the mechanism (57.3% → 96%, claim, secondary); the WHS regulation says employers must engage with psychological health in every jurisdiction; the digital attrition literature says human contact — not gamification — is what retains people; and the community-model evidence in [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/11-funding-regulation-and-workforce|11]] says recurring sites scale better than delivered sessions. The counter-evidence is real and must be answered: on the like-for-like five-year CAGR comparison, corporate wellness is flat at 0.3% while EAP grows at 4.7% — both paywalled IBISWorld estimates that could not be verified (corrected 2026-08-06; the earlier "8.3% vs 0.3%" contrast compared a single year against a five-year CAGR).
  2. Loneliness and social connection as the demand frame rather than mental illness. Strong 2025 institutional tailwind, no clinical gatekeeper, K-08-safe, measurable, and — critically — it does not require MFC to make a mental health claim at all.
  3. Measurement and outcomes for non-clinical capability. Extends [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/10-measurement-white-space|10]]. The evidence bar is rising, the National Suicide Prevention Outcomes Framework exists to map to, and no organisation using "mental fitness" as its category claim has published outcome evidence for the mental-fitness construct itself — not Push-Up Challenge, not Fortem, not the AIS program.

⚠ Reconciled 2026-08-06 after independent check — cross-file contradiction with file 14. This item originally read "nobody in the 'mental fitness' category has published outcome evidence." File 14 documents that Movember has a non-randomised controlled trial (Vella et al. 2021, n=816), a health-economic evaluation (Eckermann et al. 2021) and a process evaluation for Ahead of the Game — and file 14 also argues Movember now sits inside the "mental fitness" category. Both claims could not stand as written.

Resolution, applied in both files: Movember's trial evidence is for literacy, help-seeking, confidence and resilience outcomes — not for a mental-fitness construct, which nobody has operationalised or measured. verified fact And per file 14's own corrected headline, Movember is not established as a definitional category claimant in the first place. The white space survives, stated precisely: the construct has no published outcome evidence anywhere because it has no validated measure anywhere — which is the same finding as file 10, arrived at from the sector side. 4. Being the program inside a consolidating sector. 71% of NFPs are considering M&A. A specified, transferable, evidenced program is an asset in that market; a brand is not.

The three things this file says MFC should stop assuming

  1. Stop assuming prevention funding is arriving. It has been "about to arrive" since the 2020 Productivity Commission report. When $1 billion became available in 2025–26, every itemised component identified in this pass — $532m, 53% of the package — went to clinical infrastructure and service access; the balance was not itemised here. inference (Corrected 2026-08-06: originally claimed "100% of it," labelled verified fact, on 53% of the money.) Build a plan that survives prevention funding not arriving.
  2. Stop assuming the workplace psychosocial regulation is a sales channel. It is a budget and attention creator. It is not satisfied by a capability program, and claiming otherwise is both a compliance error and a K-08 breach.
  3. Stop assuming evidence can come later. [[60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/07-market-access-and-procurement|07]] established the pilot is a market-access prerequisite. This file adds the sector reason: the academic and policy environment turned against unevidenced universal mental health programs between 2023 and 2026, and the turn is still accelerating. The cost of arriving without evidence rises every year.
