18 Collective Participation Model

Collective participation models — mechanism, evidence, and design

The single most important finding in this file, stated up front. The Push-Up Challenge's own peer-reviewed evaluation (University of Melbourne, Journal of Prevention, 2025) found that physical activity gains were not maintained at three months (d = −0.02), resilience returned to no significant change (d = −0.04), and social connection returned to no significant change (d = 0.01) — from a starting sample of 29,069 down to 4,346 at follow-up. verified fact — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12858552/

The best-executed, best-funded, most-loved mass-participation mental-health challenge in Australia produces reach, destigmatisation and a very small wellbeing effect — and essentially no maintained behaviour. If MFC builds a challenge, it must be built knowing that time-bound challenges reliably deliver attention and reliably fail to deliver practice. MFC's entire product problem (K-07's "Build It" stage — the knowing-doing gap) is a maintenance problem. A challenge is a reach instrument. They are not the same tool and should not be conflated.

PART 1 — Deconstructing the working cases

1.1 The Push-Up Challenge (AU) — the number-as-message device

Element Finding Label
2026 rep target 3,307 push-ups over 3–26 June — one for every Australian life lost to suicide in 2024 verified fact — https://headspace.org.au/our-impact/campaigns/push-up-challenge/
2025 rep target 3,214 — lives lost in 2023 verified fact — https://lifelinedirect.org.au/bondi/news/pushupchallenge-schools-2025
2026 participation 230,000+ participants, 330m+ push-ups, $13m raised public organisational claim — https://www.thepushupchallenge.com.au/impact/our-impact
Cumulative 1 billion push-ups, 1 million participants, $80m raised since 2017 public organisational claim — same source
Students 40,000+ students; 614 Student Ambassadors trained public organisational claim — same source
Cost to participate Free. "It doesn't cost anything to do something great for the physical and mental fitness of your students and teachers." verified fact — https://www.thepushupchallenge.com.au/challenge/schools
Fundraising Optional, not a condition of participation verified fact — same source
Education payload A daily Mental Health Fact delivered alongside the day's rep target verified fact — same source
Teacher resources Free Canva templates, free mental-health awareness training for educators, classroom activities co-developed with headspace (Stress Bucket, Healthy Headspace Chatterbox, bingo, flyers) verified fact — https://www.thepushupchallenge.com.au/challenge/teachers

The number-as-message device, precisely. The target is not a fitness target. It is a fact delivered through the body: you do not read the suicide statistic, you perform it, once per rep, for 23 days. The daily target changes each day, so the number is re-encountered daily rather than stated once. This is the highest-leverage single design element in the entire case set — it converts a statistic (forgettable) into an embodied duration (memorable), and it does so without a single minute of instruction. inference — the mechanism is not described in these terms by the organisation; the components are all verified above, the synthesis is mine.

What it actually measures. Reps logged (self-reported into an app), dollars raised, participant counts, and post-event survey items (destigmatisation, conversations had, connection felt). verified fact — impact page above. Note carefully: it does not measure any mental-fitness capability. Its own evaluation had to bolt on validated instruments from outside the product.

1.2 Why it gets into schools when a wellbeing curriculum programme has to fight for a slot

This was the founder's actual question, so it gets a direct, verified answer.

Verified negative finding, and it is the important one: the Push-Up Challenge's own Schools and Teachers pages make no curriculum-alignment claim at all. No Australian Curriculum codes, no HPE mapping, no lesson-plan sequence, no stated time requirement. verified fact — both pages fetched 2026-08-06, checked specifically for this. The classroom resources are explicitly framed as usable "at any time of the year," i.e. not as a scheduled unit.

So the mechanism is not curriculum alignment. The mechanism is that it does not need a slot.

The barrier a wellbeing programme faces in Australian schools is verified and severe: wellbeing expectations are spread across multiple curriculum documents and frameworks with no single planning route; teachers are asked to deliver sensitive discussion-based content with limited time, varying confidence and inconsistent resources; ~70% of Australian teachers report unmanageable workloads. verified fact — https://www.aitsl.edu.au/research/spotlights/wellbeing-in-australian-schools and https://www.aeufederal.org.au/news-media/news/2025/students-and-teachers-need-better-wellbeing-support

A curriculum wellbeing programme must win four separate fights: a timetable slot, teacher confidence, professional development, and budget. The Push-Up Challenge wins by not entering any of those four contests:

  1. It has no slot to defend. Push-ups happen in the space schools already have — before class, at recess, in sport, in PE warm-up, at assembly, in house competition. It parasitises existing structure rather than requesting new structure. inference
  2. Zero teacher preparation, because the activity is self-explanatory. No teacher has to be confident about mental health to supervise push-ups. The education payload is a one-sentence daily fact, which requires no facilitation skill. inference from the verified resource list.
  3. Free. No budget line, therefore no procurement, therefore no approval chain. verified fact
  4. Students run it. 614 Student Ambassadors — the labour is transferred off staff. public organisational claim
  5. It is an event, not a programme. Events are approved by a principal in one conversation; programmes go to a curriculum committee. inference
  6. Fundraising benefit to the school itself: unknown. I could not verify any rebate, commission or retained-funds arrangement for participating schools. Do not assume there is one.

The transferable rule, and the trap inside it: a mass-participation programme enters schools by requiring nothing of teachers and no time of its own. The trap for MFC is that the Push-Up Challenge can do this only because the activity is physical. Physical activity has pre-existing school infrastructure (PE, sport, house systems) that a challenge can attach to for free. A Mental Rep has no such host structure. There is no timetabled period in which internal skill practice already happens. This is the single hardest structural fact in this study, and no amount of design cleverness removes it. inference, and I hold it with high confidence.

1.3 Movember — the socially costly visible signal

The moustache is a costly, unavoidable, time-bound public signal. Its properties, in mechanism terms: it cannot be hidden; it degrades the wearer's appearance (the cost is what makes it credible); it changes daily, so it re-prompts conversation for 30 days rather than once; and it forces the wearer to explain it — the explanation is the intervention, not the moustache. inference; the underlying components (conversation-starter function, visible commitment, free registration, personal "Mo Space" fundraising page) are public organisational claim — https://us.movember.com/support-us/grow

Why it repeats annually where the Ice Bucket Challenge did not: Movember has a fixed calendar slot, a re-enterable role (you can be a Mo Bro again next year), a team structure, and a signal that must be rebuilt each year from a shaved face. inference

1.4 R U OK? Day — the failure mode MFC must avoid, stated precisely

The 2019 peer-reviewed evaluation is genuinely positive on reach and intention: campaign awareness 66%→78% and participation 19%→32% between 2014 and 2017; highest-exposure respondents were ~3× more likely to intend helping actions and up to ~6× more likely to report having reached out; odds ratios 1.35–6.45. verified fact — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6744695/ (cross-sectional survey, n = 2,013, weighted).

And here is the finding that matters for MFC, in the authors' own words: knowledge of how to start a conversation using R U OK?'s own four steps was not measured. verified fact — same source; the authors recommend future evaluations include it.

So the most successful mental-health participation campaign in Australia has, after more than a decade, published evidence that it moves belief, intention and reported behaviour — and no published evidence that it moves capability. That is not a criticism of R U OK?; it is a structural property of peak-day awareness models. It is also precisely MFC's stated point of difference under K-05 ("mental health is how we are doing; mental fitness is what we are able to do"). If MFC builds a challenge that measures participation and conversations, MFC has built R U OK? Day with extra steps.

1.5 The durable counter-model: parkrun

Element Finding Label
12-month retention 63% — cited in the same review against 3.7% for unsupervised gym membership and 51% for community exercise classes. ⚠ Not a like-for-like benchmark — see note below verified fact that the review makes this comparison; inference that the figures are comparable
Model Free, weekly, same time, same place, volunteer-run, timed but explicitly non-competitive verified fact — same source
Reach 25% previous non-runners (UK), 15% (AU); engages people with mental health difficulties and chronic illness verified fact — same source
Mechanism, per the review Free low-demand participation; diversity of ability; non-competitive social environment; green space; volunteer-run structure enabling reciprocity and community ownership; weekly consistency providing routine verified fact — same source
Equity limitation Participants skew higher socioeconomic status, predominantly white and English-speaking verified fact — same source

⚠ Added 2026-08-06 after independent check — do not use 63% as a target. The three retention figures are individually accurate and the cited review does make the comparison itself, but they come from three unrelated studies with different populations, eras and definitions of retention: Stevinson & Hickson (2014), UK parkrunners; Sperandei et al. (2016), Brazilian gym joiners; Ecclestone (1998), seniors' exercise classes. verified fact

This file originally offered 63% as "a real, published comparator to be judged against." It is not a benchmark — it is an illustrative contrast, and committing MFC to a retention target derived from an apples-to-oranges comparison would set a number the design cannot fairly be held to. inference The qualitative lesson below is what this case supports, and it is the valuable part.

The design contrast that should govern MFC's choice. parkrun is recurring, indefinite, local, volunteer-owned, and rewards participation rather than performance. The review explicitly notes the model "aligns with evidence demonstrating the value of rewarding participation rather than performance." That is an almost exact structural match for Mental Rep's outcome-independent counting rule (K-07: "the outcome does not determine whether it counts"). parkrun is the closest existing analogue to what MFC's own framework logically implies — and it is nothing like a challenge.

1.6 Temporary-abstinence challenges — the one place maintenance evidence actually exists

Dry January / Dry July / FebFast are the only case class in this study with real post-challenge maintenance data:

  • At 6-month follow-up, successful participants: AUDIT-C 8.89 → 6.72; drinking days d = 0.53; drinks per drinking day d = 0.25; drunkenness frequency d = 0.40. Even unsuccessful participants improved (AUDIT-C 6.82 → 6.18; drinking days d = 0.45). verified fact — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8895623/
  • FebFast: 51% self-reported reducing drinking frequency ~4 months post-event. verified fact — same scoping review.
  • The review's own limitations: non-randomised, self-selected (skewing female, higher education, higher income), self-report, inconsistent attrition control, UK-dominated, "general paucity of studies." verified fact — same source.

Why abstinence challenges maintain and push-up challenges do not. inference, offered as the sharpest mechanistic hypothesis in this file: an abstinence challenge changes a standing rule about a recurring situation ("when offered a drink, I decline"), which is rehearsed dozens of times in the person's ordinary environment. A push-up challenge adds a novel behaviour requiring a novel occasion, which disappears when the occasion does. Lally et al. 2010's condition for habit formation — repetition of the same response in a stable context — is satisfied by the first and violated by the second.

This matters enormously for MFC, because a Mental Rep is structurally an abstinence-type behaviour, not a push-up-type behaviour: it is a different response to a situation that was going to happen anyway. K-07's Radar ("choosing which moments to work on") is literally a stable-context selection instrument. MFC's own architecture is already on the right side of this line. That is the strongest single asset MFC brings to this design problem.

1.7 Ice Bucket Challenge, streaks, and the rest, briefly

  • Ice Bucket Challenge — why it never became a practice. It had no repeatable role, no calendar slot, no team, and no second act; the nomination mechanic is terminal (once you've been nominated and done it, the loop closes). Analyses note only about one in five videos mentioned the disease at all, and that commentators explicitly contrasted it with Movember's repeat-participation model. verified fact (that these analyses exist and say this) — https://csic.georgetown.edu/magazine/slacktivism-at-its-finest/ and https://gnovisjournal.georgetown.edu/the-gnovis-blog/transforming-slacktivism-to-collective-activism-the-als-ice-bucket-challenge/ Whether virality can be engineered at all: the commentary describes it as "a viral lottery." public commentary, and I treat deliberate replication as unknown/not achievable by design.
  • Steptember. 28 days, teams of four, free registration, 10,000 steps/day or equivalent converted from 60+ activities (an accessibility design worth noting — the unit is effort, not steps). verified fact — https://www.steptember.org.au/home-challenge. Caution: the same page carries "20 million Aussies have already taken part," which is not plausible against Australia's population; treat all Steptember participation figures as unknown pending direct verification. Flagged deliberately — an unchallenged implausible number is exactly the kind of thing that gets repeated into MFC's own copy.
  • Streaks (Duolingo-style). Streaks work through loss aversion, not positive motivation, and the documented failure mode is that a broken streak destroys the identity the streak was building and triggers abandonment. public commentary / practitioner analysis — https://thedecisionlab.com/insights/consumer-insights/streak-creep-the-perils-of-too-much-gamification Peer-reviewed position on points/levels/leaderboards is genuinely mixed: Mekler et al. found they raised performance without affecting perceived autonomy, competence or intrinsic motivation (https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/2583008.2583017); a 2023 meta-analysis found gamification improved perceived autonomy and relatedness but did not satisfy competence needs better than non-gamified conditions (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11423-023-10337-7). SDT's own rule is the usable one: rewards perceived as controlling undermine autonomy; rewards perceived as informational support competence.
  • Mental Health Awareness Week models. Same structural class as R U OK? Day — see 1.4.

PART 2 — The evidence on why these work, and where it runs out

Social identity and group membership. Groups 4 Health (Haslam, Cruwys, Jetten et al.) is the strongest available evidence that building group membership itself is an active mental-health ingredient rather than a delivery convenience: RCT (n = 120) found G4H outperformed treatment-as-usual on social anxiety and multiple group membership; a later phase-3 non-inferiority trial compared G4H against CBT for depression and loneliness in young people with 12-month follow-up. verified fact (that these trials exist and report this) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26828756/ and https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/the-british-journal-of-psychiatry/article/groups-4-health-versus-cognitivebehavioural-therapy-for-depression-and-loneliness-in-young-people-randomised-phase-3-noninferiority-trial-with-12month-followup/E13DEFE06AB6B510E4E3356E780D0CDB Design implication: the team in a team challenge is not packaging. It is plausibly the most evidence-backed component available to MFC — provided the team persists past the challenge. A 30-day team that dissolves on day 31 has built nothing G4H would recognise. inference

Social contagion. Fowler & Christakis 2008 (BMJ 337:a2338) is already a registered vault source (10-sources/2026-08-06-fowler-christakis-2008-happiness-social-networks.md) and supports the "we don't practise in a vacuum" framing. Note the standard methodological caution: network-contagion estimates from Framingham are contested on confounding/homophily grounds. Treat as supporting rationale, not proof of a causal spread mechanism. inference

Public commitment and observability. Observability strengthens commitment devices — publicly labelled savings accounts raised savings 18–25% versus control, with private labelling ineffective for average savers. verified fact (as reported) — https://www.researchgate.net/publication/305695524_Observability_Increases_the_Demand_for_Commitment_Devices But the same literature supplies the countervailing finding: self-report under conditions of social evaluation is systematically distorted by social desirability, and anonymity produces more authentic self-report. verified fact — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11611177/ and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3090315/ Observability buys adherence and costs data integrity. For a self-reported internal act, that trade is much worse than for push-ups.

Habit formation. Lally et al. 2010: median 66 days to 95% of the automaticity plateau, range 18–254 days; missing an occasional repetition did not materially impair formation. verified fact — registered in-vault at 10-sources/2026-08-06-lally-et-al-2010-how-habits-formed.md.

Two consequences, both uncomfortable and both decision-relevant:

  1. A 23-to-30-day challenge does not clear the habit-formation bar for a median person. It is roughly 40% of the median. Any MFC challenge that promises a formed habit in a month would be making a claim its own registered evidence contradicts. Under K-08 that is not merely a stretch, it is the wrong side of a red line.
  2. The "missing an occasional repetition doesn't matter" finding directly contradicts streak mechanics. Streaks punish exactly the thing habit science says is harmless. MFC should not use an unbroken-streak mechanic. This is a rare case where the evidence gives a clean, unambiguous design instruction.

Post-challenge maintenance — the honest bottom line. Across the case set: strong maintenance evidence exists only for temporary-abstinence challenges, and even that is non-randomised and self-selected. For fitness/step/rep challenges, the best available evidence is the Push-Up Challenge's own evaluation, and it shows physical activity gains gone by three months (d = −0.02). verified fact — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12858552/ For peak-day awareness campaigns, capability was never measured. verified fact — §1.4.

Stated plainly, because it is itself the finding: there is no published evidence known to this study that a time-bound mass-participation challenge produces maintained skill practice. The one model with strong retention evidence (parkrun, 63% at 12 months) is not a challenge at all.

PART 3 — The hard design problem

A push-up is observable, countable, verifiable and unambiguous. A Mental Rep is none of these. Worse, it is defined as outcome-independent: K-07's locked wording is "The outcome does not determine whether it counts." Working through each consequence honestly:

3.1 Making an internal act visible without corrupting it

There are only four structural options, and three of them fail:

Option What it does Verdict
Publish the count Person reports "7 reps today" publicly Fails. Unverifiable, inflatable, and rewards the number rather than the noticing.
Publish the content Person shares what the moment was Fails hard. This is disclosure, and in schools it collides directly with K-08 safety rule 6 (do not force disclosure or public sharing) and with C-16.
Publish the commitment, not the count Person publicly names which moment they are working on, and their team knows Viable. Movember's actual mechanism: the visible thing is the commitment, not the performance.
Publish nothing; make the practice collective in time and place Everyone does it together, presence is the visible unit Viable, and strongest. parkrun's mechanism. Presence is verifiable, non-inflatable, and carries no disclosure.

The generalisable rule I would put to Hunter: make the commitment and the co-presence public; keep the count and the content private. inference, and it is the central design conclusion of this file.

3.2 Counting something only the person can see

You cannot. Any self-reported private count is inflatable, and the observability literature says the social pressure that drives adherence is the same pressure that drives inflation (§2). Three honest responses:

  1. Don't count reps publicly at all. Count sessions attended or moments named — externally verifiable proxies.
  2. If reps are counted, count them privately and never rank them. Private counting is informational (SDT-compatible); public ranking is controlling.
  3. Accept and state that any aggregate rep figure MFC publishes is a self-reported participation metric, not an outcome measure. The Push-Up Challenge can say "330 million push-ups" with a straight face because push-ups are real even if miscounted. "2 million Mental Reps" would be a number MFC could not defend if a journalist or funder asked how it knows. Under K-08's claim discipline that is a live reputational exposure, not a hypothetical one.

3.3 Does public competition break the outcome-independent principle?

Yes, and directly. This is not a soft risk, it is a definitional contradiction. The moment reps are ranked, the highest-status participant is the one who reports most, and the person who tried and it went badly is at the bottom of a list — despite K-07 stating that their attempt counts equally. A leaderboard silently converts an outcome-independent unit into an outcome-dependent one by substituting quantity for quality of outcome. It is the same corruption in a different currency.

A related governance point — stated as an inference, not a hard stop. K-08 clinical and inclusion safety rule 7 states "Do not make the State Check mandatory, scored, public, or performance-based." verified fact — 00-foundations/K-08-claims-red-lines.md.

Corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check. This paragraph previously called a leaderboard "a hard stop rather than a judgement call" and instructed that any leaderboard design "must be treated as breaching K-08." That overreached. Rule 7 governs the State Check specifically, not rep counts — and K-07's counting rule confirms a rep may be counted without an explicit Shift step. Ranking rep counts does not, on its face, make the State Check mandatory, scored or public. Telling Hunter a design option is governance-blocked when it is in fact his call is exactly the kind of false constraint this system is supposed to avoid. inference

The accurate position: a leaderboard is not established as a K-08 rule 7 breach, but it sits close enough to rule 7's intent that clinical governance should rule on it before any build. strategic hypothesis The decisive objection is the one already made immediately above and needs no governance overreach to carry it: ranking rep counts contradicts Mental Rep's own locked outcome-independent definition. That argument stands on K-07 alone.

3.4 SDT risk

Yes — and the mitigation is known. SDT's operative distinction is controlling versus informational feedback (§1.7). Team-level, non-ranked, participation-based feedback is informational. Individual ranked leaderboards are controlling. The 2023 meta-analysis finding that gamification improved autonomy and relatedness but not competence is the relevant one here: the parts of gamification that help are the social/belonging parts, which MFC can have without a leaderboard.

3.5 Safeguarding

Two things must be said plainly.

First, the blocking control-state fact. K-08 records C-16: youth/schools "Blocked until youth process reviewed"; external use "No until reviewed"; "Mandatory reporting/duty-of-care detail needed"; no named safeguarding lead (BD-05, pending). Every red-line claim in K-08 is itself unapproved (C-15/C-24, all eight board decisions pending). verified fact — 00-foundations/K-08-claims-red-lines.md. MFC currently has no authority to run anything participant-facing in schools. That is not my opinion; it is the vault's own recorded state. D-0016's six safeguarding matters also remain open.

Second, what a mental-fitness challenge creates that a push-up challenge does not. A push-up challenge in a school delivers a one-sentence fact and a physical act; disclosure risk is incidental. A challenge that asks students to notice and work with their own difficult moments manufactures disclosure occasions by design, at scale, supervised by teachers who have had no training. The research-safeguarding literature's standard requirements — disclosure limits communicated in advance via information sheets, transparency about when confidentiality will be broken, all disclosures recorded and routed to a safeguarding team, parent consent, staff briefed during recruitment — are what a competent version of this would require. verified fact (that these are the stated requirements) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10910574/ Note that the Push-Up Challenge itself does not appear to publish a safeguarding protocol on its schools pages; a "Mental health support" footer link was the only visible provision. verified fact (of what is on the page); the existence of an unpublished internal protocol is unknown.

3.6 The number that carries the message

What MFC must not do. The Push-Up Challenge's device — reps = annual suicide deaths — is unavailable to MFC. K-08's Claims Register prohibition is explicit: "Do not claim treatment, prevention, diagnosis, symptom reduction, clinical validation, guaranteed outcomes, direct reductions in prevalence, suicide-risk reduction..." verified fact — K-08. Using a suicide-death count as a practice target inescapably implies the practice is addressed to that count. The Push-Up Challenge can carry it because it is a remembrance device attached to fundraising for services; MFC would be carrying it as a skill-practice target, which reads as a prevention claim. Do not do this. C-18 (the Framework prohibits "prevents", the Constitution names prevention as principal activity) makes this territory doubly unsafe until legal advice lands.

The honest candidates, assessed:

Candidate number Source Verdict
66 — median days to habit automaticity Lally et al. 2010, registered vault source, verified fact Strongest. It is a real, citable, non-clinical number; it carries exactly the message MFC needs ("this is practice over time, not a moment"); it makes the challenge duration itself the argument; it breaches no red line; and it honestly implies the challenge is where practice starts, not where it finishes. Its wide range (18–254 days) is a feature — it lets MFC say "for some people 18, for some 254; 66 is the middle" and thereby refuse a guaranteed-outcome framing in the same breath.
7 — the seven skills (D-0076) K-07, verified fact (internal) Usable as a structural device (one skill per week/day), not as a scale number. Weak as a headline.
1 in 5 or similar prevalence figure AIHW/ABS, verifiable Reject. Attaching a practice target to a prevalence figure is the prevalence-reduction implication K-08 prohibits.
Any suicide figure — Reject. See above.
A "moments in a day" figure — unknown and unverifiable. Never estimate it.

Recommendation on the number: 66. It is the rare case where the honest number is also the better story — it says this takes longer than a campaign, which is true, defensible, and differentiating against every competitor in this file.

PART 4 — Four candidate models

Deliberately structurally different, not four skins on one idea.

Model A — "66": a time-bound team challenge

  • Mechanic: 66 days. Teams of 4–6. Each person keeps a private rep count in a simple log; the team sees only how many members showed up to the weekly 10-minute team check-in and a shared team-level total that is never broken down by person.
  • Unit counted: publicly, team check-in attendance; privately, Mental Reps.
  • Team structure: small fixed teams; a named team moment ("our Monday morning").
  • Pathway: workplaces first. Schools blocked (C-16).
  • Measures: attendance rate; number of Radar moments named; pre/post on a validated self-efficacy or wellbeing instrument if MFC ever gets ethics-grade measurement.
  • Cost: moderate — needs a logging tool, comms, team-lead materials. unknown in dollars.
  • Strongest objection: 66 days is a long challenge. Every high-participation case in this file is 23–31 days. Attrition over 66 days is likely severe, and the Push-Up Challenge's 85% survey attrition happened over ~3 months with far more resources than MFC has.
  • Verdict: the number is excellent; the duration derived from it may be commercially unviable. Conditionally viable, in workplaces only.

Model B — "Our Moments": a team Radar, no counting at all

  • Mechanic: a team (work team, sports team, staff room) collectively names one shared moment they all face — the Monday stand-up, the end-of-shift handover, the pre-game 10 minutes — and agrees to run Stop-Shift-Do in it. Recurring, indefinite, not time-bound. K-07's existing "Our moments" Radar layer, made into a product.
  • Unit counted: moments named and reviewed, not reps. A team that has named 3 moments and reviewed them monthly has a legible record with nothing internal exposed.
  • Team structure: the team is the pre-existing real team. No new social unit is created — which is the G4H insight applied correctly: the group must persist independently of the programme.
  • Pathway: workplaces, sports clubs, emergency services. Schools: staff rooms first, which is outside C-16's participant-facing block and addresses a verified acute need (70% of teachers reporting unmanageable workloads).
  • Measures: moments named; moments still in use at 3/6 months; team-level qualitative review.
  • Cost: lowest of the four. It is a facilitation artefact plus a review cadence.
  • Strongest objection: it has no mass-participation surface at all. It will never produce a headline number, a fundraising channel, or a school assembly. It does not answer the founder's question as asked.
  • Verdict: the most likely to actually work, and the least likely to feel like what was asked for. It is the model whose mechanism matches MFC's own evidence position.

Model C — "Mental Fitness parkrun": recurring, free, local, volunteer-run

  • Mechanic: a free, recurring (weekly or fortnightly), same-time-same-place 20–30 minute in-person session where people run one Mental Rep together and talk about the moment they chose — never about the content of their distress. Volunteer-led from a fixed script.
  • Unit counted: attendance. Verifiable, non-inflatable, no disclosure.
  • Team structure: the location cohort, exactly as parkrun.
  • Pathway: community first (libraries, clubs, councils), workplaces second, schools last and only post-C-16.
  • Measures: attendance, retention at 12 months (set MFC's own baseline from its first cohort — do not adopt parkrun's 63% as a target; see the warning in §2, the figures are not comparable; the parkrun case gives MFC a qualitative model, not a published comparator to be judged against — a rare gift).
  • Cost: highest ongoing operational cost. Requires volunteer recruitment, training, a safeguarding escalation route at every site, and insurance. Under K-08 safety rule 10 and D-0016 item 6 (insurer confirmation), this is not a thing MFC can stand up quickly.
  • Strongest objection: MFC does not currently have the operational capacity, the safeguarding clearance, or the volunteer base. parkrun took years and a running culture that already existed; there is no equivalent pre-existing "turn up and practise your mind in a park" culture to ride.
  • Verdict: the best long-term answer and the wrong immediate one. Structurally correct, operationally out of reach today.

Model D — "Rep Partner": a dyad, not a crowd

  • Mechanic: two people pair for 30 days. Each names one moment. They exchange one message a day — not a count, not content: a single agreed word or emoji meaning "I caught it" or "I missed it," with no penalty attached to either. Explicitly not a streak: Lally's finding that occasional missed repetitions don't impair formation is stated to participants up front.
  • Unit counted: the exchange happened. Verified by both sides, which is the only genuinely cheat-resistant unit available for an internal act.
  • Team structure: dyad, optionally aggregated into a workplace count of active pairs.
  • Pathway: workplaces and community. Peer-support framing sits inside K-07's existing "Supporting others" boundary (peer support, not treatment).
  • Measures: pairs formed; pairs still exchanging at day 30 and day 90; conversion to Model B.
  • Cost: low. Could run on SMS or an existing messaging app before any product build.
  • Strongest objection: dyads are fragile — one person dropping out kills both. And the "I missed it" signal is exactly where social-desirability inflation bites hardest; participants will over-report catching.
  • Verdict: viable as a cheap pilot instrument, weak as a public campaign. Its real value is that it is the fastest way to learn whether people will report reps honestly at all — which is the unknown blocking every other model.

Recommendation

Do not launch a public mass-participation challenge in 2026. Build Model B ("Our Moments") in workplaces and staff rooms now, run Model D as a 30-day paired pilot to test honest self-report, and hold Models A and C as the acquisition and durability layers to build once the workshop is pilot-proven and C-16/D-0016 are resolved.

Confidence: 0.75 on "not a public campaign yet"; 0.6 on Model B specifically being the right first build.

Reasoning, honestly. 1. The evidence does not support the thing being asked for. The best-executed case in the category produces no maintained behaviour at three months, and the only durable model in the set is not a challenge. Building a challenge to solve a maintenance problem is a category error. 2. MFC cannot legally or safely enter schools right now. C-16 blocks participant-facing youth use, D-0016's six matters are open, the entire claims register is unapproved, and there is no named safeguarding lead. A schools challenge is not a design question yet; it is a governance blocker. 3. A leaderboard-based rep challenge is in direct tension with K-08 safety rule 7 and with Mental Rep's own outcome-independent definition. Building it would require MFC to breach its own framework to compete with organisations that do not have MFC's constraint. 4. Model B is the only candidate whose mechanism is already what MFC's framework says. It needs no new claim, no new number, no new counting system, and no new social unit — it makes an existing K-07 layer (Our moments) into a deliverable. 5. Reputationally, a rep-count headline figure is a number MFC could not defend under scrutiny. That is a foreseeable, avoidable exposure.

What would change my mind. If Model D's pilot showed people self-report reps honestly and consistently, and if the workshop reached pilot-proven status with C-16 resolved, the ordering flips: Model A becomes a credible annual acquisition wrapper around a Model B/C practice core. That is roughly a 12–24 month sequence, not a 2026 one. strategic hypothesis

What I could not verify

  • Whether participating schools receive any financial benefit from Push-Up Challenge fundraising — unknown.
  • Whether the Push-Up Challenge has an internal, unpublished schools safeguarding/disclosure protocol — unknown; only a footer support link is publicly visible.
  • Any Push-Up Challenge outcome data specific to school students (the University of Melbourne evaluation's sample had a mean age of 35.7) — unknown.
  • Steptember participation totals — the published "20 million Aussies" figure is implausible; treat all its participation numbers as unknown.
  • Movember's repeat-participation rate year-on-year — unknown; asserted in commentary, no figure located.
  • Any published evaluation of a mass-participation challenge that measured a skill or capability outcome rather than awareness, intention, mood or activity — none found. This is the white space, and it aligns with 10-measurement-white-space.md.
  • Cost to run any of the four models in dollars — unknown. Not estimated, deliberately.

Control-state caveats

This file makes no approved claim. K-08's red lines are themselves unapproved (C-15/C-24); C-16 blocks youth/schools; D-0016 remains open. Nothing here authorises a schools pathway. The recommendation is a research recommendation requiring Hunter's decision and, for anything participant-facing, the safeguarding gates that already exist.

19 Schools And Workplace Challengers

Schools/youth and workplace challengers

Discovery and profiling pass covering the two segments MFC's existing competitor map (files 02–06) under-covers: Australian schools/youth wellbeing providers, and Australian workplace wellbeing providers plus the EAP incumbents that hold the workplace budget.

Already profiled elsewhere and deliberately excluded here: Gotcha4Life, Smiling Mind, The Resilience Project, R U OK?, AIS Mental Fitness Program, Mental Fitness Australia, Healthy Minds Australia, MHFA, batyr, Life Ed, Berry Street Education Model, Beyond Blue, Black Dog Institute, headspace, ReachOut, Movember, MATES in Construction.

Labels: verified fact · public organisational claim · inference · strategic hypothesis · unknown.

All figures carry the year they refer to. Today is 2026-08-06.

Method note — and an honest limitation

Revenue is unknown for most organisations in this file, and that is a real gap, not a rounding error.

  • Individual ACNC charity-register profile pages (acnc.gov.au/charity/charities/<uuid>/profile) are JavaScript-rendered and consistently time out on automated fetch (60s exceeded, verified 2026-08-06 against The Project Rockit Foundation's profile). Search-engine snippets of those pages return narrative text but not the financial tables.
  • The ACNC bulk AIS dataset would resolve nearly every unknown in the revenue column in one pass, but was ruled out of scope for this run (a prior agent stalled on it).
  • Therefore: no revenue figure in this file has been estimated. Where it is unknown, the verification route is stated precisely.
  • Aggregator sites (Growjo, ZoomInfo, Tracxn, PitchBook, CompWorth) surfaced revenue-looking numbers for the private workplace players. These are modelled estimates, not filed accounts, and are recorded below as unknown with the estimate noted only so a future pass does not mistake them for verified. Growjo's "$422.7M revenue" for Converge International in particular is not credible against 472 employees and should not be reused.

Standing recommendation: one bounded ACNC bulk-AIS pass, run as its own objective with a hard row-filter, would convert ~15 unknowns in this file into verified fact. Do not attempt it inside a profiling run.

PART A — SCHOOLS AND YOUTH

A1. Be You (Beyond Blue, with Early Childhood Australia and headspace)

The single most important entry in this file. It is not a competitor MFC beats; it is the price floor MFC prices against.

Field Value
What it is Australia's national mental health in education initiative, funded by the Commonwealth Department of Health and Aged Care, delivered by Beyond Blue with Early Childhood Australia and headspace verified fact — https://beyou.edu.au/
Launched November 2018 verified fact
Cost to schools Free to all Australian educators and learning communities verified fact
Reach "Almost 11,000 schools and early learning services... 70 per cent of all Australian schools and a quarter of all early learning services" since 2018 launch public organisational claim (Beyond Blue) — https://www.beyondblue.org.au/about/media/media-releases/be-you-mental-health-in-education
Funding continuity Extended a further two years following a Prime Ministerial announcement verified fact; exact expiry date and dollar value unknown — verify via Health and Aged Care portfolio budget statements
Format Professional learning for educators (not direct student delivery), consultant support, tools, and — critically — the Be You Programs Directory, a national evidence-rated catalogue of third-party school programs verified fact
Construct claimed Mentally healthy learning communities; whole-setting capability, not a named skill construct inference from positioning
"Mental fitness" language No inference — Be You's public materials use "mental health and wellbeing," not "mental fitness"
Evidence quality Be You itself is an implementation framework rather than a discrete intervention; independent effectiveness evaluation of Be You as a whole unknown — verify via Department of Health commissioned evaluation reports

Where MFC overlaps. Both address the same buyer (Australian schools), the same budget line (student wellbeing), and the same broad promise (equip people to look after their mental health before crisis). Be You's Programs Directory is the gatekeeping mechanism MFC will eventually be assessed by if it sells into schools.

Where MFC differs. Be You builds educator and setting capability; it does not itself deliver a skills curriculum to students. It is a framework and a directory, not a workshop. MFC's proposition is a specific taught skill set with dosage and practice — the thing that sits inside a Be You-aligned school, not the thing that replaces it.

What MFC could learn. 1. The price floor is zero. Any schools offer must justify a price against a free, Commonwealth- funded, 70%-penetrated national alternative. That is a positioning constraint, not a marketing one. 2. Getting listed in the Be You Programs Directory (and the NSW and SA state catalogues) is the real distribution gate — Grow Your Mind, Bounce Back, Peaceful Kids and You Can Do It! are all listed; listing appears to be what converts a program from "a workshop" to "procurable." inference 3. Be You's evidence rating system (Bounce Back carries 3/4) means MFC's evidence base will be scored by a third party on a published scale. Build for that scale now, not later.

A2. FRIENDS Resilience (Prof. Paula Barrett)

Founder flagged this as potentially the strongest evidence competitor in the schools space. Assessment: it is the strongest published evidence base — and it is also the clearest cautionary tale in this file.

Field Value
What it is A family of CBT-based anxiety-prevention and resilience programs across the lifespan (Fun FRIENDS, FRIENDS for Life, My FRIENDS Youth, Adult Resilience) developed by Prof. Paula Barrett verified fact — https://friendsresilience.org/
Origin Australian (University of Queensland) verified fact
Format and dosage Manualised group program, typically ~10 sessions plus booster sessions, delivered by a trained/accredited facilitator public organisational claim — exact per-variant session counts unknown
Reach Delivered internationally across many countries; Australian school-count and student-count unknown — verify via FRIENDS Resilience's own accreditation registry or state education program catalogues
Revenue unknown — commercial licensing/training model; verify via ASIC company extract for the operating entity
Construct claimed Resilience, operationalised as anxiety/depression symptom prevention via CBT skills (Feelings, Relax, I can try, Explore solutions, Now reward yourself, Don't forget to practice, Smile) verified fact
"Mental fitness" language No — "resilience" verified fact

Evidence base — the honest read. - Strongest claim: recognised in a WHO evidence-based review for prevention/treatment of childhood and adolescent anxiety and depression public organisational claim (FRIENDS Resilience) — the underlying WHO document and its date should be verified before MFC ever cites this second-hand. - Genuine long-term Australian RCT data exists: Barrett et al., long-term outcomes of an Australian universal prevention trial, 12/24/36-month follow-up, Grade 6 and Grade 9 — anxiety reductions maintained at long-term follow-up for Grade 6 but not Grade 9 verified fact — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16836477/ - And there are real nulls, which the organisation's own marketing does not lead with: - Canadian targeted and universal studies found no effect when FRIENDS was delivered by class teachers verified fact; a large UK randomised trial (PACES) likewise found no universal effect under school-staff delivery, with a significant effect only in the health-led arm verified fact (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12879531/).

Corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check — the earlier wording here overstated this. This file previously asserted, as verified fact, that effects appeared only when delivered by external health staff. The cited source does not support that as a general rule. The same Wigelsworth et al. review reports education-staff delivery working for children already in the clinical range (d = .67); Barrett & Turner (2001) found teacher-led and psychologist-led delivery both effective; and the health-led PACES effect the claim rested on is small (ES = 0.2, vs usual provision 95% CI −5.22 to −0.09). verified fact

Correct characterisation: delivery agent is a live moderator and an open design risk — universal school-staff delivery has repeatedly underperformed, but school-staff delivery is not established as ineffective, and it demonstrably works for higher-symptom subgroups. Treat it as a question MFC must answer with its own data, not as a settled constraint. inference - A Zambian cluster-RCT found intervention participation did not reduce anxiety or depression verified fact — https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12037358/ - A Campbell Collaboration systematic review and meta-analysis (Filges et al., 2024) exists and should be read in full before MFC characterises this evidence base either way verified fact — https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/cl2.1443 - No effect on academic performance verified fact — https://www.acamh.org/research-digest/friends-programme-reduced-anxiety-no-effect-school-academic-performance-anxiety-programmes-delivered-schools-friends-life1-demonstrated-efficacy-reducing-anxiety-s/

Where MFC overlaps. FRIENDS is the closest thing in the Australian schools market to what MFC claims to be: a specific, manualised, practised skill set with a defined dosage and a real trial record — not a values message, not an assembly, not an app.

Where MFC differs. FRIENDS is framed as clinical prevention (anxiety and depression symptom reduction) delivered under a psychology-derived model. MFC's Framework is explicitly non-clinical and does not claim symptom reduction (K-08 red lines). MFC also targets adults and general populations, not primarily Grade 3–9 anxiety prevention.

What MFC could learn — this is the most consequential lesson in the file. 1. Delivery agent is a live risk to MFC's scaling model — an open question, not a settled constraint. In several universal trials the same manualised content produced effects under trained external health staff and null results when handed to classroom teachers — but not uniformly: education-staff delivery worked for children in the clinical range (d = .67), and Barrett & Turner (2001) found teacher-led and psychologist-led delivery both effective. verified fact If MFC's growth plan is "train the host organisation's own staff to deliver it," the strongest evidence base in this category says that is the variable most likely to decide whether the effect survives — so MFC should measure delivery-agent fidelity and outcomes by arm from the first pilot, rather than assuming either that train-the-trainer works or that it doesn't. strategic hypothesis 2. A WHO citation and a real null literature can coexist in the same program. MFC should assume its own evidence will eventually be read the same way — and should publish nulls itself first. 3. Grade 6 held, Grade 9 did not. Developmental timing appears to moderate durability. MFC has an analogous open question about which populations its dosage actually holds for.

Where MFC overlaps. YCDI is a named five-part skill construct taught as a curriculum — which is structurally the closest analogue in this file to MFC's own named-skills Framework. Both make the same implicit promise: these are learnable, nameable capacities, not moods.

Where MFC differs. YCDI is embedded curriculum for children delivered by teachers over a school year. MFC is a workshop-format offer with adult reach. YCDI's five foundations are dispositional (confidence, persistence); MFC's constructs are behavioural and practised.

What MFC could learn. 1. A clean, memorable, five-part named construct has extraordinary staying power — YCDI has run 30+ years on it. Naming is not decoration; it is the durability mechanism. 2. But YCDI shows what happens when the construct outruns the evidence. Thirty years of adoption and the flagship study is still six schools, developer-authored, perception outcomes. MFC will be tempted by exactly this trade (adoption now, evidence later) and should note that it leaves a permanent, unfixable credibility gap that competitors can name. 3. Directory listing (Be You + ACER Wellbeing Program Guide) has done more for YCDI's distribution than its evidence has. That is the actual market mechanism in Australian schools. inference

Where MFC differs. Bounce Back is a book — a low-cost, self-serve, teacher-delivered resource with no facilitator dependency and no per-head cost. MFC's model is facilitated delivery.

What MFC could learn. The product-form question. Bounce Back reached national scale as a publishable, purchasable artefact with near-zero marginal delivery cost, and it did so through a mainstream publisher's existing school distribution rather than through charity fundraising. Those two lessons are in direct tension and MFC should resolve that tension explicitly rather than pick whichever suits the moment. strategic hypothesis

A5. Grow Your Mind

Field Value

A9. Tomorrow Man / Tomorrow Woman — CLOSED

A material finding. This organisation has ceased operating and should be removed from any live competitor list — but kept as a case study.

Field Value
What it was Social enterprise running facilitated workshops on healthy masculinity, emotional expression and help-seeking for young men (Tomorrow Man) and young women (Tomorrow Woman); partnered with Tomorrow Architects verified fact — https://www.tomorrowman.com.au/
Status Both organisations closed after ten years. Stated cause: "an incredibly challenging philanthropy landscape has meant they are not able to find a financially sustainable way to continue long term." Workshops booked to 30 June 2025 proceeded; anything beyond was cancelled and refunded verified fact (Tomorrow Man's own closure notice; corroborated by third-party commentary — https://www.mystrengths.com.au/educators/why-the-closure-of-tomorrow-man-matters-for-our-boys/)
Format and dosage Single facilitated workshops (schools, sports clubs, workplaces, community), typically one-off verified fact
Reach / revenue at closure unknown — verify via final ACNC AIS / ASIC deregistration filing
Construct claimed Healthy masculinity, emotional literacy, vulnerability verified fact
"Mental fitness" language No verified fact
Evidence quality "97% of young men said they would recommend Tomorrow Man to their mates" public organisational claim — a satisfaction metric, not an outcome. Independent evaluation unknown

Where MFC overlapped. Almost exactly MFC's delivery form: charismatic facilitated group workshops, skills-and-conversation framing, sold into schools, clubs and workplaces, funded substantially by philanthropy.

Where MFC differs. MFC's construct is general and non-gendered; Tomorrow Man's was gender-specific and identity-framed.

What MFC could learn — treat this as the most important commercial warning in the file. 1. A ten-year-old, well-known, well-regarded, high-satisfaction facilitated-workshop social enterprise ran out of money in 2025 in this exact market. Brand recognition and 97% recommendation did not produce sustainability. The failure was in the revenue model, not the product. 2. Philanthropy-dependence plus per-workshop delivery cost is a demonstrated failure mode, and it is the default shape of what MFC is building. Contrast with Project Rockit's dual entity (A8), Bounce Back's publishing model (A4), and Grow Your Mind's subscription (A5). 3. Satisfaction metrics do not defend a budget. When funding tightened, "97% would recommend" was not an argument. FRIENDS-style outcome data, whatever its flaws, is. 4. There is now an unserved gap in the boys'/young-men's facilitated-workshop segment — a distribution opportunity for The Man Cave and potentially others. inference

Where MFC overlaps. PBL occupies the whole-school wellbeing slot — the strategic framing, the staff professional-learning time, and the school's articulated wellbeing approach.

SA's directory, NSW's catalogue, and Be You's directory are three listings that between them determine whether an Australian school can easily buy MFC at all. Getting listed is a concrete, achievable, high-leverage objective. 3. Even a government's own evaluation of its own flagship framework rests on perception data. The evidence bar in Australian schools wellbeing is genuinely low. MFC's risk is not failing to clear it — it is clearing it and mistaking that for having proven something (K-08).

PART B — WORKPLACE

B1. The EAP incumbents — Converge International, Benestar, AccessEAP, Davidson Trahaire Corpsych, LifeWorks

The structural competitor for workplace mental health budget. Not a program competitor — a budget-line competitor, which is worse.

Field Value
What they are Employee Assistance Programs — contracted, per-employee-per-year counselling and support services verified fact
Named majors Converge International, Benestar, AccessEAP, Davidson Trahaire Corpsych, LifeWorks verified fact — https://www.opencare.com.au/blog/navigating-the-best-eap-providers-in-australia-a-comprehensive-guide
Converge reach "Supporting Australian and New Zealand organisations and their employees, delivering mental health and wellbeing support services to over 2.7 million employees and their immediate family members" public organisational claim (Converge International)
Revenue unknown. Aggregator estimates exist (Growjo: Converge $422.7M / 472 employees; Benestar $37.3M / 138 employees) — these are modelled, not filed, and the Converge figure is not credible against its stated headcount. Do not reuse them. Verify via ASIC company extracts and, for Benestar, its parent group's filings
Format and dosage Reactive, individual, confidential short-course counselling (typically 3–6 sessions), 24/7 phone/digital access, plus manager assist and critical-incident response inference from standard market structure — per-provider session caps unknown
Construct claimed Access to support; risk mitigation and WHS compliance — not a skills or capability construct verified fact
"Mental fitness" language No verified fact
Evidence quality EAP utilisation rates are the industry metric; independent effectiveness evidence for Australian EAPs unknown and, on the international literature, contested inference

Where MFC overlaps. The budget, entirely. An organisation that has bought an EAP frequently believes it has "done" mental health. That belief is the primary commercial obstacle to MFC's workplace offer — more than any program competitor.

Where MFC differs — and this is MFC's sharpest workplace argument. - EAP is reactive, individual, confidential, and clinical. MFC is preventative, collective, visible, and non-clinical. - EAP is bought as risk transfer; MFC is bought as capability building. - EAP measures utilisation (i.e. how many people were unwell enough to call). MFC would measure capability. Utilisation as a success metric is genuinely perverse and MFC should say so plainly — it is the strongest available wedge into this budget. strategic hypothesis

What MFC could learn. 1. Psychosocial-hazard regulation is the money. Australian WHS psychosocial-risk obligations are what currently forces workplace spend. MFC's workplace offer will be bought faster if it is positioned against a duty (control of psychosocial hazards) than against a benefit (wellbeing). strategic hypothesis 2. Per-employee-per-year contracted pricing is the pricing model workplaces already understand. MFC's per-workshop pricing asks buyers to think in an unfamiliar unit. 3. "Complements your EAP, doesn't replace it" is the only positioning that gets past procurement without triggering an existing-contract objection. inference

The best-capitalised workplace wellbeing challenger in Australia. Not a competitor MFC beats — a competitor that defines what "scale" now means in this segment.

Field Value

Where MFC overlaps. Same buyer (HR/WHS), same budget, same "prevention beats crisis" narrative.

Where MFC differs. Sonder is a reactive access platform at heart — better, faster access to help when something goes wrong. MFC teaches capability so fewer things go wrong. Sonder is capital- intensive and technology-scaled; MFC is human-delivered.

What MFC could learn. 1. The winning workplace narrative in 2025 Australia was "health and safety," not "wellbeing." Sonder raised $40M in a hard capital market by positioning as WHS. That is the language the budget responds to. 2. $40M of venture capital is now inside MFC's adjacent market. MFC will not out-spend or out-market this. It has to be a different kind of thing, and say so. 3. "1 million members" is a distribution claim, not an outcome claim — and it worked. Note both halves of that.

B3. Springfox (part of the Resilience Institute)

Field Value
What it is Founded 2003 by Stuart Taylor (formerly The Resilience Institute Australia); "Australia's leading provider of evidence-based resilience programmes to individuals and organisations" public organisational claim — https://www.springfox.com/

Revenue unknown — private; verify via ASIC extract

"Mental fitness" language No — "resilience" throughout verified fact

"Programmes are proven to improve individuals' and organisations' resilience by an average of 25%" public organisational claim — measured on the provider's own diagnostic instrument, no control group disclosed, no independent replication located. Publishes white papers (e.g. the ASORC-hosted "Building Resilience," Stuart Taylor) verified fact — https://www.asorc.org.au/download/?id=10314 . A CSIRO-published item on resilient leadership exists verified fact — https://www.publish.csiro.au/aj/aj20207

Where MFC overlaps. This is the closest structural analogue to MFC in the workplace segment: a named, trainable, multi-component construct, delivered by facilitators, measured on a proprietary instrument, with a founder-origin story (Taylor's cancer experience) as the brand's emotional core.

Where MFC differs. Springfox is a for-profit consultancy selling to corporate budgets; MFC is a charity with a mission audience. Springfox's construct is "resilience"; MFC's is "mental fitness" — and Springfox got 23 years of runway out of a term it did not have to defend.

What MFC could learn — and a direct warning. 1. "Improves resilience by an average of 25%, measured on our own instrument" is exactly the claim MFC will be tempted to make about its own measure, and exactly what K-08 should stop. It is commercially effective and evidentially empty. MFC should decide in advance that it will not do this, because the market clearly rewards it. 2. The founder-story-as-brand-core model works and lasts — but note it is a for-profit sustainability model. Springfox survived where charity-funded Tomorrow Man did not. 3. A proprietary diagnostic is the commercial engine, not the training. The diagnostic creates the need, benchmarks it, and sells the remedy. That is a business-model insight MFC's measurement work should sit alongside.

What MFC could learn — the most directly actionable item in Part B. 1. Giving the measurement instrument away free is the distribution strategy. The free PERMAH survey creates the demand, the credibility, and the dataset; the paid work follows. MFC's measurement ambition could take exactly this shape, and it costs less than any other channel in this file. 2. Attaching a named university academic to the instrument (Kern, Melbourne) is what makes it citable. This is the cheapest credibility purchase available to MFC and it does not require a trial. 3. An annual nationally-representative workplace survey (n≈1,000) is affordable, repeatable, and has produced eight years of owned media and AHRI co-branding. SuperFriend (B5) runs the same play at larger n. This is a proven Australian pattern for a small organisation to own a category conversation without owning a randomised trial. strategic hypothesis

B7. Thrive at Work (Centre for Transformative Work Design, Future of Work Institute, Curtin University)

Field Value
What it is University-led workplace wellbeing initiative, Curtin University, with foundational funding from the WA Mental Health Commission verified fact — https://www.thriveatwork.org.au/

Reach unknown — verify by requesting partner counts from the Future of Work Institute
Revenue unknown — sits inside Curtin University
Construct claimed Work design — the distinctive claim is that wellbeing comes from redesigning the work itself, not from fixing the worker: "give organisations the knowledge, tools and skills to re-examine the actual work their employees do" verified fact
"Mental fitness" language No verified fact
Evidence quality The strongest academic pedigree in Part B. The Centre for Transformative Work Design (Prof. Sharon Parker's group) is an internationally recognised work-design research centre with a substantial peer-reviewed literature inference from institutional standing; specific effectiveness evidence for the Thrive framework as deployed unknown. Listed on the Commonwealth Mentally Healthy Workplaces resource verified fact

Where MFC overlaps. Almost nothing on delivery. Considerable on claim territory.

Where MFC differs — and this is the most serious intellectual challenge to MFC in the file. Thrive at Work represents the strongest academic critique of everything MFC does: the position that individual-level wellbeing interventions are, at best, marginal, and that the real determinants of workplace mental health are job design, workload, control, and role clarity. On this view, teaching individuals skills is treating a symptom of a structural problem — and there is a substantial occupational-psychology literature behind that view.

What MFC could learn. 1. MFC must have a real answer to the work-design critique, not a dismissal. The honest answer is probably: both are true, they operate at different levels, and MFC's claim is bounded to what an individual can control. That is a defensible position — but only if MFC states the boundary explicitly rather than implying skills can fix a badly designed job. This belongs in K-08 territory. strategic hypothesis 2. A university-hosted, state-commission-funded model is a fourth sustainability structure — research funding rather than philanthropy, fees, or sector levy. 3. The maturity-audit format is a superb front-of-funnel product: it is cheap to deliver, it creates the diagnosis that justifies the purchase, and it positions the provider as an assessor rather than a vendor. Springfox (B3) does the commercial version of the same thing.

CROSS-CUTTING FINDINGS

1. Revenue-model fragility, not product failure, is what removes organisations like MFC

strategic hypothesis

Corrected 2026-08-06 after independent check. This section previously read "Three of the organisations closest to MFC's proposition have exited within ~18 months." The eighteen-month window was false — Uprise was acquired in March 2021, five years earlier, and by acquisition rather than closure. The heading and the grouping have been rewritten. The underlying finding survives; the compressed timeframe did not.

Two Australian organisations occupying MFC-adjacent preventive positions closed in the 2025–26 period — each on revenue model, neither on product: verified fact

  • Tomorrow Man / Tomorrow Woman — closed 2025, ten years old, facilitated workshops, unsustainable philanthropy.
  • Ahead for Business (Everymind) — closed June 2026, a decade old, $3.1M national rollout, Commonwealth funding discontinued.

A third, earlier and structurally different case: Uprise — acquired by Integrated Behavioral Health, 30 March 2021, subsequently rebranded; Australian trading status unknown pending an ASIC extract. verified fact Not a closure and not defunding — the prevention proposition was commercially resolved by being folded back into the reactive incumbent model it set out to displace.

The common feature across all three is dependence on a single funding source someone else controls. inference This is the shape of MFC's current model, and it deserves a direct strategic response rather than a note. It is corroborated independently by file 15: the Australian organisations in this sector that endure — R U OK? (merchandise 36.1% of revenue), yourtown (a lottery business), MHFA (fee-for-service since 2002) — all run on revenue engines that no single funder can switch off.

2. "Mental fitness" is being used more, and more loosely, than MFC's earlier passes recorded

New to this file: Danny Frawley Centre (DFC Mental Fitness) — a named product from an AFL-club- linked health facility selling to schools, clubs and workplaces; EQ Minds — a named "Mental Fitness" workshop with Westpac/Macquarie/Google-tier corporate distribution; Brooke McIntosh — a ten-city "Mental Fitness Tour" claiming to be Australia's first; Resilience Agenda — retail stationery. Together with the AIS/Black Dog program and Mental Fitness Australia already on the map, this reinforces 13-category-coherence.md: the word is taken, repeatedly, by parties who define it differently and defend it not at all.

3. Nobody in either segment holds the evidence high ground — and the bar is low

The best published Australian result located is The Resilience Project + Resilient Youth + Monash (100+ schools, 40,000+ students, reduced depression and anxiety). The state's own flagship framework (PBL, 1,608 schools) rests on perception data. YCDI's flagship study is six schools, developer- authored. Grow Your Mind's is one school. Springfox's "25% improvement" is measured on its own instrument. The competitive risk to MFC is not failing to clear this bar — it is clearing it easily and mistaking that for having proven something (K-08, L-003).

4. Distribution in Australian schools runs through four catalogues, not through sales

Be You Programs Directory · NSW Student Wellbeing external programs catalogue · SA External Wellbeing Programs Directory · ACER Wellbeing Program Guide. Every scaled schools program in this file is listed in at least one. Getting MFC listed is a concrete, bounded, high-leverage objective and is almost certainly cheaper than any other market-access activity available. strategic hypothesis

6. The workplace wedge is psychosocial duty, not wellbeing benefit

strategic hypothesis

Sonder raised $40M positioned as health and safety. CMHAA members have a reporting obligation. EAPs are bought as risk transfer. The buyer in this segment responds to duty and compliance language, not to flourishing language. MFC's workplace offer is currently framed in the weaker of the two registers.

7. The FRIENDS delivery-agent finding is a constraint on MFC's business model

The strongest evidence base in the schools segment shows the same content produced effects when delivered by trained external staff and null results when delivered by the host organisation's own staff. Any MFC scaling plan built on training host staff to deliver is scaling toward the null. Peaceful Kids' accredited-facilitator model is the counter-pattern. This tension between scale and effect is the central unresolved design question and should be named as such rather than resolved by convenience.

00 V1 1 Index And Executive Summary

Market Intelligence V1.1 — Adult Demand, Buyer Pathways and Commercial Model

A bounded, advisory continuation of V1. Branched from ops/market-competitor-intelligence-v1 at commit f0ed7e6. Public sources and bounded desk research only. No external outreach occurred. A-17 characterises; it does not decide MFC's response, and nothing in this package changes an authoritative MFC record.

What V1 established

  • The category is used but not owned. At least fourteen organisations use "mental fitness"; six of the most prominent never define it. SWM-02's claim that MFC is defining the category does not hold as stated.
  • An orphaned Australian expert-consensus definition exists — Robinson, Oades & Caputi (2015) — that MFC's K-04 independently converges with.
  • Nobody has built the practice layer the word promises. Every competitor sells exposure and calls it training.
  • MFC's outcome-independent rep appears genuinely unclaimed; the Radar and Stop-Shift-Do are well-evidenced but not novel structures.
  • Nobody has a validated, change-sensitive measure of the construct.

What remained unknown after V1

Everything about adult demand specifically: which segment, what purchasing pathway, what a buyer or lost-user would actually say, whether the outcome-independent-rep claim survives a wider prior-art search, and whether V1's measurement candidates (STEM-B, EMA) would hold up under closer scrutiny.

Which unknowns could materially change MFC strategy

Three, ranked by how much this package moved them:

  1. The outcome-independent rep's novelty — closed. 08 confirms "no equivalent identified in the reviewed evidence," strengthening SWM-02's replacement claim.
  2. Measurement candidate confidence — revised, not merely closed. 07 found direct evidence against STEM-B's and EMA's assumed change-sensitivity — a genuine correction to V1, not an elaboration of it.
  3. Adult segment demand — still substantially open. Desk research narrowed the question (see the sport-funding finding below) but did not answer it. This is the one item V1.1 cannot close without primary research.

What V1.1 answers

  • A four-segment comparison grounded in verified Australian procurement evidence, not assumption (01).
  • A revision to V1's measurement recommendation, with the evidence that produced it shown explicitly (07).
  • Closure of the outcome-independent-rep novelty question across ten literatures (08).
  • Ready-to-review research instruments, a comprehension-study design, and a partnership map — none executed (02, 03, 06, 10).

What still requires primary research

Everything the ten human decision gates protect: segment selection, participant recruitment, buyer/partner/academic contact, external price or concept testing, any change to public claims or measurement design, and the comprehension study's actual launch. See 11 for the full mapping of gates to what this package prepared.

Evidence, inference and proposal — how this package uses the distinction

  • Verified fact: read directly on a primary or government/official source (e.g. the NSW Mental Health Sports Fund's published grant terms).
  • Organisation claim: a self-published assertion, not independently audited (e.g. vendor-published EAP pricing).
  • Evidence-supported inference: a reasoned conclusion from verified facts, not itself independently verified (e.g. that sport's grant channel is more tractable than the other three).
  • Proposal: a design choice offered for Hunter's approval, not a finding (e.g. the interview instruments, the decision thresholds in 02).
  • Unknown: genuinely not established — recorded explicitly rather than estimated, per instruction, throughout.

The headline finding

Of the four adult segments assessed, only sport organisations and clubs have a named, currently-described, government-administered funding channel explicitly open to external-provider partnerships (the NSW Mental Health Sports Fund — up to $150,000/grant, $2.8M pool). Every other segment's purchasing pathway remains substantially unknown or structurally difficult. This is a hypothesis for primary-research testing, not a market decision — see 11.

A second finding, cutting the other way against over-confidence: this task revised, not merely confirmed, one of V1's own conclusions. STEM-B and event-contingent EMA — V1's leading measurement candidates — both turned out to have direct evidence against their assumed change-sensitivity once the actual intervention trials were retrieved. 07 records this as a correction, and it is the clearest demonstration in this package that closure research can move a finding backward as well as forward.

Honest limits of this research

  • Desk research only. No buyer, participant, lost-user, partner or academic was contacted.
  • Explicit search gaps recorded throughout, not papered over: no AU-specific work-redesign-vs-training cost comparison; no HR/WHS/L&D budget-split survey; no PHN tender for adult wellbeing programs located; no primary ACNC financial data (third-party aggregator figures used instead, flagged for verification); NSW Mental Health Sports Fund eligibility criteria not retrieved.
  • Independent review: one pass completed against this package before commit — see the commit message for its scope and findings.
  • No correction beyond one pass was required or made following that review.

Authority and boundaries

Advisory only, per the same A-17 constraints as V1. This package does not modify K-04, K-05, any Strategic World Model entry, D-0016, or D-0017. Stage 11 was not advanced. Every proposal requires the corresponding Hunter decision gate before any execution.
