01 Adult Market Segment Hypotheses

Adult market segment hypotheses

Four segments only, per scope. No segment is recommended for selection here — that decision sits with Hunter in 11, and requires gate-1 approval before any segment becomes MFC's research or delivery focus.

Explicit caution, per your instruction: lower competitor density is not evidence of higher demand. Where a segment looks less crowded in V1's competitor landscape, that is checked below against independent procurement evidence, not assumed to mean opportunity.

1. Workplaces and employers

Dimension Finding Label
Participant problem Individual employees managing stress, overwhelm, workplace relationships — the general adult problem MFC already addresses inference, carried from V1
Buyer problem Post-2022 WHS psychosocial reform creates a compliance obligation, but the obligation is discharged primarily through work redesign, not training — V1 already established this; this task's research confirms the regulatory hierarchy explicitly starts with redesign, not policy or training verified fact (regulation) + evidence-supported inference (implication)
Buyer and budget holder No single Australian dataset names the typical holder. Industry commentary suggests procurement is negotiated across WHS, HR and L&D rather than owned by one function evidence-supported inference — search failed to find a quantified split; treat as genuinely unresolved
Current substitutes Major EAP providers (Converge International, Assure Programs, TELUS Health) bundle counselling, coaching and "training & development." Published EAP benchmarks: $30–$80 per employee per year (basic), some providers from $7.99/employee/month, counselling ~$40/hour verified fact — vendor-published, treat as indicative not audited
Purchasing trigger unknown — no Australian data locates the actual trigger (WHS incident, engagement survey result, budget-cycle renewal, leadership change). This is the single most important gap 03's buyer instrument is designed to close
Procurement difficulty Comparative US data (not directly transferable) suggests vendor wellness programs can cost more than work-redesign consultancy per employee — meaning a training vendor may be competing against a cheaper compliance-satisfying alternative, not just against other trainers evidence-supported inference, non-AU source, flagged
Expected evidence threshold High, per V1's finding that credible school-adjacent channels are evidence-gated — no reason to assume the workplace channel is materially easier, and the WHS hierarchy of controls adds a second, harder bar: demonstrating the offer doesn't purport to replace redesign evidence-supported inference
Likely delivery model Single or multi-session workshop, per MFC's current capability inference
Repeat-purchase/renewal potential unknown — no data found either way
Scalability Bounded by facilitator capacity per V1's earlier findings; no new evidence changes this inference, carried from V1
Major risks The claims-boundary risk already flagged in V1 (06) and 04 of this package — a buyer purchasing under the belief it discharges a WHS duty. This risk is now sharper: the regulatory hierarchy of controls is explicit that training sits below redesign, so an uninformed buyer's misunderstanding is a predictable, not hypothetical, failure mode
Unresolved assumptions Whether MFC's non-compliance-shaped offer is even attractive to a buyer whose primary motivation is compliance; whether HR/L&D wellbeing budgets (distinct from WHS compliance budgets) are large enough to matter
Evidence that would disconfirm this segment If buyer interviews (Instrument 1, 03) show budget-holders consistently name WHS compliance as the only driver for this category of spend, and cannot separately articulate an HR/culture rationale, that would suggest MFC's non-compliance offer has no real budget line to attach to

2. Sport organisations and clubs

Dimension Finding Label
Participant problem Same general adult problem, delivered in a sport/club social context inference
Buyer problem Varies by governing body, but a consistent pattern emerged: procurement is brokered at the State Sporting Organisation (SSO) level, not by individual grassroots clubs, and is frequently co-funded or fully funded by state government verified fact, multiple independent examples below
Buyer and budget holder Evidence across codes: NRL — centrally run "State of Mind," expanded with NSW Government funding, one reported $280,000 investment across NSW clubs. Netball Queensland — formal partnership committing to ≥30 workshops/year, ≥600 participants. Netball Victoria — free wellbeing courses via a delivery partner, plus a WorkSafe Victoria-branded program, implying government co-funding. NSW Mental Health Sports Fund — a named, active grant pathway: up to $150,000 per grant, $2.8M total pool, jointly run by NSW Health and NSW Office of Sport, explicitly open to sporting bodies partnering with external providers verified fact for all of the above
Current substitutes AIS Mental Fitness Program (documented in V1) reaches "458 schools and sporting organisations," but no disaggregated club-only reach figure exists — the program's real distribution channel is very likely predominantly schools, not clubs. Movember/AFL's Ahead of the Game is the clearest existing sport-sector program verified fact (the ambiguity itself) — do not assume AIS competes directly for club-level budget
Purchasing trigger unknown at club level; at SSO/government level, the NSW Mental Health Sports Fund is a scheduled, applied-for grant round, not a reactive trigger
Procurement difficulty Lower than expected, and this is the segment where "lower density" evidence and "real pathway" evidence actually align — a concrete, government-administered, application-based grant channel exists and explicitly invites external-provider partnerships verified fact — this is the strongest procurement-pathway evidence found across all four segments
Expected evidence threshold unknown for the grant application itself — not located in this desk research pass — but grant programs of this kind typically require at minimum a program description and a delivery plan, which MFC can already produce
Likely delivery model Workshop delivery to club members/staff, likely brokered through an SSO rather than sold to a single grassroots club directly
Repeat-purchase/renewal potential unknown — grant funding is typically round-based rather than a renewing commercial relationship, which changes the nature of "repeat purchase" from a sales question to a re-application question
Scalability Potentially higher than workplace delivery if SSO-level partnerships are secured, since one SSO relationship could reach many clubs — but this is unverified and depends on relationship-building MFC has not yet attempted
Major risks Grant-cycle dependency (funding is not guaranteed to renew); the same clinical/non-clinical boundary risk as other segments if government co-funding carries expectations MFC's non-clinical model cannot meet
Unresolved assumptions Whether MFC would be a credible applicant to the NSW Mental Health Sports Fund or equivalent without existing sport-sector runs on the board; whether other states have equivalent funds (not checked in this bounded pass)
Evidence that would disconfirm this segment If a review of the NSW Mental Health Sports Fund's actual grant recipients (not attempted in this bounded task) shows it exclusively funds established, credentialed providers, that would weaken the "MFC could realistically apply" assumption

strategic hypothesis This segment produced the single most concrete, verifiable, government-administered funding pathway found across all four segments in this research. That is a materially different finding from V1's competitor-density read, which noted AIS's dominance in this space without identifying this specific grant channel as a separate, lower-barrier entry point.

3. Community organisations

Dimension Finding Label
Participant problem General adult population, potentially skewed toward specific needs depending on the commissioning body (e.g. older adults, regional/rural populations) inference
Buyer problem PHNs commission both clinical and non-clinical mental health/wellbeing services against regional priority areas verified fact
Buyer and budget holder PHNs (regional, competitive commissioning); local councils (small, fragmented); philanthropic intermediaries like FRRR verified fact for the structure; specific budget-holder names not located
Current substitutes One concrete PHN example located: Hunter New England and Central Coast PHN's "EngAGE Community Pilot" (older-adult social connection) — funding amount not published. No open PHN tender for adult non-clinical wellbeing/mental-fitness programs was locatable verified fact (the pilot exists) / explicit search gap (no tender found)
Purchasing trigger PHN commissioning is tender/RFP-based, not a direct-sale relationship — this is a structurally different and typically slower purchasing pathway than a direct workplace or sport sale verified fact
Procurement difficulty Comparatively high for PHN-level funding (competitive tender, likely requiring a track record MFC does not yet have) but comparatively low for the smaller philanthropic/council tier evidence-supported inference
Expected evidence threshold High for PHN-level commissioning (formal RFP process); lower for smaller grants evidence-supported inference
Likely delivery model Community-based workshop delivery, likely smaller cohorts than a workplace booking
Repeat-purchase/renewal potential unknown
Scalability Low at the smaller-grant tier. FRRR's "In a Good Place" program: grants up to $20,000 per project, funding pool at least $240,000 per round — this funds pilot-scale delivery, not a scaled program. Council grants are similarly small and fragmented (examples ranging $1,000–$150,000 across different councils, most well under $15,000) verified fact
Major risks The smaller-grant tier is real but capped low enough that it cannot be a primary commercial pathway on its own; the PHN tier is a real but slow and competitive pathway requiring evidence MFC does not yet have
Unresolved assumptions Whether MFC could win a PHN tender without prior delivery evidence; whether the smaller-grant tier is worth the administrative overhead relative to its funding cap
Evidence that would disconfirm this segment If partner interviews (Instrument 4, 03) with PHN-adjacent contacts confirm that PHN tenders structurally require an existing evaluated program (which V1's market-access findings on evidence-gating make plausible), that would disconfirm PHN commissioning as a near-term pathway, leaving only the low-ceiling grant tier

4. Direct-to-adult participants

Dimension Finding Label
Participant problem Same general adult problem, but here the participant is also the buyer
Buyer problem N/A — participant and buyer are the same person
Buyer and budget holder The individual adult
Current substitutes Headspace app: ~$12.99/month or $69.99/year (pricing varies by source/promotion). Smiling Mind app: free, and has been free for 12+ years by deliberate design. MHFA standard adult course: $220–$462+ per participant — the clearest genuine direct-fee Australian benchmark, though largely workplace-purchased seats rather than pure individual consumer purchases verified fact for all prices; evidence-supported inference on the workplace-vs-individual purchase mix for MHFA
Purchasing trigger unknown — no Australian data on what triggers an individual adult to pay for a non-clinical wellbeing product specifically
Procurement difficulty Lowest of the four segments structurally (no institutional gatekeeper) — but this cuts both ways, since it also means no institutional budget line exists to draw on
Expected evidence threshold unknown, likely lower than institutional buyers (individuals are known to act on less formal evidence than procurement processes require) but this is an assumption, not tested
Likely delivery model Direct booking, likely lower price point than institutional delivery
Repeat-purchase/renewal potential unknown
Scalability Structurally the most scalable if a low-cost or free-access model is used (per Smiling Mind's pattern), but this raises the same sustainability question Smiling Mind itself faces — a free-to-consumer model requires funding from elsewhere
Major risks The evidence pattern found (Smiling Mind free + cross-subsidised; MHFA paid + credential-driven) suggests direct consumer payment for pure wellbeing content, without an accompanying credential, may be structurally harder to sustain than either free-access-plus-cross-subsidy or paid-plus-credential models. This is a pattern read across two examples, not a proven rule
Unresolved assumptions Whether MFC's category (non-clinical practice, no credential) fits either successful pattern found, or falls into a harder-to-sustain middle ground
Evidence that would disconfirm this segment If participant interviews and the price/willingness-to-pay instrument (03) find adults readily naming amounts they'd pay directly and can point to past direct purchases of comparable non-credentialed wellbeing content, that would strengthen this segment. If most past examples cited by respondents turn out to be free or employer-funded, that disconfirms the direct-payment assumption specifically (though not necessarily the segment itself, which could still work as a free/philanthropy-funded channel)

Cross-segment observation — checking the "lower density ≠ higher demand" instruction directly

strategic hypothesis

  • Workplaces: V1 found this segment moderately crowded (EAPs, Uprise, Sonder) — and this task's research found the regulatory structure itself works against a training-only offer, independent of competitor density. Crowding and regulatory headwind both point the same direction here.
  • Sport: V1 found AIS dominant by reach, which reads as high density — but this task found AIS's actual grassroots-club penetration is unverified, and located a separate, concrete, government-funded pathway (NSW Mental Health Sports Fund) that AIS does not obviously occupy. This is the clearest case in this research where surface-level competitor density did not predict the actual opportunity — the opportunity sits in a funding channel, not in competing for AIS's existing distribution.
  • Community: Low density in V1's competitor landscape, but this task found the procurement structure itself (competitive PHN tendering, low grant ceilings) is the binding constraint, not competition. Low density here reflects a hard-to-enter channel, not an easy one.
  • Direct-to-adult: Low density of specialist competitors, but real substitute products exist (Headspace, Smiling Mind, MHFA) at a range of price points, and the sustainability pattern found (free+cross-subsidised or paid+credentialed) suggests the apparent openness may be illusory without one of those two supporting structures.

No segment can be ranked from this file alone. The decision synthesis is 11's job, and requires the disconfirming evidence from primary research (02, 03) that this desk-research pass cannot supply.

02 Buyer And Participant Research Plan

Buyer and participant research plan

No recruitment, contact or outreach has occurred under this file. It is a ready-to-review design. Every named step requires Hunter's approval before execution, per the V1.1 human decision gates (items 2 and 3 specifically).

Why this plan exists

V1 established that the category is contested and the evidence bar for every credible channel is real. V1.1's segment analysis (01) is built from desk research and inference — public procurement documents, published pricing, competitor behaviour. None of it is primary evidence of what an actual Australian buyer or adult participant thinks, needs, or would pay. This plan is what closes that gap, if and when Hunter authorises it.

Four research populations

Population Why it matters What desk research cannot tell us
Organisational buyers (HR/WHS/L&D leads, club administrators, PHN commissioners) They hold the budget and the procurement decision Actual purchasing triggers, actual objections, actual evaluation criteria in their own words
Delivery or referral partners (EAPs, Black Dog, university researchers, sporting bodies) They can extend reach or lend credibility MFC lacks alone Whether partnership interest is real or a research artefact
Adult participants They are the people the practice must actually work for Whether the category language lands, whether the practice is usable in real life
Lost / non-users — people who rejected, discontinued or never engaged with a comparable offer (Smiling Mind app, a corporate wellbeing program, a resilience workshop) The single most information-dense and most neglected population in this field Why offers that look similar to MFC's fail to sustain use — this is the evidence nobody in the competitive landscape publishes

inference The lost/non-user population deserves disproportionate weight. Every competitor profile in V1 shows the same failure mode — high initial reach, near-total drop-off (Gotcha4Life's 8% gym conversion; Smiling Mind's unpublished retention). Nobody has asked those people why. That is a genuinely open research question, not a repeat of existing work.

Minimum useful sample

proposal — for Hunter's approval, not a claim of statistical power. This is qualitative, hypothesis-generating research, not a validation study.

Population Minimum Rationale
Organisational buyers 8–10, spread across at least 2 of the 4 segments in 01 Enough to see whether procurement patterns repeat within a segment before generalising
Delivery/referral partners 4–6 Fewer needed — the question is partnership incentive, not population variance
Adult participants (workshop-naive) 10–12 Enough for thematic saturation on message comprehension (see 06)
Lost/non-users 8–10 Deliberately equal weight to buyers — this is the priority population

Total: ~30–38 conversations. proposal This is a scoping sample, sized to surface disconfirming evidence and sharpen the segment choice — not to prove a market exists.

Recruitment criteria

proposal — none of this has been executed.

  • Organisational buyers: must hold or directly influence a training/wellbeing budget decision within the last 24 months, across at least workplaces and one other segment (sport or community), so segment comparison isn't confounded with recruitment-channel bias.
  • Participants: adults 25–55 (the segment most workshops and comparable offers target), screened for no current engagement with MFC to avoid confirmation bias from people already favourably disposed.
  • Lost/non-users: must have started a comparable offer (app, workshop, program) and stopped within 3 months, or actively declined one after evaluating it. Screen out people who never considered any such offer — the research question is about drop-off, not disinterest.
  • Partners: identified from the V1 partnership map (10) — organisations already named as potential-fit, approached only after Hunter's item-3 approval.

inference Recruitment channel itself is a source of bias worth naming: if participants are recruited through MFC's existing network, findings will skew toward people already sympathetic to the category. A recruitment plan that only reaches warm contacts should be treated as a weaker evidence tier than one reaching cold, segment-matched respondents — this is a design quality question for whoever executes, not resolved here.

Sequence

proposal

  1. Lost/non-users and buyers first. They carry the highest-value disconfirming evidence and don't require MFC's own materials to be shown.
  2. Partners second, informed by what buyers and lost-users reveal about where MFC would need external credibility.
  3. Participants last, using the comprehension and product-format instruments (03, 04) once buyer language is understood — participant interviews can then test whether MFC's framing lands against the objections buyers and lost-users have already surfaced.

Interview duration and format

proposal - Buyers and partners: 30–40 minutes, semi-structured, one-on-one, video or phone. - Participants and lost-users: 25–35 minutes, same format. - No group sessions — group settings suppress disclosure of failure and disengagement, which is exactly the signal this research needs from lost-users.

Consent and privacy requirements

proposal — MFC-specific requirements to confirm against its own governance before any execution:

  • Plain-language information sheet stating MFC's identity, the research purpose, that no clinical or diagnostic content will be discussed, and that participation is voluntary and withdrawable at any point.
  • Explicit consent to recording (or note-taking if recording is declined).
  • No collection of identifiable health information — this research asks about purchasing and engagement behaviour, not mental health status. If a participant discloses distress, standard MFC safeguarding referral practice applies (this connects to, but does not reopen, D-0016 — the same referral-pathway question that blocks pilot-ready approval applies here and should be resolved once, not twice).
  • Data retention limited to thematic analysis notes; recordings deleted after transcription per MFC's data policy (unknown — no MFC data retention policy was located in the files reviewed for this task; flagged as a gap to close before execution, not resolved here).
  • Given the WWCC / safeguarding overlap noted in V1's market-access file, any research involving under-18s is explicitly out of scope for this plan. All populations here are adults.

Analysis method

proposal - Thematic analysis (not statistical) — code interviews for: stated problem, current alternative/substitute, purchasing trigger or barrier, reaction to MFC's category language, reaction to specific offer concepts (04). - Compare themes within each segment first (does this buyer's account match other buyers in the same segment?), then across segments (is workplace demand structurally different from sport-club demand, or superficially different?). - Explicit disconfirmation pass: for every theme that appears to support a segment hypothesis in 01, actively search the same transcripts for counter-examples before treating the theme as supported.

Stopping rule

proposal Saturation-based, not sample-size-based. Stop recruiting within a population when three consecutive interviews produce no new theme relevant to the decision questions in 11. If saturation is not reached within the minimum sample above, that itself is a finding — it suggests the population is more heterogeneous than assumed, and the segment hypothesis should be treated as less resolved, not force-closed.

Decision thresholds

proposal — for Hunter to set or amend, not decided here:

  • A segment is disconfirmed if a majority of buyers in that segment describe a purchasing pathway MFC cannot realistically enter within 12 months (e.g. requires an existing multi-year vendor panel, or a procurement threshold MFC's current capacity can't service).
  • A segment is supported for testing (not proven) if buyers describe a live, describable purchasing trigger, name a real budget line, and the objections raised are addressable rather than structural.
  • The category language is at risk if more than roughly a third of participant interviews independently produce one of the adverse interpretations flagged in 06 (blame, toughness, brain-muscle literalism, clinical confusion, corporate superficiality) without being prompted toward it.

These thresholds are starting proposals for Hunter to adjust, not fixed rules — they are not evidence-based in themselves; they are judgment calls about what result would change MFC's course.

Expected Hunter approvals

Per the V1.1 human decision gates, before any part of this plan executes, Hunter must separately approve: 1. Selecting the first segment(s) to research (gate 1) 2. Recruiting participants (gate 2) 3. Contacting buyers, partners or academics (gate 3)

This file provides the design for those approvals to be granted against — it does not itself constitute approval, and no step in it has begun.

03 Interview And Testing Instruments

Interview and testing instruments

Instruments only. None has been used. Every question below is designed against one rule: ask what someone did, not what they'd do. V1's research repeatedly found organisations measuring intention and satisfaction rather than behaviour (Gotcha4Life's post-only self-report, AIS's "likely to implement," R U OK?'s awareness metrics) — these instruments exist specifically to not repeat that error.

Design rule, applied throughout

Never ask "would you buy this?" or "would you use this?" These questions reliably overstate real demand — this is a well-documented bias in market research, not a novel observation, and it is the same failure mode this whole research programme exists to avoid repeating.

Always prefer: "What did you last do about this?" · "Tell me about the last time X happened." · "Walk me through what happened when you tried Y." Past behaviour is the best available predictor of future behaviour; stated future intention is not.

Instrument 1 — Buyer interview (organisational)

Duration: 30–40 min. Opens with: role, budget scope, and how long they've held it — establishes whether they're actually a decision-maker before spending time on hypothetical questions.

  1. "Tell me about the last time your organisation spent money on staff/member wellbeing, training, or mental health support. What was it, and what prompted it?"
  2. "Walk me through how that decision actually got made — who raised it, who approved it, how long it took."
  3. "What did you compare it against? What else did you look at and not choose?"
  4. "What's the biggest thing you needed to see before you'd sign off on something like that?"
  5. "Has anything you've bought in this space not worked out? What happened, and how did you find out it wasn't working?"
  6. "If a program in this space asked you for evidence before you'd buy it, what would actually satisfy you — a case study, a published study, a trial with your own people, something else?"
  7. "Who else needs to say yes before you can say yes?"
  8. [Only after 1–7] "Here's roughly what we're building — non-clinical, practice-based, adult-focused." [brief, neutral description] "What's your first reaction — and specifically, what would make you say no to it?"

inference Question 8 is placed last and framed to elicit objections, not enthusiasm — deliberately asking "what would make you say no" rather than "would this interest you," per the design rule above.

Instrument 2 — Participant interview (adult, workshop-naive)

Duration: 25–35 min.

  1. "Think of a recent moment where you felt overwhelmed, or knew you should respond differently than you did. Walk me through what happened."
  2. "What did you do about it afterwards, if anything? Did you look anything up, talk to anyone, try to change anything?"
  3. "Have you ever paid for or signed up to something to help with this kind of thing — an app, a course, a book, a workshop? What was it, and what happened to it? Are you still using it?"
  4. "If you stopped using it, what happened — did it stop being useful, did life get in the way, something else?"
  5. "What's the last thing that actually stuck — something you're still doing months later? What made that one different?"
  6. [Message-comprehension items — see Instrument 5]

Instrument 3 — Lost or non-user interview

Duration: 25–35 min. The most important instrument in this file — see 02 on why this population is weighted equally with buyers.

  1. "Tell me about [the specific program/app/workshop they started]. What made you try it in the first place?"
  2. "Walk me through the first week or two — what did you actually do?"
  3. "When did you notice yourself using it less, or thinking about stopping? What was happening in your life at that point?"
  4. "Was there a specific moment it stopped, or did it just fade out?"
  5. "Looking back, what would have needed to be different for you to still be doing it?"
  6. "Did it help at all, even a little, while you were doing it? How would you know?"
  7. "If someone offered you something similar again, what would make you say no this time — and what would make you say yes?"

Instrument 4 — Partner interview (delivery/referral)

Duration: 30–40 min.

  1. "What does your organisation currently do in this space, and how did that come to be the shape it is?"
  2. "Where do you feel the gaps are in what you currently offer or refer people to?"
  3. "Have you partnered with an external org on something like this before? What worked, what didn't?"
  4. "What would you need to see from a new partner before you'd refer to them or co-deliver with them?"
  5. "What's in it for your organisation, concretely, in a partnership like this — reach, credibility, evidence, something else?"
  6. "What would make this a bad idea for you, or for the people you serve?"

Instrument 5 — Category and message-comprehension testing

Design note: present each statement cold, without MFC branding, and ask participants to explain it back in their own words before offering any correction or clarification. The goal is to observe the interpretation that occurs unprompted.

  1. [Show] "Mental health is how we are doing. Mental fitness is what we are able to do." → "In your own words, what does that mean? What's the difference being made here?"
  2. "If I told you mental fitness is a developable capacity — something you can build, like a skill — does that match how you'd naturally think about it? What would you have said instead?"
  3. "Some people say the hard part isn't lacking a skill, it's not being able to access the skill you already have, in the moment you need it. Does that match your experience? Can you give me an example from your own life?"
  4. "What's the difference, if any, between this and things like 'resilience,' 'wellbeing,' 'mental toughness,' or 'positive thinking'? Are these the same thing to you?"
  5. [Show] "A mental rep is catching a moment and choosing your next move, on purpose, toward what matters — the outcome doesn't determine whether it counts." → "What do you make of that? Does 'it still counts even if it doesn't work' make sense to you, or does it sound like an excuse?"
  6. Adverse-interpretation probes — ask directly, don't wait for it to arise spontaneously: - "Does any of this sound like it's saying people are responsible for their own struggles?" - "Does it sound more like therapy, like a gym program, or like something else?" - "If your workplace gave you this, would it feel genuine or like a box-ticking exercise?"

(Full study design, including quantitative phase, is in 06 — this instrument is the qualitative component only.)

Instrument 6 — Product-format testing

Use after Instrument 2 or 3, once rapport is established. Present the four concepts from 04 one at a time, described neutrally (no pricing, no branding), and ask:

  1. "Which part of that would you actually show up for? Which part would you skip?"
  2. "What's missing that you'd need to actually keep doing this?"
  3. "Who else would need to be involved for this to work — a manager, a friend, no one?"
  4. "If this cost something, who do you think should be paying for it — you, your employer, a club, a charity/government program?"

Instrument 7 — Price and willingness-to-pay exploration

Deliberately not a direct "how much would you pay" question — that method is known to be unreliable. Instead:

  1. "What have you actually paid for something in this category before — an app subscription, a course, a workshop, a course of coaching? How much, and was it worth it?"
  2. "What's the most you've walked away from because it felt too expensive? What was the actual number, if you remember?"
  3. [For buyers] "What's the last training or wellbeing line item in your budget, and roughly what did it cost, per person or in total?"
  4. "If two options looked otherwise identical and one was free and one cost money, what would make you trust the paid one more, if anything?"

inference This is designed around the recall-of-past-spend method, which is more reliable than hypothetical willingness-to-pay questions, though still an indirect proxy — a genuine price test would require an actual purchase decision, which is out of scope for this desk-and-interview phase.

What these instruments do not attempt

  • No instrument tests MFC's actual workshop content, materials, or facilitator delivery — that would require participant-facing pilot activity, which is blocked by D-0016 and out of scope for V1.1.
  • No instrument collects identifiable health information.
  • No instrument is administered until Hunter approves recruitment (gate 2) and, for buyers/partners, contact (gate 3).

04 Product Format Test

Product format test — four concepts, not built

These are testable concepts for the research instruments in 03, not designs, prototypes, or approvals. Nothing here modifies the Stage 10 workshop package or D-0017's measurement architecture. Each concept is deliberately under-specified where specification would require product decisions outside V1.1's scope.

Why four, and why these four

inference These four concepts test the dosage and structure question that runs through the whole V1 research: every competitor profiled sells either a single event (Gotcha4Life's workshop, R U OK?'s campaign day) or an ongoing product nobody has evidenced sustains use (Smiling Mind's app, Gotcha4Life's "gym"). V1's international research (RULER, Triple P) shows the field's answer is multi-year, team-based, leadership-anchored delivery — which MFC cannot yet afford to test at that scale. These four concepts span the gap between MFC's current single-session capacity and that evidenced-but-expensive end state.

Concept 1 — Foundational workshop (current state)

Field Detail
Intended customer Whoever currently books MFC — likely a workplace L&D contact or an individual organiser
Intended participant Adults, general population, no prerequisite
Problem addressed Introduces the mental fitness distinction (K-05) and the Radar/Stop-Shift-Do practice, once
Participant experience A single session, in person, as currently built in Stage 10
Duration and dosage One session. unknown exact length — Stage 10 package deliberately leaves pacing flexible per Decision 7
Mechanism Introduce the distinction → introduce the Radar → one practice cycle → one take-home reminder/cue → one follow-up retrieval prompt at 3–4 weeks (per the existing Stage 10 design)
Deliverables Workshop delivery, participant take-home materials
Evidence requirement Lowest of the four — matches the NSW principal-checklist bar of "clear outcomes" identified in V1 (07-market-access-and-procurement.md)
Pricing logic unknown — no MFC pricing was located in the files reviewed; comparable single-session Australian offers range from free (AIS) to several thousand dollars per session (see 05)
Delivery-cost drivers Facilitator time and travel; no ongoing cost
Risks This is the exact format V1 found evidence against — Broad & Newstrom's finding that skills decay within six months absent ongoing support (documented in V1's behaviour-change review), and the training-transfer literature generally
What must be tested before development Nothing — this format already exists. The open question is whether it should remain the only format sold, given the evidence above

Concept 2 — Workshop plus 8–12 week practice system

Field Detail
Intended customer A buyer willing to commit beyond a single event — likely workplace L&D with a training budget cycle, or a sport club pre-season
Intended participant Same adults as Concept 1, now with a sustained-engagement layer
Problem addressed Directly answers V1's finding that "everyone claimed the gym, nobody built it" (Gotcha4Life's 8% conversion; Smiling Mind's unpublished retention)
Participant experience Workshop as in Concept 1, then a structured 8–12 week period of prompted practice — matched to Lally et al.'s median 66 days to habit automaticity, cited in V1's measurement research
Duration and dosage 8–12 weeks post-workshop. proposal — no evidence base yet specifies optimal cadence within that window; this is a design assumption to test, not a finding
Mechanism Existing Radar/rep structure, extended with periodic prompts (format unknown — SMS, email, app — not decided here) and the skill-use-rate measurement approach identified in V1's measurement file (10-measurement-white-space.md)
Deliverables Workshop + structured follow-up cadence + an evaluation instrument (see 07 for candidates)
Evidence requirement Higher — this format is where the field's evidence gap (no dose-response curve for adult mental fitness training) is most directly addressed, and where MFC's differentiator claim actually needs to be tested
Pricing logic unknown — likely higher than Concept 1 given the added delivery burden; no comparable Australian adult pricing was located in this task's desk research (see 05)
Delivery-cost drivers Facilitator time for the workshop, plus whatever system delivers the 8–12 week prompts — cost scales with whether that layer is human-facilitated or automated
Risks Reactivity (V1 flagged this for EMA specifically — prompting about practice may itself increase practice, confounding any resulting evidence); attrition over the 8–12 week window; cost of sustaining engagement without a person driving it
What must be tested before development Whether adults will actually engage with a multi-week follow-up at all (Instrument 6 in 03 tests this directly) — this is the single highest-priority question for primary research, because the whole concept depends on an unverified assumption

Concept 3 — Organisational package with environmental/manager supports

Field Detail
Intended customer An organisational buyer able to commit management involvement, not just individual attendance
Intended participant Employees/members, plus their direct manager or team lead as a distinct, separate participant
Problem addressed Directly answers the structural seam identified across three V1 files (06, 12, 13) — that K-04 names environment and support as determinants of access while the current intervention is purely individual
Participant experience Manager/leader training precedes or runs parallel to participant workshops — mirroring the adults-first sequencing found in RULER, Penn's MRT, and Geelong Grammar (all documented in V1's international file)
Duration and dosage unknown — depends on the manager-training component's scope, which is not specified here (see 09 for the structural requirements this concept must satisfy, without redesigning them)
Mechanism As Concept 1 or 2, plus a parallel or preceding manager stream and, potentially, environmental cues in the workplace itself
Deliverables Participant workshop, manager/leader session, any physical or digital environmental materials
Evidence requirement Highest of the four — this is the format most exposed to the WHS psychosocial-hazard critique documented in V1 (training cannot substitute for work redesign), so it carries the greatest risk of an unsupportable claim if not carefully bounded
Pricing logic unknown — likely a premium format given added delivery complexity; comparable pricing not located
Delivery-cost drivers Two delivery streams (participant + manager) instead of one; highest facilitator-time cost of the four concepts
Risks The single largest risk in this file: a buyer purchasing this format under the belief it discharges a WHS psychosocial duty. V1's finding that "training sits at the bottom of the hierarchy of controls" applies most directly here. Any go-forward on this concept requires an explicit, written claims boundary (K-08-adjacent, not resolved in this task)
What must be tested before development Whether organisational buyers actually want or will fund a manager-inclusive format, versus preferring the cheaper individual-only version — Instrument 1 in 03 tests this directly, particularly item 7 ("who else needs to say yes")

Concept 4 — Measurement-led pilot

Field Detail
Intended customer A funder, academic partner, or early-adopter organisation motivated by evidence-generation rather than immediate wellbeing delivery — e.g. a philanthropic funder identified in V1's funding file, or a university partner from the measurement file
Intended participant A smaller, deliberately recruited cohort willing to complete extended measurement (STEM-B/CompACT-15 pre-post, plus SEMA3 event-contingent EMA — all identified as candidates in V1's 10-measurement-white-space.md)
Problem addressed Directly builds the evidence base V1 identified as MFC's largest strategic opportunity — nobody in the field has a dose-response curve or a behavioural measure of skill enactment
Participant experience Workshop (Concept 1 or 2) plus a research-grade measurement burden — additional surveys and EMA prompts, explained and consented to as research participation, not as the product itself
Duration and dosage Matches whichever base format (1 or 2) it's paired with, plus the measurement period
Mechanism As Concept 1 or 2, with the added instrumentation
Deliverables Workshop delivery + a completed evaluation dataset + (if partnered per 10) a co-authored or co-owned research output
Evidence requirement This is the evidence-generation format — the requirement is methodological rigour (pre-registration, an arm's-length evaluator, as recommended in V1) rather than a pre-existing evidence bar to clear
Pricing logic unknown and likely different in kind, not just amount — this format may be funded as research (grant, philanthropy) rather than sold as a service, per the funding channels identified in V1's 11-funding-regulation-and-workforce.md
Delivery-cost drivers Facilitator time as in the base format, plus ethics approval, instrument licensing (though the leading candidates are free), and analysis capacity MFC does not currently have internally
Risks Recruitment difficulty (a measurement-heavy pilot is a harder sell to participants than a straightforward workshop) and the reactivity/attrition risks already noted for EMA in V1
What must be tested before development Whether an academic or funding partner is actually willing to co-invest — this is a partnership question (10), not a product question, and is the actual gating item for this concept

Cross-cutting notes

  • None of these concepts has been built, priced, or approved. They exist to be shown to research participants (Instrument 6, 03) in neutral terms, without branding or pricing, to see which one people would actually engage with.
  • inference Concepts 2 and 4 are not mutually exclusive with 1 and 3 — the likely real product architecture is a base workshop (1) with either a practice layer (2), an organisational layer (3), or a measurement layer (4) added depending on the buyer. This file deliberately does not resolve that architecture question, since doing so would constitute product design, which is out of scope.
  • Concept 3 carries a claims risk that the others do not and should not proceed to any external testing without the K-08-adjacent boundary work flagged above being addressed first.

05 Commercial And Buyer Pathway Model

Commercial and buyer pathway model

A minimum evaluation framework, not a business plan. No price is set here. Where evidence is unavailable, the field is marked unknown rather than estimated — per explicit instruction.

The framework, by segment

Field Workplaces Sport (SSO/grant) Community (PHN/grant) Direct-to-adult
Buyer HR/WHS/L&D, unclear which — unknown split SSO administrators, or a joint SSO/government grant panel PHN commissioning teams (tender); council grant officers; philanthropic panel (FRRR) The individual
User Employees Club members/staff Community members Same as buyer
Budget source Operating budget, unclear compliance vs culture line NSW Mental Health Sports Fund (verified: up to $150,000/grant, $2.8M pool) or club/SSO operating funds PHN commissioning budget (competitive); council community grants ($1,000–$150,000 range, most under $15,000); FRRR (up to $20,000/project, $240,000+/round) Personal discretionary spend
Purchasing pathway unknown — not established by desk research Grant application (documented, open channel) Competitive tender (PHN) or grant application (council/FRRR) Direct booking/purchase
Procurement period unknown Grant round cycles — unknown exact cadence for NSW Mental Health Sports Fund specifically PHN tender cycles typically longer than grant rounds; council/FRRR rounds recurring, unknown exact frequency Immediate, no institutional cycle
Substitute spend, where verifiable EAP: $30–$80/employee/year basic; some from $7.99/employee/month; counselling ~$40/hour (all vendor-published, not audited) unknown — no comparable per-participant sport-sector figure located unknown MHFA: $220–$462+/participant. Headspace app: $12.99–$19.99/month. Smiling Mind: free
Acceptable pricing research method Recall-of-past-spend (Instrument 7, 03) — not hypothetical willingness-to-pay Same Same Same
Facilitator requirements unknown beyond what Stage 10's existing facilitator specification already covers Same Same Same
Operational/delivery capacity Bounded by current founder/facilitator capacity — no change from V1's finding Same Same Same
Gross-margin inputs unknown — MFC has no published pricing to calculate against. Industry facilitator day-rate benchmarks found: $500–$2,000/half-day (entry), $2,000–$7,500/workshop (mid), up to $10,000+ (expert/keynote) — vendor-published, single-sourced, needs a second source before use in a financial model. MHFA-specific instructor economics (closer analogue): day rates $900–$1,800; instructor nets ~$60–$150 per participant after materials/admin — single-blog-sourced, same caveat Same cost base likely applies
Renewal mechanism unknown Grant re-application, not a renewing commercial relationship — structurally different from a repeat sale PHN/council: re-application. FRRR: repeat rounds exist but per-project, not automatic renewal unknown
Sponsorship or grant dependency unknown for MFC specifically. Comparable orgs show both models work: Smiling Mind (~$14M revenue per third-party aggregator, free-to-consumer, cross-subsidised) and MHFA (~$6.2M revenue per third-party aggregator, fee-for-service, credential-driven) — both figures from aggregators (Tracxn, Growjo), not primary ACNC filings; verify against ACNC Annual Information Statements before use in any formal document Segment is structurally grant-dependent by design (this is how the sector's funding is organised, not a weakness specific to MFC) Mixed — PHN funded, philanthropy-funded, or fee-for-service depending on channel chosen Depends entirely on whether MFC adopts a free-access or fee-for-service model — unresolved
Sales/adoption risk Highest — no established purchasing trigger found; genuine risk that HR/culture budget is separate from and smaller than WHS compliance budget, which MFC's non-compliance offer cannot draw on Grant-cycle risk (funding not guaranteed to renew); credibility risk (unproven track record vs an evidently competitive/relationship-based grant process) Tender competitiveness risk; MFC's lack of an evaluated program may be a real barrier per V1's evidence-gating finding Sustainability risk — neither of the two working patterns found (free+cross-subsidy, paid+credential) obviously fits MFC's current offer

What this file establishes and does not

Establishes: a comparable structure across four segments, using only verified or explicitly-labelled figures, so that whichever segment Hunter selects can be evaluated on the same dimensions.

Does not establish: a price for MFC's offer, a revenue projection, a margin calculation, or a recommendation. Every gross-margin and pricing cell above is either unknown or drawn from single, unaudited third-party sources flagged as needing verification — none of it should be used in a funding application or board paper without independent confirmation.

The clearest finding in this file

evidence-supported inference The sport segment's grant pathway (NSW Mental Health Sports Fund) is the only one of the four with a named, government-administered, currently-described funding mechanism explicitly open to external-provider partnerships. Every other segment's purchasing pathway is either unknown (workplace), competitively gated with an unproven track record as a likely barrier (community/PHN), or structurally ambiguous on sustainability (direct-to-adult). This does not make sport the recommended segment — that synthesis belongs in 11 — but it is the single most concrete commercial fact this research produced.

06 Category Comprehension Study Plan

Category comprehension study plan

A design, not a launched study — reconsidered and held, 2026-08-05. Briefly marked "commissioned" the same day, then reversed within the hour: Hunter's own words, "I don't think we need to test it like that as I've been testing it every day with people I speak with and refined and refined it." His continuous, informal real-world conversation testing is the validation channel in use — a formal structured study (recruited strangers, cognitive-interview script, coded transcripts) is not currently judged to add enough over that to be worth commissioning. This file stays as a ready design, not active work, unless Hunter revisits it.

Why this study matters more than it looks

V1's category-coherence audit (13-category-coherence.md) found that SWM-13— "the category claim assumes the public experiences a knowing–doing gap in these terms... untested externally" — is correct and understated. It also found that Smiling Mind ran the adjacent study, surveyed 900 Australians, found people conflate "mental health" with "mental illness," published it, and repositioned their whole organisation on it.

Correction, 2026-08-05: this file previously also said the finding was "converted... into $3.3M of federal funding" — false, verified against the primary source. That $3.3M was announced 29 April 2022, over two years before the 2024 repositioning, for the Schools Program's existing reach — unrelated to this study. See 09-five-page-findings.md's correction for detail. Doesn't change why this study is worth doing (a citable comprehension stat, informing MFC's own wording) — just removes an inaccurate funding-outcome claim.

inference This study is not a nice-to-have communications check. It is the single research activity most likely to convert MFC's category position from an assumption into an evidenced claim — closing SWM-13 and SWM-22 directly, and giving MFC a citable asset the way Smiling Mind's stigma study became one.

What is being tested

Seven specific claims, each drawn directly from MFC's own controlled kernel or internal framework language:

# Claim Source
1 "Mental health is how we are doing." K-05
2 "Mental fitness is what we are able to do." K-05
3 Mental fitness as a "developable capacity" K-04 evidence definition
4 The access gap — skills being easier or harder to access in the moment Internal framework; V1 found this is a defensible translation of established psychology (Tulving 1966, Sheppes 2011) but untested as public messaging
5 "Mental reps" Internal framework
6 Outcome-independent practice — "the outcome does not determine whether it counts" Internal framework; V1's prior-art audit (12) flagged this as MFC's strongest unclaimed asset, making it worth testing carefully
7 The distinction from resilience, wellbeing, mental toughness, therapy and positive thinking Not currently stated anywhere in MFC's public materials, per V1's finding that the public site carries none of this framing

Adverse interpretations to test explicitly

inference — each grounded in a specific V1 finding, not a generic communications caution:

Adverse interpretation Why it's a live risk, per V1
Personal blame V1's prior-art file found K-04 lists power, safety, environment and support as determinants of access, while the intervention is purely individual — "a seam three separate critiques converge on." The individualisation critique (University of Auckland, cited in V1's international file) is unanswered by anyone in the field
Toughness or optimisation The Comprehensive Soldier Fitness precedent (V1's international file) shows this exact framing drew sustained academic attack for scaling a fitness metaphor without addressing this risk first
"Brain muscle" claims K-04 explicitly states "the mind is not a muscle" — but V1 verified MFC's own public website currently uses "mental muscles" language, directly contradicting the locked kernel. This adverse interpretation is not hypothetical; it is already live on MFC's own site
Clinical misunderstanding Multiple competitors profiled in V1 (MensLine, AIS) conflate mental fitness with mental health messaging; testing whether the Australian public does the same is directly relevant to whether K-05's distinction actually lands
Corporate-wellbeing superficiality V1's WHS regulation file found real, evidenced public scepticism (Fleming 2024, n=46,336) toward individual-level workplace wellbeing interventions specifically
Implying control over all circumstances or outcomes Connects to the same individualisation risk; K-04's own boundary statement ("not a promise that people will never struggle") is the intended answer, but it is not yet tested for whether it actually reads that way to a naive respondent

Phase design

Qualitative phase (proposed first)

proposal - Method: cognitive interviewing / think-aloud protocol — respondents read each statement aloud and narrate their interpretation before any clarification is offered, matching Instrument 5 in 03. - Sample: 12–15 adults, deliberately diverse on age, gender, and prior exposure to wellbeing/mental health messaging (some workshop-naive, some with prior EAP/therapy/app experience) — comprehension is likely to vary by prior exposure, and averaging across a homogeneous sample would hide that. - Purpose: surface interpretations MFC has not anticipated, refine wording, and identify which of the seven claims above are intuitive versus which need more scaffolding than a single sentence can provide.

Quantitative phase (proposed second, contingent on qualitative findings)

proposal - Method: structured survey, likely using a comprehension-check format (e.g. "in your own words" free text, coded post-hoc, plus forced-choice items distinguishing mental fitness from the five adjacent constructs in claim 7). - Sample: large enough for basic subgroup comparison (age, gender, prior exposure) — unknown exact n, this is a design decision for whoever executes, informed by the qualitative phase's findings on variance. - Purpose: establish whether the qualitative findings generalise, and produce the citable population-level statistic Smiling Mind's study achieved (e.g. "X% of Australians surveyed correctly distinguished mental fitness from mental health without prompting").

Neither phase is launched by this file. Commissioning requires Hunter's gate-8 approval.

What this study would and would not establish

Would establish proposal: whether the category language is intuitively comprehensible to a naive Australian adult, which specific phrases produce adverse interpretations, and (if the quantitative phase runs) a population-level baseline MFC could cite the way Smiling Mind cites its 900-person study.

Would not establish: whether the program works, whether participants who understand the language actually change behaviour, or whether the category is more compelling than a competitor's framing head-to-head (that would require a comparative test, not specified here).

07 Measurement Construct Closure

Measurement construct closure

This file does not reopen or modify D-0017. It closes open questions from V1's measurement research (10-measurement-white-space.md) and, in doing so, revises one of V1's findings. That revision is flagged prominently below and should be read before anyone acts on V1's original recommendation.

⚠ Revision to V1: STEM-B and EMA are weaker change-sensitivity candidates than first reported

V1 identified STEM-B and event-contingent EMA (via SEMA3) as strong candidates specifically because they might be sensitive to change — able to detect a program's effect. Closure research this task located the actual intervention evidence, and it does not support that confidence.

STEM-B — a properly powered RCT (n=448 randomised, 326 completers; web-based emotional-skills training vs matched placebo) found no significant group × time interaction on STEM-B immediately post-training (F(1,363)=0.28, p=.600, ηp²=0.00). A weak effect appeared only at 6-month follow-up (p=.05, ηp²=0.01) as a retention pattern, not an acute training effect.

evidence-supported inference STEM-B has been tested as a pre/post outcome measure once, in an adequately powered trial, and it failed to detect an acute program effect. This does not disqualify STEM-B as a capability measure — but it means MFC should not assume it will show short-horizon program effects.

Event-contingent EMA (SEMA3 or equivalent) — the JMIR 2025;27:e69297 paper (Webb et al., secondary analysis of 4 app-based meditation trials, N=412) was retrieved in full this time. Its actual finding: conventional retrospective self-report detected a larger intervention effect (Cohen's d = 0.37) than EMA did (d = 0.14), and EMA change-score reliability was materially lower (ρ=.50–.77) than self-report change-score reliability (ρ=.71–.90), with no significant correlation between the two methods' change scores.

evidence-supported inference This directly contradicts the assumption that EMA is the more change-sensitive method. The authors' own conclusion is that EMA and self-report provide distinct information, not that EMA is superior for detecting intervention effects. MFC's candidacy for SEMA3 as "the" change-sensitive behavioural measure should now be treated as unproven, not confirmed.

What still holds from V1, on construct grounds alone (not change-sensitivity): the state-vs-capability distinction is unaffected by this revision. WHO-5, K10 and SWEMWBS still measure state, not capability, regardless of how STEM-B or EMA perform. The case for moving away from WHO-5 as the sole primary instrument stands. The case for STEM-B or EMA as the automatic replacement is now weaker and requires MFC's own pilot data before being trusted.

A. Measuring the overall mental-fitness construct

unknown, closed as fully as bounded desk research allows. Robinson's 2014 UOW PhD thesis was located (ro.uow.edu.au/theses/4269) but direct retrieval returned a 403; its companion peer-reviewed output — Robinson, Oades & Caputi (2015), International Journal of Wellbeing — was fetched in full.

Verified fact: the 2015 Delphi study is a purely conceptual/definitional consensus study, not a psychometric scale-development study. Two-round Delphi, international expert panel (n=25), evaluating a proposed definition and four guiding principles. No scale was developed, no items were written or piloted, and no reliability or validity statistics exist in this output. The paper's own framing states there are "no consistent theoretical foundations, models or reliable and valid measures" for mental fitness.

This closes the question definitively: there is no validated Robinson mental-fitness scale to source or benchmark against. It was never built, not merely unfound.

evidence-supported inference This strengthens, not weakens, the strategic case in V1's category-coherence file (13). The construct is orphaned in exactly the sense claimed — the field's best available expert-consensus definition has never been operationalised into a measure. Whoever builds that measure first genuinely has no existing instrument to compete against for the overall construct.

Whether a new construct measure is needed: evidence-supported inference — yes, if MFC wants to measure "mental fitness" as a whole construct (as distinct from measuring the enactment of a specific practice, see Part B). Nothing reviewed in either V1 or this closure pass supplies one.

B. Measuring real-world enactment of a mental rep — the behavioural question

This is a narrower, more tractable question than Part A, and it is where MFC's own Stage 10 measurement design already has a head start (identified in V1: the "did you attempt a rep?" / "did any of those moments come up?" numerator/denominator pair).

Should skill-use rate be treated as a behavioural outcome rather than a validated construct measure?

evidence-supported inference Yes — and this closure research makes that distinction sharper than V1 left it. A construct measure (like STEM-B or a hypothetical mental-fitness scale) aims to estimate a stable underlying capacity. Skill-use rate is not that — it is a count of observed behaviour (reps attempted ÷ opportunities that arose), closer in kind to a rehabilitation adherence log than to a psychometric scale. Treating it as a behavioural outcome, not a construct measure, is the methodologically correct framing, and it sidesteps the change-sensitivity uncertainty just raised for STEM-B and EMA — a behavioural count does not need to be "sensitive to change" in the same statistical sense a trait scale does; it simply needs to be reliably countable.

Instrument-by-instrument assessment

Instrument What it measures Psychometric strength Change-sensitivity evidence Burden Fit with K-04/K-05
STEM-B Performance-based capacity (situational judgement of emotion management) Strong on development (IRT-derived) Mixed/negative — one adequately powered RCT found no acute pre-post effect; weak follow-up effect only 18 items, ~10–15 min (inference) Good conceptual fit (capacity, not state) but empirically unproven for acute change detection
CompACT-15 Perceived capacity/process — openness, behavioural awareness, valued action Good — CFA-confirmed, longitudinal measurement invariance in a UK general-population sample; also validated across clinical, community, military and older-adult samples unknown — no intervention pre/post effect-size data located in this pass 15 items, likely 3–5 min (inference; no source gives an exact time) Moderate — self-reported, not directly observed, but the best cross-population evidence of the three candidates and closest existing fit to a general adult population
WHO-5 Subjective wellbeing/state Strong, extremely widely validated Yes, for state/mood 5 items, ~1 min Poor — measures state, not capability (V1 finding reaffirmed)
K10 / SWEMWBS Psychological distress / mental wellbeing state Strong, population-normed Yes, for state/distress 10 / 7 items Poor — same state/capability mismatch
SEMA3 (EMA) Momentary affect/behaviour, in situ Good design flexibility; level-score reliability high, change-score reliability notably weaker (ρ=.50–.77 in the cited trial) Weaker than V1 assumed — the one directly retrieved 4-trial analysis found conventional self-report outperformed EMA on effect size (d=0.37 vs 0.14) Low per-prompt, high cumulative burden; 72–80% compliance in the cited trial Good structural fit for capturing behaviour in situ, but the strongest available evidence now argues against assuming superior change-sensitivity

Should WHO-5 remain as a secondary contrast or safety measure?

proposal — yes, and this closure pass does not disturb that recommendation. Nothing here changes the finding that WHO-5 measures the wrong side of K-05's distinction as a primary outcome. It remains defensible as a secondary measure precisely because it is what funders and evaluators already recognise, and because a state measure alongside a behavioural one lets MFC show it is not ignoring wellbeing while still centring capability. This file does not reopen D-0017 to make that change — it is recorded here as evidence for whoever does.

What this closure pass changes about V1's recommendation

V1 said This closure finds Net effect
STEM-B + CompACT-15 + SEMA3-EMA is a fundable, credible measurement package STEM-B and EMA both have direct evidence against assumed change-sensitivity; CompACT-15's evidence is silent but its cross-population validation is the strongest of the three CompACT-15 becomes the safer initial default among the three; STEM-B and EMA should be piloted, not presumed
Skill-use rate is the differentiating, unclaimed measurement asset Confirmed and sharpened — it should be explicitly framed as a behavioural outcome, not a construct measure, which is methodologically cleaner and avoids inheriting the change-sensitivity uncertainty above Strengthened, with a clearer justification
No validated mental-fitness scale exists Confirmed with certainty — Robinson's thesis never produced one Confirmed, not merely still-unknown

08 Outcome Independent Rep Prior Art Closure

Outcome-independent-rep prior art closure

A bounded, second-pass search across ten specific literatures, closing the question V1's prior-art audit (12-stop-shift-do-prior-art.md) left open with a first-pass "no equivalent found."

The verdict

No equivalent was identified in the reviewed evidence of a formally operationalised, explicitly outcome-independent, countable unit of practice matching MFC's rep as precisely as MFC's rep is defined — a discrete, loggable unit where "catching a moment and choosing your next move, on purpose, toward what matters" is the counting criterion, independent of the downstream result.

This uses the bounded phrasing your brief specified, deliberately — the search was ten literatures, English-language, primarily open-access sources. It is not a claim of universal novelty.

The ten literatures, closest citation and verdict

# Literature Closest citation What it actually says Closeness to MFC's rep
1 Deliberate practice Ericsson, Krampe & Tesch-Römer (1993) Requires feedback-corrected success, not attempt-only counting. The unit of value is the feedback-correction cycle, not the raw attempt Low. Opposite structure — DP needs outcome-linked correction to count
2 Process goals (sport) Kingston & Hardy (1997) About attentional focus and self-efficacy; reduces cognitive anxiety versus outcome goals — but no source states a process goal is logged as complete irrespective of the outcome Moderate. Conceptually adjacent, no evidence of an outcome-independent counting operationalisation
3 Exposure therapy / inhibitory learning Craske, Treanor, Conway, Zbozinek & Vervliet (2014) The inhibitory-learning model explicitly does not require anxiety reduction during a trial for it to count — some strategies deliberately maintain elevated fear. The trial is valuable for the learning it generates, independent of symptom outcome High. A genuine structural cousin
4 Behavioural activation Jacobson, Martell & Dimidjian (2001) Explicitly separates activity completion from mood outcome via self-monitoring of the activity–mood link — the tracked unit is whether the activity occurred; mood is a separate, secondary observation High. The closest structural match found
5 ACT and committed action Hayes, Luoma, Bond, Masuda & Lillis (2006) "Workability" — not outcome success — governs whether to persist or pivot in a values-aligned action. Primary-source exact quote not retrieved (paywalled); synthesis from secondary description High — plausibly the closest match, though not confirmed against primary text
6 Rehabilitation adherence General adherence-measurement literature (2024 scoping review) Attendance/attempt-based counting is common practice, but it is a measurement convention, not a values-based rationale — thinner conceptual grounding than BA/ACT/exposure Moderate-high structurally, weaker conceptually
7 Habit lapse and recovery (Abstinence Violation Effect) Marlatt & Gordon (1985) Reframes a lapse's meaning — a harm-reduction reinterpretation of a negative outcome, not a redefinition of what "counts" as a completed unit Low-moderate. Closest conceptual, not structural, cousin
8 Self-compassion Neff (2003; 2022 review) "Common humanity" reframes failure as shared human experience — a post-hoc emotional response to failure, not a definition of a countable unit Low-moderate. Same category as AVE
9 Growth mindset / effort praise Mueller & Dweck (1998) Process praise is well-documented as attitudinal/motivational. No evidence found of a formal "counts regardless of outcome" scoring or logging system anywhere in Dweck's work Low as a countable unit, moderate as attitude — confirms V1's "close cousin" framing but the closure search confirms it stops at attitude
10 Implementation intentions Gollwitzer & Brandstätter (1997); Gollwitzer & Sheeran (2006) Discusses ceiling effects on whether if-then plans work, concentrated on getting-started problems. No concept found of a "failed but still credited" implementation intention — the outcome variable is whether the behaviour occurred Low. No equivalent identified

The closest three, ranked

  1. Behavioural activation's activity-log-vs-mood-monitoring separation (Jacobson, Martell & Dimidjian, 2001) — a completed, loggable unit (the scheduled activity) whose "count" is independent of a separately tracked outcome (mood). Embedded in a clinical depression-treatment protocol, not isolated as its own standalone user-facing practice unit.
  2. Craske et al.'s (2014) inhibitory-learning exposure trials — a trial "counts" for its learning value regardless of whether anxiety dropped. Embedded in exposure-therapy protocol design, again not extracted as a standalone construct.
  3. ACT's committed action / workability (Hayes et al., 2006) — close conceptually, already flagged in V1's first-pass audit. This closure pass could not confirm the exact "counts regardless of outcome" wording against Hayes's primary text (paywalled), so treat this match as slightly less certain than the other two.

None of these three is packaged as a discrete, self-report-loggable "rep" the way MFC's construct is — each is embedded in a broader clinical protocol rather than isolated as its own standalone practice unit carrying that specific outcome-independence framing.

The safest defensible MFC claim

"No equivalent operationalised, standalone, outcome-independent practice unit was identified in the reviewed evidence — though closely related mechanisms exist in behavioural activation, exposure therapy's inhibitory-learning model, and ACT's committed action, each embedded within a broader clinical protocol rather than extracted as an independent construct."

proposal This is the phrasing recommended for any public or funder-facing use. MFC should not claim to have originated the underlying insight — behavioural activation and inhibitory-learning exposure got there first, decades ago, in clinical contexts. What appears genuinely available is the extraction and naming: taking a mechanism that exists inside clinical protocols and making it a standalone, teachable, countable unit for a non-clinical general population.

Should MFC claim originality at all?

evidence-supported inference — No, not of the underlying mechanism. Yes, cautiously, of the specific operationalisation and framing, provided the three closest citations above are named alongside the claim, not omitted. This mirrors the recommendation already made in V1's prior-art file regarding the Radar and Gollwitzer: cite the lineage, claim the packaging.

Testable mechanisms — how attempt-based counting might support persistence

proposal, for a future research or pilot design, not tested here:

  1. Removing the pass/fail dynamic reduces avoidance. If a rep only "counts" on success, a person who anticipates failure has an incentive to avoid attempting at all — this is the mechanism behavioural activation's activity-log model is designed to counter (a scheduled activity is logged regardless of mood outcome, which keeps the person engaging with the process). evidence-supported inference from BA's design rationale.
  2. Outcome-independence may reduce the intensity of a single lapse, by analogy with the Abstinence Violation Effect literature — if a missed or "failed" rep doesn't invalidate the practice, a single bad moment is less likely to trigger disengagement from the whole practice. This is a conceptual analogy, not a tested mechanism for MFC's specific construct.
  3. Attempt-logging may function similarly to exposure therapy's inhibitory-learning trials — the value is in what the moment teaches (about the self, the situation, the available responses), independent of whether the "right" response occurred. If true, this would predict that rep frequency, not rep "success," should track with skill development over time — a testable hypothesis for MFC's eventual measurement work (see 07).

None of these three mechanisms has been tested for MFC's specific rep construct. They are transplanted hypotheses from adjacent literatures, offered as candidate explanations worth designing a pilot around, not established findings.
