09 Structural And Collective Product Requirements

Structural and collective product requirements

This file translates a tension into requirements. It does not redesign the current workshop, and no requirement here is authorised for implementation.

The tension, stated precisely

K-04's boundary statement:

"What a person can access changes with health, state, previous learning, habits, relationships, support, environment, power, safety, and the demands of the situation."

MFC's current intervention is a single individual-level workshop. It teaches a practice (the Radar, Stop-Shift-Do) that the individual is expected to deploy in moments shaped by factors — environment, power, safety, support — that the workshop itself does not touch.

V1 identified this same tension independently in three files, from three different directions:

  • 06 (adjacent fields): the WHS psychosocial hierarchy of controls places training below work redesign — a structural argument that individual-level intervention cannot substitute for environmental fix.
  • 12 (prior-art audit): "a seam critics will find quickly" — the access-gap framing lists structural determinants but intervenes only individually.
  • 13 (category coherence): "near-total individualisation" across every competitor in the category, and Robinson's own expert panel flagged a workplace discrimination hazard in judging individuals' "mental fitness" without addressing this.

Three independent lines of evidence converging on one unresolved design question is a strong signal, not a coincidence.

What this file does and does not do

Does: translate the tension into a checklist of possible future product requirements, organised by who or what they would apply to, each with the evidence basis and the open question attached.

Does not: decide which requirements MFC should adopt, specify how they would be delivered, or alter the Stage 10 workshop package or D-0017's measurement architecture in any way.

Possible requirements, by target

Managers

Possible requirement Evidence basis Open question
A manager/leader stream, separate from the participant stream, preceding or parallel to it V1's international file: RULER, Penn's MRT, and Geelong Grammar all independently converged on training the adults around a person before training the person — described in V1 as "as close to a settled design principle as this field has" Whether MFC has the delivery capacity for a second stream at all — this is a capacity question, tested in 05, not a design question
A named, bounded scope for what a manager is asked to do (e.g. "notice and encourage," not "diagnose or treat") The individualisation critique and the WHS hierarchy both suggest that asking managers to fix environment without formal authority to do so would recreate the same structural failure at one remove unknown — not tested against any buyer or manager in this task

Facilitators

Possible requirement Evidence basis Open question
A defined escalation and referral boundary, separate from and consistent with D-0016's safeguarding work V1's workforce file: the lived-experience peer-workforce precedent shows scope-of-practice boundaries are "the whole game" for a non-clinical workforce operating near real distress This connects to, but must not duplicate or reopen, D-0016's existing safeguarding validation package — flagged as a dependency, not resolved here
Explicit training in not individualising a participant's stated environmental barriers (e.g. a participant naming an unsafe or unsupportive workplace) Direct application of K-04's own boundary text — "not a way to blame people for... unsafe environments, or lack of support" Whether this is already covered in Stage 10's facilitator guide — unknown, not reviewed line-by-line in this bounded task

Teams / collective practice

Possible requirement Evidence basis Open question
A shared, visible practice artefact at the team level (not just individual take-home materials) V1's international file: RULER's Charter and Mood Meter are explicitly team/room-level artefacts, not individual worksheets — "leave behind reusable objects, not remembered ideas" Whether this is feasible without redesigning the current individual-focused Stage 10 materials — out of scope here
A daily shared ritual, socially witnessed The US Army's Master Resilience Training "Hunt the Good Stuff" — a daily gratitude practice shared aloud each morning — documented in V1 as making reps "social and public" Whether a charity workshop context (one-off, mixed strangers) can support this the way an intact team can — unknown

Organisational conditions

Possible requirement Evidence basis Open question
A pre-engagement check on whether basic environmental conditions are in place (e.g. workload, psychological safety) before selling the individual-facing product Direct response to the WHS finding that training cannot substitute for work redesign, and the risk (flagged in 04, Concept 3) of a buyer purchasing MFC's offer believing it discharges a psychosocial duty This is close to a claims-boundary question (K-08-adjacent) more than a product question — noted, not resolved
A standard, written statement to every organisational buyer: MFC's offer does not discharge, satisfy or substitute for any WHS psychosocial duty V1's regulation file made this recommendation directly This is a claims decision requiring committee-level sign-off, not something V1.1 can authorise

Environmental prompts

Possible requirement Evidence basis Open question
Physical or digital cues in the participant's actual environment (not just a take-home reminder card) Gollwitzer's implementation-intention literature (cited extensively in V1's prior-art file) — cue accessibility is the mechanism, and an environmental cue is stronger than a remembered one Whether this constitutes a new instrument or deliverable, which would exceed V1.1's scope ("do not create a new validated instrument")

Workload and job-design boundaries

Possible requirement Evidence basis Open question
An explicit statement of what MFC's offer is not responsible for fixing — workload, scheduling, role clarity, procedural justice (the named psychosocial hazards from V1's regulation file) Direct application of the hierarchy-of-controls finding This is the same claims-boundary question as above, not duplicated as a separate requirement

Referral and escalation boundaries

Possible requirement Evidence basis Open question
A single, consistent referral pathway used across every product format in 04, not designed separately per format D-0016 already names this as one of six unresolved matters blocking pilot-ready approval This file does not attempt to resolve it. It notes that whatever V1.1's research surfaces about buyer and participant expectations should feed into the existing D-0016 process, not create a parallel one

Safeguards against individual blame

Possible requirement Evidence basis Open question
Explicit language, tested via the comprehension study (06), confirming that K-04's existing boundary statement actually prevents the blame interpretation in practice, not just on paper V1's finding that the individualisation critique "has no good published answer from anyone in the field," and that K-04's boundary is MFC's best available answer but is untested This is precisely what 06's adverse-interpretation testing is designed to check — the two files are directly linked

The honest summary

inference None of these requirements is validated. All of them are plausible responses to a real, independently-corroborated tension. The single most important open question across all of them is whether MFC's current individual-only delivery model can absorb a structural/collective layer without a full product redesign — which this file is explicitly not authorised to undertake.

The nearest-term, lowest-cost action available is the claims-boundary statement (organisational conditions, row 2) — it requires no product change, only a written commitment, and it is the one item here that several V1 files independently recommend regardless of which product format MFC eventually pursues.

10 Partnership And Ecosystem Map

Partnership and ecosystem map

No contact has been made with any organisation or individual named in this file. All information is drawn from public institutional sources. Approach is deliberately institutional (department, centre, or organisation contact points), not personal.

⚠ Correction to the brief's assumptions

Two factual corrections surfaced during this research, worth flagging before the map itself:

  1. Lindsay Oades is at the University of Melbourne, not the University of Sydney. He directs the Centre for Wellbeing Science, Faculty of Education, University of Melbourne (a centre originally founded by Lea Waters). His earlier career (1996–2015) was at the University of Wollongong. He has no current University of Sydney affiliation.
  2. "Robinson" of the Delphi study is most consistently identified as Dr Paula Robinson, not "Trish/Patricia Robinson." If a different Robinson was intended, verify the first name before any approach — this correction is carried forward from the desk research, not independently re-verified against the original 2015 paper's author list in this file.

University of Sydney remains correctly associated with Carolyn MacCann (STEM/STEU), so the "Sydney" institutional link in V1 and V1.1's measurement files is accurate — it is specifically the Oades/Delphi-study association with Sydney that needs correcting.

MFC's potential contribution Varies by body; for sport specifically, this task identified the NSW Mental Health Sports Fund (jointly run by NSW Health and NSW Office of Sport) as a concrete, named, currently-described grant channel explicitly open to external-provider partnerships
Their possible incentive Government bodies administering this fund have an interest in funding credible external providers to meet program objectives
Conflicts or competitive tension Low — this is a funding body, not a competing service provider
Evidence/capability MFC would seek Grant eligibility criteria and application requirements — unknown, not located in this bounded desk-research pass
Reputational risk Low for an initial enquiry
Dependencies Whether MFC meets whatever eligibility bar the fund sets — unknown
Smallest credible first approach proposal, not executed: reviewing the fund's published guidelines (not retrieved in this task) before any application, and identifying whether a State Sporting Organisation partner is required or whether MFC could apply directly

Cross-cutting observation

evidence-supported inference The map splits cleanly into two categories: genuine potential collaborators where MFC has something distinct to offer (the academic partners, Black Dog/AIS on the concept-and-practice gap specifically, and the NSW sport grant channel), and direct category-language competitors (Smiling Mind, Gotcha4Life) where an approach is more likely to create reputational risk than partnership value. This mirrors, and confirms, the competitive landscape V1 already established — this task adds no new competitive finding, only the institutional-contact-point correction and the sport-funding-channel discovery noted above.

11 Hunter Decision Brief

Hunter decision brief

This file recommends nothing MFC is authorised to act on without your explicit approval. It synthesises V1.1's findings against the ten questions your brief specified. A-17 characterises; it does not decide.

1. Is there sufficient evidence to approve adults as MFC's initial primary market?

No — not in the sense of a validated market decision. What exists is:

  • V1's finding that the adult segment is the least contested on category-language grounds (schools are crowded by Gotcha4Life, Smiling Mind, The Resilience Project and the free AIS program; adults are not).
  • This task's finding that none of the four adult segments has a fully evidenced purchasing pathway — the sport segment's grant channel is the clearest, but even that is unverified against actual grant recipients or eligibility criteria.
  • No primary research has been conducted. Every segment finding in 01 is desk research plus inference, not evidence from an actual buyer or participant.

evidence-supported inference The adult-market thesis is weakened from where V1 left it, not strengthened — but for a specific, useful reason: V1.1 found real procurement complexity in every segment, where V1's competitor-landscape read alone might have suggested adults were simply "open." That is a more honest and more useful position than an unqualified endorsement would have been.

2. Which adult segment appears most promising?

Sport organisations and clubs, provisionally — but flagged as a hypothesis requiring primary-research confirmation, not a conclusion.

Why: it is the only segment where this task located a named, currently-described, government-administered funding channel explicitly open to external-provider partnerships — the NSW Mental Health Sports Fund (up to $150,000/grant, $2.8M pool, jointly run by NSW Health and NSW Office of Sport). Every other segment's pathway is either unknown (workplace), structurally slow and competitive (community/PHN), or sustainability-ambiguous (direct-to-adult).

What would change this: if partner or buyer interviews (once approved) find the fund requires an existing track record MFC doesn't have, or if equivalent workplace or community pathways turn out to exist but weren't locatable in bounded desk research, this ranking should be revisited.

3. Which conclusions remain hypotheses rather than decisions?

Everything in 01 and 05. Specifically: - That sport is the most promising segment (hypothesis — see above) - That the workplace segment's regulatory headwind (training below work-redesign in the hierarchy of controls) makes it structurally harder, not merely as competitive as others — plausible, not tested against actual buyer behaviour - That direct-to-adult sustainability requires either a free/cross-subsidy model or a paid/credential model — a pattern read across two examples (Smiling Mind, MHFA), explicitly flagged as low-N

4. Which offer formats should enter testing?

Concepts 1 and 2 from 04 (foundational workshop; workshop plus 8–12 week practice system) are the lowest-risk to test first, since Concept 3 (organisational package) carries the WHS claims-boundary risk flagged repeatedly across this package, and Concept 4 (measurement-led pilot) depends on a partnership (10) not yet pursued.

proposal Test format preference within whichever segment is prioritised, using Instrument 6 in 03, before committing development effort to any one format.

5. What primary research must occur before a market decision?

The full plan in 02 — at minimum, the lost/non-user and buyer populations, which carry the highest-value disconfirming evidence and have not been substituted for by any desk research in this package. No amount of further desk research closes this gap — it requires actual conversations, which are gated behind Hunter's approval (decision gates 1–3).

6. What measurement approach is credible now?

evidence-supported inference, revised from V1 by this task's closure research (07):

  • CompACT-15 is now the safer initial default among the capability-adjacent instruments — its cross-population validation evidence is stronger than STEM-B's or SEMA3-EMA's, and neither of those two has supporting change-sensitivity evidence; STEM-B actually has evidence against acute change-sensitivity, and EMA underperformed conventional self-report on effect size in the one directly retrieved trial.
  • Skill-use rate should be treated explicitly as a behavioural outcome, not a construct measure — this is methodologically cleaner and was confirmed, not merely repeated, by this closure pass.
  • WHO-5 remains defensible as a secondary contrast/safety measure, not as the primary instrument — this task did not disturb that conclusion, and did not reopen D-0017 to act on it.

7. What claims can MFC safely make?

  • That its category definition (K-04) independently converges with the only peer-reviewed expert-consensus definition of mental fitness in existence (Robinson, Oades & Caputi, 2015) — confirmed further by this task: the 2015 paper produced no competing validated scale, so the construct genuinely remains unclaimed at the measurement level.
  • That its outcome-independent rep has no directly equivalent operationalised construct identified in the reviewed evidence — using that precise phrasing, per 08's closure finding, and citing behavioural activation, exposure therapy's inhibitory-learning model, and ACT's committed action as the closest (embedded, not standalone) relatives.

8. What claims remain unsupported?

  • That MFC understands adult buyer demand in any segment — no primary evidence exists.
  • That the outcome-independent rep, the Radar, or Stop-Shift-Do are original mechanisms — V1's prior-art audit and this task's closure research both confirm they are, at best, novel packaging of established or closely related mechanisms, not new discoveries.
  • That STEM-B or EMA will reliably detect MFC's program effects — the opposite is now the better-evidenced expectation, pending MFC's own pilot data.
  • That any adult segment's purchasing pathway is well understood — every pathway identified in 01 carries unknown fields on the questions that matter most (trigger, budget holder, evidence threshold).

9. What evidence would change the recommendation?

  • Primary buyer/lost-user interviews finding a workplace or community pathway is in fact more tractable than sport, once real conversations (not desk research) surface actual purchasing behaviour.
  • Confirmation that MFC would not meet NSW Mental Health Sports Fund eligibility criteria (not checked in this bounded task) — this would meaningfully weaken the sport-segment hypothesis.
  • Comprehension study results (06, once commissioned) showing the category language does not land with a naive adult audience regardless of segment — this would be a finding that precedes and outranks any segment decision.

10. What must Hunter approve before execution?

The ten gates already specified in your brief, restated against what this package has prepared for each:

Gate What V1.1 prepared for it
1. Select the first adult segment 01, 05, 11 — a provisional hypothesis (sport), explicitly not a decision
2. Recruit interview/survey participants 02 — a ready-to-review plan, unexecuted
3. Contact buyers, partners or academics 03, 10 — instruments and a map, no contact made
4. Test prices or product concepts externally 04, Instrument 7 in 03 — concepts and a testing method, untested
5. Treat adults as MFC's authoritative primary market Not supported by current evidence — see Q1
6. Change the measurement design 07 — findings ready to inform a future, separate D-0017 reopening, not enacted here
7. Change MFC's public claims 08, and V1's 12 — safest claim wording proposed, not published
8. Commission the comprehension study 06 — full design, not launched
9. Initiate an Indigenous-led SEWB process Out of scope for this package; carried forward from V1 as an outstanding item
10. Develop a new product format 04 — concepts only, nothing built

12 Category Comprehension Study Realistic Proposal

Category comprehension study — realistic proposal for clinical advisers and committee

Decisions confirmed by Hunter, 2026-08-05

  • Scope: adults 18+. Confirmed — matches the recommendation above, keeps this outside D-0016.
  • Heaps Normal: funding/visibility partner, confirmed as the intended role — not the research- credibility source.
  • Paula Robinson: chosen as the first research-partnership outreach target. Outreach note drafted, not sent — [[60-projects/market-intelligence-v1-1-adult-demand/13-paula-robinson-outreach-draft|13]].
  • Next conversation: Debra Fidler and Eimear Quigley, framed as raising an opportunity for their reaction, not presenting a committed plan — briefing notes drafted at [[60-projects/market-intelligence-v1-1-adult-demand/14-clinical-adviser-conversation-briefing|14]].
  • Timeline named honestly by Hunter: "something that happens in six months' time or a year" — this is being raised now as a direction, not committed to a near-term launch.
  • UNSW added as a fourth research-partner candidate (Hunter, 2026-08-05, clarifying the earlier ASR mis-transcription "NFPG"), alongside ACU and Sydney — not yet individually researched to the depth 10-partnership-and-ecosystem-map.md gave Robinson/Oades/Caputi, MacCann, and the Melbourne FEEL Lab. A follow-up pass should map a specific department/contact for ACU, Sydney (general psychology, distinct from the MacCann/STEM-B angle already mapped), and UNSW the same way, rather than treating "university" as interchangeable.
  • Split into two tiers, 2026-08-05 — the formal funded study is no longer the only path forward. Hunter pushed directly on what the formal study actually buys once the (now-corrected) "it got Smiling Mind funded" story is removed, and landed on a genuine two-tier strategy — see "Two-tier strategy" below. The free tier starts now; the funded tier waits for money and a partner.
  • Tier 1 instrument decided, 2026-08-05: the anonymous survey, not the conversational kit. A concurrent session independently built [[60-projects/informal-gap-survey-v1/01-survey-instrument-and-methodology|an anonymous 5-question form]] testing a related but distinct claim (taught-and-practiced skill gap, from K-07) at the same time this session built a conversational question kit testing category-language comprehension. Hunter reviewed both and chose the anonymous form directly — the conversational kit is parked at 15-tier-1-fieldwork-question-kit.md. Tier 1 fieldwork now means: distribute the anonymous form.

Alternative pathway — approach established charities directly, not just academics

Hunter's own instinct, 2026-08-05: "if we can't get Paula Robinson... do we reach out to Smiling Mind, Gotcha4Life, already-established charities and say — this is what we're doing, can you help us, will you be a part of this? Your approach is dealing with kids, we're trying to deal with this, but you've got the relationships, you've got the resources... we're on the same mission."

This directly contradicts the existing partnership map's own recommendation — 10-partnership-and-ecosystem-map.md flagged both Smiling Mind and Gotcha4Life as "Not recommended at this time", citing high competitive tension (both are direct category-language competitors) and reputational risk (an approach could read as free-riding on their existing positioning work). That finding isn't wrong on its own terms — the risk is real. But Hunter's framing is a genuinely different strategy, not an oversight: lead with shared mission, not competition — they've built the adult/schools reach and government relationships MFC lacks; MFC has the adult-specific, evidence-architecture depth they haven't built. Explicitly acknowledging their space (kids/schools) rather than MFC's (adults) is the move that could make this land as collaborative rather than territorial.

Not resolved here — worth flagging honestly: whether this outreach happens before or after a Robinson/university conversation matters. Going to a direct competitor asking for help while also building an independent academic partnership could read inconsistently if they compare notes. This is a sequencing decision, not just a "who to ask" decision — worth thinking through before either outreach happens, not after.

Also raised, not yet actionable: Hunter's own personal/professional network as a research-partner source — "who do we know that could be a research partner perhaps" — this needs Hunter's own input (who he actually knows), not desk research, and hasn't been explored yet.

No contact has been made with anyone named below. This is the "what this would actually look like" document Hunter asked for, 2026-08-05, after reconsidering and reopening the (previously held) [[60-projects/market-intelligence-v1-1-adult-demand/06-category-comprehension-study-plan|study plan]] — now reframed not just as internal validation, but as a strategic asset: something to bring to clinical advisers, put to committee, and use to strengthen MFC's case for existence and future grant applications.

The pitch, in one line — reframed 2026-08-05

Not "copy what Smiling Mind did." "Mental fitness" is an active, contested category — eleven-plus organisations already use the term, most without defining it consistently, and MFC's own market research has already mapped who they are and what they claim (60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/01-category-language-and-positioning-risk.md, 13-category-coherence.md). Nobody has tested whether the public actually understands any of it. That's the opportunity — understanding the landscape that already exists, not chasing a funding story that turned out not to be real.

Correction, 2026-08-05, checked against the primary source: an earlier version of this pitch said the research "turned it into $3.3M in federal funding" — verified false. That $3.3M was announced 29 April 2022, over two years before Smiling Mind's 2024 repositioning, and was explicitly for expanding the Schools Program's reach (300 more schools, support for 800 existing) — not connected to the stigma study. This is exactly why the pitch was reframed above, rather than patched.

Two-tier strategy — what's free and starts now, vs. what needs funding and waits

Hunter's own stress-test, 2026-08-05: if the funding story wasn't the real reason to do this, what is this actually for, and is it different from him just talking to people, which he's already doing? The honest answer split the study into two genuinely different things:

Tier 1 — narrative fieldwork Tier 2 — the funded, citable study
What it is The same comprehension questions, asked consistently to people Hunter/MFC already talk to, logged rather than left informal A representative national sample, proper methodology, a named credible partner
What it buys Real, quotable human testimony — "in early conversations with X people, we consistently heard Y." Builds relationships, sharpens wording, feeds grant narratives and committee conversations A statistic that survives scrutiny from someone who wasn't already inclined to believe MFC — a funder, journalist, or academic reviewer
What it can't do Cannot become a defensible population statistic no matter how much volume accumulates — a convenience sample (people Hunter already talks to) stays biased regardless of size. Presenting it as "X% of Australians" would be a real evidence-integrity problem, not a rigor nitpick Costs real money and needs a partner in place first
Cost Free ~$3k–$10k+ (Phase 2 estimate above), plus partner cost
When Now — could start this week Later — when funding and a partner relationship both exist

Recommendation, matching where Hunter landed: don't hold the whole opportunity on the funded tier. Start Tier 1 immediately and call it exactly what it is — early qualitative fieldwork, not a study — so it stays honest and still usable. Keep Tier 2's groundwork moving in parallel (partner mapping, cost clarity) without committing money until it's actually needed. The two tiers aren't sequential steps toward the same deliverable — they produce genuinely different things, and MFC can have the free one immediately.

What Tier 1 needs to actually happen, not yet built: the specific question set (can reuse the seven claims already drafted in 06-category-comprehension-study-plan.md), and a simple, consistent way to log responses (even a plain notes doc works — this doesn't need infrastructure to start).

Two separate jobs — don't conflate them

This is the most important structural point. Smiling Mind's credibility came from two distinct things bundled together, and MFC doesn't need to source them from the same place:

Job What it does Who Smiling Mind used MFC's realistic options
Research/methodology credibility Designs the survey properly, runs it on a real representative sample, and puts a name on the finding that a funder or journalist trusts without re-checking KPMG See academic candidates below — arguably better fits than a firm like KPMG, because they're the actual authors of the definition MFC already converges on
Funding/visibility partner Pays for it, and/or lends brand visibility and audience unknown for Smiling Mind (likely government/philanthropic, not disclosed in this vault's research) Heaps Normal — an existing MFC relationship, already a named pilot candidate for workplace delivery testing (60-projects/workshop-evidence-informed-adult/11-two-format-build-v1/09-case-study-cohort-model.md)

Heaps Normal is a good, real option for the second job — money and visibility, and there's already a relationship to build on. It is not a substitute for the first job. A funder's name on a study doesn't make it citable; the methodology and who stands behind it does. Using Heaps Normal as both funder and sole credibility source would be a weaker asset than Smiling Mind's, not a comparable one.

Who could actually do the research-credibility job — already mapped, never contacted

This vault already did the legwork ([[60-projects/market-intelligence-v1-1-adult-demand/10-partnership-and-ecosystem-map|10 — Partnership and ecosystem map]], 2026-08-01) — three academic candidates, each with a specific angle:

  1. Paula Robinson (and co-authors Oades & Caputi) — authored the 2015 Delphi consensus definition of mental fitness that MFC's own K-04 independently converged on. This is the strongest fit conceptually — MFC wouldn't just be buying survey credibility, it would be partnering with the people whose own definition MFC is arguably completing and stewarding (per the "the word is taken, the category is vacant" strategic reframe in 60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/13-category-coherence.md). Caveat: Robinson now operates through a private consultancy, not a university — this is closer to a paid commercial collaboration than a free academic partnership, which changes the cost picture (see below).
  2. Carolyn MacCann, University of Sydney — owns the STEM-B measurement instrument, under-tested in general adult populations. A narrower, more methodological fit than a broad category study.
  3. FEEL Lab, University of Melbourne (Assoc. Prof. Pete Koval) — research infrastructure (SEMA3), not a natural fit for a one-off comprehension survey specifically, but relevant if this later grows into ongoing measurement work.

None of these have been approached. The partnership map itself proposes the smallest credible first approach for each — a short institutional note, not a general partnership pitch. That's the actual next action if this path is chosen, and it's a message MFC would send, not something I can send on MFC's behalf.

A fourth candidate to map the same way, per Hunter's direction 2026-08-05: UNSW. Not yet researched to the depth given to the other three — no specific department, academic, or contact point identified. Should get the same treatment (an actual named person/centre, their likely incentive, smallest credible first approach) before being treated as equivalent to the others.

Who could do the funding/visibility job — beyond Heaps Normal

Hunter's direction, 2026-08-05: look at sport/lifestyle companies specifically, because "there's a big upsell and a benefit for these organisations" in being associated with this kind of work. Two real Australian candidates found, neither contacted or vetted beyond a public web search:

  • LSKD — Australian activewear brand, already runs mental-health-linked partnerships: a limited-edition tee with The Good Human Factory (proceeds fund student mental-health workshops — a genuinely similar mechanism to what MFC would be asking for), a Movember partnership, and Through Strangers Eyes (a mental-health/suicide-prevention community initiative). This is a brand that has already shown it's willing to fund exactly this kind of cause-linked mental-health work — a real, warm lead, not a cold one.
  • Vital Apparel (vitalapparel.com.au) — a smaller Australian activewear brand built explicitly around mental health as its cause; states each order contributes toward mental health research. Less scale than LSKD, but the closest direct mission-match found.

Not yet done: actually vetting either beyond what's publicly visible — reach, existing charity partnerships (any conflicts?), whether they fund research specifically vs. only program delivery sponsorship (LSKD's own examples are workshop-access funding, not comprehension research — worth confirming they'd extend to this specific kind of ask before pitching it as a foregone conclusion).

What it would realistically cost

Two phases, per the existing study plan, and the cost profile is very different between them:

Phase 1 — qualitative (12–15 cognitive interviews). Low cost. Mostly time: recruiting a deliberately diverse small sample, running/recording the sessions, coding the transcripts. If run in-house or with a research-savvy volunteer/adviser rather than an agency, this could cost close to nothing beyond people's time. This phase also directly produces the wording refinements needed before spending real money on Phase 2.

Phase 2 — quantitative (a real, representative national sample, ~900 to match Smiling Mind's own benchmark). This is where actual money is spent. As a general order-of-magnitude range (not a quote — nobody has been asked): a straightforward panel-only survey (recruiting via a provider like Pureprofile, YouGov Australia, or Qualtrics Panels, with demographic quotas matching ABS data) is typically a few thousand to around ten thousand dollars for a sample this size, depending on question complexity and whether weighting/analysis is included. Adding a named credible partner (academic collaboration fee, or a firm like KPMG) adds cost but is also most of what buys the citability — a report with no credible name attached is much less useful for exactly the grant/press purposes this proposal is for.

What's still unknown and needs Hunter, not assumed: the actual figure of community-raised funds currently available for this. I don't have a documented number for this in the vault — this proposal should not proceed with a specific budget line until that's confirmed directly, rather than guessed.

Scope decision worth flagging now, not after commissioning

Smiling Mind's own 900-person sample was nearly half aged 5–18 — a minors-inclusion decision that adds real complexity (parental consent, ethics considerations). Recommend MFC's version be adults-only at this stage: it matches MFC's current adult-focus positioning, avoids extra ethics overhead, and keeps this cleanly separate from D-0016's six safeguarding matters (which govern youth/participant-facing delivery specifically, not this kind of comprehension survey — but there's no reason to blur that line by including minors in the sample when MFC's own current focus doesn't require it).

What this buys, concretely, if it's done properly

  • A citable, external-facing statistic MFC currently has no equivalent of — exactly the asset the category-comprehension study plan named as the reason this "is not a nice-to-have communications check."
  • A credible answer to a clinical adviser or committee member who asks "how do you know your language actually works?" — the honest current answer is "Hunter refines it through direct conversation continuously," which is real but not the kind of evidence a grant panel weighs.
  • A stronger case-for-existence and grant-funding narrative — "here is evidence of a public understanding gap, and here is MFC's answer to it." (Not, per the correction above, a claim that this specific structure is what funded Smiling Mind — but it's still the right shape of argument for a grant panel on its own merits.)
  • Material for the evidence page itself — this would become one of MFC's own "10 things the evidence explains" cards eventually, not just an internal validation exercise.

The gap-evidence case — already documented, worth using directly

Hunter's own framing, 2026-08-05: show what MFC's own scan finds — who else claims to teach these skills, and what their actual evidence shows. This exact table already exists (09-five-page-findings.md, "Everyone claimed the gym. Nobody built it.") and is a strong, ready-to-use asset:

Organisation What they promise What the numbers actually show
Gotcha4Life A "Mental Fitness Gym" 114,177 workshop participants → 9,566 gym members — an 8% conversion
Smiling Mind "Lifelong" Mental Fitness 9.8M app downloads · no retention data published
AIS Mental Fitness "Strategies to stay mentally fit" 85% "likely to implement" — an intention measure, not a behaviour measure
R U OK? A conversation skill Peak-day awareness only · no skill measurement at all
The Resilience Project Whole-school wellbeing The field's best evidence here — and it shows nothing measurable before year 6

This is the real version of Hunter's "if we ask these questions, it shows the gap" instinct — not a future finding to go looking for, an existing one. Downloads, participants, and "likely to implement" scores are everywhere in this sector; a measured skill or behaviour change essentially isn't, anywhere, including from the best-resourced player. The comprehension study adds a second, complementary gap-finding (nobody understands the language) to a gap MFC's own research has already established (nobody measures whether the skill sticks). Together, that's the actual case-for- existence argument — not "we have a good idea," but "here is what everyone else's own numbers show is missing, twice over."

What this proposal does not do

  • Does not commit any money or contact any organisation.
  • Does not resolve which academic partner (if any) is realistic — Robinson's consultancy structure in particular needs a direct cost conversation before it can be compared against a university-department option.
  • Does not confirm what funds are actually available — needs Hunter's number before a real budget can be attached to this.
  • Does not replace the still-open naming/wording refinement Hunter is doing through live conversation — Phase 1's interview script should be informed by what Hunter has already learned informally, not built from scratch as if starting cold.

Suggested next step

A short, concrete decision list rather than more research: (1) confirm the actual funds figure available for this; (2) decide whether to approach Robinson's consultancy or a university-department option first, given the cost/relationship trade-off; (3) map UNSW the same way the other three candidates were mapped; (4) decide whether LSKD or Vital Apparel is worth a first conversation alongside/instead of Heaps Normal; (5) if proceeding, draft the Phase 1 interview script next, informed by what Hunter has already learned through direct conversation.

13 Paula Robinson Outreach Draft

Outreach draft — Positive Psychology Institute (Paula Robinson)

Drafted only. Not sent. Nothing has been contacted. Per the partnership map's own guidance: institutional contact point, not a personal address — Positive Psychology Institute's general contact channel (positivepsychologyinstitute.com.au), verified live 2026-08-05 via web search, not a guessed personal email.

Purpose: a first, low-pressure note — gauge interest, not propose a formal partnership yet. Per the partnership map: "a short written note referencing the 2015 paper specifically and MFC's independent convergence on its definition."

Draft message

Subject: MFC — a charity that independently arrived at your 2015 mental fitness definition

Hi Paula (or team),

I'm Hunter [surname], founder of MFC, an Australian charity building a practical mental fitness framework and workshop program for everyday adults.

I'm reaching out because your 2015 Delphi study with Oades and Caputi (Conceptualising and measuring mental fitness) named a definition and set of guiding principles that — without having read your paper when we started — MFC's own framework independently converged on. When we found the paper, it read like a confirmation of work already underway, not a starting point.

We think that definition is still largely unclaimed in practice — most Australian organisations using "mental fitness" publicly don't define it the way your panel did, and none we've found have built a sustained practice layer underneath it. We'd love to explore whether there's an opportunity to connect what you and your co-authors established conceptually with what we're building operationally — including, potentially, some primary research on how the Australian public actually understands "mental fitness" versus "mental health," in the same spirit as the comprehension research Smiling Mind ran before their own 2024 repositioning.

No specific ask yet — genuinely just want to know if this is interesting to you, and if so, whether a short call makes sense.

[Hunter's sign-off]

Notes for whoever sends this

  • Confirm current preferred contact route on positivepsychologyinstitute.com.au before sending — a contact form vs. a direct email may be the live option, this wasn't independently re-verified beyond the site existing.
  • Keep the tone exactly this modest — the partnership map flagged reputational risk as low but explicitly recommended a "smallest credible first approach," not a partnership pitch.
  • Robinson operates through this private consultancy now, not a university — expect any real collaboration conversation to include a commercial/cost dimension, not a free academic one. Don't promise funding or a specific study design in this first note; that's a second-conversation topic.

14 Clinical Adviser Conversation Briefing

Conversation briefing — Debra Fidler & Eimear Quigley

Prep notes for Hunter's own conversation, not a document to hand over verbatim. Structured around what Hunter described wanting to say, 2026-08-05: an opportunity being raised for thinking and reaction, not a decision already made.

The shape of the conversation, as Hunter framed it

"I've been having a think... this is what I think we should really do, this is why. Yes, there might be something that happens in six months' time or a year because we need certain things to be in place. However, there is a big opportunity here for us."

That's the right framing to open with — an idea being brought to them honestly, timeline uncertainty named upfront, not oversold as imminent or already committed.

The core argument, in sequence

  1. What Smiling Mind actually did. They surveyed 900 Australians, found people conflate "mental health" with "mental illness," published it, and repositioned their whole organisation on it (Sept 2024). Important correction, checked against the primary source after this briefing was first drafted: Smiling Mind's $3.3M federal funding was announced in April 2022, two years before this study — for the Schools Program's reach, unrelated to the stigma finding. Don't say the research led to the funding; that's not true, and saying it to clinical advisers/committee would be repeating a false claim. The research and the repositioning are still real and still the actual argument here — just without the funding-outcome story attached.
  2. The uncomfortable overlap. That finding is essentially MFC's own founding argument — independently arrived at, per the market-intelligence work already done (60-projects/market-and-competitor-intelligence-v1/). Smiling Mind tested and published it first; MFC hasn't tested its version at all.
  3. The gap is bigger than one competitor. This isn't just "Smiling Mind got there first" — the category-coherence research found the whole sector (eleven-plus organisations using "mental fitness") largely doesn't define the term consistently, and nobody has built a sustained everyday-practice layer under it for adults. That's MFC's actual proof-of-claim: the problem (people don't get taught this, and it shows up as struggling in ordinary moments) is real and undersolved, not invented.
  4. What proper research would add. Right now MFC's confidence in its own language comes from Hunter's continuous direct conversations — real, but not the kind of evidence a grant panel or an external reviewer weighs. A properly run comprehension study (scoped to adults 18+, per Hunter's decision) would produce a citable statistic and feed directly into the evidence-and- research page work already underway, and into the next phase of MFC's own rapid-research/evidence program.
  5. The ask. Not "approve a budget today." It's: does this direction make sense to you, is there anything from a clinical-governance angle we should build in from the start (informed consent design, question wording safety, anything under your remit), and would you want to be involved as it develops.

What NOT to imply

  • Not a commitment to spend money yet — the funds figure and the research-partner cost (Paula Robinson's consultancy vs. a university alternative) are both still open, per 12-category-comprehension-study-realistic-proposal.md.
  • Not framed as "we're behind Smiling Mind" in a defensive way — framed as "here's a real, mapped opportunity, and here's evidence it's worked for a comparable organisation."
  • Scope is adults 18+ only, explicitly — keeps this outside D-0016's youth-safeguarding gate, and it's worth saying that out loud so it reads as a deliberately bounded, careful proposal rather than scope creep.

If they ask "what would you actually need from us"

Honest current answer, per the realistic proposal: mainly their read on whether the survey questions (once drafted) are asked in a psychologically safe, non-leading way — the same kind of review K-09 already expects of any evidence-facing work — and whether either of them would want to be named as the study's clinical-governance reviewer, which itself becomes part of what makes the eventual finding credible.

15 Tier 1 Fieldwork Question Kit

Tier 1 fieldwork question kit

Parked, 2026-08-05. Hunter reviewed this alongside a parallel, independently-built instrument — [[60-projects/informal-gap-survey-v1/01-survey-instrument-and-methodology|the informal gap survey]] (anonymous 5-question form, built by a concurrent session) — and chose that one directly: "I want the other one, I don't like what you've done here." No further work should go into this file. Kept for record, not active. The two tested different claims (this kit: category-language comprehension; the other: whether stress-handling skills were ever taught and practiced) — Hunter's choice was about the method (anonymous structured form vs. conversational listening+logging), not about which claim matters more. If the category-comprehension questions still need testing, that would mean adapting them into the surviving instrument's format, not reviving this one.

What this is: the free, start-this-week half of the two-tier strategy in [[60-projects/market-intelligence-v1-1-adult-demand/12-category-comprehension-study-realistic-proposal|12]]. Not a survey, not a study — the same seven claims already drafted in [[60-projects/market-intelligence-v1-1-adult-demand/06-category-comprehension-study-plan|06]], turned into questions that fit naturally into a conversation Hunter's already having, logged so the narrative doesn't evaporate. Call it fieldwork, not research, when talking about it externally — that distinction is what keeps this honest per the two-tier proposal's own limit (this can never become a defensible population statistic, no matter the volume).

The seven, as real questions — not survey language

Ask however feels natural in the actual conversation — these are what to listen for, not a script to read verbatim.

# What's being tested A natural way to ask it
1 Do people separate how they're doing from what they're able to do? "When I say 'mental health,' what comes to mind? ...What about 'mental fitness' — same thing, or different?"
2 Do people think mental fitness is fixed or buildable? "Do you reckon mental fitness is something you're just born with, or something you can actually build, like a skill?"
3 Do people recognise the access gap (knowing something helps, not doing it in the moment)? "Ever known something helps — like taking a breath before reacting — but in the moment you just don't do it? Why do you reckon that happens?"
4 Does "mental rep" mean anything to a naive listener? "Have you heard the phrase 'mental rep' before? If not, what would you guess it means?"
5 Do people accept outcome-independent practice, or judge by result? "If you tried using a skill in a tough moment and it still didn't go well — you still lost it — would that attempt still count for something, or does it not matter if it didn't work?"
6 Do people distinguish mental fitness from resilience/wellbeing/toughness/therapy/positive thinking? "Is mental fitness the same as resilience? Or wellbeing? Or just being positive? What's the difference to you, if any?"
7 (Cross-check) Does the whole thing land as personal responsibility, without naming what's outside a person's control? Listen for this rather than asking directly — does their own explanation put everything on the individual, with no mention of context/support/circumstances?

What to listen for — the adverse interpretations already flagged as live risks

From 06's own research, not generic caution — each is a specific, evidenced risk:

  • Personal blame — do they hear this as "it's on you to fix yourself," with no room for what's actually outside someone's control?
  • Toughness/optimisation — do they hear "push through" or "be tougher," rather than a practical skill?
  • "Brain muscle" literalism — do they take the fitness metaphor literally (the mind as a muscle)? Worth knowing MFC's own current public site still has this exact contradiction live.
  • Clinical mix-up — do they think this is therapy, or for people who are already struggling, rather than for everyone?
  • Corporate-wellbeing cynicism — if raised in a work context, does it land as another tick-box wellness initiative?

How to log it — five minutes, right after the conversation

No infrastructure needed — a plain notes doc, voice memo transcribed later, or a running document is enough. Capture, per conversation:

  • Rough date (not exact time needed)
  • Rough context — who broadly (age range, relationship to Hunter, prior exposure to wellbeing/ therapy language if it came up) — no names or identifying detail, this is informal fieldwork, not consented research
  • Which of the seven came up, and roughly what was asked
  • What they actually said — their own words where possible, not paraphrased into MFC's language (paraphrasing defeats the point — you want to know how they'd say it)
  • Any adverse interpretation that showed up
  • Any quote worth keeping — this is the actual output. A handful of vivid, honest quotes over a few months is more useful for a grant narrative or a committee conversation than a summary would be

What this becomes, over time

A running qualitative record Hunter can point to — "in conversations with roughly N people over M months, here's what we kept hearing" — usable in a grant application, a conversation with Debra and Eimear, or just to sharpen MFC's own public wording. When (and if) Tier 2 is ever commissioned, this same set of questions is most of the qualitative-phase design already done.

00 Index And Executive Summary

MFC Case for Existence, Corporate Entry and Equitable Public Access V1

A governed strategy-and-evidence synthesis, built from an isolated worktree at d19e84f. No authoritative MFC record was changed. A-05/A-06/A-17 characterise; they do not decide.

⚠ Correction notice, 2026-08-01

The first version of this package incorrectly stated that C1, the Rapid Review manuscript, the Evidence & Measures Bank, and the Committee Business Plan had not been read. A subsequent, separately authorised correction task obtained genuine Google Drive access and read all four in substantial or full detail. See 10-source-verification-and-reference-register.md for the complete verification.

The headline results of that correction: this package's independent synthesis converges closely with C1's own argument (§6, §10.1 and §24.2 of C1 read almost as direct sources for this package's own claims) — a stronger finding than "untested." Two material gaps were closed: MFC already has a named collective-measurement design (Team Pulse, Team Radar Lab, in the Evidence & Measures Bank), and MFC already has a working commercial position (~$1,800 price point, in the Commercial Model) — both corrected into 05 and 06. The Rapid Review's actual scope is now confirmed, not merely presumed: it supports the general trainability of psychological skills; it does not test Stop-Shift-Do or any MFC-specific mechanism. The Hunter decision brief (09) was also corrected — it was titled "ten decisions" but numbered seven; it now correctly numbers ten, with three genuine new decisions surfaced by the source-verification work itself (a Committee Business Plan duplicate-document conflict, correcting the retired definition at its source, and unblocking the long-pending Claims Register).

The strategic direction, stated once

Your authorised inputs — young adults and adults as primary beneficiaries, corporate workplaces as the initial paid channel, corporate delivery not as the mission's boundary, funded/subsidised/pro bono access as a genuine commitment, and social architecture/norm change as the longer ambition — are treated throughout this package as given, not re-opened. No file in this package re-ranks adult market segments; that work is V1.1's, already done, not repeated here.

The core gap, tested rather than assumed

02 tests the working thesis directly. The defensible conclusion: information reliably changes what a person knows; it does not reliably determine what a person does in a specific, activated, real-life moment — because retrieval, selection and action under activation are governed by different mechanisms (inert knowledge, state-dependent retrieval, stress-impaired executive function) than knowledge acquisition. This is well-evidenced as a general mechanism. It is not evidence that MFC's specific model closes the gap — that remains untested, and this package does not claim otherwise.

MFC's proposed contribution

A non-clinical, moment-based practice architecture. Two elements of it are inherited from well-established traditions and should be presented as such, not as inventions (03, and V1/V1.1's completed prior-art work): the three-step Stop-Shift-Do loop, and the Radar's pre-selection of moments (structurally close to Gollwitzer's implementation intentions). One element appears to be genuine packaging contribution: the outcome-independent mental rep — no equivalent standalone, countable, attempt-based practice unit was identified anywhere in a ten-literature search (04).

Strongest supporting evidence

  • MFC's own K-04 definition independently converges with the only peer-reviewed expert-consensus definition of "mental fitness" in existence (Robinson, Oades & Caputi, 2015) — a finding from V1.1, restated in 01.
  • Behavioural spillover between coworkers is genuine, field-experimental evidence (Mas & Moretti, 2009), not merely theoretical — the strongest single data point supporting any part of the social-architecture chain (05).
  • MFC's own claims-discipline system (K-08, K-09) is, per KN-0005's own synthesis (reused and confirmed here), unusually rigorous by early-stage-organisation standards.

Strongest counterarguments

  • The individual-to-organisational link in the social-change chain is the field's most common failure point, not MFC's unique risk — a 2025 systematic review of 44 workplace interventions found only 4 used structural, goal-directed techniques (05).
  • Training sits below work redesign in the WHS psychosocial hierarchy of controls (V1, reconfirmed throughout this package) — MFC's corporate offer must never be positioned as discharging an employer's psychosocial duty.
  • No study was found testing durable, correct application of any comparable taught mnemonic sequence at a follow-up interval — this is a gap for the whole field, not a deficiency specific to MFC, but it means the "three steps aid retention" intuition is currently unproven (03).
  • The public MFC website does not yet reflect the Framework's own stated breadth (ordinary, meaningful, performance and enjoyable moments, not only difficult ones) — a real gap between internal design intent and current public delivery (04, 08).

Government and funding implications

07's headline finding, stated without softening: across eleven Australian and NSW policy areas researched, no currently open, competitive, adult-non-clinical-appropriate government funding door was found for MFC at its present scale. SafeWork NSW's dedicated $5.6m workplace psychological-health budget is already committed to Black Dog Institute and Transitioning Well — adding a funding-competitor dimension to Black Dog's status alongside the potential-partnership case V1 already made. The two most concrete funding pathways found across the whole research programme remain V1.1's findings: the NSW Mental Health Sports Fund and FRRR's "In a Good Place" program — neither of which was re-researched here.

Unresolved decisions

Ten genuine decisions are identified in 09, none approved by this package. The two most consequential: whether to adopt the revised case-for-existence thesis (from "we define the category" to "we translate established science into a testable practice architecture for a real, evidenced gap"), and the Indigenous SEWB gap, which this package restates as unowned and requiring an Indigenous-led process, not an AI-drafted resolution — carried forward unresolved from V1 and V1.1, and independently reconfirmed by 07's finding that a national SEWB implementation framework (Gayaa Dhuwi, 2025–2035) now formally governs any engagement in this space.

What this package does and does not answer

Answers: whether the access-gap thesis is defensible (yes, with the general mechanism well-evidenced and MFC's specific effectiveness untested); what is and isn't distinctive about Stop-Shift-Do and the mental rep (largely inherited, with one genuine packaging contribution); how the corporate and equitable-access model separates roles and risks; where government policy aligns with MFC's mission without translating into accessible funding.

Does not answer: whether MFC's model actually works (requires the pilot and measurement programme V1.1 already designed), which adult segment to prioritise (V1.1's question, not reopened here), or any question requiring primary research, outreach, or an authoritative record change.

Reading order

  1. This file, for orientation
  2. 01 — source reconciliation, including the honest limitation that most canonical documents named in this task's brief exist only as unread metadata stubs in this vault
  3. 02, 03, 04 — the core thesis, tested piece by piece
  4. 05 — the social-architecture chain, with its failure points named explicitly
  5. 06, 07 — the commercial and government landscape
  6. 08 — the claims register, the practical output every other file feeds into
  7. 09 — the draft case for existence and the decision brief, read last because it draws on everything before it

Structure, for orientation

Six parts: I The causal story (why the public model of mental health became reactive) · II The problem MFC is actually facing (§6, why awareness and information alone do not create skill) · III The missing middle (§8–10, what mental fitness names, why moments matter, §10.1 not only for hard moments) · IV The MFC Framework as the practical response (Stop-Shift-Do, Human Operating System, seven skills, reps) · V What MFC is proposing societally (§19.3 why workplaces matter early, §20 why this must stay collective, partnered and staged) · VI Strategic implications and staging (§24.2 what is supported, what is synthesis, what still needs testing).

What remains valid — drawn from verified-extraction sources

The core definition and distinction (Framework, K-04, K-05) — valid, locked, well-evidenced internally

"Mental fitness is how well we navigate life's everyday moments." — Framework, Category lock-in, locked 20 July 2026

"Mental health is how we are doing. Mental fitness is what we are able to do." — Framework, K-05

"MFC conceptualises mental fitness as a developable capacity to access and coordinate relevant human skills across changing situations: to think flexibly, recognise and work skilfully with internal states, direct attention and action towards what matters, and relate constructively to ourselves and others." — Framework §2

Cross-checked against V1.1's category-coherence finding: this definition is close to a paraphrase of Robinson, Oades & Caputi's (2015) peer-reviewed expert-consensus definition — "the modifiable capacity to utilise resources and skills to flexibly adapt to challenges or advantages, enabling thriving." MFC's internal definition and the only orphaned academic consensus definition of the category converge independently. Still valid; strengthened, not weakened, by V1.1.

Non-diagnostic, non-scoring design discipline — valid, and unusually rigorous

"Mental fitness is not a fixed identity, a judgement of worth, or a promise of control." — Framework §2

"Do not label people skilled/unskilled or mentally fit/mentally unfit." — Framework, Category lock-in and Appendix B

evidence-supported inference The pattern of explicit prohibitions across the four-position model, the State Check, and whole-person labelling is consistent enough to describe as a deliberate design principle (KN-0001's own synthesis language, reused here).

Access-not-possession framing — valid, and independently corroborated by V1.1's closure research

"A person does not need to change their whole life to begin. They need one real moment, one intentional next move, and enough support to keep practising." — Framework §3

V1.1's own prior-art closure work (external to this file, already completed) found this framing restates Tulving & Pearlstone's (1966) availability-vs-accessibility distinction and Bransford/Whitehead's inert knowledge — not new theory, but a defensible translation of established psychology into public language. See 02 of this package for the full test of this claim.

The claims-discipline system itself — valid and MFC's genuine organisational strength

"MFC should describe this framework as evidence-informed and evidence-aligned… It should not be described as a clinically validated standalone protocol unless directly tested." — Framework §16

"The strongest evidence sits behind the underlying processes… MFC's exact packaging — including the five public skills, seven deeper skills, mental reps, radar, and Stop, Shift, Do — should be tested through delivery, feedback, evaluation, and advisor review over time." — Framework §18

KN-0005's own synthesis, reused here because it is accurate and important: "MFC's evidence discipline is... its strongest organisational asset. It distinguishes what informed the design from what validates the design — a distinction most early-stage organisations collapse."

What is now incomplete — gaps V1.1 and this task's own reading exposed

  1. No published construct measure exists for "mental fitness" as MFC or Robinson et al. define it (confirmed in V1.1's measurement closure). The Measurement Blueprint's own construct list already names PRE-02 (knowing–doing/access gap) and EDU-02 (mental health vs. mental fitness distinction) as recommended constructs — but every row's status reads "MFC recommended; advisor review" — none is advisor-approved, per the source's own status column.
  2. The Learning Science Evidence Library's own text is explicit that its cited studies do not validate MFC's workshop: "They do not prove that the full MFC workshop improves mental fitness or creates lasting behaviour change. MFC must evaluate those outcomes directly." This is the organisation's own stated position, not an external critique — it should anchor, not undermine, the case for existence.
  3. The Radar and Stop-Shift-Do lineage is not publicly cited anywhere in MFC's own materials found in this task or V1.1 — see 03 of this package.

02 Information To Practice And Access Gap

Information-to-practice and the access gap

Testing, not assuming, the core working thesis. The question is not whether information matters — it demonstrably does — but whether information alone is sufficient, and what the evidence says the remaining gap actually is.

What information and psychoeducation can achieve — stated plainly, not minimised

evidence-supported inference, well-established across decades of health psychology and education research:

  • Information changes knowledge and, under the right conditions, attitudes and stated intentions. Psychoeducation is a real, evidenced component of many effective interventions — it is not inert on its own.
  • Information is a necessary precondition for informed choice: a person cannot act on a skill they have never encountered.
  • AI materially increases information availability. A person can now retrieve a technically accurate description of almost any evidence-based psychological technique in seconds. This is real and growing, not a fixed prior condition.

The thesis is not that information is worthless. A defensible statement, and the one this file settles on: information changes what a person knows; it does not reliably determine what a person does in a specific, activated, real-life moment.

Why information alone may be insufficient — the mechanisms, not an assertion

The knowledge–doing and intention–behaviour gaps

evidence-supported inference, carried forward from prior research already in this vault's evidence base (Pfeffer & Sutton on the knowing–doing gap; Sheeran 2002 and Webb & Sheeran 2006 on the intention–behaviour gap — intention change of d=0.66 translating to behaviour change of only d=0.36). This is a well-established, replicated finding across health and organisational psychology: intending to act and acting are measurably different constructs, with a real and quantifiable gap between them.

Inert knowledge

evidence-supported inference. Whitehead (1929) named the phenomenon of knowledge that is "welded" to the context in which it was learned — expressible on demand but unusable when the relevant real-world situation arises. Bransford and colleagues (Cognition and Technology Group at Vanderbilt, 1980s–90s) developed this into a working research programme showing that knowledge acquired abstractly, without anchoring to the situations where it will be needed, frequently fails to transfer. This is precisely the mechanism MFC's Framework gestures at without naming, per KN-0001's own synthesis: "The framework's recurring question is not 'does this person have the skill?' but 'what is shaping access right now?'"

State- and context-dependent retrieval

evidence-supported inference. Tulving & Pearlstone's (1966) foundational availability-vs-accessibility distinction in memory research — a memory trace can be present in storage yet inaccessible without the right retrieval cue — has since been extended into state-dependent and context-dependent memory research generally. The practical implication for MFC's model: a skill learned in a calm classroom setting is not automatically retrievable in a heated, activated, real-life moment, because the retrieval context differs from the encoding context.

Cognitive load and recall under activation

evidence-supported inference. Arnsten's (2009, Nature Reviews Neuroscience) body of work on stress and prefrontal cortex function is directly relevant here: even mild, uncontrollable stress rapidly impairs the brain systems responsible for flexible, effortful thinking, while strengthening the more automatic, habit-driven systems. This supplies the neuroscience of "skills a person has but cannot reach" — precisely the access-gap language K-04 and KN-0001 already use, independently.

Knowing, remembering, selecting, and acting are four different things

MFC proposal, synthesised from the above rather than a single cited source: the evidence base above supports separating at least four distinct steps that are routinely collapsed into a single word — "knowing":

  1. Knowing — encountering and understanding a piece of information (what psychoeducation achieves)
  2. Remembering — being able to retrieve that information on demand, outside the original learning context
  3. Selecting — under time pressure, in an unfolding moment, choosing which of several possible responses actually fits
  4. Acting — executing the chosen response, often under emotional or physiological activation that itself impairs the executive function required for steps 2 and 3

This four-step separation is a proposed MFC framing, not a citation from a single paper — but every individual step is independently evidenced above.

Repeated practice, cues, reinforcement and environment

evidence-supported inference, already established in this vault's research: Lally et al. (2010) found habit automaticity takes a median 66 days with an 18–254 day range; Gollwitzer & Sheeran's (2006) implementation-intention meta-analysis (d=.65 across 94 tests) shows that pre-specifying a cue measurably increases the likelihood a behaviour occurs when that cue arises — cue-based retrieval, not information volume, is what the strongest evidence in this space actually targets.

AI changes information availability without necessarily solving enactment

evidence-supported inference, a direct and defensible extension of everything above: if the bottleneck is retrieval-under-activation rather than information access, then a technology that makes information easier to find does not, by the same mechanism, make a skill easier to retrieve in the moment it is needed. This is a reasoned inference from the retrieval-cue literature above, not a tested finding about AI specifically — no direct study of AI's effect on real-time skill enactment was located or should be assumed to exist.

Avoiding the absolute claim

MFC must not claim, and this file does not claim, that information never changes behaviour. The correct, defensible, and considerably more interesting claim is narrower and stronger:

Information reliably changes what a person knows. It does not reliably determine what a person does in a specific, activated, real-life moment — because retrieval, selection and action under activation are governed by different mechanisms than knowledge acquisition, and those mechanisms are where the evidence base is thinnest and the practical gap is largest.

⚠ Correction, 2026-08-01: this is already MFC's own stated position, not an external framing

With genuine Drive access, this correction task read C1 ("Why Mental Fitness, Why Now") directly. verified fact, C1 §6:

"Awareness matters. It can reduce stigma, improve willingness to talk, and encourage help-seeking. But awareness is not the same as capability... They ask people to behave differently without giving them a coherent model for what is happening in the moment and how to work with it. The gap is not hypocrisy. It is the distance between understanding and usable skill."

This is, almost precisely, the statement this file arrived at independently. The correct framing is that this file's external psychological evidence (Tulving, Arnsten, the intention-behaviour gap) deepens and grounds an existing MFC position, not that it introduces one. This should be cited as such in any future public or committee use.

verified fact, further confirmation from MFC's current, approved Public Messaging Source Library (23 Jul 2026, status: controlled messaging authority):

"Access means what a person can recognise, remember and draw on in a particular situation. Access is affected by learning and practice, but also by health, energy, disability, neurodivergence, pressure, habits, relationships, safety, support and environment."

This is the current, fixed, approved MFC language — not a synthesis this task proposed.

The strongest defensible statement of MFC's gap

MFC proposal, offered for the case-for-existence draft in 09:

The mental-health and self-development environment already contains an enormous and growing volume of accurate information, much of it now instantly retrievable. What remains scarce is a structured way to practise retrieving and applying a relevant skill inside the specific, often activated, moments where it is actually needed — repeatedly, across a person's real life, with enough support that the practice continues.

This statement is directly supported by the mechanisms above (inert knowledge, state-dependent retrieval, cognitive load under activation, the intention–behaviour gap) and does not require any claim about MFC's own effectiveness, which remains untested per K-09's evidence-role framework and the Measurement Blueprint's own unapproved status.

What remains untested

  • Whether MFC's specific practice architecture (the Radar, Stop-Shift-Do, mental reps) closes this gap better than any other practice-based intervention — untested, and explicitly out of scope for this claim.
  • Whether the four-step knowing/remembering/selecting/acting separation proposed above is itself a validated model, as opposed to a useful organising synthesis — MFC proposal, not an established four-stage model in the literature under this exact framing.

The thesis, sharpened by Hunter, 2026-09-24

Why this section exists. A literature search on 2026-09-24 tested the claim MFC had been making — that these skills have not been tested in the everyday adult population — and refuted it from MFC's own shelves. Schäfer 2024 (101 trials, 20,010 explicitly non-clinical adults), Vanhove 2016, Fleming 2024 and Gayed 2019 were already held, and Bermudez 2025 tested universal skills programmes on 10,809 unselected adults. One citation from MFC's own library would have killed the claim in front of a reviewer.

Told that, Hunter sharpened it rather than defended it. What follows is his framing, and it is stronger than the claim it replaces because it survives the literature.

The physio distinction

"It's not therapy. People have gone to the physiotherapist, they've learned new things and they're feeling better in their life. Awesome, but we're not here around physiotherapy. We're here on how we can actually be stronger so we don't have to go to the physio in the first place. Even though they might be learning some basics that are similar and overlap, it's a different entry point."

This does the work the old claim could not. It concedes everything the evidence establishes — these programmes exist, they have been tested in adults, some of the content overlaps — and still names something genuinely different. The distinction is the entry point, not the content. A therapeutic or symptom-reduction programme is entered because something is wrong. MFC's premise is entered because everyone has moments, all the time, and no condition is required to want to handle them better.

What MFC may therefore say: not that this is untested, but that it has been tested as a different thing, for a different reason, in a different frame.

What has actually not been captured

Hunter: "not that it doesn't exist, but that hasn't really been captured, taught or measured in that way."

The evidence supports this in a specific and defensible form:

  1. Symptom outcomes have been tested and are null. Bermudez 2025: universal programmes given to unselected adults produced SMD -0.02 on quality of life, -0.09 on depression, -0.03 on anxiety. None significant. This is why MFC does not make symptom claims — not preference, but because the question has been asked and answered.
  2. Certainty is low even where effects appear. Miguel 2023, the WHO-commissioned umbrella review behind the global guidelines on mental health at work: small to moderate effects, GRADE certainty low to very low in almost all examined outcomes. Verified against the full text 2026-09-24.
  3. Enactment is the outcome the field has largely not measured. Forthal 2021 on Mental Health First Aid — 31 studies, only 9 rigorous enough to judge. Knowledge moves. Intent moves. On whether trainees actually used the skills: 3 of 9 found an effect, 6 found none. On recipients' mental health at 12, 24 and 36 months: no effect. The authors' own words are that implementers "should take particular care when describing the intervention as evidence-based."

That third point is the differentiator, and it is evidenced. Hunter: "We measure for intention, not so much the skill enactment. And it's the skill enactment part that... really differentiates us."

The system-level claim, stated as a claim and not as a finding

"Every single person in every single moment of their life depends on these skills. But we don't have a place where we can teach them, we can practice them, we can normalise them, and we can reward them. There's no systems and no norms around that. And this is why it's going to take so much time."

This is MFC's position, not a research finding, and it must be written as one. No paper searched on 2026-09-24 states it. The search terms and databases are recorded in 10-sources/evidence-library-searched-and-not-found-2026-09-23.md. The nearest supported statement found was that mental-health-literacy research concentrates on children and young adults, sourced to a commentary that failed MFC's authoritative-source rule and was not admitted.

K-08's category-confidence rule already handles a structurally identical problem — MFC states publicly that no construct-validation literature distinguishes mental fitness from resilience training, and that this is "a genuinely open external question, not settled either way." Say this the same way.

What must not be said

  • Not that this has never been tested in adults. It has, and MFC holds the papers.
  • Not that CBT's effects are declining. Cuijpers 2023, 409 trials and 52,702 patients, found no reduction in effect size by publication year, with trial quality rising.
  • Not that loneliness is rising in Australia. AIHW/HILDA to 2024 shows a COVID spike that largely returned; and the global trend evidence does not exist, per Surkalim 2022 in the BMJ.
  • Not that rising prevalence is why MFC exists. MFC holds Foulkes 2023, which proposes that awareness efforts may inflate reported prevalence. Arguing from a rising trend while holding that paper hands a reviewer the contradiction. Use absolute burden and unmet need instead: under half of Australian adults with a 12-month disorder sought any treatment (Teesson 2024, n = 15,893).
