03 Stop Shift Do And Traffic Light Retrieval

Stop, Shift, Do and traffic-light retrieval

Do not claim Stop, Shift, Do is novel — it is not, and this file does not attempt to argue otherwise. It reviews the lineage already established elsewhere in this vault's research, then adds a genuinely new question: is the three-step, traffic-light-associated design well-supported by cognitive-load and retrieval evidence?

The lineage — restated briefly, not re-litigated

V1.1's prior-art audit (already completed) found Stop-Shift-Do occupies a crowded genre — DBT's STOP, MBSR's STOP, Google's SBNRR, RULER's Meta-Moment, and ACT's Choice Point all share the identical interrupt→shift/reorient→act structure, with DBT and MBSR converging independently on the identical word "STOP." That finding is not repeated here in full — see V1's 12 and V1.1's 08 for the complete comparison table and sourcing.

The safest defensible description, carried forward unchanged: Stop-Shift-Do is a wording choice within a well-established genre. Cite the lineage — Linehan, Goldstein, Tan, Brackett, Harris — rather than presenting it as invented.

Is three steps easier to retrieve than four or more?

The cognitive-load case for three steps

verified fact. Miller (1956) proposed ~7±2 items in short-term memory; Cowan's (2001) more rigorous reconsideration — controlling for chunking strategies across verbal/non-verbal, visual/auditory and attended/unattended paradigms — found the underlying focus-of-attention capacity averages ~4 chunks, not 7.

evidence-supported inference, not directly tested: a 3-step sequence sits inside Cowan's ~4-chunk ceiling with margin; a 4-step sequence sits at the estimated ceiling itself, with zero margin. Combined with Arnsten's already-established finding (see 02) that stress reduces effective prefrontal working-memory capacity below baseline, the inference that 3-step recall is more robust under activation than 4-step recall is reasonable — but no study was found that directly manipulates sequence length under acute stress and measures recall. This is the honest state of the evidence: a plausible extrapolation from two well-established facts, not a directly tested finding.

The complicating finding

verified fact. Radović & Manzey (2019), Frontiers in Psychology, two experiments (n=65, n=20) on an 8-step task with a mnemonic acronym found the acronym sped initial learning (910.5s vs 1150.5s, p=.001) but gave no execution-speed or accuracy advantage once learned, and no general protection against interruption. What did help resumption after an interruption was the task's internal hierarchical structure — grouping into sub-chunks — not the acronym or step-count itself (resumption time 2041ms at a structural boundary vs 3222ms elsewhere, p=.005).

This is the single most relevant empirical data point located, and it complicates rather than confirms the "3 steps is simply better" intuition. It supports chunking and structure generally; it does not support a simple claim that fewer steps produce better real-time execution once a sequence is learned. The safest statement: fewer steps very plausibly aid initial learning and memorability; the evidence that they aid execution under pressure, once learned, is weaker than assumed.

Does the traffic-light association improve timed recall?

verified fact. Colour-coded (red/yellow/green; "amber" in some sources) signalling has a robust, general human-factors evidence base for improving message comprehension and reaction time under time pressure, across domains including road signage and aviation/cockpit coding.

unknown, an important gap: no evidence was found isolating colour-coding's specific contribution independent of underlying content, and no study was found testing a traffic-light system specifically for self-regulation retrieval.

The direct comparator, and why it doesn't transfer cleanly

verified fact. The Zones of Regulation (Kuypers) is a real, widely-used four-colour system (Blue/Green/Yellow/Red) — not three — used in schools to teach emotional self-regulation. It is a classification system (which zone am I in) rather than a sequential action system (do step 1, then 2, then 3).

evidence-supported inference Zones of Regulation is not directly evidence for MFC's traffic-light retrieval design, because the two are structurally different mechanisms — one asks "where am I," the other asks "what do I do next." They should not be conflated as equivalent evidence.

A further caveat on Zones itself: the positive outcome findings circulating for it (SEL-domain gains in a 2019 study; reduced irritability/hyperactivity in autistic youth in a 2024 study) are relayed through the developer's own marketing and evidence pages, not independently verified primary sources in this task. unknown / vendor-sourced claim — should not be cited as independently confirmed.

Does "Stop" risk suppression, avoidance or oversimplification?

This is a genuine, evidence-grounded risk, not a hypothetical one, and the file treats it as such.

verified fact. Gross's process model of emotion regulation (1998, 2001) distinguishes antecedent-focused strategies (occurring early, before the emotional response is fully generated — e.g. reappraisal) from response-focused strategies (occurring late, after the response is generated — e.g. expressive suppression). Suppression is associated with greater physiological activation, reduced positive-emotion experience without reduced negative-emotion experience, poorer memory for concurrent events, and worse interpersonal functioning.

evidence-supported inference — the risk assessment this file exists to make: whether MFC's "Stop" functions as (a) a brief attentional pause preceding a chosen response (antecedent-focused, lower-risk, consistent with mindfulness-pause literature) or (b) response inhibition (higher-risk, closer to suppression) depends entirely on how "Stop" is instructed and what happens in "Shift." No study tests MFC's specific sequence — this is inference, not a finding about MFC.

A structural comparison worth naming directly: DBT's STOP skill is four steps — Stop, Take a step back, Observe, Proceed mindfully — not three. Its "Observe" step is explicitly designed to prevent suppression by requiring noticing and naming before any action is taken.

evidence-supported inference, a genuine design-risk flag: MFC's three-step compression may fold what DBT deliberately keeps as two separate steps (pause, then observe) into one ("Stop"). This could be read as removing the observational safeguard DBT includes on purpose. This is not a proven finding — no study tests MFC's compression directly — but it is a specific, evidence-grounded risk worth naming rather than dismissing.

The design mitigation the evidence implies, not a decision made here: instructional framing that has participants name the feeling or urge (not block it) during "Stop," reserving change-effort for "Shift," would keep the sequence closer to Gross's lower-risk, antecedent-focused end of the spectrum.

Does durable, correct application follow from teaching a mnemonic?

unknown — a genuine and important evidence gap, not specific to MFC. No study was located measuring retention or correct application of a taught mnemonic self-regulation sequence (STOP, ALEC, or any comparable protocol) at a follow-up interval of months, as distinct from recognition at time of teaching.

evidence-supported inference: this absence is consistent with the already-established training-transfer-failure literature (Blume et al. 2010; Broad & Newstrom) — plausibly extending to mnemonic sequences specifically, but this is extrapolation across domains, not direct evidence. No comparable organisation in this field — including the ones MFC's protocol structurally resembles — has published this evidence either. MFC is not behind the field here; the field does not have it.

⚠ Correction, 2026-08-01: the Rapid Review's actual scope, confirmed by full read

The first draft cautioned against presenting the Rapid Review as evidence for Stop-Shift-Do without having read it. It has now been read in full (Fidler & Prout, MFC working manuscript; 10 included studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs). The caution was correct, and is now confirmed rather than merely inferred:

verified fact The review tested general psychological intervention modalities — cognitive-behavioural, mindfulness-based, acceptance-based, compassion-focused and positive psychology approaches, plus resilience training, breathwork and guided imagery — finding small-to-moderate effects (g≈0.20–0.50) across all of them, with no single modality showing consistent superiority.

verified as absence The review did not test Stop-Shift-Do, three-step versus four-step sequences, traffic-light coding, or outcome-independent reps. None of MFC's specific packaging was an object of study. The review's own conclusion states this limitation directly: "mental fitness remains an emergent construct rather than a clearly operationalised system for intervention and evaluation" and interventions are "largely implemented in fragmented and modality-specific ways... rarely integrated into a unified framework."

evidence-supported inference This is exactly the gap C1 itself identifies (§7, "why fragmented tools do not add up to a public model") and exactly the role MFC's own K-09 evidence-role framework assigns the Rapid Review: a "foundational principle" and "representative source" for the general trainability of psychological skills, not "claim-specific" or "MFC-specific" evidence for Stop-Shift-Do. Citing the review to support the general premise that psychological skills are trainable is fully defensible. Citing it to support any claim about MFC's specific three-step design would not be.

What is inherited, what MFC's integration changes, and what needs testing

Status
The three-slot interrupt-shift-act structure Inherited — a well-established genre, per V1.1's closure work
The specific word "Stop" Inherited — shared with DBT and MBSR independently
Compressing pause-and-observe into one step MFC's integration change — plausible design risk, untested
Traffic-light colour association MFC's integration choice — general human-factors support for colour-coding exists; no direct evidence for this specific application
Whether 3 beats 4+ steps under real-world activation Untested. Plausible from chunking theory; not directly evidenced
Whether it produces durable, correct application months later Untested — and unanswered for every comparable protocol in the field, not just MFC's

What would need to be experimentally tested

MFC proposal, not committed to here: a study comparing recall and correct application of the three-step sequence under simulated time pressure or activation, against at least one four-step comparator (e.g. a version with an explicit "Observe" step reinstated), with a follow-up interval of weeks to months — directly targeting the two evidence gaps this file found nowhere else in the field either.

04 Moments Positive Use And Outcome Independent Reps

Moments, positive use, and outcome-independent reps

Building the case for moments as MFC's unit of recognition, choice, practice, reflection and measurement — deliberately not deficit-only or crisis-centred.

Moments as the unit — what the Framework already establishes

verified fact, Framework §2, quoted in KN-0001:

"Mental fitness is relevant in ordinary, meaningful, and difficult moments. It is not only about coping."

This is not a new claim this task is introducing — it is already the Framework's own stated position, though V1.1's prior-art audit found it is not currently reflected on MFC's public website, which instead runs a conventional "Daily 1% Model" of five fixed daily exercises. The gap identified there is real: the moment-based, non-deficit framing exists in the internal Framework and is not yet the public front door.

The six moment types, and why breadth matters

Moment type Function
Difficult and high-pressure moments The intuitive, deficit-associated use case — conflict, stress, overwhelm
Ordinary everyday moments Low-friction, high-frequency practice ground — per KN-0004's own synthesis, "lower-friction reps are not less important. They are the training ground"
Relational moments Interactions with others — the bridge to the social-architecture claim in 05
Meaningful and values-based moments Not stress-triggered; oriented toward what matters to the person
Performance moments Where a person wants to act well, not merely cope
Enjoyable, connecting and appreciative moments Positive-affect moments — gratitude, connection, savouring
Early-action moments Where an early, small intentional move may prevent avoidable escalation later — distinct from crisis intervention, and explicitly not a claim that MFC prevents crises

MFC proposal This breadth is the direct, structural answer to the deficit-only critique that follows every fitness-framed wellbeing organisation profiled in prior research (Gotcha4Life, Smiling Mind, and others, per V1's competitor research) — provided it is genuinely built into delivery and measurement, not only stated. The Measurement Blueprint's own construct list (per this task's source reconciliation, 01) does not yet visibly distinguish moment types in its item set — this is a design gap worth naming, not resolved here.

⚠ Correction, 2026-08-01: this is already C1's stated position, verbatim

C1 has now been read in full. verified fact, section titled exactly "10.1 Mental fitness is not only for hard moments" — the same claim this section develops is already an explicit, named section of MFC's own authoritative case-for-existence document. This should be attributed to C1 directly rather than presented as this task's own elaboration; the six-moment-type table above is a legitimate development of an existing C1 position, not a new claim.

The outcome-independent mental rep, reviewed against V1.1's completed prior-art work

KN-0004, quoting the Framework §8:

"A mental rep is catching a moment and choosing your next move, on purpose, toward what matters. You may catch the moment before it happens, while it is happening, or afterwards. The outcome does not determine whether it counts."

V1.1's prior-art closure (already completed, this task does not repeat it) searched ten literatures — deliberate practice, sport process goals, exposure therapy, behavioural activation, ACT committed action, rehabilitation adherence, relapse prevention, self-compassion, growth mindset, and implementation-intention failure — for any equivalent, standalone, outcome-independent countable practice unit.

The finding, restated precisely for this file

No equivalent was identified in the reviewed evidence. The closest relatives, in order: behavioural activation's separation of activity-completion from mood-outcome (Jacobson, Martell & Dimidjian, 2001); exposure therapy's inhibitory-learning model, where a trial "counts" for its learning value regardless of whether anxiety dropped (Craske et al., 2014); and ACT's committed action / workability (Hayes et al., 2006), where the primary source could not be independently confirmed for the exact wording. All three are embedded inside a broader clinical protocol; none is extracted as a discrete, standalone, user-facing, countable unit the way MFC's rep is.

Distinguishing what is genuinely MFC's from what is inherited

Element Status
The underlying mechanism — that attempt-based, outcome-independent practice may support persistence better than success-gated practice Has precedent. Behavioural activation and inhibitory-learning exposure both rest on structurally similar logic, decades earlier, in clinical contexts
A standalone, publicly nameable, countable unit ("a rep") extracted from that mechanism Appears to be MFC's genuine packaging contribution. No source found extracts this logic into a lay-facing, gym-metaphor-compatible, self-administered unit
The gym/fitness-reps metaphor itself Not MFC's. Already documented elsewhere in this vault's competitive research: Positive Intelligence (Chamine, 2012) has used "mental muscles" and "PQ reps" in a "mental fitness" brand since 2012

The safest defensible description

"No equivalent operationalised, standalone, outcome-independent practice unit was identified in the reviewed evidence — though closely related mechanisms exist in behavioural activation and exposure therapy's inhibitory-learning model, each embedded within a broader clinical protocol rather than extracted as an independent, lay-facing construct."

MFC proposal. This is the wording this task recommends for any public or funder-facing use, and it is the wording carried into 08's claims register and 09's draft case for existence.

What must not be implied

Per this task's explicit brief and consistent with K-08's existing claim boundaries:

  • Mental reps do not prevent mental illness. No claim to this effect appears anywhere in this file or should appear in any derived public material.
  • Mental reps do not guarantee positive outcomes. The Framework's own language — "the outcome does not determine whether it counts" — is in tension with any framing that promises reps produce good outcomes; the honest position is that the outcome is not the measure of whether the practice occurred, not that the practice is guaranteed to produce a good outcome.
  • The "early action may prevent avoidable escalation" moment type must not be read as a crisis-prevention or clinical-triage claim. It describes a category of everyday moment (e.g. noticing early irritation before it escalates into a bigger conflict), not a mechanism for preventing self-harm, crisis, or clinical deterioration. This distinction should be made explicit wherever this moment type is used publicly.

05 Social Architecture And Behavioural Norm Change

Social architecture and behavioural norm change

A testable theory of change, stress-tested for where it may fail — not a validated model. Your stated long-term ambition includes social architecture, norm change, and helping people show up better for one another; this file develops what that would require, and where the evidence says the chain is weakest.

The proposed pathway

shared understanding → shared language → repeated individual practice → visible interpersonal behaviour → relational reinforcement → group norms → organisational practices and conditions → broader cultural diffusion

Each link is examined below against real evidence, not generic theory summaries.

Link by link

Shared understanding → shared language

evidence-supported inference. This is the least contested link — it is essentially what MFC's category work (K-04, K-05) already does: giving people a common vocabulary (mental fitness, moments, reps, Stop-Shift-Do) is a precondition for the links that follow, not yet a behaviour-change claim in itself.

Shared language → repeated individual practice

Covered in 02 and 04 of this package — the access-gap literature and the outcome-independent rep. Not repeated here.

Repeated individual practice → visible interpersonal behaviour → relational reinforcement (modelling and contagion)

verified fact. Bandura's foundational modelling research (Bandura, Ross & Ross, 1961, 1963) established that observing a model's behaviour — and critically, the consequences the model receives — produces imitation in the observer, mediated by four processes: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. All four must be present, not just observation.

evidence-supported inference — a genuine check on MFC's assumption: a colleague observing another colleague use "Stop-Shift-Do" does not itself guarantee retention, reproduction capability, or motivation to reproduce it. Visibility is necessary but not sufficient.

On contagion specifically — the evidence is stronger for adjacent constructs than for the exact claim MFC would need:

  • verified fact, experimental, large-scale: Kramer, Guillory & Hancock (2014), PNAS, manipulated the emotional valence of ~689,003 users' social-media feeds and found matching shifts in users' own subsequent emotional expression — genuine experimental evidence of emotional contagion without direct interaction.
  • verified fact, field-experimental, workplace-specific, the closest true analogue found: Mas & Moretti (2009) — introducing a highly productive supermarket cashier into a shift raised co-present, visually-proximate coworkers' productivity by 1–2%, an effect that depended on line-of-sight (no effect where workers could not see the high performer). This is the strongest direct evidence for MFC's "individual practice → visible behaviour → spread" link — genuine behavioural spillover among coworkers, field-tested, not merely correlational.
  • unknown, explicitly: no study was found testing contagion of an emotion-regulation skill specifically (as opposed to mood or general productivity) spreading interpersonally in a workplace. MFC proposal: the modelling mechanism and the productivity-spillover finding together make skill contagion for something like Stop-Shift-Do plausible by analogy — this must be labelled plausible-but-untested extension, not verified fact.

Relational reinforcement → group norms

This is where the evidence introduces a real risk MFC's messaging must actively manage, not simply where it becomes weaker.

verified fact. Kallgren, Reno & Cialdini's (2000) focus theory of normative conduct establishes that descriptive norms ("what most people do") and injunctive norms ("what most people approve of") operate through separate psychological channels and do not automatically reinforce each other. Critically: descriptive-norm messaging that inadvertently communicates an undesired behaviour is common can increase that undesired behaviour — the "boomerang effect." Cialdini's own applied guidance explicitly recommends never pairing "many people don't do X" with a message intended to increase X.

evidence-supported inference, directly load-bearing for MFC's own communications: any MFC messaging that says or implies "not enough people currently practise this" — even as a call to action — carries a documented risk of reinforcing the low-uptake norm rather than changing it. Messaging must pair descriptive information with injunctive framing (this is valued and approved here), never state low current uptake alone. This is not a hypothetical risk; there is an active, ongoing academic effort specifically investigating when descriptive-norm interventions backfire, indicating the field itself treats this as unsettled and real.

Group norms → organisational practices and conditions — the chain's most defensible point of critique

This is where the evidence becomes genuinely thin, and it should be named as such rather than assumed away.

verified fact. Edmondson's (1999) foundational study of 51 work teams found team psychological safety predicted team learning behaviour (feedback-seeking, idea-offering, help-seeking), which in turn mediated the relationship between safety and performance. verified fact. Bandura's collective efficacy construct — group-level self-efficacy — is well-evidenced as predictive of group performance, with Bandura himself characterising it as subject to reciprocal causality with group action, not a simple one-way cause.

evidence-supported inference, a genuine circularity worth naming: psychological safety and some baseline collective efficacy plausibly need to already exist at the team level before individual practice can become visible rather than privatised. This means part of MFC's chain may be circular — safety is both a precondition for visible practice and an outcome the chain hopes to produce. This is a structural risk in the theory of change, not a flaw specific to MFC.

verified fact, directly on point: a 2025 systematic review (Translational Behavioral Medicine, Oxford Academic) of 44 workplace interventions aimed at changing staff behaviour found that only 4 of 44 made substantial use of goal-directed, structural behaviour-change techniques — the large majority (27 of 44) relied on awareness-raising and roleplay, i.e. individual-level, lower-intensity techniques. This is direct systematic-review evidence that the individual-to-organisational jump is empirically rare in the wider intervention literature, not a risk unique to MFC's design.

evidence-supported inference, drawing on a wider read of the organisational-change literature (leader-modelling and transfer-climate research broadly, not a single study): the transition from group norms to organisational practices typically requires leader modelling specifically (not peer modelling alone), structural/systemic reinforcement (hiring, performance conversations, work design — not training), and pre-existing psychological safety. This connects directly, and is fully consistent with, the already-established finding that training sits below work redesign in the WHS psychosocial hierarchy of controls (V1) — the new evidence here explains the mechanism: individual training structurally lacks the goal-directed, systems-level techniques the rare successful structural interventions use.

Organisational practices → broader cultural diffusion

verified fact. Rogers' diffusion-of-innovations model: adoption spreads via five categories along an S-curve, and the rate of diffusion depends on relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability, and observability. evidence-supported inference: diffusion characteristically stalls at the gap between early adopters and the early majority, because the early majority requires social proof from trusted peers, not conviction from enthusiasts — looping back to the group-norms risk above.

On Stop-Shift-Do's specific diffusion properties: MFC proposal, an assessment against Rogers' five attributes — low complexity and high trialability are genuine strengths (a three-step mnemonic is easy to try); observability is the more uncertain factor, since emotion regulation is often an internal, private act, and a practice that is not visible to others cannot generate the peer modelling the diffusion literature says is required.

Where the causal chain may fail — summarised

Link Strength of evidence Where it may fail
Shared understanding → shared language Strong (MFC's own existing work) Low risk
Shared language → individual practice Moderate (see 02, 04) The access/enactment gap itself
Individual practice → visible behaviour Moderate — real spillover evidence exists (Mas & Moretti) but not for this exact skill type Requires Bandura's four conditions (attention, retention, reproduction, motivation) all present; requires the practice to be observable, which emotion regulation often isn't
Visible behaviour → relational reinforcement / group norms Genuine risk — descriptive-norm messaging can backfire Messaging discipline required; not yet designed
Group norms → organisational practices Weakest, most evidenced failure point Requires leader modelling, structural reinforcement, and pre-existing psychological safety — none of which individual training alone produces, per the 2025 systematic review
Organisational practices → cultural diffusion Theoretically modelled (Rogers) but contingent on the prior link succeeding Stalls without social proof from trusted peers at the early-majority stage

⚠ Correction, 2026-08-01: MFC already has a collective-measurement concept

The first draft of this file, and V1.1's parallel treatment, implied MFC has no existing collective/organisational component beyond the individual workshop. That was incomplete. A subsequent correction task, with genuine Google Drive access, read MFC's Evidence & Measures Bank directly and found MFC already names and partially designs a collective layer: Team Pulse and Team Radar Lab, with fortnightly follow-through, evaluated as an explicit, separate evidence layer from individual application.

verified fact, from the Evidence & Measures Bank's "Revised Evaluation Strategy" (29 Jun 2026, prepared for Eimear Quigley, Debra Fidler and the MFC research working group):

"MFC should evaluate two connected but separate pathways: Individual application... Collective workplace implementation — Whether a workplace makes shared priorities visible, agrees on one achievable team practice, supports it through leadership and normal routines, repeats it and reviews whether it is helping... Those components must be evaluated rather than assumed to work."

"Measuring only the individual risks implying that employees are solely responsible for overcoming workplace conditions. Measuring only the collective process risks missing whether people gained practical skills they can use beyond work."

This second sentence is, almost verbatim, MFC's own internal statement of the individualisation risk this file and V1's earlier research treated as an external critique MFC had not yet addressed. That framing needs correcting: MFC has already identified and is already designing against this risk.

The document further specifies a six-layer evaluation model, already distinguishing understanding/acceptability, individual application, collective preference and direction, and collective implementation as separate, explicitly-not-conflated evidence layers — directly relevant to, and more developed than, this file's proposed "observability design" requirement below.

evidence-supported inference This does not resolve the weakest-joint finding below — the group-norms-to-organisational-practices transition remains evidenced as the field's most common failure point, and MFC's Team Pulse/Team Radar Lab design has not itself been tested. But the correct framing is that MFC has already started building toward this, not that it hasn't started. The recommendations below should be read as refinements to an existing design direction, not as identifying an absent one.

What MFC would need to build beyond an individual workshop for the social-change claim to be credible

MFC proposal, none of this decided or committed here:

  1. A norm-messaging discipline that never states low current uptake alone, consistent with the boomerang-effect evidence above.
  2. A defined leader-modelling component, not only participant delivery — per the evidence that leader modelling, not peer modelling alone, is the empirically supported conduit from individual to group behaviour.
  3. Some structural or systemic reinforcement beyond training — connects directly to 09's structural and collective product requirements, and to the WHS hierarchy-of-controls finding already established in V1.
  4. An explicit account of psychological safety as a precondition, not an assumed outcome — meaning MFC's offer may need to assess or build safety conditions before, not only after, individual practice is introduced.
  5. A deliberate observability design — since emotion regulation is often private, MFC's practice architecture may need an explicit, safe way to make practice visible (without making it mandatory, scored or public, per K-06's existing prohibitions on the State Check).

The honest summary

evidence-supported inference Every individual link in this chain has real, if uneven, evidence behind it. The evidence is strongest at the start (shared language, individual practice, modelling) and weakest exactly at the joint between "group norms" and "organisational practices" — a gap the wider intervention literature shows is common, not a defect specific to MFC. A credible social-change claim requires naming this weak joint explicitly and building toward it deliberately, not assuming the chain completes itself once individual practice begins.

06 Corporate Entry And Equitable Access Model

Corporate entry and equitable access model

This file develops, it does not decide. Per your stated direction, workplaces are treated as the initial paid channel and corporate delivery is treated as not the boundary of MFC's mission — those are inputs to this file, not questions it re-opens. This task does not set a price or design a final commercial product.

⚠ Correction, 2026-08-01: MFC already has a working commercial position

The first draft implied MFC had no existing commercial framework to reconcile against. With genuine Drive access, this correction task read MFC's actual Commercial Model, Pricing and Revenue Pathway (FY2026–27) — a confidential management/committee review paper — directly. It exists, it is specific, and this file's earlier framing understated that.

verified fact, from the Commercial Model's own text:

"MFC will validate one core programme, Mental Fitness Foundations, through two bounded formats: Foundations Session — practical education and immediate application; Workplace Implementation Engagement — the same core teaching plus deeper intake, a shared workplace practice, structured follow-up, evidence and findings. They are two formats of the same programme, not separate products and not an automatic sequence."

"The principal early direct-payment market is small-to-medium workplaces and purpose-led organisations with a current need, accessible decision-maker and some budget. Larger organisations are selective opportunities. Schools, sport and community are primarily funded-access pathways where the host, sponsor and payer may differ."

Working direct-payment price point: approximately $1,800, within a test range of approximately $1,500–$2,200 (per the related Committee Business Plan). Year 1 planning sensitivity: 5–11 engagements, of which 5–8 should be paid or fully funded, no more than 3 partly or fully subsidised.

Explicitly, and importantly: "This is a controlled testing model, not an approved budget, public price schedule, revenue forecast or claim that the model is proven."

This changes what this file should do. Rather than developing a corporate model from first principles, the correct task is to check the existing model against the risks and evidence this research programme has surfaced — which is what the sections below now do, with the existing figures reported (not invented) and clearly attributed to MFC's own working document.

Separating the roles — who is who

Role Definition Note
Primary beneficiaries Young adults and adults, per your stated direction Not re-litigated in this file
Paying buyer The organisation (initially, a corporate workplace) that purchases delivery Distinct from the participant
Participant The individual who attends and practises May or may not be the buyer's direct employee (e.g. contractors, casual staff)
Delivery setting Where the practice occurs — a workplace, a community venue, online Shapes what environmental/collective supports (09) are feasible
Partner An organisation that extends reach, credibility, or delivery capacity without paying directly E.g. a potential academic or clinical-credibility partner, per V1's partnership map
Funder Government, philanthropy, or sponsorship money that subsidises access for someone who is not the buyer The mechanism for equitable access
Mission beneficiary Anyone MFC's north star ultimately serves, whether or not they ever pay or are paid for The widest circle — includes people reached only through funded or pro bono access

MFC proposal Naming these roles separately matters because V1 and V1.1 both found that competitors and adjacent organisations routinely blur buyer and beneficiary — e.g. an employer buying a workshop to satisfy a WHS optic, where the employee is nominally the beneficiary but the actual purchasing logic serves the employer's compliance anxiety. Keeping the roles distinct is what allows MFC to serve corporate buyers without letting corporate purchasing logic define the mission.

A. Paid adoption — corporate workplaces and purpose-led organisations

Why workplaces are a useful first environment

evidence-supported inference, drawing on V1.1's own commercial research (already completed, not repeated here):

  • Workplaces are structurally organised environments with an existing budget line (however contested — see below) and a captive, repeat-contact population — properties few other adult-facing channels share as cleanly.
  • V1.1 found real, if uneven, procurement evidence: EAP substitute pricing ($30–$80/employee/year for basic providers, published but vendor-sourced and unaudited), and a regulatory environment (the 2022 WHS psychosocial reform) that has already created board-level and HR-level attention to non-clinical wellbeing spend, even if it has not resolved into a clean purchasing pathway.
  • Workplaces provide a plausible route to the manager/leader-inclusive delivery model identified as good practice in prior research (RULER, Penn's MRT, Geelong Grammar — all converging on training the adults around a person before or alongside the person) — a structural advantage schools and direct-to-consumer channels do not offer as readily.

Where workplace purchasing demand is still unverified

evidence-supported inference, carried directly from V1.1: no primary research has established an actual workplace purchasing trigger, budget-holder identity, or willingness-to-pay for MFC's specific offer. V1.1's own buyer-instrument design (02/03 of that package) exists precisely because this gap has not been closed. This file does not close it either — it restates it as the binding uncertainty in the paid-adoption channel.

The role of leaders, managers and teams

evidence-supported inference. Every well-evidenced adjacent program reviewed in prior research sequences adult/leader capability before or alongside participant delivery (RULER's "adults first," Penn's MRT 5:3 "live it/teach it" ratio, Geelong Grammar's "learn it, live it, teach it, embed it"). MFC proposal: a corporate offer that includes a distinct manager stream, even a small one, is more consistent with this evidence base than a participant-only delivery — but this is a design recommendation, not a decision, and 09 develops the structural requirements this would create without redesigning the current workshop.

The risk of becoming an individual-resilience or compliance product

This is the single most important risk in this file, and it is not hypothetical. V1's adjacent-fields research (already completed) found:

  • Training sits at the bottom of the WHS hierarchy of controls — the 2022 psychosocial reform requires employers to address hazards through work redesign first, with training and coping strategies as lower-order controls. A mental fitness program cannot discharge an employer's psychosocial duty.
  • Fleming (2024), Industrial Relations Journal, n=46,336 across 233 organisations, found no wellbeing benefit from individual-level workplace interventions generally, and that resilience-training participants specifically reported worse mental health than non-participants (very plausibly a selection effect, not a causal harm — but the finding has circulated widely and buyers may have absorbed it as settled).

MFC proposal MFC's offer must be positioned, in writing, as a complement to psychosocial risk controls, not a substitute for them. This is not a new finding — V1 already recommended it — but it belongs in the case for existence explicitly, because a corporate-entry strategy that lets buyers believe otherwise is both a claims risk (K-08) and a reputational risk once (not if) a buyer or regulator notices the gap.

How the offer complements rather than replaces psychosocial hazard controls

MFC proposal, a candidate structural answer, not adopted here: MFC's own evidence and claims discipline (K-08) already prohibits claiming the framework "manages all psychosocial hazards" or "transforms workplace culture." The corporate-entry model should make this boundary a selling point — explicit written acknowledgement that MFC does not replace work redesign is a differentiator against providers who imply otherwise, per V1's original finding that "honesty about the boundary is cheap for MFC and expensive for competitors to match."

What corporate revenue could responsibly subsidise

MFC proposal, not a financial model — no price is set. The structural logic: if corporate delivery generates a margin, that margin is the most obvious internal funding source for the equitable-access commitments below, reducing (not eliminating) dependency on external grant cycles that V1.1 found to be uncertain, slow, or capped low (e.g. FRRR's $20,000/project ceiling, most council grants under $15,000).

B. Funded access — government, philanthropy, sponsorship, host organisations, cross-subsidy, pro bono

How pro bono commitments can remain sustainable rather than ad hoc

MFC proposal. The failure mode named directly, because it is common and avoidable: an organisation announces a pro bono commitment as a mission statement, then delivers it inconsistently because it has no defined capacity, budget, or decision process behind it. A sustainable structure requires — at minimum, none of this decided here — a named percentage or unit allocation (e.g. a fixed proportion of paid-delivery capacity reserved), a defined selection process for who receives funded access, and a funding source identified in advance, not assembled reactively per request.

Priority populations requiring future evidence and consultation

MFC proposal, explicitly not decided or consulted on here:

  • Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities — V1 already identified that MFC has no stated position on Indigenous Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEWB), an existing, policy-recognised, Indigenous-led Australian framework. This file does not resolve that gap. It restates it as a precondition for any equitable-access work involving Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander communities specifically — see 07 for the current national SEWB policy landscape, and human decision gate 9 in 09.
  • Young adults outside employment (not reached by the corporate channel by definition) — a genuine gap in the paid-adoption model that funded access exists specifically to close.
  • Regional and rural communities — V1.1 found a real but capped funding channel here (FRRR's "In a Good Place" program), pilot-scale only.
  • Culturally and linguistically diverse communities, people with disability, and other populations requiring adapted delivery — not assessed in this task; named here as a gap, not resolved.

Funding pathways — pointer only

07 of this package maps the current Australian and NSW government policy and funding landscape in detail, including which pathways are genuinely accessible now versus merely policy-aligned. This file does not duplicate that map.

The honest summary

evidence-supported inference The paid-adoption channel has a plausible structural logic and a real regulatory headwind that must be managed explicitly. The funded-access commitment has a clear moral logic and, per V1.1, a fragmented and mostly small-scale set of actual funding channels to draw on. Neither side of this model is validated by primary research. Both require the research programme V1.1 already designed and this task does not repeat.

07 Australian And Nsw Government Policy And Funding Map

Australian and NSW government policy and funding map

No agency was contacted. No application was drafted or submitted. Every pathway below distinguishes policy alignment from a genuinely accessible funding route — the two are not the same, and this file does not treat the first as evidence of the second.

Labels: verified fact (read directly on an official source) · source claim (a secondary or search-summary source, flagged where a primary fetch failed) · evidence-supported inference · unknown.

The headline finding

Across all eleven policy areas researched, no currently open, competitive, adult-non-clinical-appropriate government funding door was found for MFC at its current scale. Two live small grants exist and are either too narrow (single-event, $500–$1,000) or gender-restricted and currently closed. The larger NSW Health funding lines are structurally invitation-only. SafeWork NSW's dedicated workplace budget is already committed to two named incumbent providers. Commonwealth activity clusters around clinical service expansion, peer-workforce credentialing, and research — none of which fit MFC's model as it currently stands.

This is stated plainly because policy language in this sector is abundant and funding access is not — conflating the two would misrepresent MFC's actual position to a committee or a funder.

10. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEWB) policy — landscape note only

verified fact. The Gayaa Dhuwi (Proud Spirit) Declaration Framework and Implementation Plan 2025–2035 launched in Brisbane in late February 2026 — a 10-year roadmap embedding Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander leadership across mental health and suicide prevention systems, built on five themes: Cultural Strength, Best Practice, Best Evidence, Presence, Leadership/Influence.

This is a policy-landscape note only, per your explicit instruction, not a partnership recommendation. This Framework establishes that any MFC engagement with First Nations communities or SEWB-linked funding must be Indigenous-led and governed under this Framework's own leadership principles. MFC has no standing to initiate here. This restates, and does not resolve, the SEWB gap already identified in V1 and carried into 06/08/09 of this package as human decision gate 9.

The adjacent Closing the Gap SEWB Budget line ($1.2bn over 5 years) is administered through First Nations-controlled structures — not an access route for MFC.

11. National Lived Experience (Peer) Workforce policy

verified fact. The National Mental Health Commission's Peer Workforce Development Guidelines define a specific, separate, credentialed workforce category — distinct from general non-clinical facilitators. NSW Health launched its own "Elevating Lived Experience Expertise" framework on 16 October 2025.

evidence-supported inference MFC's model — non-clinical, not lived-experience-credentialed, facilitator-delivered — sits outside this framework entirely. This is not a barrier to operating, but it does mean MFC cannot claim "peer workforce" status or access peer-workforce-specific funding without a different organisational design choice. Worth naming explicitly in the case for existence as a category MFC deliberately sits outside of, rather than leaving ambiguous.

08 Claims Evidence And Testing Register

Claims, evidence and testing register

A decision-quality register, not a decision. Every row requires committee or Hunter approval per K-08's existing (currently unadopted, per C-15/C-24) claims-governance system, which this register is designed to slot into, not replace.

⚠ Correction, 2026-08-01

Two rows below are updated with real, now-verified citations in place of the first draft's necessarily generic wording. The Rapid Review manuscript (Fidler & Prout) has now been read in full: 10 included studies, systematic reviews/meta-analyses of RCTs, testing CBT, mindfulness, ACT, self-compassion, positive psychology, resilience training, breathwork and guided imagery, with small-to-moderate pooled effects (g≈0.20–0.50). It supports the general trainability of psychological skills as a "foundational principle" per K-09's evidence-role framework — it does not test any of MFC's specific mechanisms. See row 1 and 7 below, and 10 for the full verification.

Register

1. Information alone is insufficient

Field Content
Exact wording "Information alone does not reliably change what a person does in a specific, activated, real-life moment."
Evidence strength Moderate-to-strong, indirect
Direct or indirect support Indirect — no study tests "MFC's information vs MFC's practice" head to head. Supported by well-established adjacent findings (intention–behaviour gap, inert knowledge, state-dependent retrieval)
Counterevidence None found suggesting information is inert; the opposite absolute claim would be the error
Safe internal wording As above, framed as a mechanism-based inference from established literature
Safe public wording "Knowing what to do and being able to do it in the moment are different things — and the gap between them is where most people get stuck."
Prohibited overclaim "Information never changes behaviour" (false); "MFC has proven this gap exists in its own audience" (untested)
Required test None required to state the general mechanism; MFC-specific version requires the comprehension study already designed in V1.1
Decision owner Hunter / committee (public-messaging authority)

2. The main gap is access or enactment

Field Content
Exact wording "The main remaining gap is retrieving and applying a relevant skill inside the moments where it is needed, not a lack of information."
Evidence strength Moderate, well-triangulated across independent literatures (Tulving, Bransford, Arnsten, Sheeran)
Direct or indirect support Indirect for MFC specifically; direct for the general psychological mechanism
Counterevidence None found against the general mechanism; MFC's own effectiveness at closing this gap is separately untested
Safe internal wording As in 02 of this package
Safe public wording "You already know more than you think. The hard part is reaching it in the moment."
Prohibited overclaim "MFC closes this gap" (unproven — no pilot data exists)
Required test MFC's own pilot, per K-09's stage-gate framework, Stage 2 ("do participants notice relevant moments and attempt a Mental Rep?")
Decision owner Hunter / committee

3. Three steps improve recall

Field Content
Exact wording "A three-step sequence is easier to recall under pressure than a four-or-more-step sequence."
Evidence strength Weak-to-moderate, inferential
Direct or indirect support Indirect — extrapolated from Cowan's (2001) ~4-chunk working-memory ceiling and Arnsten's stress-impairment findings; no direct study of 3 vs 4 vs 5-step recall under stress was located
Counterevidence Radović & Manzey (2019) found step-count/mnemonic presence made no difference to execution speed or interruption-resistance once a sequence was learned — internal chunk structure mattered more
Safe internal wording "Plausible from cognitive-load theory; not directly tested"
Safe public wording None recommended as a standalone public claim — too easily overstated
Prohibited overclaim "Research shows three steps are easier to remember than four" (overstates an inference as a finding)
Required test A direct comparison study, per 03 of this package
Decision owner Hunter (public claims) / A-06 (evidence standard)

4. Traffic-light coding improves retrieval

Field Content
Exact wording "Colour-coding the three steps improves retrieval speed and accuracy."
Evidence strength Weak for this specific application
Direct or indirect support Indirect — general human-factors evidence for colour-coding exists (aviation, road signage); no study isolates colour-coding's contribution for self-regulation retrieval specifically, and Zones of Regulation (the closest comparator) is a 4-colour classification system, structurally different from a 3-step action sequence
Counterevidence None found; simply untested for this application
Safe internal wording "General human-factors support for colour-coding exists; no direct evidence for this specific design"
Safe public wording None recommended as an evidence claim
Prohibited overclaim Citing Zones of Regulation's outcome studies as evidence for MFC's system (structurally different mechanism, and Zones' own positive findings are vendor-sourced, not independently verified)
Required test Not yet designed
Decision owner Hunter / A-06

5. Moments are a useful unit of practice

Field Content
Exact wording "Everyday moments are a useful unit for recognising, practising and reflecting on mental fitness."
Evidence strength Moderate — internally consistent with K-04's own definition and design logic
Direct or indirect support Indirect — no external study validates "the moment" as a construct; internally, the Framework's own design (per KN-0001) treats it as foundational
Counterevidence None found directly; the general critique that moment-level intervention may under-address structural/environmental determinants applies (see item 11 below)
Safe internal wording As stated
Safe public wording "Change doesn't require changing your whole life. It starts with one moment."
Prohibited overclaim Implying moment-based practice alone resolves structural or environmental barriers
Required test Participant comprehension and usability testing (V1.1's comprehension study design)
Decision owner Hunter / committee

6. The framework is useful beyond difficult moments

Field Content
Exact wording "Mental fitness practice applies to ordinary, meaningful, performance and enjoyable moments, not only difficult ones."
Evidence strength Strong as an internal design commitment (Framework §2, quoted in 04); untested as a public perception
Direct or indirect support Direct for the Framework's stated intent; indirect for whether public materials or delivery actually reflect it
Counterevidence V1.1's prior-art audit found MFC's own public website currently runs a conventional, largely deficit-adjacent "Daily 1% Model," not this broader framing — a real gap between stated intent and current public delivery
Safe internal wording As stated, with the gap named
Safe public wording Should not be claimed publicly until the public site reflects it, per the gap just named
Prohibited overclaim Claiming this breadth is already delivered when V1.1 found the public site does not yet reflect it
Required test An audit of current public materials against this claim before it is used externally
Decision owner Hunter (public-messaging authority)

7. Outcome-independent reps support persistence

Field Content
Exact wording "Counting a rep by attempt rather than outcome supports continued practice over time."
Evidence strength Weak-to-moderate, by structural analogy only
Direct or indirect support Indirect — behavioural activation and exposure therapy's inhibitory-learning model use structurally similar logic in clinical contexts; no study tests MFC's specific standalone, lay-facing unit
Counterevidence None found against the mechanism; the standalone packaging itself is simply untested
Safe internal wording "No equivalent operationalised, standalone, outcome-independent practice unit was identified in the reviewed evidence — though closely related mechanisms exist in behavioural activation and exposure therapy's inhibitory-learning model"
Safe public wording "Every attempt counts, whether or not it goes the way you hoped."
Prohibited overclaim "Research proves outcome-independent reps build lasting change" (no such research exists for this construct)
Required test An MFC-specific pilot tracking rep frequency against persistence over time
Decision owner Hunter / committee

8. Shared language and practice can change norms

Field Content
Exact wording "As more people share this language and practise it, it becomes a normal, expected part of how people interact."
Evidence strength Weak at the group-norms link specifically; moderate at earlier links (modelling, spillover)
Direct or indirect support Indirect — Bandura's modelling mechanism and Mas & Moretti's workplace spillover finding support plausibility; no study tests contagion of an emotion-regulation skill specifically
Counterevidence Cialdini's boomerang-effect research shows norm messaging can backfire if mishandled — a real risk, not merely a caveat
Safe internal wording "Plausible-but-untested extension of established modelling and spillover research"
Safe public wording Should avoid any framing implying current low uptake (backfire risk); should not be stated as an established outcome
Prohibited overclaim "MFC's practice is spreading through workplaces and changing norms" (no evidence this has occurred)
Required test Longitudinal organisational-level measurement, not yet designed
Decision owner Hunter / committee

9. Workplace delivery can support collective change

Field Content
Exact wording "Delivering in workplaces can produce team- or organisation-level behaviour change, not only individual change."
Evidence strength Weak at this specific link — this is 05's identified weakest joint in the whole causal chain
Direct or indirect support Indirect and contrary evidence exists: a 2025 systematic review of 44 workplace interventions found only 4 used structural, goal-directed techniques; the rest (including most individual-training formats) did not reliably produce organisational-level change
Counterevidence The WHS hierarchy-of-controls finding (V1) — training sits below work redesign — is direct, official-source evidence against assuming training alone changes organisational conditions
Safe internal wording "Organisational change requires leader modelling and structural reinforcement beyond individual training; this is not yet built into MFC's offer"
Safe public wording "We start with individuals and teams — real organisational change also needs support from leaders and the conditions people work in, which is why we don't claim to do it alone."
Prohibited overclaim "MFC transforms workplace culture" — already explicitly prohibited in K-08's existing claims boundaries, and independently confirmed here
Required test Requires the structural/leader-modelling components identified in 05 and 09, none of which currently exist
Decision owner Hunter / committee

10. MFC fills a gap not met by existing services

Field Content
Exact wording "MFC addresses a gap that existing mental health and self-development services do not."
Evidence strength Moderate, drawing on V1/V1.1's completed competitive research
Direct or indirect support Indirect — V1 found the category term is contested but the practice architecture (a sustained, opportunity-sensitive, outcome-independent practice loop) is largely unbuilt by competitors; direct evidence of MFC's own effectiveness is absent
Counterevidence Positive Intelligence, Smiling Mind, Gotcha4Life and others (per V1) occupy adjacent territory with more scale, though V1 found each has real, documented weaknesses MFC does not automatically avoid by existing
Safe internal wording "A genuinely under-occupied practice-architecture gap exists in the category, per completed competitive research; MFC's ability to fill it is untested"
Safe public wording Consistent with V1's own recommended positioning: "Australia has been told what mental fitness is. Nobody has yet shown what training it actually takes."
Prohibited overclaim "MFC is the only organisation doing this" or "MFC invented mental fitness" — both directly contradicted by V1's research
Required test The pilot and measurement work already designed in V1.1
Decision owner Hunter (positioning decision, per SWM-02's existing status)

11. MFC's model is accessible and non-clinical

Field Content
Exact wording "MFC's practice is non-clinical, accessible, and appropriate for the general population."
Evidence strength Strong as a design commitment (K-08's twelve safety rules); untested as a delivered outcome
Direct or indirect support Direct for the design intent; indirect/absent for whether delivery consistently achieves it
Counterevidence K-04's own boundary names power, safety, environment and support as determinants of access — while current delivery is purely individual, a structural tension identified independently in V1.1's prior-art audit, this task's 05, and the individualisation critique documented in V1. No MFC position exists on Indigenous SEWB, a specific, named accessibility gap for a defined population
Safe internal wording "Strong design commitment to non-clinical, accessible practice; the individual/structural tension and the SEWB gap remain open and unresolved"
Safe public wording Should not claim universal accessibility until the SEWB gap is addressed through an Indigenous-led process (human decision gate 9)
Prohibited overclaim "MFC is accessible to everyone" while the SEWB gap remains unaddressed
Required test The Indigenous-led process itself, not a research task
Decision owner Hunter — explicitly flagged as requiring an Indigenous-led process, not an AI-drafted resolution

Summary — what this register makes visible

evidence-supported inference Every claim in this register that touches MFC's own effectiveness, as opposed to the general psychological mechanisms MFC draws on, is currently unsupported by direct evidence — not because the underlying science is weak, but because MFC has not yet piloted. This is consistent with, not contradictory to, K-09's own stage-gate framework and KN-0005's finding that MFC's claims-discipline system is well-designed and currently unadopted. This register is built to slot into that existing system, not replace it.

09 Case For Existence And Hunter Decision Brief

Case for existence and Hunter decision brief

This file recommends nothing MFC is authorised to act on without explicit approval. Section A is a draft, offered for adaptation, not a published position. Section B identifies genuine decisions only. A-06/A-17 characterise; they do not decide.

Section A — Draft case for existence

A committee- and public-adaptable draft. Every substantive claim below is traceable to a file in this package or in V1/V1.1, and none should be read as already approved MFC public messaging.

The societal problem

People are not short of information about how to manage difficult emotions, handle conflict, or build better habits. Books, courses, apps, and now AI-generated advice on every one of these topics are more available than at any point in history. And yet the gap between knowing what to do and actually doing it — in the specific, often stressful, always fast-moving moments where it matters — has not closed. If anything, the sheer volume of available advice can make the gap harder to see, because it is easy to mistake having read something for being able to use it.

What already exists

Evidence-based psychological skills for managing emotion, attention and relationships are real and well-established — decades of research in cognitive-behavioural therapy, dialectical behaviour therapy, mindfulness-based approaches, and acceptance and commitment therapy have produced genuinely effective techniques. Australia also has a substantial mental health service system, a growing prevention and promotion sector, and a wide field of workplace wellbeing providers. None of this is being invented anew, and none of it should be claimed as MFC's own discovery.

Where the current environment falls short

What is fragmented is the translation of these established skills into something a person can reliably retrieve and use in an ordinary moment of their own life, without a clinician in the room, without specialist language, and without waiting for a crisis to justify the effort. Most of what exists is either clinical (requiring a diagnosis or a referral to access), abstract (delivered as information rather than practice), or crisis-oriented (built around difficult and high-stakes moments rather than the far more frequent ordinary ones).

The access and enactment gap

The evidence reviewed in this package — from memory research on why learned information stays "inert" outside its original context, to neuroscience on how stress narrows the brain's capacity for flexible thinking exactly when a skill is most needed — points to a specific, well-evidenced mechanism: retrieving and applying a skill under real-world activation is a different task from acquiring the skill in the first place, and it is the task almost nothing in the current landscape is built to train.

MFC's proposed solution

MFC's approach treats the everyday moment — not the day, the diagnosis, or the person as a whole — as the unit of practice. Every person picks a small number of specific, recurring moments in their own life to pay attention to. When one arises, a simple three-step process — Stop, Shift, Do — helps create a pause, reorient, and choose an intentional next move. Each attempt is a "rep," and — deliberately — the rep counts because the person tried with intention, not because of how it turned out. This removes the pass/fail pressure that research shows suppresses continued practice, and it is the one element of MFC's model that a wide search of the relevant clinical and behavioural literature did not find an existing equivalent for.

Why it applies to good and ordinary moments, not only difficult ones

Mental fitness, as MFC defines it, is not only about coping with hardship. It shows up just as much in the good moments — noticing something to be grateful for, choosing to connect with someone, showing up well in a moment that matters to you, or simply catching an ordinary interaction and doing it a little more intentionally. A model built only around crisis and difficulty would reach people only when they are already struggling. MFC's model is designed to be practised on an ordinary Tuesday, not only on a bad day.

Why young adults and adults matter now

MFC's initial focus is young adults and adults — the population most often left out of school-based prevention programs on one side and clinical mental health services on the other, and the population for whom "no one has taught me this since school, if ever" is common. This is a deliberate initial focus, not a statement about who else matters — MFC's ambition, and its commitment to funded and pro bono access, extends well beyond this starting population.

Why workplaces are the first paid channel

Workplaces bring together an existing population, some existing structure, and — increasingly, following Australia's 2022 psychosocial safety reforms — genuine organisational attention to non-clinical wellbeing. This makes workplaces a practical first environment to build and test a paid offer. It is not where MFC's mission ends. MFC does not claim, and must never claim, that its workplace offer discharges an employer's legal duty to manage psychosocial risk through safer work design — that duty sits with the employer, and MFC's role complements it rather than substituting for it.

Why equitable public access remains essential

A practice this simple should not be available only to people whose employer happens to buy it. MFC's model is built from the outset to generate funded, subsidised, and pro bono access — through government and philanthropic funding, sponsorship, host-organisation partnerships, and a defined, sustainable allocation of capacity, not an ad hoc afterthought. Specific priority populations, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, require dedicated, community-led engagement before MFC can responsibly claim to serve them — that work has not yet begun, and this document does not pre-empt it.

How showing up for one another and social architecture fit

MFC's longer ambition is not only that individuals build a private practice, but that enough people share the same simple language and practice that it becomes normal to notice, support, and model this for one another — at home, in teams, and eventually more broadly. The evidence for the early steps of this chain — that people learn by watching others, and that behaviour can genuinely spread between people who work alongside each other — is real. The evidence for the later steps — that this spreads into lasting organisational or cultural change without deliberate structural support — is the weakest link in the whole model, and MFC does not yet have that structural support built. Naming that honestly is part of taking the ambition seriously, not a reason to abandon it.

What MFC is testing rather than claiming as proven

MFC has not yet run a pilot. No outcome evidence exists yet for MFC's own program. What exists is a well-reasoned design, built from established science, with an unusually disciplined internal system for saying what it can and cannot yet claim. The task now is to test it — starting with whether people understand the language, whether they attempt a rep in real life, and only later, honestly and patiently, whether it produces the changes it is designed to support.

Section B — Hunter decision brief: ten decisions

Corrected 2026-08-01. The first draft of this section was titled "ten decisions" but numbered only seven, with three further items folded into a padded final entry. This correction separates every genuine decision, drops nothing, and adds nothing to reach a target count — it resolves to exactly ten because that is how many distinct, real decisions this research programme surfaced once the source-verification work (10) was complete.

For each decision: what it is, what happens after approval, and whether it requires a governed change to an authoritative MFC record.

1. Approval of the updated case-for-existence thesis

Reframes MFC's founding claim from "we are defining a category no one occupies" to "we translate established psychological science into a practice architecture for a real, evidenced access gap." Strengthened by this correction: C1 itself already argues substantially this position (§6, §24.2) — this is closer to adopting C1's own framing explicitly than to introducing a new one. After approval: this framing becomes available for committee and public use, subject to decisions 2–3 below. Governed record change: none required — consistent with SWM-02's existing direction, not a change to it.

2. Approval of the safest description of Stop, Shift, Do

Cite the lineage (DBT, MBSR, SBNRR, RULER, ACT); do not claim novelty of the structure; name the pause/observe compression risk rather than omitting it. After approval: this description becomes the standard internal and external reference for Stop-Shift-Do, replacing any framing that implies invention. Governed record change: none — clarifies existing usage, does not alter K-06's fixed language.

3. Approval of the positive and non-deficit framing, and correction of the public website

Moments include difficult, ordinary, relational, meaningful, performance and enjoyable categories — already C1's own position (§10.1), not yet reflected on MFC's public site. After approval: triggers a website content correction, separate from this task and requiring its own resourcing. Governed record change: none to K-04/K-05; a public-messaging execution task, not a definitional change.

4. Approval of the corporate-entry and equitable-access model as authoritative strategy

Per 06, now reconciled against MFC's actual Commercial Model: the existing ~$1,800 working price point, the Foundations Session / Workplace Implementation Engagement structure, and explicit non-substitution for WHS psychosocial duties. After approval: the reconciled model becomes the reference point for future commercial decisions; no price is set or changed by this task. Governed record change: none — the Commercial Model itself remains the controlling document; this task reports on it, does not amend it.

5. Approval of the proposed social-norm theory of change

The eight-link causal chain, with its weakest joint (group norms → organisational practices) named explicitly, now corrected to reflect that MFC's Evidence & Measures Bank already contains a Team Pulse/Team Radar Lab collective-measurement design — this is a refinement of an existing direction, not a proposal from nothing. After approval: becomes the basis for any public claim about organisational or cultural change. Governed record change: none to authoritative records; may inform future Measurement Blueprint work, which remains D-0017's territory, not reopened here.

6. Approval of priority government and funding pathways for later action

No currently open, competitive, adult-appropriate government funding door was found across eleven policy areas (07). The two most concrete pathways remain V1.1's findings (NSW Mental Health Sports Fund, FRRR). After approval: authorises which pathway, if any, receives future attention — no outreach has occurred. Governed record change: none.

7. Resolution of the Committee Business Plan duplicate-document conflict

New, from this correction. Two documents share the title "MFC Committee Business Plan," different formats (Google Doc vs PDF), different dates (6 Jul vs 2 Jul 2026), different owners, and materially different content — one carries the retired public definition (C-13), confirmed directly from source in this correction. After approval: Hunter confirms which document is current; the other should be marked superseded or archived in the Document Register. Governed record change: yes — this is a Document Register update, a genuine authoritative-record action.

8. Correction of the retired definition in circulating committee papers

C-13 is now confirmed directly from source, not inferred: the Committee Business Plan (Google Doc variant) carries "Mental fitness is how well we can think, feel, act and connect in life's everyday moments" — the formulation the Public Messaging Source Library records as retired. After approval: the affected document(s) are corrected to the locked 20 July 2026 definition. Governed record change: yes — a correction to a circulating internal document, not merely a finding.

9. Decision on unblocking the Claims Register

C-15/C-24: the Claims Register — containing the five-level claim ladder and the red-line prohibitions — remains unadopted; all eight board decisions have been pending since May 2026. After approval: authorises scheduling the board decisions that would formally adopt the register. Governed record change: yes — this is the single largest pending governed-record action identified across this entire research programme, and it predates this task.

10. Initiation of an Indigenous-led process on Social and Emotional Wellbeing (SEWB)

Carried forward from V1 and V1.1, independently reconfirmed by 07's finding that a national SEWB implementation framework (Gayaa Dhuwi, 2025–2035) now formally governs this space. After approval: authorises identifying an appropriate Indigenous-led process — not resolved by this or any AI-drafted document. Governed record change: none by this task; the process itself, once run, may produce one.

What this brief does not do

It does not approve the thesis, the corporate model, the social-change claim, or any public wording. It does not resolve any of the five conflicts named above. It does not select government funding pathways for pursuit. Every item above is a decision for Hunter, not a conclusion of this research.

evidence-supported inference Four of the eleven studies the manuscript cites (Gu, Kirca, Zemla, Schäfer) could not be independently cross-verified against an external database within this task's time budget — they are recorded exactly as the manuscript itself cites them, per K-09's "representative source" evidence role, not as independently confirmed by this task.

Inaccessible-source record

No source classified as required by the correction brief was found to be inaccessible once genuine Drive access was used. One named source — the "MFC Workplace Collective Mental Fitness Pathway" — does not exist under that title anywhere in Drive, per a direct title search returning zero results. This is recorded as a non-existent source, not an access failure.

Several non-critical supporting materials (the full Commercial Model beyond its opening sections; the second, PDF copy of the Committee Business Plan; the Measurement Blueprint's full current content beyond the existing K-09 extraction) were located but not read in full, within this task's 90-minute time budget. This is disclosed as a limitation, not concealed.

What this means for the first draft's honesty framing

The first draft's own discipline — labelling claims and disclosing limitations rather than overclaiming — was sound in method. Its error was factual, not methodological: it stated sources were unread when, with proper Drive access, they were readable. This correction does not change the package's evidentiary discipline; it corrects the specific factual claim about what had and had not been consulted, and updates every downstream claim that depended on that gap.
